## The State Buddha Sāsana
## The Great Chronicle of Buddhas
## (Volume Four)
## The Chronicle of Gotama Buddha
**********
Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## The Buddha Treasure
## Chapter 28
## Journey to the Village of Bālakaloṇaka
Bālakaloṇaka was the revenue village of the householder Upāli. (A village named Bālakaloṇakāra also exists in Sri Lanka). When the Buddha journeyed to that village, he did not inform or consult even one of the Chief Disciples or Great Disciples, nor even the Venerable Ānanda at the very least. He took his own bowl and robes and departed alone, like a great tusker elephant that has separated from the herd.

The reason was that during the upcoming tenth Vassa (rainy season retreat), there were no beings to be converted by the Buddha (Buddha-veneyya). Therefore—
3:
3
When the Venerable Bhagu saw the Blessed One coming from afar, he prepared a seat, set out water for washing the feet, a foot-stool, and a foot-scrubber. He went out to welcome him and took the bowl and robes. The Blessed One sat on the seat prepared by the Venerable Bhagu and washed his feet. Then, the Venerable Bhagu, having paid homage and sat in a suitable place, was asked by the Blessed One: "Monk, are you keeping well? Are you comfortable? Are you not weary in your quest for alms?"

The Venerable Bhagu replied, "Blessed One, I am keeping well. Blessed One, I am comfortable. Blessed One, I am not weary in my quest for alms." Then the Blessed One, having delivered a discourse on the benefits of living in solitude to the Venerable Bhagu, journeyed toward the Eastern Bamboo Grove (Pācīnavaṃsadāya).

## Arrival at the Eastern Bamboo Grove
At that time, the three elders—Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimala—were residing in the Eastern Bamboo Grove. The forest guard saw the Blessed One coming from afar and, regarding him as an ordinary monk, spoke to restrain him:

"O monk, do not enter this forest. In this forest, there are three noble sons who, desiring their own spiritual welfare, are residing here. Do not cause discomfort to those three noble sons."
4:
4
(In this regard: Just as a hungry person delights in and longs for food, a thirsty person for water, one oppressed by cold for heat, one oppressed by heat for cold, and a suffering person for happiness—similarly, the Blessed One, having experienced the wearisome disputes of the monks of Kosambī who were not in harmony, considered those virtuous ones who lived in unity. The three noble elders then appeared in his divine wisdom. Wishing to favor those three elders, he reflected, "By doing so, this practice will serve as a good strategy to eventually admonish the monks of Kosambī." Thus, he journeyed to the Eastern Bamboo Grove where the three elders resided.

The forest where Venerable Anuruddha and the others lived was an enclosed and guarded forest, fenced so that people could not enter at will to pick flowers, fruits, or sap, or to cut timber.

When the man who was the forest guard saw the Blessed One coming from afar, he thought:

"Within this forest, these three noble sons are living in harmony. Some individuals cause quarrels and disputes wherever they go; such a person wanders about destroying and butting like a fierce bull with sharp horns. When such destruction occurs, divisions arise so that even two people cannot travel together on one path. This elderly monk who is coming now might at some time cause such division and destroy the harmonious and happy living of these three noble sons. Looking at this elderly monk, he is inspiring and has a golden complexion. He seems like one who might be attached to good flavors. This elderly monk—
5:
5
—from the time he arrives here, he might destroy the three noble sons' practice of heedfulness by speaking words of praise to his donors who offer good alms food, and so on.

Furthermore, regarding the dwellings, there are exactly three small monasteries, three walkways (caṅkama), three daytime resting places, and three couches and stools for these three noble sons; there are no extras. This monk who is coming now is large in stature. He might be a senior monk (vassa-elder). This monk might cause these three noble sons to rise from their existing places at an improper time. If this happens, it will cause discomfort to these three noble sons in every way." Thinking thus, and having no desire for the discomfort of the three noble sons, he spoke to restrain him, saying, "Do not cause discomfort to those three noble sons."

A question may arise: Did this forest guard restrain the Blessed One knowing he was the Buddha, or not knowing? The answer is: He restrained him because he did not know. To elaborate: When the Blessed One journeys with a retinue of monks in his full glory, everyone knows he is the Buddha without having to ask, "Who is this?" However, when journeying to the Eastern Bamboo Grove, the Blessed One thought, "Let no one know that I am the Buddha." By his psychic power, he concealed his Buddha-glory, such as the rays, with his robes, like the full moon covered by a mass of clouds. He took his own bowl and robes and journeyed in an inconspicuous form. Therefore, not knowing the Blessed One was the Buddha, the forest guard restrained him.)

The Venerable Anuruddha, from his daytime resting place, heard the voice of the forest guard saying, "O monk, do not enter this forest," and so on.
6:
6
He thought, "Only the three of us live in this forest; there are no other monks. Yet this forest guard is speaking as if to a monk. Who could it be?" He rose from his daytime resting place, stood at the entrance, and looking toward the path, he saw the Blessed One.

As soon as the Venerable Anuruddha saw him, the Blessed One released his bodily radiance. The radiance of the Blessed One, beautiful with the various major and minor marks, was exceedingly magnificent, like a golden cloth spread out. The Venerable Anuruddha thought, "This forest guard, like a man stretching out his hand to grab a hooded cobra by the neck, is speaking to the most supreme person in the world without knowing he is the Buddha; he is speaking as if to an inconspicuous monk." He then told the forest guard, "Lay follower forest guard, do not restrain the Blessed One. Our teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived."

## The Three Elders Welcoming the Buddha in Unity
Then, the Venerable Anuruddha did not go to welcome the Blessed One alone. He thought, "The three of us are now living in harmony. If I alone welcome the Blessed One, it would not be called living in harmony. I will welcome him only after calling my dear friends. Just as I love and revere the Blessed One, my friends also—"
7:
Thinking, “They have great love and devotion for the Blessed One,” he wished to welcome the Buddha together with his two friends. He went to where the Venerable Nandiya and Venerable Kimala were spending the day and called out to them, “Come, Venerables! Come, Venerables! Our teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.” Then, the three venerable ones went together to welcome the Blessed One. One took the Blessed One’s bowl and robes, another prepared the seat, and the third placed water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-scrubber nearby.

The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat and washed his feet.

(In this regard: The Blessed One, using his golden hands which were as red as a newly blossomed lotus, took the water that was as clear and white as crystal, poured it over his golden-hued feet, and washed them by rubbing them together.

One might ask: Since no dust or impurity ever clings to the body of the Buddhas, why did he wash his feet? The answer is: He washed them to obtain the physical coolness of the body and for the benefit of gladdening the hearts of those three venerable ones. To clarify further: By the Blessed One washing his feet, those attendant monks could feel great joy and happiness, thinking, “The Blessed One is washing his feet and making use of the water we brought.” Therefore, even though no dust or impurity clung to his body, he washed his feet.)
8:
The three venerable ones also paid their respects to the Blessed One with great reverence and sat down in a suitable place. Then the Blessed One asked the Venerable Anuruddha, “Anuruddha, are you keeping well? Are you enduring? Are you not troubled by alms-food?” The Venerable Anuruddha replied, “We are keeping well, Blessed One. We are enduring, Blessed One. We are not troubled by alms-food, Blessed One.”

(In this regard: Among the three venerable ones, Venerable Anuruddha was the eldest. Since honoring the eldest, Venerable Anuruddha, meant honoring the others as well, the Blessed One addressed him specifically. Alternatively, by using the plural form “Anuruddhas,” he was addressing the other two as well through the method of ellipsis [virūpekatthesa].)

The Blessed One asked again, “Anuruddhas, are you living in harmony, in mutual delight, without dispute, blending like milk and water, looking at each other with eyes of affection?” The Venerable Anuruddha replied, “Indeed, Blessed One, we are living in harmony, in mutual delight, without dispute, blending like milk and water, looking at each other with eyes of affection.” When he had said this, the Blessed One asked, “Anuruddhas, in what way are you living in harmony, in mutual delight, without dispute, blending like milk and water, looking at each other with eyes of affection?” Then the Venerable Anuruddha said:
9:
“Venerable Blessed One, while living in this forest, the thought occurs to me: ‘It is a gain for me, it is a great gain for me, that I am living with such fellow practitioners.’ Venerable Blessed One, I maintain bodily actions of loving-kindness, verbal actions of loving-kindness, and mental actions of loving-kindness toward these two venerable ones both in their presence and in their absence. Venerable Blessed One, the thought occurs to me: ‘Why should I not set aside my own will and act according to the will of these two venerable ones?’ Then, Blessed One, I set aside my own will and act according to the will of these two venerable ones. Venerable Blessed One, we are different in body, but we are, as it were, one in mind.”

Thus he spoke. Then the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimala each spoke in the same way as the Venerable Anuruddha had spoken.

(In this regard: Concerning the statement about maintaining the three types of loving-kindness in presence and absence—loving-kindness in bodily and verbal actions in presence is practiced when living together; loving-kindness in bodily and verbal actions in absence is practiced when living apart. Loving-kindness in mental actions is practiced both when living together and when living apart.

To elaborate: Among those living together, if one sees a bed, a stool, or wooden or earthenware items left out improperly—
10:
—and without showing disregard by thinking, ‘Who used this?’, he picks it up and puts it away as if it were his own improperly placed item; or if a monk cleans a place that needs cleaning—all such bodily actions of monks are called bodily actions of loving-kindness in presence.

Among those living together, if one monk goes elsewhere, and another monk tidies up the monastery requisites that the departed monk had left improperly, or cleans a place that needs cleaning—all such bodily actions are called bodily actions of loving-kindness in absence.

While living together, the verbal actions of a monk who speaks pleasant, delightful, and harmonious words with the elders—words that should be remembered for a lifetime, Dhamma talk, preaching the Dhamma clearly, discussing the Dhamma, and asking and answering questions—all such verbal actions are called verbal actions of loving-kindness in presence.

When the elders have gone elsewhere, the verbal actions of a monk who praises their virtues, saying, ‘My dear friend Venerable Nandiya or Venerable Kimala is one endowed with such virtue, endowed with such conduct,’ are called verbal actions of loving-kindness in absence.

Whether in their presence or absence, the mental action of a monk who reflects, ‘May my dear friends Venerable Nandiya and Venerable Kimala be free from enmity, free from the anger of ill-will that disturbs and destroys, and may they be happy in body and mind,’ is called mental action of loving-kindness.

As for how these three venerable ones set aside their own will and acted according to the will of the other two: suppose the alms-bowl of one venerable one became encrusted with grime,
11:
the robes of another became soiled, and the meditation hut of the third became dusty and needed cleaning. Suppose these three tasks arose simultaneously. If the monk whose bowl was grimy and needed firing said first, ‘Friends, my bowl is grimy; it should be fired,’ the other two would not mention their own tasks—the soiled robes or the dusty hut. Instead, they would go into the forest and help that monk with his bowl-firing task, and only afterward would they attend to their own robe-washing or hut-cleaning. Similarly, if the monk with soiled robes spoke first, or the monk with the dusty hut spoke first, they would first help the one who spoke first before attending to their own tasks. This is how those three venerable ones set aside their own will and acted according to the will of the other two.)

In this way, the Blessed One inquired about the essence of their harmony, and after hearing that they possessed the full essence of harmony, he wished to ask about their diligence (appamāda). He asked, “Anuruddhas, are you living diligent, ardent, and resolute, with minds directed toward Nibbāna?” The Venerable Anuruddha replied, “Indeed, Blessed One, we are living diligent, ardent, and resolute, with minds directed toward Nibbāna.” The Blessed One continued, “Anuruddhas, in what way are you living diligent, ardent, and resolute,
12:
with minds directed toward Nibbāna?” Then the Venerable Anuruddha said:

“Venerable Blessed One, among the three of us living in this forest, whoever returns first from the village after the alms-round prepares the seats, sets out the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-scrubber. He sets out the bowl for receiving the first portion of alms-food and sets out the drinking water and utility water.

Whoever returns last from the village after the alms-round eats the leftover food if he wishes. If he does not wish to eat, he throws it away where there is no green grass or pours it into water that has no living beings. That monk who returns last also puts away the seats, the foot-washing water, the footstool, and the foot-scrubber. He washes and puts away the bowl for the first portion of alms-food and puts away the drinking water and utility water. He sweeps the refectory.

If anyone sees that the drinking water pot, the utility water pot, or the water pot in the toilet is empty, he refills it. If it is too heavy for him to carry, he signals a companion with his hand, and they carry the water pot together by joining hands. Venerable Blessed One, we do not break our silence for the sake of refilling the water. Venerable Blessed One, every five days, we spend the entire night together in Dhamma talk.”
13:
13
“Venerable Sir, we live in this manner as we have described, being heedful, possessing strenuous effort, and having our minds directed towards Nibbāna.”

(In this regard, what is worthy of inspiration and note is that those three Elders did not enter for alms together as a group. Indeed, as those three Elders were ones who delighted in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), they performed their personal hygiene early in the morning, fulfilled their major and minor duties, and then entered their respective meditation cells. They remained there for a designated period, dwelling in the attainment of fruition.

Among those three Elders, the one who first entered and dwelt in the attainment of fruition would arise first according to his designated time. Having gone for alms first, upon returning and reaching the dining area, he would know, “Those two monks are late; I have arrived first.” Then, after putting away his bowl and preparing the seats and so on, if he had received enough alms-food in his bowl, he would sit quietly and consume it. If there was extra food, he would place that extra food in the bowl designated for surplus food, cover that bowl, and then eat. After eating, he would wash and dry the bowl, making it clean, place it in the bowl-bag, take his bowl and robes, and enter his place for the day-rest.

When the second Elder reached the dining area, he would also know, “One monk has gone before me, and one is still behind me.” If that Elder had enough food in his bowl, he would sit quietly and consume it. If it was insufficient, he would take food from the surplus food bowl (left by the first monk) and consume it. If the food in his bowl was more than enough, he would place the extra food in the surplus food bowl
14:
14
and after setting it aside, he would eat only what was sufficient for him. Then, in the same manner as the first Elder, he would enter his place for the day-rest.

When the third Elder reached the dining area, he would know, “Two monks have arrived and gone before me; I am the last.” After eating his meal like the second Elder, when the meal duties were finished, he would wash and dry the bowl, making it clean, place it in the bowl-bag, and then lift and store the seats. After discarding the remaining water from the drinking water pots and washing water pots, he would turn the pots upside down. If there were any leftovers in the surplus food bowl, he would discard them in a place without green grass or in water without living insects, following the prescribed method. He would then wash, dry, and store the bowl. After sweeping the refectory (dining area) and discarding the sweepings, he would store the broom in a place free from termites. Then, taking his bowl and robes, he would enter his place for the day-rest. This which has been described is the duty to be performed at the refectory in the forest outside the monastery.

The provision of drinking water and utility water is a duty to be performed within the monastery. To clarify further: if any of those three noble Elders saw that one of the water pots was empty, the Elder who saw it would take that pot, go to the pond, wash the inside and outside of the pot, filter the water, and fill it. (If it was a heavy burden), he would leave the water pot at the bank and signal with his hand to call a companion monk. He would not make a sound, whether by calling out a name or otherwise, to get a companion monk.

The reason is that if he called out a name, the sound of the call could be a disturbance to the meditation work of the monk being called. Therefore, he did not make a sound by calling a name. If he made a sound without calling a name, both monks might think, “I will go so that I arrive first; I will go so that I arrive first,”
15:
15
and both would come out from their meditation cells. If they came out like that, in a task that could be completed by two people (by three people doing it), the third person's part would be superfluous, and the meditation work would be interrupted. For this reason, he did not make a sound even without calling a name.

If he did not make a sound, how did he do it? The monk who had filtered the water would walk quietly, so that the sound of footsteps could not be heard, near the day-rest place of another monk, and only when that monk saw him would he signal with his hand. Upon that signal, the companion monk would come. Then, the two monks, joining hands and placing the water pot upon their four hands, would carry it together and set the drinking and utility water in place.

Regarding the statement, “Once every five days, we spend the whole night together in Dhamma discussion”: the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of both the waxing and waning moon are the three regular days for listening to the Dhamma. Without neglecting these three days of Dhamma assembly, on every fifth day, the two Elders, Venerable Nandiya and Venerable Kimala, would bathe before noon and go to the presence of the noble Elder Anuruddha. At the dwelling place of Venerable Anuruddha, the three Elders would assemble and sit, and they would ask and answer questions among themselves regarding one of the three Pitakas. While these noble Elders were thus engaged in asking and answering questions, dawn would break.

By this much, the noble Elder Anuruddha, having been asked by the Blessed One about the characteristic of non-negligence (appamāda), reported their state of non-negligence even in those situations where (other persons) are usually negligent. To elaborate: for other monks, the time of entering for alms, the time of leaving the monastery to collect alms, the time of adjusting the undergarment, the time of donning the robes, the time of wandering for alms within the village or town, the time of preaching the Dhamma, the time of giving thanks (anumodanā), the time of eating after leaving the town, the time of washing the bowl, the time of putting the bowl into the bag,
16:
16
and the time of storing the bowl and robes—these are occasions for expansive talk, which are occasions for negligence in meditation work by engaging in talk devoid of meditation. Therefore, the Elder Anuruddha replied, “Venerable Sir, even during those times and occasions which are for other monks occasions for negligence in meditation work, we do not perform any extra activities such as expansive talk devoid of meditation that is contrary to meditation work (except for not entering the dwelling attainments when it is not the proper time).” Thus, he explained their characteristic of non-negligence which had reached the summit, even in the situations where others are negligent.

By this statement, he also indicated the meaning that, apart from the eleven occasions mentioned, there was no time when they were negligent by not dwelling in the attainments of the vihāras in other situations.

The account of the journey to the Eastern Bamboo Grove ends.
**********
## The Journey to the Pālileyyaka Region
As mentioned previously, the Blessed One, after preaching the benefits of dwelling alone for half a day and a whole night to the Elder Bhagu at the village of Bālakaloṇaka, went for alms in Bālakaloṇaka village on the following day with that same Elder Bhagu as his attendant monk. After letting the Elder Bhagu remain in that place, the Blessed One thought, “I shall go to see the three young men of good family who are living in harmony,” and he journeyed alone to the Eastern Bamboo Grove. There, he preached the Dhamma on the benefits of living in harmony for a whole night to the Elder Anuruddha, the Elder Nandiya, and the Elder Kimala. After letting those three Elders
17:
17
remain in that Eastern Bamboo Grove, the Blessed One journeyed alone and arrived at the village of Pālileyyaka.

At that time, the villagers of Pālileyyaka came out to meet him and offered alms to the Blessed One. Not far from the village of Pālileyyaka, there was a great forest called Rakkhita. The villagers built a leaf hut for the Blessed One to reside in within that forest and requested him, saying, “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One dwell in this Rakkhita forest monastery,” and they invited him to stay.

In that Rakkhita forest, near the leaf hut built for the Blessed One, there was a great Sal tree named Bhaddasāla. The Blessed One, depending on the village of Pālileyyaka as his resort village, dwelt near that great Bhaddasāla tree in the Rakkhita forest. Then, while the Blessed One was dwelling alone in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind:

“Formerly, I did not live in comfort, being crowded by those Kosambī monks who were quarrelsome, contentious, disputatious, and given to bickering, and who created disputes in the Saṅgha. Now, I live in comfort, alone and without a companion, away from those Kosambī monks who were quarrelsome, contentious, disputatious, and given to bickering, and who created disputes in the Saṅgha.”

Such was the thought that arose in him.
18:
18
## About the Pālileyyaka Elephant King
At that same time, a certain bull elephant was also living crowded by young elephants, female elephants, mid-sized elephants, and nursing calves. Because he lived thus crowded, he had to eat grass with the tips broken off. Other elephants ate the branches and twigs that the bull elephant had broken down. He had to drink muddy water, and when he came up from the watering place, the female elephants would go along brushing against and bumping into his body.

Then, a thought arose in the mind of that bull elephant: “I live crowded by young elephants, female elephants, mid-sized elephants, and nursing calves. Because I live thus crowded, I have to eat grass with the tips broken off. Other elephants eat the branches and twigs that I have broken down. I have to drink muddy water, and when I come up from the watering place, the female elephants go along brushing against and bumping into my body. It would be well if I were to live alone, separated from the herd.” After this thought, the bull elephant left the herd and approached the Blessed One near the great Sal tree in the Rakkhita forest of Pālileyyaka.

(In this context: the name Pālileyyaka is the original name of the village. The original name of the forest is Rakkhita. Because that Rakkhita forest is situated near the village of Pālileyyaka, it is also called the Pālileyyaka forest by way of proximity. The aforementioned bull elephant who arrived in that forest is also commonly known as the Pālileyyaka Elephant King.)
19:
## The Pālileyyaka Elephant King’s Service to the Buddha
That great noble elephant, becoming weary of living with the herd, entered the Rakkhita forest. There, he saw the Buddha sitting at the foot of a Sal tree. With a peaceful and devoted mind, as if his heat had been quenched by a thousand water pots, he stood near the Buddha. From that day forward, as a gesture of service, he cleared the grass and plants around the great Bhaddasāla tree and the monastery, sweeping with a tree branch. He offered water for washing the face, carried water for bathing, and offered tooth-wood. He brought sweet and excellent fruits, large and small, from the forest and offered them to the Buddha. The Buddha partook of the fruits offered by the Pālileyyaka elephant king.
The Pālileyyaka elephant king brought firewood with his trunk, rubbed the sticks together to start a fire, and kindled the wood. He then placed stones in the fire to heat them. When the stones were hot, he rolled them with a stick into a stone pool or vessel. After testing whether the water was hot, and knowing it was ready, he went to the Buddha and stood nearby. The Buddha, knowing that "this Pālileyyaka elephant king desires me to bathe," went to the stone pool and bathed. The same method was used for providing drinking water; specifically, when the drinking water was cool, he would approach the Buddha.
20:
(Based on this, it should be noted that the Buddha used warm water that had been boiled and cooled). (This is an excerpt from the Vinaya Mahāvagga Commentary and the Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā).
(The following is a collection of passages from the Kosambaka Vatthu in the first volume of the Dhammapada Commentary)—
When the Buddha entered the village for alms, the Pālileyyaka elephant king would take the Buddha’s bowl and robes, place them on his forehead, and follow the Buddha. When the Buddha reached the outskirts of the village, he would say, "Pālileyyaka, from here on it is not suitable for you to follow further. Give me my bowl and robes." He would have the bowl and robes lowered from the elephant's forehead and, taking them himself, enter the village for alms.
The Pālileyyaka elephant king would remain in that spot until the Buddha returned. When the Buddha returned, he would welcome him, take the bowl and robes as before, and upon reaching the forest monastery, place them in their proper positions. He would then serve the Buddha by fanning him with a tree branch. When night fell, to ward off dangers from lions, leopards, and tigers, he would carry a large stick with his trunk and patrol the forest until dawn with the intention, "I will protect the Buddha."
21:
Note: From that time on, because it was guarded by the Pālileyyaka elephant king, that great forest became known as the Pālileyyaka Rakkhita forest.
At dawn, he would begin by offering water for washing the face and perform all the major and minor duties in the same manner.
In this way, the Buddha, accepting the care and service of the Pālileyyaka elephant king as described, spent his tenth Vassa (rainy season retreat) residing in the Pālileyyaka forest.
## Events in Kosambī
While the Buddha was thus residing in the Pālileyyaka forest for the Vassa, the group of lay devotees in Kosambī, such as Ghosaka the merchant and others, went to the Ghositārāma monastery. Not seeing the Buddha, they asked, "Venerable sirs, where is the Buddha residing?" The monks gave a sorrowful reply, "Lay devotees, the Buddha has gone to the Pālileyyaka forest." When the devotees asked, "For what reason?", the monks replied, "The Buddha made efforts to make us, who were divided, united. However, we (being filled with anger and pride) did not become united. (Therefore, he has gone to the Pālileyyaka forest)." The devotees then asked, "Venerable sirs, how is this? Did you not become united even though the Buddha himself tried to make you so after you had ordained under him?"
22:
When the monks admitted that this was true, the many laymen and laywomen of Kosambī thought, "These monks ordained under the Buddha, yet they did not become united even though the Buddha himself tried to reconcile them. Because of these monks, we have lost the opportunity to see the Buddha for a long time. Let us not provide them with seats; let us not pay them respects." They made a mutual agreement, and from that time on, they no longer showed respect to those quarreling Kosambī monks (let alone offering the four requisites).
Due to the scarcity of alms food, those quarreling monks became emaciated day by day. Within two or three days, they regained their right minds and honesty. They confessed their faults to one another and apologized. Then they pleaded with the devotees, "Lay devotees, we have now become united. Please treat us as you did before." The devotees then spoke skillfully, saying, "Venerable sirs, have you apologized to the Buddha?" When the monks replied, "Lay devotees, we have not yet apologized," the devotees said, "If that is so, please apologize to the Buddha. After you have apologized to the Buddha, we will treat you as we did before." Since it was during the Vassa, those Kosambī monks did not dare to go to the Buddha.
23:
They had to spend the three months of the Vassa in hardship and distress.
## The Monkey who was Inspired by the Pālileyyaka Elephant King
The Buddha, accepting the care and service of the Pālileyyaka elephant king (as previously described), resided peacefully in that Pālileyyaka forest throughout the three months of the Vassa.
At that time, a monkey saw the Pālileyyaka elephant king endowed with great effort and diligence, performing major and minor duties for the Buddha every day. Feeling inspired, he thought, "I, too, shall perform some meritorious deed for the Buddha." While wandering about, one day he found a honeycomb on a branch without any bees. He broke off the branch and brought the honeycomb along with the branch to the Buddha. He cut a banana leaf, placed the honeycomb on it, and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha accepted it.
The monkey watched to see, "Will he partake of it or not?" Seeing the Buddha just sitting and holding the honeycomb without eating it yet, he wondered, "Why is this?" He then took the edge of the honeycomb branch, turned it around, and inspected it. Finding bee larvae, he gently removed them and offered it to the Buddha again. Only then did the Buddha partake of it.
The monkey, with a heart full of joy and delight, moved from branch to branch, pulling himself along.
25:
Etaṃ nāgassa nāgena,
īsādantassa hatthino.
Sameti cittaṃ cittena,
yad-eko ramatī vane.
"Just as I, the Teacher of the three worlds, being alone without a companion, delight and enjoy myself within this forest called Rakkhita; so too, this noble elephant named Pālileyyaka, being alone without a companion, delights and enjoys himself within this forest called Rakkhita. Therefore, this mind of the great elephant named Pālileyyaka, who has tusks as large as plow-poles, meets and perfectly accords with the mind of the Buddha-Nāga, as both find joy in being alone in the forest."
He uttered this solemn verse (Udāna).
## Venerable Ānanda Goes to Invite the Buddha
The fact that the Buddha was residing in the Pālileyyaka forest, accepting the care and service of the Pālileyyaka elephant king, became famous throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. Great families in the city of Sāvatthī, such as the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and the great female lay devotee Visākhā, went to the Venerable Ānanda...
26:
26
“Venerable Sir, please support and assist us so that we may have the opportunity to pay homage to the Blessed One.” Such was the message they sent.

After the rains retreat, five hundred monks residing in various regions also approached the Venerable Ānanda and requested, “Friend Ānanda, it has been a long time since we have heard the Dhamma directly from the Blessed One. Friend Ānanda, we beg of you; we wish to have the opportunity to hear the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.”

Then, the Venerable Ānanda took those five hundred monks and went to the Pālileyyaka forest. Thinking, “It is not appropriate to approach the Blessed One, who has been living in solitude for the entire three months of the rains retreat, with such a large number of monks,” he left the five hundred monks outside and approached the Blessed One alone.

When the elephant king Pālileyyaka saw the Venerable Ānanda, he picked up a large wooden stick with his trunk and ran toward him (mistaking him for an enemy). The Blessed One, seeing this, said, “Pālileyyaka, move aside, move aside! Do not stop him. This monk is the attendant of the Buddha.” Upon hearing this voice, the elephant king Pālileyyaka dropped the large stick right where he stood and showed a gesture of requesting to take the Venerable Ānanda’s bowl and robes. The Venerable Ānanda, however, did not give him the bowl and robes.
27:
27
Then the elephant king Pālileyyaka thought, “If this monk is one who has been trained in and knows the proper etiquette, he will not place his personal requisites upon the stone slab where the Blessed One sits.” The Venerable Ānanda placed his bowl and robes only on the ground. (It is particularly noteworthy that those who are accomplished in etiquette—who understand the proper conduct—do not place their requisites upon the seat or bed of teachers who are worthy of respect.)

After the Venerable Ānanda had approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat at a suitable place. When the Blessed One asked, “Dear Ānanda, did you come alone?” and heard the reply that he had come together with five hundred monks, He asked, “Where are those five hundred monks now?” The Venerable Ānanda replied, “Since I did not yet know the Blessed One’s will, I left them outside and came alone, Bhante.” Then the Blessed One said, “Dear Ānanda, call those five hundred monks.”

When the Venerable Ānanda called the five hundred monks as instructed by the Blessed One, they came, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat at a suitable place. While the Blessed One was engaging in friendly conversation with those monks, they said, “Exalted Blessed One, though You are the Buddha, You are so delicate and refined. Though You are of the warrior caste, You are so delicate and refined. For the entire three months of the rains retreat, living alone...
28:
28
...You, who have remained and lived alone, have performed a difficult task. It seems there was not even anyone to perform the major and minor duties, or to provide water for washing the face and so on.” When they said this, the Buddha replied, “Monks, the elephant king Pālileyyaka performed all my various major and minor duties. Indeed, if one finds such a good companion, one should live together with that companion. For one who does not find such a person, living alone is truly praiseworthy.” He then uttered these verses:

If one finds a prudent companion,
A wise person who lives well to journey with,
One should overcome all dangers
And wander with them, joyful and mindful.

If one does not find a prudent companion,
A wise person who lives well to journey with,
Then, like a king leaving behind a conquered kingdom,
One should wander alone, like an elephant in the Matanga forest.

Living alone is better;
There is no companionship with a fool.
One should wander alone and do no evil,
With few concerns, like an elephant in the Matanga forest.

The Blessed One preached these three verses from the Nāgavagga. (The meaning of these verses was already written on pages 764-5 at the end of the third volume, Chapter 27). At the conclusion of the verses, those five hundred monks were established in the Fruit of Arahantship.

The Venerable Ānanda then conveyed the messages sent by the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, the great lay-supporter Visākhā, and others, saying:
29:
29
“Exalted Blessed One, the five hundred million noble lay followers living in Sāvatthī, headed by the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, are greatly longing and hoping for Your arrival, Bhante.” The Blessed One said, “Dear Ānanda, if that is so, take the bowl and robes.” Having had the bowl and robes taken, He departed from the Pālileyyaka forest.

At that time, the elephant king Pālileyyaka stood across the path where the Blessed One and the Saṅgha would travel. When the monks saw this behavior, they asked the Blessed One, “Exalted Blessed One, what is the elephant king Pālileyyaka doing?” The Blessed One said, “Monks, the elephant king desires to offer alms-food to you. In truth, this elephant king has been of great service to Me for a long time; it is not proper to cause his mind to be distressed. Monks, turn back for a while.” Saying this, He led the monks and turned back.

The elephant king Pālileyyaka entered the forest, gathered various kinds of delicious fruits such as jackfruit and bananas, placed them in heaps, and offered them to the monks the next day. The five hundred monks were unable to consume all the fruits.

When the meal was finished, the Blessed One had the bowl and robes taken and departed from the forest. The elephant king Pālileyyaka walked in between the monks and...
30:
30
...stood across the path directly in front of the Blessed One again. When the monks asked, “Exalted Blessed One, what is the elephant king Pālileyyaka doing?” the Blessed One said, “Monks, the elephant king wants to let you go but wants Me to turn back.” He then said to the elephant king Pālileyyaka, “Pālileyyaka, this current departure of Me is a departure without turning back. For you, in this current existence, there is no possibility for the arising of Jhāna, Vipassanā, Magga, or Phala. You must remain behind.” Upon hearing these words, the elephant king Pālileyyaka put his trunk into his mouth and followed behind the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, weeping. Indeed, if that elephant king had been given the chance to make the Blessed One turn back, he would have continued to serve Him in that manner for his entire life.

When the Blessed One reached the vicinity of the village of Pālileyyaka, He spoke His final words to the elephant king, “Pālileyyaka, from this point on, it is no longer your roaming ground. The dwelling place of humans is full of many dangers. You must remain behind.” The elephant king Pālileyyaka remained there weeping and watched the Blessed One until He was out of sight. When the Blessed One was no longer visible (having left the area where he could be seen), the elephant's heart broke, and he died right there. Due to the wholesome merit of his devotion to the Blessed One, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in a great golden mansion thirty yojanas wide, surrounded by a thousand celestial nymphs, and became a deity famously known as “Pālileyyaka Devaputta.”

The story of the elephant king Pālileyyaka ends.

## The Eighteen Grounds of Dhamma
Dear Sāriputta, by eighteen grounds, a person who speaks Dhamma (dhamma-vādī) is to be known. Dear Sāriputta, in this Dispensation, a monk—
(1) represents what is not Dhamma as not Dhamma,
(2) represents what is Dhamma as Dhamma,
(3) represents what is not Vinaya as not Vinaya,
(4) represents what is Vinaya as Vinaya,
(5) represents what was not spoken or uttered by the Blessed One as not spoken or uttered by the Blessed One,
(6) represents what was spoken and uttered by the Blessed One as spoken and uttered by the Blessed One,
34:
(7) represents what was not practiced by the Blessed One as not practiced by the Blessed One,
(8) represents what was practiced by the Blessed One as practiced by the Blessed One,
(9) represents what was not prescribed by the Blessed One as not prescribed by the Blessed One,
(10) represents what was prescribed by the Blessed One as prescribed by the Blessed One,
(11) represents what is not an offense as not an offense,
(12) represents what is an offense as an offense,
(13) represents a light offense as a light offense,
(14) represents a heavy offense as a heavy offense,
(15) represents an offense with a remainder as an offense with a remainder,
(16) represents an offense without a remainder as an offense without a remainder,
(17) represents a gross offense as a gross offense,
(18) represents a non-gross offense as a non-gross offense.
Dear Sāriputta, it was taught that by these eighteen grounds, a person who speaks Dhamma (dhamma-vādī) is to be known.
(In this context, since this is a teaching given in terms of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna), (1) representing what is not Dhamma as Dhamma, (2) representing what is Dhamma as not Dhamma [and so on] (17) representing a gross
35:
offense as a non-gross offense, (18) representing a non-gross offense as a gross offense—these eighteen are called the eighteen grounds of non-Dhamma (adhamma-vatthu). They are also called the eighteen grounds for causing a schism (bhedakara-vatthu). A person who possesses any one of these eighteen should be known as a person who speaks what is not Dhamma (adhamma-vādī).
Similarly, on the side of the grounds of Dhamma (dhamma-vatthu): (1) representing what is not Dhamma as not Dhamma, (2) representing what is Dhamma as Dhamma [and so on] (17) representing a gross offense as a gross offense, (18) representing a non-gross offense as a non-gross offense—these eighteen are called the eighteen grounds of Dhamma (dhamma-vatthu), meaning the eighteen grounds that are righteous and true. A person who possesses any one of these eighteen should be known as a person who speaks Dhamma (dhamma-vādī). This is the summary of the Blessed One's intended meaning that should be noted.
## Distinctions of Dhamma, Adhamma, etc.
Among these eighteen grounds, according to the Suttanta method, the ten wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha) are called Dhamma. The ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kammapatha) are called Adhamma. Likewise, the thirty-seven qualities contributing to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), such as the four foundations of mindfulness and the four right efforts, are called Dhamma. The following are called Adhamma: [incorrect sets such as] 3 foundations of mindfulness, 3 right efforts, 3 bases of power, 6 faculties, 6 powers, 7 factors of enlightenment, 9 path factors (this collection of false teachings), as well as the 4 types of clinging (upādāna), 5 hindrances (nīvaraṇa), 7 underlying tendencies (anusaya), 8 factors of wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi), and other such collections of bad qualities.
Taking any one of the aforementioned collections of Adhamma and consulting together, saying: "Let us represent and speak of this Adhamma as Dhamma. If we represent and speak in this way, we will achieve high status by relying on our teacher's lineage, and we ourselves will become famous in the world."
36:
If they agree and speak of that Adhamma as Dhamma, saying "This is Dhamma," then they are said to (1) represent what is not Dhamma as Dhamma.
Similarly, if they take any one of the collections of Dhamma and speak of it as "This is Adhamma," then they are said to (2) represent what is Dhamma as not Dhamma.
According to the Vinaya method, an act (kamma) performed by making an accusation based on a true incident, causing the person to remember, and acting according to their confession, is called a Dhamma-kamma. An act performed by making an accusation based on a false incident, without causing them to remember, without obtaining a confession, is called an Adhamma-kamma. If one speaks of an Adhamma-kamma as a Dhamma-kamma, it is said that they represent what is not Dhamma as Dhamma. If one speaks of a Dhamma-kamma as an Adhamma-kamma, it is said that they speak of or represent what is Dhamma as not Dhamma. (Speaking itself is called representing.)
According to the Suttanta method, the removal of lust (rāga), the removal of hatred (dosa), and the removal of delusion (moha)—namely the five types of restraint (saṃvara): restraint through virtue (sīla-saṃvara), restraint through mindfulness (sati-saṃvara), restraint through wisdom (ñāṇa-saṃvara), restraint through patience (khanti-saṃvara), and restraint through energy (vīriya-saṃvara); the five types of abandonment (pahāna): abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), abandonment by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-pahāna), and abandonment by escape (nissaraṇa-pahāna); and reflecting with wisdom to prevent the arising of lust, hatred, and delusion—this collection of qualities is called Vinaya. Conversely, the failure to remove, the lack of restraint, and the lack of reflection regarding lust, etc., is called Avinaya.
According to the Vinaya method, the completeness of the five factors—the basis (vatthu), the boundary (sīmā), the motion (ñatti), the assembly (parisā), and the proclamation (kammavācā)—is called Vinaya. The incompleteness, distortion, or failure of these five factors is called Avinaya.
According to the Suttanta method, the Blessed One taught and spoke of the collection of qualities consisting of: 4 foundations of mindfulness, 4 right efforts, 4 bases of power, 5 faculties, 5 powers, 7 factors of enlightenment, and 8 path factors. The Blessed One did not teach them as: 3 foundations of mindfulness, 3 right efforts, 3 bases of power, 6 faculties, 6 powers, 8 factors of enlightenment, or 9 path factors.
37:
According to the Vinaya method, the Blessed One taught the 4 Pārājikas, 13 Saṅghādisesas, 2 Aniyatas, 30 Nissaggiya Pācittiyas, and so on. The Blessed One did not teach 3 Pārājikas, 14 Saṅghādisesas, 3 Aniyatas, 31 Nissaggiya Pācittiyas, and so on. (The collection of teachings that were taught is also called the collection of prescribed rules; the collection that was not taught is called the collection of non-prescribed rules.)
According to the Suttanta method, the Blessed One practiced (i.e., performed) these tasks: entering the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) every day, entering the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti), surveying the world of beings with the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakkhu, consisting of the knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies of beings and the knowledge of the degree of maturity of the faculties of beings), and teaching the relevant Suttas or Jātakas when an occasion (atthuppatti) arose. The Blessed One did not practice such things as not entering the attainment of fruition or not entering the attainment of great compassion every day.
According to the Vinaya method, the Blessed One practiced (i.e., performed) these tasks: entering the rains retreat in various towns and villages upon the invitation of the respective donors, and after the retreat, informing the donors before departing on a journey; departing on a journey after performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony; and greeting visiting monks who arrived in his presence with detailed words such as, "Dear monks, are you healthy? Are you keeping well in your postures?" and so on. Performing these aforementioned tasks was the Blessed One's practice; not performing them was not his practice.
In various Vinaya training rules, the collection of points taught such as "anāpatti ajānantassa = there is no offense for a monk who does not know; there is no offense for a monk who has no intention to steal; there is no offense for a monk who has no intention to kill" is called the category of non-offense. The collection of points taught such as "jānantassa theyyacittassa = there is an offense for a monk who knows; there is an offense for a monk who has the intention to steal; there is an offense for a monk who has the intention to kill"
38:
is called the category of offense or the collection of points where an offense is incurred.
Among the seven classes of offenses—Pārājika, Saṅghādisesa, Thullaccaya, Pācittiya, Pāṭidesanīya, Dukkaṭa, and Dubbhāsita—the last five classes are called light offenses or offenses that are not very gross or severe. The first two classes (Pārājika and Saṅghādisesa) are called heavy offenses or gross and severe offenses.
Among the seven classes of offenses, the last six classes are called offenses with a remainder (sāvasesa-āpatti) regarding the status of a monk. (This means that if one transgresses any of the last six classes, although there is a fault, the status of a monk still remains in that person.) The Pārājika offense is called an offense without a remainder (anavasesa-āpatti). (This means that if one transgresses a Pārājika training rule, the status of a monk no longer remains at all in that person.)
In this way, these nine pairs such as Dhamma and Adhamma should be specifically noted and understood. (This collection of words is extracted and presented from the commentary on the Saṅghabhedaka-kkhandhaka of the Vinaya Cūḷavagga.)
Just like the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, Venerable Mahākassapa, Venerable Mahākaccāna, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, Venerable Mahākappina, Venerable Mahācunda, Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Revata, Venerable Upāli, Venerable Ānanda, and Venerable Rāhula also heard the news that the Kosambī monks were coming to Sāvatthī. Just like the Venerable Sāriputta, they went to the Blessed One and made their inquiries. On those occasions too, the Blessed One taught those elders the eighteen grounds of Dhamma and the eighteen grounds of non-Dhamma, just as he had to the Venerable Sāriputta.

She went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. She then inquired of the Blessed One in the same manner as the Venerable Sāriputta. At that time, the Blessed One said to the great Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī:
"Gotamī, if that is the case, you should listen to the Dhamma from both sides of the Saṅgha. Anāthapiṇḍika the treasurer, the donor of the Jetavana Monastery, and Visākhā, the great female donor of the Pubbārāma Monastery, also heard the news and went to the Blessed One to make their inquiries. To Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā, the Blessed One said:
"Great Treasurer (Visākhā), if that is the case, you should give alms to both sides of the Saṅgha. Having given alms to both sides, you should listen to the Dhamma from both sides of the Saṅgha. Having listened to the Dhamma from both sides, you should favor the view, the intention, the preference, and the opinion of the monks who speak Dhamma (dhamma-vādī) among those two sides of the Saṅgha."
40:
Thus He spoke. (These statements are excerpts from the Vinaya Mahāvagga Pāḷi, its Commentary, and Sub-commentary).

(The following is from the Dhammapada Commentary): King Pasenadi of Kosala heard the news that "those monks of Kosambī who have been quarreling are coming to Sāvatthī." He approached the Buddha and submitted, "Exalted Buddha, I do not wish to allow those Kosambī monks to enter my kingdom."

The Buddha replied, "Great King, those Kosambī monks are virtuous; it is only because they were in dispute with one another that they did not follow My words. Now they are coming to pay respects to Me. Let them come, Great King."

Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant also submitted, "Exalted Buddha, I do not wish to allow those Kosambī monks to enter the monastery." Having been similarly refused by the Buddha, he remained silent.

Furthermore, when those Kosambī monks arrived at Sāvatthī, the Buddha had them stay in a secluded area at the edge of the monastery and had lodgings prepared for them. Other monks not only refrained from sitting or standing together with those Kosambī monks, but whenever conscientious (lajjī) monks arrived, they would ask the Buddha, "Exalted Buddha, who are those Kosambī monks who have been quarreling and disputing?" The Buddha would point them out, saying, "These are the ones."
41:
"These are the ones, those Kosambī monks who quarreled and did not listen to the Buddha's words; these are the ones, those Kosambī monks who quarreled and did not listen to the Buddha's words." Being thus pointed out and spoken of by every conscientious monk who arrived, those Kosambī monks felt great shame. Not daring to lift their heads, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha's feet and begged for His forgiveness. Then the Buddha said:

"Monks, you have been ordained in the presence of an Omniscient Buddha like Me, yet even when I Myself tried to bring harmony, you did not follow My words. You have committed a grave wrong.

In the past, wise men of virtue, the Bodhisattas, heard the advice and instructions of their parents who were about to be killed. Even though those parents were killed, they did not transgress their parents' advice and instructions, and later they came to rule as kings over two great kingdoms."

Having said this, He again preached the Kosambaka Jātaka (the story of Dīghāvu) in detail and said:

"Monks, in this way, the Bodhisatta Prince Dīghāvu, even though his parents were killed, did not transgress their advice and instructions. Later, he even won the hand of King Brahmadatta's daughter and came to rule as king over two great kingdoms, the Kāsī and Kosala realms. You, My sons, who did not follow My words,
42:
have committed a grave fault by not following My words."

Then He spoke this verse:

*Pare ca na vijānanti, mayamettha yamāmase.*
*Ye ca tattha vijānanti, tato sammanti medhagā.*

(Ettha = In the midst of this Saṅgha, crowded with people. Pare ca = Those monks who lack wisdom and engage in quarrels. "Mayaṃ = We. Yamāmase = Are constantly moving toward the presence of Death." Na vijānanti = Do not know or see, as their eye of wisdom is closed. Tattha = In the midst of that Saṅgha, crowded with people. Ye ca = Those wise monks whose intelligence shines. Vijānanti = Know clearly with the presence of mindfulness on death (maraṇassati) that we are constantly moving toward the presence of Death. Tato = Because of such realization. Medhagā = Quarrels and disputes. Sammanti = Are ceased and extinguished through the practice of Right Conduct (Sammā-paṭipatti).)

At the conclusion of the verse, the monks who had gathered there were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The Buddha, through many such Dhamma teachings (from the time He finished the Vassa in the Palileyyaka forest until nearly eleven years had passed), delivered humans, devas, and brahmās.

## Regarding the 5 Buddha-duties

In connection with the Buddha-duties, many commentaries such as the Saṃyutta Commentary explain them as the five Buddha-duties. However, the Sutta Nipāta Commentary combines the later four Buddha-duties into one, naming it the post-meal Buddha-duty (pacchābhatta-buddhakicca), thus presenting two Buddha-duties: the morning Buddha-duty (purebhatta-buddhakicca) and the post-meal Buddha-duty. The meaning, however, is the same. Therefore, according to the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, there are two Buddha-duties as mentioned; according to other commentaries, there are five types of Buddha-duties (the Buddha's daily routine): purebhatta-kicca, pacchābhatta-kicca, purimayāma-kicca, majjhimayāma-kicca, and pacchimayāma-kicca. I shall describe these five Buddha-duties in order to increase your devotion and faith:

## (1) Purebhatta-buddhakicca = The Morning Buddha-duty

The Buddha rises early and, to favor the attendant monk and for the comfort of His physical body (rūpakāya), performs personal hygiene such as washing His face. Then, until it is time to enter for alms,
45:
He spends the time in a secluded place in the Attainment of Fruition (phalasamāpatti). When the time for alms-round arrives, He adjusts His lower robe, fastens His waistband, puts on His outer robe, and taking His alms-bowl, He enters the village or town for alms, sometimes alone and sometimes surrounded by a company of monks. When He enters, He sometimes does so in an ordinary manner and sometimes with many miraculous displays of psychic power. The manner of His entry is as follows:

When the Buddha enters for alms, gentle breezes blow ahead of Him, cleaning the surface of the earth. Clouds release fine droplets of water, settling the dust along the path, and follow above His head like a canopy or ceiling. Other winds bring flowers blooming in various places and blow them along, spreading a carpet of flowers along the path He travels. Naturally high ground becomes low and level on its own. Naturally low ground rises and becomes level on its own. Stones, rocks, gravel, potsherds, stumps, and thorns move away of their own accord.

When He places His feet on the ground, the earth's surface is already level; or else, great paduma lotuses, the size of well-crafted chariot wheels, appear spontaneously to receive His feet.

As soon as He places His right foot inside the threshold of the gates of various towns and villages, six-colored rays radiate from His body. They make buildings such as four-cornered palatial
46:
houses and apartments appear as if they were cast in liquid gold or wrapped and covered with exquisite cloths, making them glitter and shine, and the rays dart here and there. Animals such as elephants, horses, and birds, while remaining in their respective places, utter sweet and pleasant sounds, trumpeting, neighing, and singing. Similarly, musical instruments such as drums and gongs sound melodiously without being struck by humans. Ornaments worn by people, such as beads, earrings, bracelets, and armlets, also spontaneously produce pleasant sounds. By these signs, people know, "Today, the Buddha has entered our town or village for alms."

Those people, wearing their best clothes and wraps, carrying perfumes, flowers, and so on, come out from their respective houses and gather on the main street. They respectfully worship the Buddha with perfumes and flowers and request, "Venerable Sir, please give us ten monks; please give us twenty monks; please give us a hundred monks," and so forth, taking as many as they can manage. They also take the Buddha's alms-bowl, prepare seats, and respectfully serve the meal.

When the Buddha has finished His meal, He looks into the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of those people and preaches so that some are established in the Three Refuges, some in the Five Precepts, and some in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).
48: Thus, he exhorted them with the discourse on heedfulness (appamāda-ovāda). In that assembly, some monks requested meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Blessed One. The Blessed One gave those monks meditation subjects suitable to their temperaments. Thereafter, all the monks paid respectful homage to the Blessed One and departed to their respective places for the day's rest and the night's rest. Some went to the forest, some to the foot of trees, some to mountains and other such places. Some went to the Cātumahārājika deva realm, some to Tāvatiṃsa, Yāma, Tusita, Nimmānarati, and Paranimmitavasavatti deva realms. Thereafter, the Blessed One entered the Gandhakuṭī and, if he so desired, would lie down for a moment on his right side in the noble lion's posture, remaining mindful and clearly comprehending. Then, with his body refreshed, he would rise from his rest and, in the second part of the day, survey the world of beings. In the third part of the day, the people living in various towns and villages depending on the alms-resort village, having given alms in the morning, would dress in their best clothes and robes in the afternoon, and carrying perfumes, flowers, and so on, would gather in the monastery to hear the Dhamma. At that time, the Blessed One would proceed to the assembly with suitable psychic power (pāṭihāriya) and sit upon the noble Buddha's seat prepared in the Dhamma hall (the pavilion for preaching).
51: to relieve the physical fatigue of his noble body (rūpakāya) caused by the sitting posture. In the second part, he would enter the Gandhakuṭī and lie down on his right side in the noble lion's posture, remaining mindful and clearly comprehending. In the third part, rising from his rest, he would sit cross-legged and survey the world of beings with his pair of Buddha-eyes (buddha-cakkhu)—namely, the Knowledge of the Inclinations and Latent Tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) and the Knowledge of the Maturity of the Faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa)—to clearly see those individuals who had performed special meritorious deeds (adhikāra) such as generosity (dāna) and virtue (sīla) in the presence of previous Buddhas. This is the explanation found in the Saṃyutta Commentary, the Sīlakkhandha Commentary, and others. The explanation in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is as follows: The last watch is divided into four parts. In the first part, he performs walking meditation. In the second part, he enters the Gandhakuṭī and lies down on his right side in the noble lion's posture, mindful and clearly comprehending. In the third part, he enters the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala-samāpatti). In the fourth part, he enters the attainment of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) and then surveys the world of beings with the aforementioned pair of Buddha-eyes to clearly see beings with little dust in their eyes (apparajakkha), beings with much dust in their eyes (mahārajakkha), and so on. (This is the Pacchimayāma-buddhakicca = the last watch of the night duty). The section on the five duties of the Buddha is finished. ********** Thus, it was the natural custom (dhammatā) of the Blessed One to diligently perform these five daily duties of the Buddha in every place where he resided. Following this
52:
52

Naturally, while residing at the great Dakkhinagiri Monastery during this 11th Vassa, the Buddha performed his duties. One day, during the duties of the last watch (pacchima-yāma), while surveying the world of beings with his 'Buddha-eye' (Buddha-cakkhu), he perceived through his omniscient wisdom the Brahmin Kasi Bharadvaja, who was endowed with the supportive merit (adhikāra) and the potential (upanissaya) for the Fruit of Arahatship. Upon further reflection, he clearly saw: 'Today, the Brahmin Kasi Bharadvaja will hold a plowing ceremony. When I go to the place where he is plowing, there will be a conversation. At the end of that conversation, having heard my Dhamma teaching, the Brahmin will ordain and attain the Fruit of Arahatship.' Thus, he waited for the right time, residing in the Gandhakuti within the Dakkhinagiri Monastery.

## The Plowing Ceremony of the Brahmin Kasi Bharadvaja
That day was the day of the plowing ceremony of the Brahmin named Kasi Bharadvaja, a resident of Ekanālā village. (He is called Kasi Bharadvaja because he belongs to the Bharadvaja lineage and earns his living by plowing/farming). The arrangement for the first day of sowing in Kasi Bharadvaja's field was as follows:
Three thousand pairs of draught oxen were prepared. All the oxen had beautiful gold covers on their horns and silver covers on their hooves...
53:
...were already harnessed; all the oxen were decorated with white flowers and five-finger marks of sandalwood paste. They were beautiful in their five limbs—the head and four legs—and possessed all the auspicious characteristics of noble oxen. Some oxen were dark blue like the color of collyrium. Some were white as crystal, some were bright red like coral, and some were variegated like masaragalla stone.

Likewise, all five hundred laborers were dressed in brand-new white clothes, decorated with flowers and sandalwood. They wore large garlands draped uniformly over their right shoulders, and their entire bodies were smeared with orpiment and realgar, making them shine brilliantly. When they set out, they moved in groups of ten plows each. The tips and ends of the plows, the yokes, and the goads were all plated with gold. Among the five hundred plows, the first plow was drawn by eight strong lead oxen, while the remaining plows were drawn by four oxen each. The rest of the oxen were brought along as spares to replace those that became tired. For every group of ten plows, there was one seed cart, and the farmers took turns plowing. They also took turns sowing the seeds.

The landowner Brahmin Kasibharadvāja himself had his beard trimmed beforehand, bathed, and smeared his body with highly fragrant sandalwood. He wore a lower garment worth five hundred...
54:
...wearing a lower garment and an upper robe worth a thousand draped over his left shoulder. He wore twenty rings, two on each finger, and lion-mouth shaped earrings in both ears. On his head, he wore a turban like that of the Brahma King, and a golden flower garland around his neck. Surrounded by a host of Brahmins, he managed the work.

Afterward, the Brahmin's wife had many pots of milk-rice (pāyāsa) cooked and loaded onto large carts. After bathing in scented water and dressing in full finery, she went to the workplace surrounded by a host of Brahmin women.

The Brahmin's house was also well-smeared with sandalwood in every corner. Popped rice was scattered everywhere. It was decorated with full water pots, banana trees, banners, streamers, and jasmine flowers, and offerings of fragrant flowers were made. In the fields, tall banners and flags were planted here and there. The crowd that gathered at the workplace, including attendants and laborers, numbered two thousand five hundred. Every person wore new clothes, and milk-rice and other foods were prepared for all two thousand five hundred people.

When everyone was ready at the workplace, the Brahmin had his usual golden bowl washed clean, filled it with milk-rice, and garnished it with ghee, honey, and molasses. He then had an offering made to the deity of the plow. The Brahmin's wife gave golden, silver, bronze, and copper bowls...
55:
...to the five hundred laborers respectively. She herself, holding a golden ladle, went around serving the milk-rice in order. The Brahmin, after having the sacrificial offerings (bali) made, wore sandals with red straps and held a large red golden staff. He moved about directing as needed: "Give milk-rice in this person's bowl; give ghee in this person's bowl; give sugar in this person's bowl."

This was the elaborate ceremony and arrangement at the plowing festival of the landowner Brahmin Kasibharadvāja.

## The Arrival of the Blessed One

At that time, the Blessed One, while staying at the Gandhakuṭī monastery, perceived that the Brahmin's milk-rice feast was taking place. He reflected, "It is now time to discipline this Brahmin." He then adjusted his inner robe, fastened his waistband, put on his outer robe, took his alms-bowl, and departed alone from the Gandhakuṭī monastery toward the place where the Brahmin Kasibharadvāja's plowing festival was being held.

(In this regard: When the Blessed One wishes to go for alms, just as a bee naturally comes to a pair of blooming lotus flowers, the sapphire-colored stone bowl—donated by the Four Great Kings—would spontaneously arrive between his two hands without the Blessed One having to go and pick it up.

In this regard: One might ask, "Why did the monks not follow the Blessed One?" The answer is: If the Blessed One wishes to go alone...
56:
...at the time of the morning alms-round, he would close the door and remain inside the Gandhakuṭī. At that, the monks would understand the sign: "Today the Blessed One wishes to enter the village or town alone; he must have seen some being who is ready to be converted." They would then take their own bowls and robes, circumambulate the Gandhakuṭī to the right, and go for alms elsewhere. On the day he was to convert the Brahmin Kasibharadvāja, the Blessed One acted in this manner. Therefore, the monks did not follow the Blessed One. This is the answer.)

When the Blessed One arrived, the Brahmin Kasibharadvāja was still serving milk-rice to his attendants. The Blessed One then went to the place where the milk-rice was being served and stood in a suitable spot.

(In this regard: The Blessed One's arrival and standing at the place where milk-rice was served was solely to bless the Brahmin. Indeed, the Blessed One did not go to the serving area because he wished to eat like a destitute man. To elaborate: The Blessed One's relatives numbered one hundred and sixty thousand—eighty thousand from his mother's side and eighty thousand from his father's side. These relatives, with their wealth, could constantly provide him with perpetual alms-food. In truth, the Blessed One did not become a monk for the sake of food. Rather, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) and made the five great sacrifices throughout countless aeons, he became a monk with the intention: "Having liberated myself from the round of rebirth, I shall liberate other beings as well; having tamed my own six senses, I shall tame other beings as well; having extinguished all the heat of defilements, I shall cool other beings as well; having...
57:
...attained the element of Parinibbāna, both of the aggregates and of defilements, I shall lead other beings to attain it as well." Thus, because he himself is liberated from the round of rebirth, he wishes to liberate other beings; because he himself has tamed his six senses, he wishes to tame other beings; because he himself has cooled the heat of defilements, he wishes to cool other beings; and because he himself has attained the two types of Parinibbāna, he wishes to lead other beings to attain them as well. It was for this purpose of blessing the Brahmin Kasibharadvāja that he traveled through the world and stood at the place where the milk-rice was being served.)

The Blessed One stood on a high spot where the Brahmin Kasibharadvāja could see him and hear his words. He then emitted the golden radiance known as Pīta-rasmi, which was more brilliant than the light of a thousand suns or moons, appearing like a blend of liquid gold and yellow orpiment, extending to a distance of eighty cubits all around. Because they were enveloped by this radiance, the walls of the Brahmin's workshop, the surrounding trees, and the turned clods of earth appeared as if they were made of solid gold.

Then, all the people who were eating the milk-rice saw the Blessed One standing there, shining brilliantly with incomparable Buddha-glory. They washed their hands and feet, raised their joined palms in reverence, and stood surrounding the Blessed One. While the multitude stood surrounding him...
58:
...the Brahmin, seeing the Blessed One standing there, thought, "He has come specifically to disturb my work." Because of this, he felt displeased. Furthermore, looking at the Blessed One's possession of the major and minor marks of a Great Man, he had the following wrong thoughts: "If this monk Gotama had engaged in productive work, he would have been like a crest-jewel of rubies upon the heads of all people in the whole of Jambudīpa. Any kind of prosperity would have been achievable for this monk Gotama. Yet, this monk Gotama, out of laziness, does not perform any work. He merely wanders about, prioritizing physical fitness, and eats by begging at people's plowing festivals and such."

With such wrong thoughts, the Brahmin spoke to the Blessed One disparagingly:

"O monk, I plow and I sow. Having plowed and sown, I eat. (Even though I am not one endowed with major and minor marks like you, these works of mine have not failed.) O monk, you too should plow and sow. Having plowed and sown, eat happily like me. (For one like you, endowed with major and minor marks, what kind of prosperity could not be achieved?)"

(In another way, this Brahmin Kasibharadvāja thought: "It is said that in the royal palace of the Sakyans in the city of Kapilavatthu, the meritorious Prince Siddhattha was born. That prince..."
59:
He was one who had previously heard the news that 'Prince Siddhattha has renounced the luxury of a Universal Monarch and become a monk.' Therefore, now, knowing that 'this monk is indeed that Prince Siddhattha,' he spoke in this manner, wishing to accuse and disparage him by saying, 'Having renounced the luxury of a Universal Monarch (to become a monk), are you now still so weary and exhausted?' (Alternatively, this Brahmin was a sharp intellectual. He did not speak thus with the intent to disparage the Buddha; rather, seeing the Buddha’s physical form clearly and wishing to praise his endowment of wisdom, he spoke in this way to initiate a conversation.)

At that time, the Buddha, knowing that the person to be tamed (the Brahmin Kasibhāradvāja) was a farmer and a sower, wished to teach the Dhamma by showing that he himself was the most supreme and noble farmer and sower in the world of beings, including devas and Brahmas, in accordance with the Brahmin's inclination and disposition:

'Brahmin, I too plow and sow; having plowed and sown, I eat and live happily.'

Then the Brahmin Kasibhāradvāja thought, 'This ascetic Gotama says, "I too plow and sow like you." However, I do not see the coarse farming equipment such as the yoke or the goad of this ascetic Gotama. Could this ascetic Gotama be telling a lie?'
60:
After considering this, he examined the Buddha from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair. Being an expert in the science of body marks (aṅgavijjā), he clearly saw that the Buddha was endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. He reflected, 'For a noble person endowed with such marks of a Great Man, there is no reason or occasion to speak a lie.' At that moment, great devotion arose in him. He abandoned the rude address of 'Samaṇa' (ascetic) and, wishing to address the Buddha by his lineage, he said:

'We do not see the venerable Gotama's yoke, nor the plow, nor the plowshare, nor the goad, nor the oxen. Yet the venerable Gotama says, "Brahmin, I too plow and sow; having plowed and sown, I eat and live happily."' 

After saying this, the Brahmin Kasibhāradvāja addressed the Buddha with this verse:

'You claim to be a farmer,
But we do not see your farming.
Being asked, tell us about your farming,
So that we may know your farming.' (1)

(O venerable Gotama, you) claim to be a farmer. (We) do not see the equipment (such as the yoke and plow) for your farming.
61:
We do not see the collection of equipment (such as the yoke, plow, etc.) for your farming. Please speak the answer to us, who ask out of a desire to know, in such a way that we may clearly understand your farming.

The Buddha answered the Brahmin's incomplete question fully with four verses (three verses of answers and one concluding verse). The meaning of the words in those verses is as follows:

## Answer Verse (1)

'Faith is the seed, austerity is the rain,
Wisdom is my yoke and plow.
Shame is the pole, mind is the tie,
Mindfulness is my plowshare and goad.' (2)

(O Brahmin of the Bhāradvāja lineage), my four types of faith—namely, faith through learning (āgama), faith through attainment (adhigama), faith through conviction (okappana), and faith through devotion (pasāda)—are called the "seed," as they are the true root cause when plowing the field. (For the four types of faith, see the Pāthikavagga Commentary, page 212, etc.)
62:
My restraint of the six sense faculties is called "rain," as it is greatly beneficial in making the special plant of faith thrive and grow. (b)

My collection of Dhamma, consisting of the four Path-wisdoms along with insight-wisdom (vipassanā), is called the "yoke and plow." (c)

My two qualities of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri and ottappa) are the "pole" of the plow. (d)

My concentration (samādhi), which is led by the mind, is called the three types of "ties" or "ropes." (e)

My mindfulness associated with insight-wisdom and mindfulness associated with Path-wisdom is the "plowshare and goad." (f)

(A special point to note here: The Brahmin only asked about the equipment for farming, such as the yoke and plow. However, the Buddha, by the power inherent in all Buddhas, supplemented the answer with what was necessary by using metaphors, even though it was not in the question, because the preceding Dhammas were similar in nature. Thus, showing this power, he said, 'My faith is the seed.')

Here, one might ask: 'What is the similarity of the preceding Dhammas? Did the Brahmin not only ask about the equipment like the yoke and plow? Why then did the Buddha add the "seed," which the Brahmin did not ask about, and explain faith by way of a metaphor? If he answers what was not asked,
63:
would this discourse not become disconnected in meaning?' (That is: Why did the Buddha provide an extra answer about the seed of faith when the Brahmin only asked about the tools? Does this not make the discourse inconsistent?)

The answer is: There is no such thing as a disconnected discourse for the Buddhas. It is the natural custom of Buddhas to supplement the preceding similar Dhammas by using metaphors. 

In this regard, the connection of meaning should be understood as follows:

This Brahmin Kasibhāradvāja asked the Buddha about farming in relation to the equipment like the yoke and plow. The Buddha, out of compassion for the questioner, did not omit anything by thinking, 'The Brahmin did not ask about this part.' Instead, wishing to make him understand the process of farming along with the four factors—(1) the root Dhamma, (2) the supporting Dhamma, (3) the equipment Dhamma, and (4) the result Dhamma—he began from the very root, saying, 'Faith is the seed.' (This means that although the Brahmin could not ask fully due to his limited wisdom, the Buddha, out of great compassion, supplemented the missing parts in his answer.)

To clarify further: Farming can only be done if there is seed; it cannot be done without seed. Farming is done only to the extent of the seed available; it is not customary to plow beyond the available seed. Therefore, the seed is the primary root cause of farming.
64:
Since the seed is the primary root cause of farming, the Buddha wished to show the process of farming starting from the cause. Because it is similar in nature to the seed, which is the basic root cause of worldly farming that the Brahmin asked about, the Buddha wished to teach by using a metaphor for the basic root cause of his own Dhamma-farming. Thus, he said, 'My faith is the seed.' (One should understand the profound meaning: the root cause of worldly farming is the seed, and the root cause of Dhamma-farming is faith.)
