Here, another question arises: 'One should first answer what the Brahmin asked, and only then answer what was not asked. Why did the Buddha answer what was not asked first?'

The brief answer is: (1) Because it was of great benefit to the Brahmin, he taught the seed of faith first, even though it could have been taught later. (2) Because the rain of sense restraint and the seed of faith are connected as cause and effect, he taught the rain of sense restraint immediately after the seed of faith.

The detailed meaning is: (1) This Brahmin was a wise man, but having been born into a family of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), he was deficient in faith. A person who is deficient in faith but possesses great wisdom does not trust others (even teachers) and does not practice the Dhamma they should practice, and thus cannot attain the Path and Fruit. In the continuum of this Brahmin Kasibhāradvāja, even the devotional faith (pasāda-saddhā) that is free from the turbidity of defilements was weak (due to his birth in a wrong-view family). Therefore, that weak faith of the Brahmin...
65:
Accompanied by great wisdom, it cannot complete the extraordinary benefit of attaining the Path and Fruition; it is like an ox yoked to a single harness along with a great elephant. Therefore, for that Brahmin, faith is the factor that will support the attainment of the Path and Fruition. Thus, wishing to establish that Brahmin in the (lacking) faith, the Blessed One, being incomparably skilled in the methods of teaching Dhamma, taught the seed of faith first, although it should normally be taught later.

(2) Rainfall is very beneficial to the seed. Since the causal relationship can only be fully completed when rainfall is mentioned immediately after the seed, although it should be taught later, this meaning of rainfall is taught first (immediately after the seed of faith). (Not only this rainfall, but the Blessed One also taught the plow-pole and so on in their appropriate places).
(In this regard, the characteristics of faith, etc., should be noted from the scriptures.)

Regarding the comparison between faith and the seed: Just as the natural seed, which is the fundamental cause of the Brahmin's worldly plowing, performs two tasks—(1) taking root below and (2) sprouting above—likewise, the seed of faith, which is the fundamental cause of the Blessed One's Dhamma-plowing, performs and completes two tasks: (1) taking root in virtue (sīla) below and (2) sprouting in tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā) above.

Just as a natural seed absorbs the essence of the earth and water through its roots and grows to reach the maturity of the grain through its stalk, likewise, this seed of faith absorbs the essence of tranquility and insight through the root of virtue and grows to attain the maturity of the grain of Noble Fruition (ariya-phala) through the stalk of the Noble Path (ariya-magga).
66:
Just as a natural seed, established in good soil, reaches growth and abundance through roots, sprouts, leaves, stalks, and ears, producing milk and resulting in a harvest of rice full of many grains, likewise, this seed of faith, established in the good soil of the mind-stream, reaches growth and abundance through the six worldly purifications such as purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi), producing the milk of purification by knowledge and vision (ñāṇadassana-visuddhi), which is the Noble Path, and resulting in the harvest of the Fruition of Arahatship (arahatta-phala) full of many analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and supernormal powers (abhiññā). Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Saddhā bījaṃ = My faith is the seed."

Regarding the phrase: "My restraint of the six sense faculties is the rainfall."
Just as the Brahmin's seeds and the crops arising from those seeds are always lush and complete without withering when they receive the support of rainfall, likewise, the seed of faith and the qualities of virtue, concentration, and wisdom rooted in that seed of faith are always lush and complete without withering when they receive the support of the Blessed One's restraint of the six sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara). With that phrase, the Blessed One indicated this profound meaning:

"Brahmin, just as it is good if it rains after you have planted and sown the seeds, and if it does not rain, you pour fresh water; likewise, I have bound the plow-pole of shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) with the yoke and plowshare of insight-wisdom and Path-wisdom using the rope of concentration (samādhi). Having yoked the oxen of effort (vīriya), I drive them with the goad of mindfulness (sati) to plow and plant the seed of faith in the good soil of my own mind-stream. In this planted seed of faith, there is never a lack of rainwater. The rain of my restraint of the six sense faculties is constantly falling upon the good soil of my mind-stream."
67:
Regarding the phrase: "My insight-wisdom and Path-wisdom are the yoke and the plowshare."
The Brahmin's yoke and plowshare are similar to the Blessed One's insight-wisdom and Path-wisdom. The yoke is the support for the plow-pole; it goes in front, is connected to the plow-pole, is the support for the ropes, and assists the oxen to move together. Likewise, wisdom is the strong support (upanissaya) for many blameless qualities headed by shame and fear of wrongdoing. It is the leader of blameless qualities. Since it cannot exist without the qualities of shame and fear of wrongdoing, which are like the plow-pole, the plow-pole of shame and fear of wrongdoing is connected to the yoke of wisdom. As it is the causal support for the rope of concentration, it is also the support for the ropes of concentration. Because wisdom prevents the two extremes of over-exertion and laxity, it assists the oxen of effort to move together with a steady pace.

A plowshare attached to a plow-base breaks up clods of earth when plowing and destroys large and small tree roots. Likewise, the Blessed One's plowshare of wisdom, equipped with the share of mindfulness, when plowing through the work of insight, breaks up the four types of compactness (ghana): compactness of continuity (santati-ghana), compactness of group (samūha-ghana), compactness of function (kicca-ghana), and compactness of object (ārammaṇa-ghana). It breaks and destroys all large and small roots of defilements (kilesa). Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "My two types of wisdom, insight-wisdom and Path-wisdom, are the yoke and the plowshare."

Regarding the phrase: "Hiri īsā = My shame is the plow-pole."
Since shame (hiri) and fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) are co-arisen associates, by taking shame, fear of wrongdoing is also taken. Therefore, it was translated as: "My two qualities of shame and fear of wrongdoing are the pair of plow-poles."
68:
Just as the Brahmin's natural plow-pole carries the yoke and the plowshare, likewise, the Blessed One's pair of shame and fear of wrongdoing (the plow-pole) carries the yoke and plowshare of mundane insight-wisdom and supramundane Path-wisdom (since these two types of wisdom can only exist if those two qualities are present). Only when the yoke and plowshare are connected to the plow-pole can they perform their respective tasks (as mentioned before); they are steady and firm (tightly bound). Likewise, only when connected with the pair of shame and fear of wrongdoing can the two types of wisdom perform their respective tasks; they are steady, firm, and remain tightly established without mixing with the unwholesome states of shamelessness (ahirika) and fearlessness of wrongdoing (anottappa). Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "My two qualities of shame and fear of wrongdoing are the pair of plow-poles."

Regarding the phrase: "Manoyottaṃ = The mind is the rope."
With the mind as the head, the intention is to teach concentration (samādhi). Therefore, it was translated as: "My concentration, with the mind at the forefront, is the three types of ropes: the binding rope, the yoke-rope, and the pole-rope."

There are three types of ropes: (1) the pole-rope that binds the plow-pole and the yoke, (2) the yoke-rope that binds the yoke and the oxen, and (3) the tethering rope that connects the driver and the oxen. Just as the Brahmin's three types of ropes prevent the plow-pole, yoke, and oxen from being separate and make them a single unit to complete their tasks, likewise, the Blessed One's rope of concentration binds this group of qualities—the plow-pole of shame and fear of wrongdoing, the yoke of wisdom, and the oxen of effort—by preventing them from scattering away from a single object, thereby completing their respective tasks. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "My concentration, with the mind at the forefront, is the three types of ropes."

Regarding the phrase: "My mindfulness associated with insight-knowledge and mindfulness associated with Path-wisdom are the plowshare and the goad."
69:
Just as a natural plowshare protects the plow-base and goes before it, likewise, mindfulness protects the plowshare of wisdom by investigating the nature and course of wholesome states and by being clear regarding the object. Therefore, in many Pali scriptures, the Blessed One taught mindfulness as a protective quality. That plowshare of mindfulness also goes before the plowshare of wisdom by way of non-forgetfulness. Indeed, after mindfulness leads and observes the group of states, wisdom follows and understands them through penetration.

Just as a natural goad shows the oxen the danger of being prodded or struck, not allowing them to slacken or stop, and preventing them from leaving the path, likewise, the goad of mindfulness shows the oxen of effort the danger of falling into the lower realms (apāya), not allowing them to be lazy, slacken, or stop. It prevents the mind from wandering into improper areas of sensual pleasures, engages it in the work of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), and prevents it from going down the wrong path. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "My mindfulness associated with insight-knowledge and mindfulness associated with Path-wisdom are the plowshare and the goad."

## Answer Verse (2)
Kāyagutto vacīgutto,
āhāre udare yato.
Saccaṃ karomi niddānaṃ,
soraccaṃ me pamocanaṃ. (3)

(O Brahmin of the Bhāradvāja lineage... Just as you protect your field with a fence... I, the Teacher of the three types of beings) am guarded in body (kāyagutto); I protect the field of the mind-stream with the fence of good bodily conduct.
70: Vacīgutto = One is secured by the fence of the four types of good conduct in speech. (By this phrase, the Virtue of Restraint according to the Pātimokkha [Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla] is expounded). Āhāre = In the four requisites to be used. Yato = One is well-restrained so that the twenty-one types of wrong livelihood [anesana] do not arise. (By this, the Virtue of Purity of Livelihood [Ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla] is expounded). Udare = In the stomach. Yato = One is well-restrained by consuming food with wise reflection. (By this, the Virtue regarding the Use of Requisites [Paccaya-sannissita-sīla] is expounded, with Moderation in Eating [Bhojane mattaññutā] as the foremost). Saccaṃ-Saccena = With truthful speech consisting of the eight types of noble modes of speech [ariya-vohāra]. Niddānaṃ = The clearing, reaping, and uprooting of the weeds (the eight types of ignoble modes of speech [anariya-vohāra]). Karomi = I perform. Soraccaṃ = The Fruit of Arahantship [arahatta-phala], which is the delight and enjoyment in the excellent Dhamma called Nibbāna. Me = For Me, the Teacher of the three worlds. Pamocanaṃ = The final rest, unyoking the plow and releasing the field. (The meaning here is: Brahmin, after sowing seeds, you build a fence of thorns, wood, or bamboo to protect the crops. By doing so, cattle, buffaloes, and deer cannot enter and destroy your crops. Similarly, I, the Buddha, having planted the seed of faith, build three great layers of walls—Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla, Ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla, and Paccaya-sannissita-sīla—to protect the various crops of merit. By doing so, the cattle, buffaloes, and deer of unwholesome states such as greed, hatred, and delusion cannot enter and destroy the various crops of merit of Me, the Great Farmer).
71: Brahmin, just as you, after performing external farming, perform the task of pulling, reaping, and clearing the weeds that destroy the crops by hand or with a sickle; similarly, I, after performing the internal farming of the Dhamma, perform the task of pulling, reaping, and clearing with the sickle of truth—the eight noble modes of speech—the weeds of the eight ignoble modes of speech [anariya-vohāra] that destroy the crops of merit. These ignoble modes are: saying one saw what one did not see, saying one heard what one did not hear, saying one sensed what one did not sense, saying one knew what one did not know, saying one did not see what one saw, saying one did not hear what one heard, saying one did not sense what one sensed, and saying one did not know what one knew. I clear these with the eight noble modes of speech: saying one did not see what one did not see, saying one did not hear what one did not hear, saying one did not sense what one did not sense, saying one did not know what one did not know, saying one saw what one saw, saying one heard what one heard, saying one sensed what one sensed, and saying one knew what one knew. Brahmin, your unyoking of the plow, releasing of the field, and resting is not a final rest, because you must plow again in the evening, the next day, or the next year.
72:
72

It is not a matter of taking a rest. My unyoking the plow and letting the field go to stand and rest is not like that. Indeed, O Brahmin, until I reached the Fruit of Arahatship, there was no such thing as unyoking the plow and letting the field go to stand and rest. To make it clearer: O Brahmin, I (the Great Farmer), starting from the time of Dipankara Buddha, harnessed the four great oxen of Right Effort (Sammappadhana) to the plow of Wisdom. For a period of four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, I performed the great internal plowing of the Dhamma. Until I reached the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscient Wisdom (until becoming a Buddha), I did not unyoke the plow or let the field go to rest.

O Brahmin, only after I had performed this ceaseless plowing of the Dhamma for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, and after reaching the Fruit of Arahatship—surrounded by all the special qualities of a Buddha—while sitting on the Unconquerable Golden Throne (Aparajita Pallanka) at the foot of the Mahabodhi tree, did I reach the final peace where all anxieties end. Only then did I unyoke the oxen of Energy from the plow of Wisdom and let go of the field, which is the mental continuum. I then entered the attainment of the Fruit of Arahatship for as long as I wished, thus taking a final rest. For me, there is now no further task of plowing.

## The Third Answer Verse
Vīriyaṃ me dhuradhorayhaṃ,
yogakkhemādhivāhanaṃ.
Gacchati anivattantaṃ,
yattha gantvā na socati. (4)

(O Brahmin of the Bharadvaja lineage... My physical and mental energy are called the pair of draught oxen harnessed to the front of the plow. Alternatively...)
73: Vīriyaṃ = The four types of Right Effort. Dhura-dhorayhaṃ = Is called the four beasts of burden yoked respectively to the primary and secondary yokes (two pairs). (Taṃ = That single pair of My bodily and mental effort; or, those two pairs of My Right Effort). Yogakkhema-adhivāhanaṃ = Because it can carry one forward to Nibbāna, where one is not oppressed by the four bonds [yoga] such as the bond of sensual desire. Yattha = To which Nibbāna. Gantvā = A farmer like Me, having gone there. Na socati = Has no sorrow at all. Taṃ = To that Nibbāna, the state free from sorrow. Anivattaṃ = Without turning back or retreating. Gacchati = One goes by the power of wisdom. (The meaning is: The plow yoked to the pair of beasts of burden at the Brahmin's plow-head breaks the clods of earth and removes large and small roots. Similarly, the plow of Wisdom, pulled vigorously by the pair of My bodily and mental effort, breaks and destroys the four types of 'density' [ghana]—density of continuity, mass, function, and object—and removes the large and small roots of defilements. (Alternatively) Just as the Brahmin has two pairs of oxen (four in total) yoked to the primary and secondary yokes of a single plow, so too in the Buddha's Dhamma-plow, there are two pairs of oxen (four in total), which are the four Right Efforts. Just as the Brahmin's two pairs of oxen, by pulling vigorously, accomplish two tasks—destroying existing and future weeds and fulfilling the growth of crops—similarly, the two pairs of great oxen of My four Right Efforts,
74:
74

...striving with intense effort, it accomplishes two tasks: the task of abandoning unwholesome states that have arisen or are yet to arise, and the task of fulfilling wholesome states.

O Brahmin, just as your pair of draught oxen go forward to the east or west as you drive them, so my pair of draught oxen of Right Effort go straight, pulling towards Nibbana where I drive them. In this pulling and going, there is a distinction: when your oxen pulling the plow reach the edge of the field (the bund), they turn back. But my oxen of Right Effort have been going towards Nibbana without turning back since the time of Dipankara Buddha.

Your oxen cannot reach a place where a farmer like you is free from sorrow. But my oxen of Right Effort reach Nibbana, the place where a farmer like me is free from sorrow, without retreating.

## Concluding Verse
Evamesā kasī kaṭṭhā, sā hoti amatapphalā.
Etaṃ kasiṃ kasitvāna, sabbadukkhā pamuccati. (5)

(O Brahmin of the Bharadvaja lineage... I, the Teacher of the three worlds, have thus plowed this internal Dhamma field for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons without interruption. This plowing of mine has Nibbana, the essence of peace, as its fruit. It is not for me alone...)
75: But indeed, whoever—whether Brahma, deva, or human—plows this internal Dhamma-farming by yoking the oxen of Right Effort incessantly, will be completely released from all suffering). Thus, the Buddha concluded the Dhamma teaching with the Fruit of Arahantship as the climax and Nibbāna as the end for Kasī Bhāradvāja Brahmin. At that time, Kasī Bhāradvāja Brahmin, having heard the very profound Dhamma teaching, clearly realized: "The crops I obtain from my farming, though eaten, leave me hungry again the next day. But this Dhamma-farming of Master Gotama bears the fruit of the Deathless, Nibbāna. By consuming the fruit of this Dhamma-farming, one can be released from all suffering forever." Being greatly inspired, he wished to perform the customary act of a devotee. He poured milk-rice into his own golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, garnished it with ghee, honey, and molasses to make it appetizing, covered the golden bowl with a fine white cloth, and personally carried it to the Buddha. He respectfully offered it, saying: "May Master Gotama consume this milk-rice. Master Gotama is indeed a plowman because he performs the Dhamma-farming which has Nibbāna as its fruit."
76: Having said this, he respectfully offered it. Then the Buddha spoke this verse to Kasī Bhāradvāja Brahmin: Gāthābhigītaṃ me abhojaneyyaṃ, sampassataṃ brāhmaṇa nesa dhammo. Gāthābhigītaṃ panudanti buddhā, dhamme sati brāhmaṇa vuttiresā. Brāhmaṇa = O Brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. Gāthābhigītaṃ = Food obtained by chanting verses. Me = By Me. Abhojaneyyaṃ = Is not to be eaten at all. Esa-eso = Eating food obtained by chanting verses. Sampassataṃ = For the Buddhas who see the purity of livelihood. Na dhammo = Is not the custom or nature. (Tasmā = Therefore). Buddhā = The Buddhas. Gāthābhigītaṃ = Food obtained by chanting verses. Panudanti = They reject. Brāhmaṇa = O Brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. Dhamme = When the principle of pure livelihood. Sati = Exists. Eso = This seeking of the four requisites righteously, without any attachment to any family, like stretching out a hand in the sky. Vutti = Is the pure livelihood of the Buddhas. Thus, He spoke this verse.
77:
(In this context, a question may arise: "Did the Blessed One recite and preach Dhamma verses in order to obtain the milk-rice, so that it might be called food obtained by reciting verses?" The answer is: The Dhamma verses were not preached for the purpose of obtaining the milk-rice. Rather, having stood near the field since early morning and not receiving even a single spoonful of food, the Blessed One fully manifested his virtues through three Dhamma verses illustrating his spiritual farming. This milk-rice obtained in such a manner is like the property obtained by performers through dancing and singing. Therefore, it was preached as "food obtained by reciting verses." Such food is not suitable for the Buddhas; hence, he preached, "It is not fit to be consumed at all."

In this verse, there are four lines. With the first three lines, the Blessed One demonstrated the purity of his teaching, freeing himself from the danger of being blamed or accused by ignorant people who might say, "The ascetic Gotama made an unfaithful, non-devout Brahmin who did not wish to give, desire to give by singing verses, and then he accepted the food; this ascetic Gotama's Dhamma teaching is rooted in the desire to obtain alms-food." With the fourth line, he demonstrated the purity of his livelihood.)

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the Brahmin Kasībhāradvāja became displeased, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama has rejected my milk-rice. He says this food is unsuitable. I am indeed one of little merit; I did not get the opportunity to give my offering." Then he further reflected, "If he does not accept this milk-rice, it would be good if the ascetic Gotama would accept another of my offerings." Knowing this, the Blessed One—
78:
"I have come here, having determined the time for alms-round, thinking, 'Within this much time, I will inspire faith in this Brahmin.' Now the Brahmin has become displeased. If he were to offend me with that displeasure, he would no longer be able to penetrate the noble Dhamma of Nibbāna." Having reflected thus, and wishing to fulfill the desire of the Brahmin's heart to increase his faith—

Aññena ca kevalinaṃ mahesiṃ,
Khīṇāsavaṃ kukkuccavūpasantaṃ.
Annena pānena upaṭṭhahassu,
Khettaṃ hi taṃ puññapekk hassa hoti. (7)

(Brāhmaṇa = O Brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan.) Aññena = with other than the milk-rice. Annena ca = with food and. Pānena ca = with drink. Kevalinaṃ = who is complete and perfect in all the Buddha's attributes. Mahesiṃ = the Great Seer who constantly seeks the mass of virtues such as noble morality. Kukkuccavūpasantaṃ = whose remorse is entirely stilled. Khīṇāsavaṃ = the noble Arahant whose taints are exhausted. Upaṭṭhahassu = attend to and serve him. (Although the Blessed One inspired the desire to give in the Brahmin, he spoke only in this indirect way; he did not directly say, "Give" or "Bring it.") Taṃ = that Dispensation of the Buddha with its eight wonders. Puññapekk hassa = of you who desire merit. Khettaṃ hi - khettaṃ eva = is indeed the great fertile field for planting and sowing the seeds of merit. Hoti = it is.

Thus he preached this verse.
79:
Then the Brahmin Kasībhāradvāja thought, "This milk-rice was brought for the Blessed One; therefore, I should not give this milk-rice to anyone else according to my own will." He then asked, "Venerable Gotama, if that is so, to whom shall I give this milk-rice?" The Blessed One said, "O Brahmin, in the world of devas, Maras, and Brahmas, and among the generation of recluses and Brahmins, princes and men, I do not see anyone (even a single person) who could properly digest this milk-rice if eaten, except for the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata. Therefore, O Brahmin, discard this milk-rice where there is no green grass, or drop it into water that is free from living beings."

(In this context, a question may arise: "Why would this milk-rice not be digested by anyone among devas and humans?" The answer is: It would not be digested because divine essence (dibba-ojā), which is subtle and delicate, was added to the coarse human food. To elaborate: In this milk-rice of the Brahmin Kasībhāradvāja, as soon as it was set aside for the Blessed One, the devas added divine essence. (If it were purely divine essence, it could be digested by devas; if it were purely milk-rice, it could be digested by humans.)

Now, because this food contains subtle and delicate divine essence within coarse human food, it cannot be digested by devas. Indeed, devas have subtle and delicate bodies; therefore, coarse human food (milk-rice) cannot be properly digested by them. If humans eat it, it cannot be digested because it contains divine essence. Indeed, humans have coarse bodies; therefore—
80:
—that subtle and delicate divine essence cannot be properly digested by those humans.

For the Blessed One, however, that milk-rice mixed with divine essence can be digested by his natural digestive fire (pācaka-tejo). (Some teachers say it can be digested due to the power of his knowledge.) For a disciple of the Blessed One who is an Arahant, that milk-rice mixed with divine essence can be digested due to the power of concentration (samādhi) and knowing the proper measure. For others besides the Buddha and Arahants, it cannot be digested even by those with psychic powers. (Alternatively, one should not speculate on the reason here; this is the domain of the Buddhas.)

Then the Brahmin Kasībhāradvāja dropped that milk-rice into water free from living beings. As soon as it was thrown into the water, that milk-rice sizzled; it made the sound 'ciṭi-ciṭi, ciṭi-ciṭi'. Smoke came out from all sides. Much smoke came out from all sides. Just as a plowshare (iron block) that has been heated all day, when thrown into water, sizzles and makes the sound 'ciṭi-ciṭi, ciṭi-ciṭi', and smoke comes out from all sides, and much smoke comes out from all sides; even so, as soon as that milk-rice was thrown into the water, it sizzled. It made the sound 'ciṭi-ciṭi, ciṭi-ciṭi', smoke came out from all sides, and much smoke came out from all sides.

Then the Brahmin Kasībhāradvāja, terrified and with his hair standing on end, approached the Blessed One, touched the Blessed One's feet with his head, and said to the Blessed One:

"O Venerable Gotama, it is wonderful! O Venerable Gotama, it is wonderful! O Venerable Gotama, just as one might set upright what was overturned—
81:
—or reveal what was hidden, or point out the way to one who is lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms; even so, the Dhamma has been clarified in many ways by the Venerable Gotama. O Venerable Gotama, I go to the Venerable Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May the Venerable Gotama grant me the going forth (pabbajjā) and the higher ordination (upasampadā) in his presence."

After receiving the going forth and the higher ordination in the presence of the Blessed One, not long after becoming a monk, the Venerable Bhāradvāja, dwelling alone, secluded, diligent, and ardent, with his mind directed towards Nibbāna, while practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, attained the fruit of Arahantship and became one among the Arahants.

The story of the Brahmin Kasībhāradvāja ends.
(This story of the Brahmin Kasībhāradvāja is extracted and described from the commentary on the Kasībhāradvāja Sutta in the first volume of the Sutta Nipāta Commentary.)

## Here ends Chapter 29.
83:
He is a Sammāsambuddha because he has perfectly realized all Dhammas by himself.

He is Vijjācaraṇasampanno because he is perfect in true knowledge (vijjā) and conduct (caraṇa).

He is Sugato because he has gone well.

He is Lokavidū because he is a knower of the three worlds.

He is Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi because he is the incomparable leader of persons to be tamed.

He is Satthādevamanussānaṃ because he is the teacher of devas and humans.

He is Buddho because he has realized the Four Noble Truths himself and awakens others to them.

He is Bhagavā because he is endowed with the six sublime glories and virtues.'

Thus his reputation has spread far and wide.

That Blessed One, having known through his own direct knowledge, realizes and preaches to this world of existence with its devas, Maras, and Brahmas, and to this world of beings with its recluses and Brahmins, its princes and men."
84:
84
That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing. He proclaims the holy life, which is perfectly complete and entirely pure. It is good indeed to see such Arahants.

Then the Brahmin Verañja went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. After concluding the pleasant and memorable conversation, the Brahmin Verañja sat at a respectful distance and said to the Blessed One:

“Master Gotama, I have heard this: ‘The recluse Gotama does not pay homage to, nor rise up for, nor offer a seat to Brahmins who are old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage.’ Master Gotama, what I have heard is indeed true. For Master Gotama does not pay homage to, nor rise up for, nor offer a seat to Brahmins who are old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage. Master Gotama, this failure to show respect is certainly not proper.”

Thus he spoke words of blame and reproach. At that time, the Blessed One, without falling into the faults of self-exaltation (attukkaṃsana) or disparaging others (paravambhana), and with a heart cooled by the sprinkling of the waters of great compassion,
85:
85
wishing to dispel the Brahmin's ignorance and delusion and to show what is appropriate, said:

“Brahmin, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its princes and people, I do not see anyone whom I should pay homage to, or rise up for, or offer a seat to. Indeed, Brahmin, if the Tathāgata were to pay homage to, or rise up for, or offer a seat to anyone, that person's head would fall off.”

Even though the Blessed One spoke thus, the Brahmin Verañja, being unwise, did not realize or understand that the Blessed One was the greatest person in the world. Unable to bear the Blessed One's truthful words, he said:

“(1) Master Gotama is a person without taste (arasarūpo).”

Then the Blessed One, in order to soften the Brahmin's heart, did not give a direct contradictory answer but wished to show that there is a certain sense in which one might say he is “without taste”:

“Brahmin, there is a sense in which one might rightly say of me: ‘The recluse Gotama is without taste.’ For, Brahmin, the taste for forms, the taste for sounds, the taste for smells, the taste for flavors, the taste for
86:
86
tangibles—these tastes have been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Brahmin, it is in this sense that one might say of me: ‘The recluse Gotama is without taste.’ But the sense in which you mean it does not exist in the Tathāgata at all.”

(Note: The Brahmin's intention was that in the world, acts such as bowing, rising, and saluting are called the 'taste of social harmony' (sāmaggī-rasa). Since Master Gotama does not perform these, he accused him of being “without taste,” meaning one who lacks the taste of social harmony.

The Blessed One's intention was that in the world, delight in forms (rūpa-rasa), sounds (sadda-rasa), smells (gandha-rasa), flavors (rasa-rasa), and tangibles (phoṭṭhabba-rasa) are called 'tastes of harmony' because they arise from the meeting of objects and senses. Since the Blessed One has eradicated all these five types of tastes, he is indeed free from them. Referring to this sense—that he is entirely free from the 'taste of harmony' which is the delight in the five sense objects—he said one might say he is “without taste,” but that the Brahmin's intended meaning did not apply to him.

Here, one might ask: Why did the Blessed One say, “The sense in which you mean it does not exist in me at all”? By saying this,
87:
87
does it not imply that he admits to having the 'taste of social harmony' (such as bowing) that the Brahmin referred to?

The answer is: It does not imply that. To elaborate: Only one who is supposed to perform the 'taste of social harmony' (like bowing) but fails to do so can be accused of being “without taste” due to lacking that social etiquette. However, the Blessed One is not one who should perform such acts, as he is the greatest in all three worlds. Therefore, wishing to make it clear that he is not one who should perform such acts of homage, he said, “The sense in which you mean it does not exist in me at all.”)

Thus, the Brahmin, unable to find fault regarding the lack of social harmony, changed his approach and tried to blame him in another way:

“(2) Master Gotama is one without use (nibbhogo).”

Then the Blessed One, wishing to show that there is another sense in which he could be spoken of in that way, said:

“Brahmin, there is a sense in which one might rightly say of me: ‘The recluse Gotama is without use.’ For, Brahmin, the use of forms through craving and greed, the use of sounds, smells, flavors, and tangibles—these acts of use (paribhogas) have been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Brahmin, in this sense (of not using the five sense objects through craving), one might say of me: ‘The recluse Gotama is without use.’
88:
88
But the sense in which you mean it does not exist in the Tathāgata at all.”

(Note: The Brahmin's intention was that in the world, paying respect to elders is recognized as 'the use of social harmony' (sāmaggī-paribhoga). Since the Blessed One lacks this kind of social use, he accused him of being “without use.”

The Blessed One's intention was that the use of forms, sounds, smells, flavors, and tangibles through craving and greed—these five types of use (paribhoga) have been eradicated by him. Therefore, he is free from those five types of paribhoga. Referring to this sense, he allowed that one might say he is “without use.”)

In this way too, the Brahmin was unable to find fault with the Blessed One, so he changed his approach again and said:

“(3) Master Gotama is one who teaches non-action (akiriya-vāda).”

The Blessed One, following the previous method, wished to show there is another sense in which he could be spoken of in that way:

“Brahmin, there is a sense in which one might rightly say of me: ‘The recluse Gotama is one who speaks of non-action, a teacher of non-action.’
89:
89
For, Brahmin, I teach the non-doing of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; I teach the non-doing of various kinds of evil and unwholesome states. Brahmin, in this sense (of teaching that evil misconduct should not be done), one might say of me: ‘The recluse Gotama is one who speaks of non-action, a teacher of non-action.’ But the sense in which you mean it does not exist in the Tathāgata at all.”

(Note: The Brahmin's intention was that people in the world practice 'family customs' (kula-cāritta) such as paying respect to elders. Because the Blessed One does not perform these family customs, he accused him of being a “teacher of non-action.”

The Blessed One's intention was that he teaches that evil misconduct should not be done. Therefore, referring to this sense of non-action regarding evil deeds, he allowed that one might say he is a “teacher of non-action.”)

In this way too, the Brahmin could not find fault, so he changed his approach once more and said:

“(4) Master Gotama is an annihilationist (uccheda-vāda).”
90:
Thus he spoke again. The Blessed One, wishing to show that there is indeed another sense (pariyāya) in which such a thing could be said, in order to soften the Brahmin's heart, spoke as follows:

“Brahmin, there is a sense in which one might rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of annihilation (ucchedavāda).’ For, Brahmin, I teach the Dhamma for the annihilation of greed (rāga), the annihilation of hatred (dosa), and the annihilation of delusion (moha). I teach the Dhamma for the annihilation of various other evil and unwholesome states. It is in this sense, Brahmin, that one might rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a teacher of annihilation.’ But that which you are referring to, Brahmin, does not exist in me at all.”

(In this context: The Brahmin, not seeing the Blessed One perform acts of respect such as bowing to elders, assumed that ‘Because of this ascetic Gotama, the traditional worldly custom of paying respect is being annihilated.’ Thus, he accused the Blessed One of being a teacher of annihilation.

The Blessed One, however, teaches the Dhamma to cut off and annihilate greed, hatred, delusion, and other unwholesome states through their respective Paths (magga). Therefore, referring to this sense of annihilating unwholesome states, he allowed that one might say ‘The ascetic Gotama is...’)
91:
‘...a teacher of annihilation.’)

Again, as the Brahmin could not find fault with the Blessed One in this way, he changed his approach to find fault in another way:

“(5) Master Gotama is one who loathes (jegucchī).”

Then the Blessed One, as before, wishing to show that there is another sense in which such a thing could be said, spoke as follows:

“Brahmin, there is a sense in which one might rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is one who loathes.’ For, Brahmin, I loathe bodily misconduct (kāya-duccarita), verbal misconduct (vacī-duccarita), and mental misconduct (mano-duccarita). I loathe the commission of various other evil and unwholesome states. It is in this sense, Brahmin, that one might rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is one who loathes.’ But that which you are referring to, Brahmin, does not exist in me at all.”

(In this context: The Brahmin thought that the Blessed One did not perform the family custom of bowing to elders because he loathed it. Thus, he accused him, saying, “Master Gotama is one who loathes.”

The Blessed One, however, loathes evil misconduct. Therefore, referring to this sense of loathing evil misconduct...)
92:
...he allowed that one might say ‘The ascetic Gotama is one who loathes.’)

Again, as the Brahmin could not find fault with the Blessed One in this way, he changed his approach to find fault in another way:

“(6) Master Gotama is a destroyer (venayika).”

Then the Blessed One, as before, wishing to show that there is another sense in which such a thing could be said, spoke as follows:

“Brahmin, there is a sense in which one might rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer.’ For, Brahmin, I teach the Dhamma for the destruction of greed, for the destruction of hatred, and for the destruction of delusion. I teach the Dhamma for the destruction of various other evil and unwholesome states. It is in this sense, Brahmin, that one might rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer.’ But that which you are referring to, Brahmin, does not exist in me at all.”

(In this context: The Brahmin, not seeing the Blessed One perform acts of respect such as bowing to elders, assumed that ‘This ascetic Gotama is a destroyer of this great merit of honoring elders (vuddhāpacāyana), which is the highest in the world.’ Thus, he accused the Blessed One of being a destroyer.

The Blessed One, however, teaches the Dhamma to abandon and destroy greed, hatred, delusion, and other unwholesome states. Therefore, referring to this sense of teaching the destruction of unwholesome states, he allowed that one might say ‘The ascetic Gotama is a destroyer.’)
93:
Again, as before, the Brahmin changed his approach to find fault in another way:

“(7) Master Gotama is a burner (tapassī).”

The Blessed One, as before, wishing to show that there is another sense in which such a thing could be said, spoke as follows:

“Brahmin, there is a sense in which one might rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a tapassī (one who has abandoned the states that burn).’ For, Brahmin, I declare that bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct—and other unwholesome states—are ‘burning states’ (tapanīyā dhammā) because they cause distress to all beings. Brahmin, one who has abandoned and relinquished these unwholesome states called ‘tapa’ is what I call a tapassī—one who has abandoned the unwholesome states that cause distress. Brahmin, the Tathāgata, who has come well like the Buddhas of old, has abandoned and relinquished those unwholesome states called ‘tapa’.

Brahmin, in this sense—that of having abandoned and relinquished the unwholesome states called ‘tapa’—one might rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is a tapassī.’ But that which you are referring to, Brahmin, does not exist in me at all.”

(In this context: The Brahmin's intention was that those who perform acts of respect, such as bowing, make the elders feel pleased and joyful, whereas those who do not perform them make the elders feel distressed (burn) in their hearts. Since the Blessed One did not perform such acts of respect, the Brahmin assumed, “This ascetic Gotama is one who causes distress to elders,” and thus accused the Blessed One of being a ‘tapassī’ in the sense of one who causes distress to elders.

The Blessed One, however, calls unwholesome states ‘tapanīyā dhammā’ or ‘tapa’ because they cause distress to the world of beings. Since he has abandoned those unwholesome states that cause distress, he is called a ‘tapassī’ (according to the etymology: *tape assīti tapassī* — ‘one who has abandoned the unwholesome states called tapa’). Referring to this sense, he allowed that one might say ‘The ascetic Gotama is a tapassī.’)
94:
94

The Blessed One has already abandoned and relinquished those unwholesome states called 'tapa'. O Brahmin, (by the method of having abandoned unwholesome states called 'tapa', you may say of me: 'The ascetic Gotama is a Tapassī = one who has abandoned unwholesome states called tapa.' But the kind of reason or sense you intend does not exist in me at all.)

Thus he replied.

(In this context: The Brahmin's intention was that those who perform acts of respect, such as bowing, make the elders happy and joyful. Those who do not do so cause the elders mental distress. Since the Buddha did not perform such acts of respect, the Brahmin considered him 'one who causes distress to elders' and accused him of being a 'Tapassī' in that sense.

The Buddha, however, explained that unwholesome states are called 'tapaniya' or 'tapa' because they cause distress to the world of beings. Since he had abandoned those unwholesome states, he could be called a 'Tapassī' according to the etymological definition: 'One who has abandoned the unwholesome states called tapa is a Tapassī.' He thus allowed the term to be used in this sense.)
95:
The great Brahmin Verañja, being unable to find fault with the Blessed One in this way, changed his approach for one final accusation:

“(8) Master Gotama is one who is free from the womb (apagabbha).”

Then the Blessed One, wishing to show that he could indeed be called ‘apagabbha’ (one free from rebirth) because he had abandoned all four types of future rebirth, spoke as follows:

“Brahmin, there is a sense in which one might rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is an apagabbha person (one who is free from remaining in a womb).’ For, Brahmin, I declare that a person (an Arahant) who has abandoned the four types of origin (yoni) and rebirth in the future is an ‘apagabbha’ person. Brahmin, the Tathāgata, who has come well like the Buddhas of old, has cut off at the root all four types of rebirth in the future. Brahmin, in this sense—that of having cut off rebirth in the future at the root—one might rightly say of me: ‘The ascetic Gotama is an apagabbha person.’ But that which you are referring to, Brahmin, does not exist in me at all.”

(In this context: The Brahmin believed that performing acts of respect to elders was a meritorious deed that could lead to rebirth in the heavenly world. Seeing that the Blessed One did not perform such acts, he accused him of being “one who is free from rebirth in the heavenly world.” His intention was to say, “The ascetic Gotama is free from heavenly rebirth and is one who will have to dwell in a loathsome human womb in a future life.”

The Blessed One, however, has no future rebirth at all, having cut it off at the root. Therefore, referring to this sense, he allowed that one might say ‘The ascetic Gotama is an apagabbha person.’)
96:
Thus, from the moment he arrived in the presence of the Blessed One, the Brahmin Verañja insulted, accused, and reviled him with eight kinds of abuse, starting with “being devoid of taste.” However, the Blessed One, out of great compassion for the Brahmin, looked upon him only with his cool and peaceful eyes. Being the Possessor of Omniscience, he wished to dispel the dark clouds of ignorance (avijjā) and delusion (moha) dwelling in the Brahmin's mind, like the full moon rising in a cloudless sky or the sun rising in the autumn season. Thus, he answered the Brahmin's words of insult and accusation by turning them into words of praise through various senses (pariyāya).

Furthermore, at this time, he clearly demonstrated his Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā), his mind which is like the earth—unshaken by the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma)—and his cool heart that does not give way to anger no matter how much others may revile him.
97:
97
“This Brahmin, without using his power of discernment and relying merely on worldly conventions such as grey hair, broken teeth, and wrinkled skin, considers himself to be older than I. He does not know in the least that he is pursued by the danger of birth, surrounded by the danger of aging, oppressed by the danger of sickness, and afflicted by the danger of death. He is a great stump in the cycle of rebirths, yet he does not realize that after dying today, he will become a mere infant (a messenger of death) lying on his back tomorrow. Indeed, it is with great effort that he has come into my presence. May this visit of the Brahmin to my presence be a fruitful one.”

Having reflected thus, and wishing to clearly demonstrate His state as the foremost and eldest person in this world, the Buddha expanded and preached the Dhamma in the following manner:

“Brahmin, suppose there were eight, ten, or twelve hen’s eggs. Suppose the hen had properly sat on them, properly warmed them, and properly scented them with her own scent. Among those chicks (within the eggs), which one should be called the eldest—the one who first breaks through the eggshell with the tip of its claws and the tip of its beak and emerges safely? Should it be called the eldest or the youngest?”
98:
98
When the Buddha asked this, the Brahmin replied, “O Venerable Gotama, it should be called the eldest. Among those chicks, the one who first breaks the shell and emerges is indeed the eldest.”

Then the Blessed One said, “Brahmin, in the same way, among the multitude of beings who are within the eggshell of ignorance, enveloped by the eggshell of ignorance, I alone in this world have first broken through the eggshell of ignorance and attained the peerless and supreme Knowledge of the Arahat Path and Omniscience. Therefore, Brahmin, I am the eldest and the most supreme among all beings in the world.”

(In this context, the comparison between the simile and its meaning should be noted: On the side of the simile of the chicks, the three actions of the mother hen—sitting on the eggs, warming them, and scenting them—ensure that the eggs do not rot. The moisture on the outer membrane of the eggs dries up, and the shell becomes thinner day by day. The tips of the claws and beaks of the chicks inside become mature and hard, and the chicks grow. As the shell thins day by day, the light from outside reaches the inside. Then, the chicks inside the shell think, ‘We have lived for a long time in this cramped and narrow place with our legs and wings curled up. This light is visible outside; now we shall live happily in the place where this light is.’ Desiring to come out, they kick the shell with their feet and stretch their necks forcefully. Thus, the shell breaks into two. Then, the chicks shake their little wings...)
99:
99
...chirping according to the moment, they emerge. Among those who emerge, the one who comes out first is called the eldest.

On the side of the Blessed One, who is the subject of the comparison (I shall now correlate the simile and the meaning): The three actions of the hen—sitting, warming, and scenting her eggs—are similar to the three types of contemplation (Anicca, Dukkha, Anatta) performed by the Buddha while sitting on the Mahābodhi throne as a Bodhisatta. The fact that the eggs do not rot due to the hen’s three actions is similar to the non-decline of Insight-knowledge (Vipassanā-ñāṇa) due to the Great Being’s development of the three contemplations. The drying up of the moisture on the outer membrane of the eggs is similar to the drying up of the sap of craving (nikanti-taṇhā) that attaches to the three planes of existence. The thinning of the eggshell day by day is similar to the thinning of the shell of ignorance and delusion (avijjā-moha) through successive thought-moments (javana) during the Great Being’s development of the three contemplations. The hardening and maturing of the chick’s claws and beak is similar to the Insight-knowledge (the beak) becoming sharp, firm, clear, and courageous. The maturing and growth of the chick is similar to the maturing and growth of Insight-knowledge, reaching the essence of wisdom. Then, just as the chick kicks with its feet and pecks with its beak to break the shell and emerges safely shaking its wings...
100:
100
...so too, after attaining the essence of Insight-knowledge through the three contemplations, the Great Being broke the eggshell of ignorance with the Path of Arahatship attained in due order. Shaking the wings of Higher Knowledge (Abhiññā), He safely realized all the special qualities and attributes of a Buddha.

Thereafter, the Blessed One continued to show the Brahmin Verañja how He attained the state of the peerless and supreme Eldest One through this practice. He preached in detail how He strove in meditation at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree with fourfold effort; how He attained the mundane jhānas through such striving; and how, based on those mundane jhānas, He attained the Higher Knowledge of Recollecting Past Lives (Pubbenivāsānussati-abhiññā) in the first watch of the night (on the full moon day of Kason, 103 Great Era). With the beak of that knowledge, He broke the eggshell of ignorance that veiled the past sequence of aggregates and was born for the first time into the Ariya fold. In the middle watch of that night, He attained the Higher Knowledge of the Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu-abhiññā). With the beak of that knowledge, He broke the eggshell of ignorance that veiled death and rebirth and was born for the second time into the Ariya fold. In the last watch of that night, He attained the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints (Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), also known as the third True Knowledge (Vijjā), and with the beak of that knowledge, He broke the eggshell of ignorance that veiled the Four Noble Truths and was born for the third time into the Ariya fold. (The details of this preaching should be noted from the section concerning the Brahmin Verañja in the Burmese translation of the Pārājika Pāḷi.)
101:
101
## The Brahmin Verañja Taking the Refuges

Thus, because the Blessed One had great compassion for the Brahmin, He preached the Dhamma clearly showing how He became the eldest and most supreme in the Ariya fold through the three True Knowledges (Vijjā): Pubbe, Dibba, and Āsava. When He had finished, the Brahmin Verañja was suffused with joy in both body and mind. Realizing clearly that the Blessed One was indeed the eldest and most supreme in the Ariya fold, he reproached himself, saying: “I have wrongly spoken to the Omniscient Buddha—who is the eldest and most supreme among the three types of people and is endowed with all virtues—saying that He does not pay respect to elders. Friends, how loathsome indeed is the delusion of ignorance!” He then made a firm decision: “This Venerable Gotama is now the eldest because He was the first to be born into the Ariya fold in this world. He is the most supreme because He is peerless in all virtues.” He then addressed the Buddha:

“Venerable Gotama is indeed the eldest in the world. Venerable Gotama is indeed the most supreme in the world. O Venerable Gotama, it is excellent! O Venerable Gotama, it is excellent! O Venerable Gotama, just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so...
102:
102
...has the Dhamma been clearly illustrated by the Venerable Gotama in many ways. O Venerable Gotama, I go to the Venerable Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May the Venerable Gotama recognize me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day onwards for as long as life lasts.”

Having thus taken the refuges, he made a request: “May the Venerable Gotama consent to spend the Rains Retreat (Vassa) in the city of Verañjā together with the Saṅgha of monks to show me favor.” The Blessed One accepted the invitation to spend the Rains Retreat in Verañjā by remaining silent. Then the Brahmin Verañja, being skilled in observing signs, thought: “If the monk Gotama did not accept my request, he would have refused by body or speech. Now, as he does not refuse but maintains an inner acceptance, he has accepted my request in his mind.” Knowing the Buddha’s acceptance, he rose from his seat, paid respectful homage to the Buddha from the four directions, and circumambulated Him three times. Although he had previously criticized the Buddha for not paying respect to elderly Brahmins, he now recognized the Buddha’s virtues. Even after paying homage many times with his body, speech, and mind, he was not yet satisfied. Keeping his hands raised in prayerful salutation (añjali) above his head, he retreated while facing the Buddha as long as He remained in sight.
103:
After paying his respects to the point of leaving the range of sight, he finally departed with satisfaction.

Following the request and invitation of the Brahmin Verañja, the Blessed One entered the twelfth rainy season retreat (vassa) in the city of Verañjā together with five hundred monks.

## The Famine in the City of Verañjā

At that time, the city of Verañjā was suffering from famine; it was difficult to find food to sustain life, the ground was bleached with white bones, and people had to subsist on food distributed by ration tickets. Consequently, it was not easy for the monks to sustain themselves by going for alms with their bowls.

During that period, horse merchants from the northern region (Uttarāpatha) were taking shelter from the rain in Verañjā with five hundred horses. These horse merchants provided a daily ration of one pattha measure of steamed barley for each monk at the horse stables. In the morning, when the monks entered the city of Verañjā for alms and received nothing, they would go to the horse stables, receive the one pattha measure of steamed barley, bring it back to the monastery, pound it in small mortars, and consume it.

(A special note here: During the four months of the rainy season in the region of Verañjā, travel was impossible due to heavy rains. Therefore, the horse merchants from Uttarāpatha had to take shelter in Verañjā. While staying there, they built houses for themselves and sheds for their horses in an area outside the city that would not be flooded, surrounding the area with fences. These locations of the horse merchants were recognized as horse stables.

To ensure the barley lasted a long time and remained free from pests, the horse merchants had steamed and husked it to use as horse feed in places where grass was unavailable. These horse merchants from Uttarāpatha, unlike those from the southern region (Dakkhiṇāpatha),
104:
were not lacking in faith; they were people of faith who cherished the Triple Gem. One morning, when these horse merchants entered the city for some business, they saw groups of seven or eight monks wandering for alms in the city for two or three consecutive days without receiving anything. They thought, "These noble ones have entered the rainy season retreat depending on this city of Verañjā. Now a famine has struck, and they are greatly exhausted as they receive nothing. Since we are guests, we cannot prepare congee or rice for these noble ones every single day. Our horses receive fodder twice—once at night and once during the day. It would be good if we could donate one pattha measure of barley from each horse's morning ration to each monk. If we do this, the noble ones will not be exhausted, and the horses will still have enough to subsist."

After consulting and agreeing among themselves, they went to the monks, informed them of this matter, and requested, "Venerable sirs, please accept one pattha measure of barley ration each and use it as you see fit." Thus, they established a daily offering of one pattha measure of barley for each monk.

When the monks entered the city of Verañjā for alms in the morning, they would wander through the whole city and receive not even a word of polite refusal, let alone food. Only when they went to the horse stables outside the city did they receive the one pattha measure of barley. They brought it back to the monastery. Since there were no lay attendants (kappiya-kāraka) to boil congee or cook rice, and it was not suitable or allowable for them to cook it themselves, they considered: "In this way, we shall have a light livelihood (sallahukavutti), and we shall also be free from the offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding self-cooking (sāmapāka)." Thus, they gathered in groups of eight or ten, pounded the barley in small mortars, and took their respective shares.
105:
They mixed it with water and consumed it. Having eaten, they lived without anxiety, striving and exerting themselves in the practice of the Dhamma.

For the Blessed One, the horse merchants offered one pattha measure of barley along with suitable ghee, honey, and sugar. The Venerable Ānanda took that barley, ghee, honey, and sugar and ground them on a stone slab. It is the nature of things prepared by a meritorious and wise person to be delightful. After grinding the barley and mixing it with the ghee and other ingredients, he offered it to the Blessed One. At that time, devas infused divine essence (ojā) into that barley powder. The Blessed One consumed that very barley powder and spent his time entering the Attainment of Fruition (phalasamāpatti). From the time the famine began, he did not go out for alms.

(In this regard, one might ask: Was Venerable Ānanda the permanent attendant (upaṭṭhāka) of the Blessed One during the retreat in Verañjā? The answer is: He was indeed serving, but he had not yet received the formal position of permanent attendant. To elaborate—during the first twenty years after Enlightenment (paṭhamabodhi), the Blessed One did not have a permanent attendant. Sometimes the Venerable Nāgasamāla served the Blessed One; sometimes Venerable Nāgita, sometimes Venerable Meghiya, sometimes Venerable Upavāna, sometimes Venerable Sāgata, and sometimes the Licchavi prince, the monk Sunakkhatta, served the Blessed One. These monks served according to their own will and departed whenever they wished.

Venerable Ānanda remained unconcerned while those various monks were serving, but whenever those monks departed, he himself performed the major and minor duties. The Blessed One also considered, "Although my noble kinsman Ānanda
106:
has not yet received the formal position of attendant (upaṭṭhāka), in matters of such service, this Ānanda is indeed the most suitable." Thus, the Blessed One accepted his service. Therefore, during this retreat in Verañjā, as there were no other attendant monks, Venerable Ānanda ground the barley on a stone slab, mixed it with ghee, honey, and sugar, and offered it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One consumed the barley powder offered by Venerable Ānanda and spent the time in the Attainment of Fruition (phalasamāpatti).

In this matter, the following questions and answers should be specifically noted:

(Question) Do not people strive greatly to perform meritorious deeds during times of famine? Do they not think that they should give to the monks even if they do not consume it themselves? Why, then, did not a single person offer even a spoonful of alms-food when the Blessed One stayed for the retreat in Verañjā? And why did the great Brahmin Verañja, who had requested the Blessed One to stay for the retreat with great effort, not even know that the Blessed One was there?

(Answer) It was because Māra, the Evil One, had possessed and deluded them, causing both the people and the Brahmin Verañja to be forgetful. To clarify—as soon as the Brahmin Verañja departed from the presence of the Blessed One, Māra possessed and confused him, as well as the citizens of Verañjā and all the people within a one-league (yojana) radius of Verañjā—the distance one could travel to and from for morning alms. Having made all those people forget and lose mindfulness of the Blessed One and the Sangha, Māra departed. Therefore, not a single person remembered to perform even the slightest act of respect.

(Question) Did the Blessed One enter the retreat in Verañjā without knowing
107:
about Māra's possession and delusion?

(Answer) He did not enter the retreat without knowing; he did so while fully aware.

(Question) If he knew that Māra would delude and possess them, why did he not enter the retreat in one of the cities such as Campā, Sāvatthī, or Rājagaha, but instead stayed only in Verañjā?

(Answer) Let alone Campā, Sāvatthī, or Rājagaha; even if the Blessed One had gone to the northern continent of Uttarakuru or to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to spend the retreat that year, Māra would have deluded and possessed the inhabitants of Uttarakuru or the devas of Tāvatiṃsa as well. For that year, Māra's mind was overwhelmed and oppressed by intense malice, grudge, and anger toward the Blessed One. However, in this city of Verañjā, the Blessed One foresaw this: "The horse merchants will support and honor the monks." For this reason, he spent the retreat only in Verañjā.

(Question) To ask further—was Māra not able to possess and delude the horse merchants?

(Answer) It is not that he was unable; he was indeed able. However, those horse merchants arrived in the city of Verañjā only after Māra had already possessed and deluded the others.

(Question) Even if they arrived later, why did Māra not return to possess and delude the horse merchants?

(Answer) He did not possess or delude them because he was unable to do so. To elaborate—Māra, for the sake of the Blessed One...
108:
108
(1) No one can cause any danger or obstacle to the almsfood that has been cooked and brought to be offered; (2) to the perpetual offering (nibaddha-dāna) that has been determined and designated as a regular alms-offering to the Buddha for a certain period; (3) or to the requisites that have been brought to the monastery and offered with the verbal dedication, “This object is offered for the use of the four requisites of the Blessed One.”

To elaborate further: No one can cause danger to the following four things: (1) The four requisites dedicated to the Blessed One, whether they are almsfood just about to be offered or offerings arranged and dedicated as perpetual gifts. (2) The lifespan of the Buddhas, which remains for four-fifths of the age-limit (āyu-kappa) of the era in which they appear. (For our Blessed One, who appeared when the human lifespan was one hundred years, no one was able to cause the danger of destroying His life-continuum before He reached eighty years, which is four-fifths of one hundred). (3) The major and minor physical marks of the Blessed One, as well as His bodily radiance. Indeed, the radiance of the moon, the sun, devas, and Brahmas disappears when it reaches the area illuminated by the Blessed One’s major and minor marks and His bodily radiance. (4) The Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) of the Buddhas. No one can cause danger to these four things: (1) the four requisites, (2) the lifespan, (3) the major and minor marks and radiance, and (4) the golden Omniscient Wisdom of the Blessed One. Therefore, it should be understood that the Blessed One, together with the five hundred disciple monks, partook of the barley almsfood in the city of Verañjā, which Māra could not obstruct.
109:
109
## The Past Kamma Leading to the Famine
That the Blessed One, along with the five hundred monks, had to undergo this famine in the city of Verañjā was due to a past deed. Ninety-two aeons ago, during the era of the Dispensation of Phussa Buddha, the Great Bodhisatta, having associated with bad friends, became a jester and spoke wrongly to the disciple monks of Phussa Buddha, saying: “Eat and chew coarse barley; do not eat fine rice almsfood.” Because of that unwholesome kamma, He encountered the danger of famine during this rainy season residence in the city of Verañjā. (This account is directly mentioned in the Apadāna Pāḷi, Khuddaka Nikāya, page 349).

## The Blessed One’s Words of Approval
The Blessed One heard the sound of the small mortar.

Buddhas ask questions even though they know;
They also do not ask even though they know. (There is nothing they do not know).
They ask at the proper time;
They do not ask when it is not the proper time.
Buddhas ask only what is connected with benefit; they do not ask what is not connected with benefit. (This means they ask only about things that will be beneficial and do not ask about things that will not be beneficial).
110:
110
Regarding matters not connected with benefit, the Buddhas have already performed the act of eradicating them through the Path (Magga).

The Buddhas question the monks for two reasons: “Either to preach the Dhamma or to prescribe training rules (sikkhāpada) for the disciples.”

Then the Blessed One asked the Venerable Ānanda: “Dear Ānanda, what is this sound of the mortar that is heard now?” The Venerable Ānanda then explained and reported the aforementioned matter to the Blessed One. At that time, the Blessed One said:

“Excellent, Ānanda! Excellent, Ānanda! You, who are virtuous, have overcome the desire for almsfood of fine rice mixed with meat (since you did not give in to famine, craving, or evil desires). Future generations, however, will look down upon such almsfood of fine rice mixed with meat that you virtuous ones have already conquered.”

## The Bold Proposal of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was a great person who reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) on the seventh day after his ordination. The Blessed One also designated him as the foremost (etadagga) in the possession of great psychic powers.
111:
111
Relying on his great psychic powers, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna thought: “At present, this city of Verañjā is in famine; the monks are weary. It would be good if I were to turn over the earth and feed them the nutritive essence (ojā) from the lower layer.” Then he thought again: “While I am living with the Buddha, it is not proper for me to act in this way without asking the Blessed One; it would be like competing with the Blessed One.” Having thought thus, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place, saying:

“Magnificent Blessed One, at present, the city of Verañjā is in famine. It is difficult to survive; the ground is white with bones; people live by food tickets; it is not easy to subsist by wandering for alms with the bowl. Magnificent Blessed One, the lower layer of this earth is sweet, excellent, and pleasant, like honey without bees or larvae. Magnificent Blessed One, I request permission to turn this great earth (mahāpathavī) upside down. The monks will then be able to consume the nutritive essence of the lower layer.”

Then the Blessed One asked: “Dear Moggallāna, what will you do with the creatures that depend on the earth?” Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied:
112:
112
“Magnificent Blessed One, I will create one hand to be like the earth. I will move the creatures that depend on the earth onto that hand created like the earth. With the other hand, I will turn this earth upside down.”

Then the Blessed One refused him, saying: “Dear Moggallāna, it is not fit. Do not wish to turn the earth, dear son. Beings might also fall into wrong views.”

In this context, the point to be noted regarding the phrase “Beings might also fall into wrong views” is as follows: This famine is not occurring only now; it will also occur in the future. At that time, where will the monks find a companion in the holy life who is endowed with psychic powers like you? Those future monks might only be Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), Non-returners (Anāgāmī), or dry-insight Arahants (Sukkhavipassaka), or even Arahants who have attained the analytical insights (Paṭisambhidāpattā) but lack psychic powers, and thus they will have to go to the houses of donors for alms. When that happens, the thought will arise in the minds of people: “In the time of the Buddha, the monks fully practiced the three types of training. The monks of that Buddha’s time developed the qualities of higher knowledge (abhiññā), and when there was famine, they turned the earth upside down and consumed the nutritive essence. Now, there are no monks who fully practice the three types of training. If there were, they would act in the same way (as in the Buddha’s time); they would not let us eat anything raw or cooked (meaning they would only feed us the earth’s essence).” Having had such thoughts,
113:
113
they would fall into the wrong view that “there are no Noble Ones (Ariyas)” even regarding those who are indeed Noble Ones. By falling into wrong views and disparaging, insulting, and accusing the Noble Ones, they would fall into the lower realms (apāya). Therefore, the Blessed One refused him, saying: “Do not wish to turn the earth, dear son.”

Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, not receiving permission for this request, wished to request in another way and said:

“Magnificent Blessed One, I request that the entire Saṅgha of monks go to Uttarakuru for alms.”

The Blessed One refused him in the same manner as before, saying: “Dear Moggallāna, it is not fit. Do not wish for the entire Saṅgha of monks to go to Uttarakuru for alms.”

(In this context, although it was not directly stated that “beings might fall into wrong views,” it should be understood that the Blessed One forbade going to Uttarakuru for alms for that very reason, as it had been stated previously. The meaning should be understood in the same way as before.

If the Blessed One had given permission, what would the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna have done? He would have created the Great Ocean to be like a small trench that could be crossed in one step, and he would have created a new direct path from the Naḷerupucimanda tree to the northern continent of Uttarakuru. He would have used his psychic power to place Uttarakuru in a position with a complete return path, making it as easy for the monks to enter and leave for alms as if it were their regular resort village (gocaragāma).)

This was the bold proposal of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
115:
115
(In this regard, a question may arise: Could the Venerable Sāriputta Thera not decide this matter of his own reflection by himself? The answer is: There are matters he could decide, and matters he could not. To elaborate—this noble Elder Sāriputta could decide that “The Sāsana of such and such Buddhas did not last long; the Sāsana of such and such Buddhas lasted long.” However, he could not decide, “For such and such a reason it did not last long; for such and such a reason it lasted long.”

The Elder Mahāpaduma, however, said: “For the Chief Disciple, who has reached the pinnacle of the sixteen kinds of knowledge, it was not a heavy burden to decide even this reason. Nevertheless, while living in the same place as the Blessed One, to make a decision by himself would be like discarding the scales and weighing with the hand. Therefore, he approached the Blessed One and asked the question.”)

Then, the Blessed One, desiring to answer the question asked by the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, said:

“Sāriputta, the Sāsana of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, and the Blessed One Vessabhū did not last long (through the succession of disciples). Sāriputta, the Sāsana of the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed One Kassapa lasted long (through the succession of disciples).”

Then, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera continued to ask:
116:
116
“Exalted Buddha, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the Sāsana of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, and the Blessed One Vessabhū did not last long?”

When asked thus, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Sāriputta Thera:

“Sāriputta, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, and the Blessed One Vessabhū were not weary in teaching the Dhamma in detail to their disciples. The ninefold Dhamma, such as Sutta and Geyya, of those Buddhas was very little. They did not prescribe training rules (sikkhāpada) for their disciples. They did not recite the (authoritative) Pātimokkha. When those Blessed Ones attained Parinibbāna and disappeared, and when the immediate disciples of those Blessed Ones attained Parinibbāna and disappeared, the later disciples of various names, clans, and castes caused that Sāsana to disappear quickly.

Sāriputta, just as various flowers placed on a wooden board without being tied together by a string are scattered, blown away, and destroyed by the wind (precisely because they are not tied by a string); even so, Sāriputta, when those Blessed Ones attained Parinibbāna and disappeared, and when the immediate disciples of those Blessed Ones attained Parinibbāna and disappeared, the later disciples of various names, clans, and castes caused that Sāsana to disappear quickly.
117:
117
Sāriputta, those (three) Blessed Ones, knowing the thoughts of their disciples with their own minds, were diligent in admonishing them.

Sāriputta, there is a special past event: the Blessed One Vessabhū, in a certain fearsome forest, knowing the minds of the monks with his own mind, admonished a thousand monks thus:

‘Think such thoughts as the three right thoughts, beginning with the thought of renunciation (nekkhamma-vitakka); do not think such thoughts as the three wrong thoughts, beginning with the thought of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka). Reflect thus: impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), non-self (anatta), and foulness (asubha); do not reflect thus: permanence (nicca), happiness (sukha), self (atta), and beauty (subha). Abandon these unwholesome states; dwell having fulfilled these wholesome states.’

Sāriputta, those thousand monks who were thus instructed and admonished by the Blessed One Vessabhū became Arahants with the destruction of taints (āsavas). Thus, the minds of those thousand monks, being completely free from the grasping of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ through craving and views regarding any state whatsoever, were clearly liberated from the taints, which were extinguished by the cessation of non-arising (a cessation that is called cessation even though it is non-arising).

Sāriputta, regarding the term ‘fearsome forest,’ because of the fearsome nature of that forest, if those who are not free from lust enter that forest, for the most part, their hair stands on end and they experience goosebumps.
118:
118
Sāriputta, this which has been said is the reason why the Sāsana of the Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, and the Blessed One Vessabhū did not last long.”

Thus the Buddha replied and spoke.

(A special note to be observed here: In the phrase “those three Blessed Ones were not weary in teaching the Dhamma in detail to their disciples,” it does not mean they were not weary due to laziness. Indeed, the Blessed Ones have no laziness or decline in energy (vīriya) at all. To make it clear—whether the Blessed Ones teach the Dhamma to one person, two people, or to many beings filling the entire universe, they teach only with equal effort and energy. They do not decrease their energy upon seeing a small audience, nor do they increase their energy upon seeing a large audience. For example, when a lion, the king of beasts, goes out to hunt after seven days, he runs and catches small prey or large prey with the same equal speed. The reason is that he has the intention: “Let my speed not diminish.” In the same way, the Blessed Ones teach the Dhamma with equal energy to even a small audience or to a very large audience. The reason is that they have the noble intention: “Let the respect for our Dhamma not diminish.”

In fact, just as our Blessed One taught the Dhamma in detail like filling the great ocean, those three Blessed Ones did not have to teach the Dhamma in detail. The reason is that in those times, the dust of defilements in the eye of wisdom of beings was very little. To elaborate—in the time of those three Buddhas, beings had long lives and
119:
119
the dust of defilements in their eye of wisdom was also little. Therefore, the veneya beings of those times, upon hearing even a single verse related to the Four Truths, would realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation. For this reason, they did not have to teach the Dhamma in detail. Consequently, the ninefold Dhamma, such as Sutta and Geyya, of those Buddhas was very little.

In the time of those three Buddhas, because the disciple monks were entirely free from faults, the authoritative training rules (sikkhāpada) related to the seven classes of offenses, which are prescribed according to faults, were not prescribed.

The authoritative Pātimokkha was not recited once every half-month (15 days). Those Blessed Ones recited only the Exhortatory Pātimokkha (Ovāda Pātimokkha), and even that Exhortatory Pātimokkha was not recited once every half-month. (This has been described in detail in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, Chapter 16, regarding the two kinds of Pātimokkha, on page 19.)

For the long-lived Blessed Ones, there were two successions of disciples: (1) the immediate generation of disciples, and (2) the later generation of disciples who were ordained under those immediate disciples. When the time of the second generation of later disciples arrived, because there were no original prescriptions of training rules, and because those disciples were of different names, clans, and castes, they felt as if they had no responsibility to protect and maintain the small collection of Dhamma taught by those long-lived Blessed Ones. Thinking, “Such and such an Elder will know, such and such an Elder will know,” they acted with laxity as if shifting the burden to one another. Because they did not protect it by holding a Council (Saṅgāyana), that Sāsana disappeared quickly.

When it is said, “The Sāsana of those long-lived Blessed Ones did not last long,” it only means that it did not last for many successions of disciples.
120:
120
In terms of the number of years, however, the life span of the Blessed One Vipassī was 80,000 years. The life span of the immediate disciples was also 80,000 years.
