Among the later disciples who were ordained under those immediate disciples, the life span of even the last disciple was 80,000 years. Therefore, after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, the life of the Sāsana through two successions of disciples lasted for 160,000 years. Since there were only two successions of disciples, it was taught as “did not last long” with reference to the few successions of disciples. It should be specifically noted that it was not taught with reference to the fewness of the duration of years.)

Thus, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, having heard the reason why the Sāsana of the three Buddhas—the Blessed One Vipassī, the Blessed One Sikhī, and the Blessed One Vessabhū—did not last long (through the succession of disciples), desired to hear the reason why the Sāsana of the three Buddhas—the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed One Kassapa—lasted long. He continued to ask the Blessed One:

“Exalted Buddha, what is the cause, what is the reason, why the Sāsana of the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed One Kassapa lasted long?”

When asked thus, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Sāriputta Thera:

“Sāriputta, the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed One Kassapa were diligent in teaching the Dhamma in detail to their disciples. The ninefold Dhamma, such as Sutta and Geyya, of those Blessed Ones
121:
121
was also very extensive. They prescribed training rules (sikkhāpada) for their disciples. They recited the (authoritative) Pātimokkha. (Therefore,) when those Blessed Ones attained Parinibbāna and disappeared, and when the immediate disciples attained Parinibbāna and disappeared, the later disciples (of successive generations) of various names, clans, and castes caused that Sāsana to endure for a long time.

Sāriputta, just as various flowers tied with a string and placed on a wooden board are not scattered, blown away, or destroyed by the wind (precisely because they are tied by a string); even so, Sāriputta, when those Blessed Ones attained Parinibbāna and disappeared, and when the immediate disciples attained Parinibbāna and disappeared, the later disciples (of successive generations) of various names, clans, and castes caused that Sāsana to endure for a long time.

Sāriputta, these aforementioned factors (teaching the Dhamma in detail, the extensiveness of the Dhamma, the prescription of training rules, and the recitation of the Pātimokkha) are the cause and the reason why the Sāsana of the Blessed One Kakusandha, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and the Blessed One Kassapa lasted long.”

Thus the Buddha replied and spoke.

(In this regard: Regarding the long duration of the Sāsana of those three Blessed Ones, both in terms of life span and the succession of disciples...)
122: It should be understood that the long endurance of the Sasana is due to the duration of the lifespan, the succession of disciples, or both. To elaborate: the lifespan of the Buddha Kakusandha was forty thousand years, the lifespan of the Buddha Koṇāgamana was thirty thousand years, and the lifespan of the Buddha Kassapa was twenty thousand years. The lifespans of the direct disciples of these Buddhas were also of similar duration. Many successive generations of those direct disciples established and maintained the Sasana. Thus, the Sasana of those three Buddhas lasted for a long time due to both the length of the lifespan and the succession of disciples. Regarding our Inconceivable Buddha, the Pinnacle of the Three Worlds, he ought to have appeared during the age when the human lifespan was ten thousand years, which is half the lifespan of the Buddha Kassapa. If not during the ten-thousand-year age, he should have appeared during the five-thousand, one-thousand, or five-hundred-year ages. However, his wisdom did not reach maturity for Buddhahood until the age when the lifespan had decreased to one hundred years. Because his wisdom matured only then, he appeared during the very short period of the hundred-year lifespan. Therefore, for our Buddha, although the Sasana may endure for a long time through the succession of disciples, it should be said that it does not endure as long in terms of the number of years according to the lifespan as the Sasanas of the previous Buddhas. Having heard the reasons for the long endurance of the Sasanas of the three Buddhas—Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa—the Venerable Sāriputta concluded that the prescription of training rules is the fundamental cause for the long endurance of the Sasana. Desiring the long endurance of this Buddha's Sasana, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, arranged his robe over his left shoulder,
123: and having paid homage to the Blessed One with joined palms, he addressed the Buddha: 'It is time, O Blessed One, for the Buddha to prescribe training rules for the disciples and to recite the Pātimokkha, so that this Sasana may endure for a long time. It is time, O Fortunate One, for the Buddha to prescribe training rules and to recite the Pātimokkha, which are the roots for the long endurance of the Sasana.' Thus he earnestly requested. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show that it was not yet the time to prescribe training rules, said: 'Wait, Sāriputta! Wait, Sāriputta! The Buddha alone will know the proper time for that (prescribing training rules and reciting the Pātimokkha). Sāriputta, the Buddha does not prescribe training rules for the disciples nor recite the Pātimokkha as long as certain states that are the grounds for taints (āsavaṭṭhānīya dhamma) have not yet appeared in the Saṅgha. Sāriputta, only when certain states that are the grounds for taints appear in the Saṅgha does the Buddha prescribe training rules for the disciples and recite the Pātimokkha for the sake of warding off those states.'
124: 'Sāriputta, as long as the Saṅgha has not reached greatness of seniority (rattaññumahatta), certain states that are the grounds for taints do not appear in the Saṅgha. But when the Saṅgha has reached greatness of seniority, then certain states that are the grounds for taints appear in the Saṅgha. Then the Buddha prescribes training rules for the disciples and recites the Pātimokkha for the sake of warding off those states. (2) Sāriputta, as long as the Saṅgha has not reached greatness of expansion (vepullamahatta), certain states that are the grounds for taints do not appear in the Saṅgha. But when the Saṅgha has reached greatness of expansion, then certain states that are the grounds for taints appear in the Saṅgha. Then the Buddha prescribes training rules for the disciples and recites the Pātimokkha for the sake of warding off those states. (3) Sāriputta, as long as the Saṅgha has not reached greatness of gain (lābhaggamahatta), certain states that are the grounds for taints do not appear in the Saṅgha.'
125: 'But when the Saṅgha has reached greatness of gain, then certain states that are the grounds for taints appear in the Saṅgha. Then the Buddha prescribes training rules for the disciples and recites the Pātimokkha for the sake of warding off those states. (4) Sāriputta, as long as the Saṅgha has not reached greatness of learning (bāhusaccamahatta), certain states that are the grounds for taints do not appear in the Saṅgha. But when the Saṅgha has reached greatness of learning, then certain states that are the grounds for taints appear in the Saṅgha. Then the Buddha prescribes training rules for the disciples and recites the Pātimokkha for the sake of warding off those states. (5) Sāriputta, at present the Saṅgha of monks is free from dross, free from blemish, free from impurity, pure, and established in the pith of virtue. Sāriputta, even the least of these five hundred monks is a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), not subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and headed for the three higher paths.' Thus he spoke.
126: (In this context, 'āsava' refers to the suffering and defilements experienced in the present life, such as being accused, killed, or bound by others, as well as the suffering of the lower realms in the next life. Because they are the causes of these taints, various transgressions such as engaging in sexual intercourse, stealing, and killing humans are called 'āsavaṭṭhānīya'—states that are the grounds for taints. In short, transgressions are called āsavaṭṭhānīya states. At the time the Venerable Sāriputta requested the prescription of training rules, these transgressions had not yet appeared at all. If the training rules such as the four Pārājikas had been prescribed prematurely before any transgression occurred, it would not have been possible to avoid backbiting, blame, and face-to-face criticism. How so? If the training rules were prescribed in advance, all necessary rules such as 'If a monk should engage in sexual intercourse...' would have to be prescribed in their entirety. If people were to know these rules before seeing or encountering any actual wrongdoing, others would engage in backbiting, blame, and face-to-face criticism in the following manner: 'Why does the ascetic Gotama bind the Saṅgha with training rules and prescribe Pārājika rules just because they follow him and obey his words? Have these sons of good family not renounced even royal majesty, having come into possession of great wealth and large circles of relatives, to become monks? Do they not live content with mere food and clothing, being extremely respectful of the three trainings and disregarding their own bodies and lives? Among such virtuous ones, who would engage in sexual intercourse, which is a worldly lure? Who would steal another's property? Who would take another's life? Who would make a living by speaking of false spiritual attainments?'
127: 'Even if the four Pārājika rules were not prescribed, has it not already been made clear that sexual intercourse, stealing, and so on are improper and should not be done by the undertaking of the novice's (sāmaṇera) precepts, such as "I undertake the training rule to abstain from taking life"? Thus, they would engage in backbiting, blame, and face-to-face criticism. Furthermore, people would not recognize the power of the Buddha, and the prescribed training rules would be destroyed and would not endure. To use a worldly analogy, an unskilled physician might call for a man who does not yet have an abscess (but will soon develop one) and say, "My dear man, come here. A large abscess will break out on this part of your body and cause you ruinous destruction. Treat that abscess early." If the man replies, "Very well, doctor, please treat it," and entrusts himself, the doctor would cut open the part of the body that does not yet have an abscess, drain the blood (that would have caused the disease), apply medicine, bind it, and wash it with medicinal decoctions. After making the skin and flesh healthy where the abscess was to appear, he might say to the man, "I have treated your large abscess; give me the fee for the medicine and treatment." The man who was treated would say to that unskilled physician, "What is this foolish doctor saying? What disease of mine has this foolish doctor treated? In truth, has this foolish doctor not caused me suffering? Has he not drained my blood?" In this way, he would backbite, blame, and criticize him to his face. He would not recognize the doctor's merit. Similarly, if the Buddha were to prescribe training rules for his disciples before the fault of transgression appeared, he would not be free from backbiting and so on, and people would not recognize the power of the Buddha.'
129:
On the day of the Great Pavāraṇā, the full moon of the month of Thadingyut (Assayuja), after performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, the Buddha called the Venerable Ānanda and said: "Ānanda, it is the custom of the Buddhas that when they have spent the Rains Retreat being invited by hosts, they do not depart for wandering without taking leave of those hosts. Come, Ānanda, let us go; let us take leave of the Brahmin Verañja."

After finishing His meal and letting the afternoon pass, the Buddha, with the Venerable Ānanda as His attendant monk, set out toward the house of the Brahmin Verañja. From the gate of Verañjā city, He made the various large and small roads shine brilliantly with the Buddha-rays.

As soon as the Blessed One stood at the gate of the Brahmin's house, the Brahmin's attendants saw Him and informed the Brahmin. Only then did the Brahmin remember, and rising in haste from his seat, he had a seat prepared that was worthy of noble ones. He went out to welcome the Blessed One and respectfully invited Him, saying, "May the Blessed One come this way."

The Blessed One went as invited by the Brahmin and sat on the prepared seat. (This was the time when Māra withdrew his deception.)

Then the Brahmin Verañja approached the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, and sat in a suitable place free from the six faults. At that time, the Blessed One said to the Brahmin Verañja:
130:
"Brahmin, according to your invitation, we have completed the Rains Retreat. We now take leave of you; we wish to depart for wandering."

Then the Brahmin Verañja said to the Blessed One:

"Master Gotama, it is true. According to my invitation, Master Gotama and the monks have spent the Rains Retreat. However, I have not yet offered any gifts. This is not because I have no gifts to offer, nor because I do not wish to give. Those living in the world have many duties and concerns. Where could I find the opportunity to give? May Master Gotama, for the sake of merit, accept my meal tomorrow together with the community of monks."

(The Brahmin did not know he had been deceived by Māra; he thought, "My forgetfulness was due to the impediments and preoccupations of a householder's life," and thus made this request.)

Then the Blessed One reflected: "If I do not accept the Brahmin's invitation, the Brahmin and all the citizens of Verañjā might think, 'This ascetic Gotama seems angry because he received no offerings throughout the three months of the Rains Retreat; therefore, even though I apologize, he does not accept even a single meal. This ascetic Gotama has no patience; this ascetic Gotama is not an Omniscient One.' Thus, they would increase much demerit. Let not the increase of their demerit—
131:
—come to pass." Out of compassion for them, the Blessed One accepted the Brahmin Verañja's invitation by remaining silent. After accepting, the Blessed One made the Brahmin Verañja realize that "there is no benefit in worrying about the impediments of household life." He then showed him the benefits of both this life and the next with a Dhamma discourse suitable for the occasion, established him in wholesome states, inspired and gladdened him in those wholesome states, and then rose from His seat and departed.

## The Great Offering of the Brahmin Verañja

After the Blessed One had departed, the Brahmin Verañja called together his family and household members and instructed them: "Friends, we invited the Blessed One to stay for the three months of the Rains Retreat, yet we failed to offer even a single meal for a single day. Come, now arrange things so that the offerings that should have been given throughout the three months can be completed in just one day tomorrow."

He then had excellent gifts prepared. When the next morning arrived, he had the place decorated and seats worthy of noble ones prepared. After arranging wonderful offerings of perfumes, incense, and flowers, he sent word to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, it is time; the meal is ready."

Then the Blessed One, surrounded by five hundred monks, went to the house of the Brahmin Verañja and sat on the prepared seats with the community of monks. Then the Brahmin Verañja—
132:
—personally attended to and served the community of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft food until they were satisfied and refused more. When the Blessed One had finished His meal and removed His hand from the bowl, the Brahmin Verañja offered a set of triple robes to the Blessed One. (In that set, each robe was worth a thousand kahāpaṇas. Thus, the Brahmin offered a set of triple robes worth three thousand to the Buddha.) To each and every monk, he offered a pair of robe-cloths. (In each pair, each cloth was worth five hundred. Thus, he offered robe-cloths worth five hundred thousand to the five hundred monks. This much is stated in the Pāḷi text; I shall further mention the explanation from the Commentary.)

Even after giving this much (robes worth five hundred and three thousand), the Brahmin Verañja was still not satisfied. He further offered many rolls of woolen blankets worth seven or eight thousand each, and many rolls of cloth made in the Paṭṭuṇṇa country, to be used for making 'āyogapaṭṭa' (binding straps), 'aṃsabaddha' (shoulder straps), waistbands, water filters, and so on.

He also filled jars and bottles with medicinal oils that had been cooked a hundred or a thousand times, and offered medicinal oil worth a thousand to each and every monk for the purpose of massage. (How could one finish describing so much?) Among the four requisites, there was not a single requisite used by monks that he did not offer. He offered all the requisites of a recluse (samaṇa-parikkhāra).
133:
After making such a great offering, the Brahmin Verañja, together with his wife and children, paid respectful homage and sat down. The Blessed One, wishing to fulfill the Brahmin's desire and compensate him for the loss of the opportunity to enjoy the nectar of the Dhamma during the whole Rains Retreat due to Māra's deception, showered down the rain of the Deathless Dhamma. He showed him the benefits of both this life and the next through a Dhamma discourse, established him in wholesome states, inspired and gladdened him in those wholesome states, and then rose from His seat and departed.

The Brahmin Verañja, together with his wife and children, respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One and the community of monks, saying, "Exalted Buddha, please favor us again another time," and after following to see them off, he returned with tears flowing.

Thereafter, the Blessed One stayed in Verañjā as long as He wished. Departing from Verañjā (among the three circuits of wandering mentioned before), He shortened the route for the Great Circuit (Mahāmaṇḍala). Wishing to lead the community of monks, who were exhausted from the famine throughout the Rains Retreat, along a straight path, He did not enter the cities of Soreyya, Saṅkassa, and Kaṇṇakujja, but went to the Payāga landing. From that landing, He crossed the Ganges River and arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī. In Vārāṇasī, the Blessed One—
134:
—stayed as long as He wished. From there, He gradually wandered toward the country of Vesālī. Upon reaching Vesālī, He stayed at the Kūṭāgārasālā (the Gabled Hall) in the Mahāvana forest.

## Here ends Chapter 30.
135:
## Chapter 31
## The Story of the Venerable Sudinna, the Son of the Kalanda Merchant

At that time, in the village of Kalanda near the city of Vesālī, there lived a merchant's son named Sudinna, of the Kalanda clan. On one occasion, Sudinna, the son of the Kalanda merchant, arrived in the city of Vesālī with many friends to attend to some business.

(The village was named Kalanda because it was abundant with black squirrels. The Kalanda merchant was a wealthy man, possessing forty crores and recognized by the King. The merchant's son Sudinna had come to Vesālī for matters such as trade, collecting debts, and making appointments. Some teachers also say he came with the intention of enjoying the Kattika festival. Indeed, the Blessed One arrived in Vesālī during the waxing half of the month of Kattika. The Kattika festival in Vesālī was very grand, and it was for this festival that the merchant's son Sudinna had come.)

After having his morning meal in Vesālī, Sudinna, the son of the Kalanda merchant, dressed in clean clothes and, carrying flowers and perfumes, saw a great crowd of people going out to see the Buddha and listen to the Dhamma. He asked, "Where are you all going?" When the people replied, "We are going to see the Buddha and listen to the Dhamma," he said, "If that is so, I shall go as well." He followed the crowd and saw the Blessed One, who was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, preaching the Dhamma with a voice like that of the Great Brahmā. Seeing the inspiring presence of the Buddha, and being urged by his past meritorious deeds, he thought, "If only I too could listen to the Dhamma..."
136:
it would be well." However, because the crowd was so large, he could not get close to the Blessed One. He sat down at a suitable place on the edge of the assembly and listened to the Dhamma.

While listening to the Dhamma, having heard even a little of the discourse concerning the three trainings—virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā)—as taught by the Blessed One, a thought arose in the mind of Sudinna, the son of the Kalanda merchant:

"As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living in a household to practice this holy life (the three trainings) in its complete and utter purity, like a polished conch shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?"

Such was his noble thought.

Then, after the Dhamma talk, Sudinna, the son of the Kalanda merchant, followed the departing crowd for a short distance. This was because many of his relatives and friends were among the crowd. He considered that they might say, "You are the only son of your parents; you will never get permission to ordain," and they might even grab him by the arm and take him away. Thinking that this would be an obstacle to his ordination, he walked with the crowd for a while, then pretended he had some personal business to attend to, turned back, and approached the Blessed One.
137:
"Venerable Sir, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living in a household to practice this holy life in its complete and utter purity, like a polished conch shell. Venerable Sir, I wish to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. May the Blessed One please grant me ordination."

At that time, since the ordination of Prince Rāhula, the Blessed One did not grant ordination to a son without the permission of his parents. Therefore, He asked, "Sudinna, have you been permitted by your parents to go forth from the household life into homelessness?" Sudinna replied, "Venerable Sir, I have not yet been permitted by my parents to go forth from the household life into homelessness." The Blessed One then said, "Sudinna, the Buddhas do not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his parents." Sudinna replied, "Venerable Sir, I will see to it that my parents permit me to go forth from the household life into homelessness."

Thereafter, Sudinna, the son of the Kalanda merchant, completed his business in Vesālī and went to his parents in Kalanda village. He said to them:
138:
"Dear mother and father, as I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy for one living in a household to practice this holy life in its complete and utter purity, like a polished conch shell. I wish to shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. Please give me your permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness."

When he had said this, his parents replied to Sudinna:

"Dear Sudinna, you are our only son, very dear and beloved. You have been raised in comfort and nurtured in happiness. Dear Sudinna, you know nothing of suffering. Even when you die, we shall have to be separated from you against our will. How then could we give you permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness while you are still alive?"

When they had refused him, Sudinna asked for permission a second time in the same way, and his parents refused him again. He asked for permission a third time, and for the third time, his parents refused him in the same manner.
139:
Then Sudinna, the son of the Kalanda merchant, realizing, "My parents will (by no means) give me permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness," lay down on the bare ground, saying, "Either my death or my ordination will happen right here." He expressed his great wholesome desire by refusing to eat one meal, two meals, three, four, five, six, and even seven meals (undertaking a hunger strike).

Then his parents said to Sudinna:

"Dear Sudinna, you are our only son, very dear and beloved. You have been raised in comfort and nurtured in happiness. Dear Sudinna, you know nothing of suffering. Even when you die, we shall have to be separated from you against our will. How then could we give you permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness while you are still alive? Dear Sudinna, arise! Eat, drink, and be merry. While eating, drinking, and being merry, enjoy sensual pleasures and perform meritorious deeds. We can (by no means) give you permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness."

When they spoke thus, Sudinna remained silent. When his parents spoke to him a second time and a third time,
140:
Sudinna remained silent just as before.

Then Sudinna's parents, having spoken three times and receiving no response, sent for Sudinna's friends and said, "Friends, your friend Sudinna wants to become a monk. Please dissuade him." Sudinna's friends went to him and spoke to him three times in the same way the parents had. To these friends also, Sudinna gave no reply and remained silent.

Then Sudinna's friends thought: "If this Sudinna dies because he does not get permission to ordain, there will be no benefit at all. However, if he ordains, both his parents and we ourselves will be able to see him whenever we wish. Furthermore, the life of a monk is a very heavy burden. Every day, one must wander for alms carrying an earthen bowl. One must sleep alone and eat only one meal in the morning; such a holy life is very difficult to practice. This Sudinna is a delicate city youth. He will never be able to practice that holy life of sleeping alone and eating only one meal in the morning, and he will certainly return to this house. Come, let us persuade his parents to give him permission." Having consulted and agreed, they went to Sudinna's parents and said:

"Mother and father, this Sudinna is lying on the bare ground, saying that either his death or his ordination will happen right here. If you do not permit him to go forth
141:
from the household life into homelessness, he will meet his death right there where he lies. If you give him permission to ordain, you will still see Sudinna as a monk. If Sudinna, after ordaining, does not find delight in the monkhood, where else would he go but back to his parents' house? He will surely return to this house. Therefore, please give Sudinna permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness."

Then Sudinna's parents said, "Friends, we give Sudinna permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness." Sudinna's friends then went to him and said, "Friend Sudinna, arise! Your parents have given you permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness."

Then Sudinna, with a joyful and uplifted mind, thinking, "My parents have given me permission to ordain," rubbed his limbs with his hands and arose from his place. After regaining his strength for a day or two, he went to the Blessed One, paid homage with his head at the Buddha's feet, sat down at a suitable place, and said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, my parents have given me permission to ordain. May the Blessed One please grant me ordination."

Because Sudinna had made this request, the Blessed One addressed a monk nearby who was a practitioner of the dhutanga of alms-gathering, saying, "Monk, [ordain him]..."
142:
"You, dear son, should give Sudinna the going-forth (pabbajjā) and the full ordination (upasampadā)." That monk who was a practitioner of the alms-food dhutanga replied, "Very well, Bhante," and having accepted Sudinna as his pupil (saddhivihārika), he gave him the going-forth as a novice (sāmaṇera) and then the full ordination as a monk.

Not long after becoming a monk, the Venerable Sudinna undertook and practiced the noble dhutanga austerities for the shaking off of defilements: he was a forest-dweller (āraññika), an alms-food eater (piṇḍapātika), a wearer of rag-robes (paṃsukūlika), and a house-to-house alms-collector (sapadānacārika). He resided near an obscure small village in the Vajjī country.

At that time, there was a famine in the Vajjī country; food was scarce and it was difficult to subsist. The ground was white with bones, and people had to live on food rations distributed by tickets. It was not easy to sustain oneself by wandering for alms with a bowl. Then, the following thought arose in the mind of Venerable Sudinna:

"At present, the Vajjī country is famine-stricken; food is scarce and it is difficult to subsist. The ground is white with bones, and people live on food rations. It is not easy to sustain oneself by wandering for alms. In the city of Vesālī, I have many relatives who are wealthy, possessing great hoards of buried treasure, abundant resources, much gold and silver, many delightful possessions and ornaments, and plenty of wealth and grain. If I were to live supported by my relatives, they would be able to
143:
give gifts and perform meritorious deeds, and the monks would also receive gains. I, too, would not be weary in the search for alms."

After having this thought, Venerable Sudinna set his lodgings in order, took his bowl and robes, and departed for the city of Vesālī. In due course, he arrived at Vesālī and stayed in the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in the Great Wood (Mahāvana) near the city.

The relatives of Venerable Sudinna heard the news: "Sudinna, the son of the Kalandaka merchant, has arrived in Vesālī." Those relatives then sent sixty pots of rice-milk to Venerable Sudinna (each pot contained enough for ten monks). Then, Venerable Sudinna, according to his original intention, gave those sixty pots of food to other monks (six hundred monks). As for himself, being a strict practitioner of the alms-food dhutanga, he adjusted his robes, took his bowl, and entered Kalandagāma for alms. While wandering for alms from house to house in Kalandagāma, he approached the door of his father's (the Kalandaka merchant's) house.

(A special note: The events described from Venerable Sudinna's return from the Vajjī country occurred when he had been a monk for eight years, which was the twentieth year of the Buddha's ministry. However, they are described here to maintain the continuity of Venerable Sudinna's story.)

At that time, a slave woman of Venerable Sudinna's relatives was about to throw away some stale barley bread from the previous night (which was so spoiled that even male slaves, laborers, or oxen could not eat it).
144:
She was coming out to discard it outside the house. Then, Venerable Sudinna said to that slave woman, "Sister (a term used by the Noble Ones), if that bread is to be thrown away, pour it into this bowl of mine."

As the slave woman was pouring the stale barley bread into Venerable Sudinna's bowl, she did not recognize him as her master's son, Sudinna, because they had been separated for eight years. However, she noted the appearance of his hands and feet and the tone of his voice. She then went to Venerable Sudinna's mother and said, "O Lady, please know that your son Sudinna has returned!" Venerable Sudinna's mother said, "O girl, if you are telling the truth, I will release you from slavery."

At that time, Venerable Sudinna was leaning against the wall of an alms-hall in Kalandagāma, eating that stale barley bread with relish.

(In that region, some donors had built alms-halls at their houses. In these halls, seats were prepared, and drinking water, utility water, and sour gruel were provided. Monks would sit and eat their alms-food in these halls after their rounds. If they wished, they would accept the offerings provided by the donors. Therefore, the "base of the wall" where Venerable Sudinna ate the stale barley bread refers to the wall of such an alms-hall built by a donor. Indeed, monks never sit and eat in unseemly or inappropriate places like lonely beggars. — From the Commentary, page 174.)

When Venerable Sudinna's father, the great merchant, was returning from his work, he saw Venerable Sudinna eating the stale barley bread with relish.
145:
He approached Venerable Sudinna and, being unable to bear the sight, said to him:

"How can this be, dear son Sudinna! That you should eat stale barley bread from the previous night! Surely, you should have gone to your own home!"

Venerable Sudinna replied, "O householder, I did go to your house, and it was from your house that I received this stale barley bread." Then, Venerable Sudinna's father, the merchant, took him by the arm and said, "Dear son Sudinna, come, let us go to the house." Because of his affection for his father, Venerable Sudinna was easy to speak to; he followed him to his father's house and sat down on the prepared seat.

Then, Venerable Sudinna's father said to him, "Dear son Sudinna, please eat." Venerable Sudinna replied, "O householder, enough; I have already finished my meal for today." The father then invited him, saying, "Dear son Sudinna, please accept an invitation for tomorrow's meal." Although Venerable Sudinna was a strict practitioner of the alms-food dhutanga, he reflected, "If I do not accept even one meal, my parents and relatives will be very distressed." Out of compassion for his relatives, he accepted the invitation by remaining silent, then rose from his seat and departed.

After that night had passed, Venerable Sudinna's mother had the ground smeared with fresh cow-dung and
146:
had two piles of treasure made, one of gold and one of silver. These piles of treasure were so large that a man standing on one side could not see a man standing on the other side, and vice versa; they were that large and high. She had these piles of treasure covered with mats, had a seat prepared in the middle, and a curtain drawn around. Then she called Venerable Sudinna's former wife and said, "Dear daughter (daughter-in-law), I urge you: wear the ornaments and clothes that my son Sudinna used to find pleasing." The former wife replied to Sudinna's mother, "Very well, mother (lady)."

The next morning, Venerable Sudinna adjusted his robes, took his bowl and robes, and approached his father's house. He sat down on the prepared seat (between the two piles of treasure). The father, the merchant, came to Venerable Sudinna, had the piles of treasure uncovered, and said:

"Dear son Sudinna, this gold and silver is only the wealth that came from your mother's side. It is merely the 'women's wealth' intended for a woman's use (meaning it is only enough for cosmetics and flowers). The wealth from my side is separate, and the wealth inherited from your grandfathers and great-grandfathers is also separate. Dear son Sudinna, it is possible to return to the lay life, to enjoy wealth, and to perform meritorious deeds. Dear son Sudinna, come, return to the lay life, enjoy and consume these riches, and perform meritorious deeds."
147:
When he said this, Venerable Sudinna replied, "Father, I cannot return to the lay life. I do not dare to return to the lay life. I am living the holy life (brahmacariya) with great joy, practicing the three trainings (sikkhā)."

A second time, the father spoke as before, and Venerable Sudinna gave the same reply. When the father spoke for the third time in the same manner, Venerable Sudinna changed his approach and said, "O householder, if you will not be angry, I would like to tell you something." The father, thinking, "My son probably wishes to honor me," joyfully gave permission, saying, "Speak, dear son Sudinna."

Then Venerable Sudinna said to his father:

"O householder, if that is the case, you should have large hemp bags sewn, fill them with gold and silver, load them onto carts, and throw them into the middle of the current of the river Gaṅgā. Why should you do this? Because, O householder, on account of that gold and silver, you will experience fear, trembling, the standing of hair on end, and the burden of guarding it. If it were not there, such dangers as fear would not happen to you. That is why I say this."

When he spoke these firm words of Dhamma, the father was displeased, thinking, "How could my son Sudinna say such a thing?"
148:
## Enticing Again Through the Wife
Then, the wealthy merchant, Sudinna's father, being unable to entice his son back to the lay life by showing him wealth, thought to himself, "There is no bond for men like that of a woman." He then called Sudinna's former wife from his lay life and said, "Dear daughter, I urge you. My son Sudinna loves you and is fond of you. He might listen to your words."

Then, Sudinna's former wife embraced Sudinna's feet and said to him:

"Noble son, for the sake of what kind of celestial nymphs do you practice the holy life? What are those celestial nymphs like?"

(To clarify: At that time, many princes, sons of Brahmins, and sons of wealthy merchants were seen renouncing great wealth to become monks. People who did not understand or know the benefits of monkhood would ask, "Why do these people become monks?" and those who pretended to be knowledgeable would answer, "They become monks because they want to obtain celestial nymphs and heavenly dancers." This talk among the ignorant was widespread. Taking up this talk, Sudinna's former wife asked and spoke as mentioned above.)

"Sister, I do not practice the holy life for the sake of celestial nymphs," Sudinna replied.
149:
When he spoke thus, the former wife thought, "From today onwards, the noble son Sudinna addresses me with the term 'sister.' Now, the noble son Sudinna no longer desires me. Because he no longer desires me, he regards me, his former legal wife and life partner, as a biological sister born from the same womb." Feeling sorrowful and distressed, she fainted and fell right there.

Then, Ven. Sudinna said to his father, the wealthy merchant, "Lay follower, if you wish to offer alms-food, please do so. Do not harass us by showing various kinds of wealth and women. Enticing us by showing wealth and women in this manner is a form of harassment to monks." Thereafter, the parents themselves served and attended to Ven. Sudinna with excellent alms-food and delicacies until he was satisfied and refused more.

## Requesting an Heir
Then, Sudinna's mother said to Ven. Sudinna after he had finished his meal:

"Dear son Sudinna, this family of ours is very wealthy. The buried treasure is abundant. There is much wealth for daily use. There are many delightful ornaments and jewels. There is much grain and goods for trade. Dear son Sudinna, it is possible to return to lay life, enjoy the riches, and perform meritorious deeds. Dear son Sudinna, come! Return to lay life, use and enjoy the riches, and perform merit."
150:
When she said this, Ven. Sudinna replied to his mother just as he had told his father, "Mother, I cannot return to lay life. I do not dare to return to lay life. I am living the holy life (the three trainings) with great delight," thus rejecting her plea. When the mother spoke a second time in the same manner, Ven. Sudinna rejected her again. On the third time, the wealthy merchant's wife, Sudinna's mother, said to him:

"Dear son Sudinna, this family of ours is wealthy. The buried treasure is abundant. There is much wealth for daily use. There is much gold and silver. There are many delightful ornaments and jewels. There is much grain and goods for trade. Dear son Sudinna, if that is the case (if you, dear son, are so delighted in the Dispensation), then at least give us an heir (a seed). Let not the Licchavī princes seize our property as heirless property (crown property)."

Thus, she spoke requesting him to give an heir.

Then Ven. Sudinna thought and reflected, "I alone am the rightful heir to the property of my parents. There is no one else. These parents of mine will follow me constantly to guard the property (as long as I do not give an heir). If they follow me like this, I will not be able to develop and practice the Dhamma of a monk without anxiety. Only when they get an heir will my parents give up. Only then will I be able to strive and develop the Dhamma of a monk in peace." Having thought so, he replied (not knowing it would be an offense):

"Mother, as for this matter of giving an heir,
151:
I can do it."

Then the mother, the wealthy merchant's wife, asked, "Dear son Sudinna, where are you staying now?" When he replied, "Mother, I am staying in the Mahāvana forest," Ven. Sudinna rose from his seat and departed.

Then Ven. Sudinna's mother called his former wife and said, "Dear daughter, let me ask you to obtain a son. When your season comes and you have your monthly period, please tell me." Ven. Sudinna's former wife replied, "Very well, noble lady."

## Giving an Heir
Not long after, when Ven. Sudinna's former wife had her season and her monthly period, she told the mother, "Noble lady, my season has come and I have my monthly period." The mother then said, "Dear daughter, if that is so, wear the clothes and ornaments that my son Sudinna used to like." Ven. Sudinna's former wife replied, "Very well, noble lady," and wore the clothes and ornaments that Ven. Sudinna liked when he was a layman.

Then the mother took Ven. Sudinna's former wife and went to Ven. Sudinna in the Mahāvana forest. She spoke to Ven. Sudinna twice as before, urging him to return to lay life, enjoy the wealth, and perform merit.
152:
Ven. Sudinna also replied as before, saying that he could not return to lay life, did not dare to return to lay life, and was living the holy life (the three trainings) with great delight. On the third time, Ven. Sudinna's mother spoke to him as mentioned before, saying that if he was so delighted in the Dispensation and could not return to lay life, he should give an heir to continue the lineage. Ven. Sudinna said, "Mother, as for this matter of giving an heir, I can do it." He then took his former wife by the arm and entered the Mahāvana forest. Since the first Pārājika rule had not yet been laid down, and not seeing the fault in sexual intercourse, he successfully engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife three times. By that act of intercourse, the former wife became pregnant.

## Eight Ways of Conception
In this regard, women can become pregnant due to these eight causes:
(1) Engaging in sexual intercourse,
(2) Physical contact,
(3) Inserting a cloth or rag (with semen),
(4) Swallowing semen,
(5) Touching the navel,
(6) Seeing a man's form,
(7) Hearing his voice,
(8) Smelling his scent.
Among these:
153:
(1) Becoming pregnant through sexual intercourse is well-known. (Ven. Sudinna's former wife became pregnant through this first cause.)

(2) Some women, when their season comes, have such intense lustful desire that they may become pregnant by delighting in pulling a man's hand, pulling his hair, or touching other major or minor limbs. This is becoming pregnant through physical contact.

(3) During the time of the Buddha, Ven. Udāyī stared lustfully at the private parts of his former wife, who was a nun, and consequently discharged semen. He then asked his former wife to wash the robe that was stained with the semen. That nun swallowed a portion of the semen with her mouth and inserted another portion into her private parts using a cloth. By doing so, that nun became pregnant. This is becoming pregnant through inserting a cloth.

(4) In the Five Hundred and Fifty Jātakas, the doe who was the mother of the hermit Migasiṅga came to the place where the father hermit had urinated during her season and swallowed the urine along with the semen. By doing so, the doe became pregnant and gave birth to the youth Migasiṅga. This is becoming pregnant through swallowing semen.
154:
(5) In the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka, Sakka, the king of devas, foreseeing that the parents of the Bodhisatta Suvaṇṇasāma would go blind, wished to give them a son. He asked the wise hermit Dukūla, "Is sexual intercourse permissible for hermits?" The wise hermit Dukūla replied, "Whether it is permissible or not, we do not desire this practice of sexual intercourse, which is why we have become hermits." Sakka then said, "If that is so, when this hermitess Pārikā has her season, please touch the navel of the hermitess Pārikā with your thumb, O wise Dukūla." The wise hermit Dukūla did as Sakka had instructed. By that act, the hermitess Pārikā became pregnant and gave birth to the Bodhisatta youth Suvaṇṇasāma. This is becoming pregnant through touching the navel.

In the same way, when the merchant's daughter Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā had her season, the Bodhisatta hermit Mātaṅga touched her navel, and she became pregnant and gave birth to the youth Maṇḍavya. The mother of King Caṇḍapajjota, during her season, felt delight when a centipede crawled over her navel and became pregnant, giving birth to Prince Caṇḍapajjota.

(6) In this world, some women, when their season comes and they do not have union with a man, may become pregnant by staring intensely at a man, like royal concubines staying within the palace, through the power of lustful desire. (In the island of Sri Lanka...
155:
(A certain palace maiden once experienced this). In this way, conception occurs through seeing the male form.

(7) Among cranes, there is not a single male. These female cranes conceive when they hear the sound of thunder during their fertile season. Hens also sometimes conceive when many of them hear the crowing of a single rooster. Similarly, cows sometimes conceive when many of them hear the bellowing of a single bull. In this way, conception occurs through hearing the male sound.

(8) Even cows sometimes conceive by smelling the scent of a bull. In this way, conception occurs through smelling the male scent.

These eight ways of obtaining conception should be specially noted. (From the Vinaya Pārājika Commentary, Vol. 1, p. 179).

## The Great Uproar and Blame of Devas and Brahmās

When Venerable Sudinna committed sexual intercourse with his former wife (there is no such thing as a secret place for one who commits an unwholesome deed in this world. Indeed, first, the perpetrator knows of that evil unwholesome act. Then, the guardian devas and forest devas know; thereafter, other devas and Brahmās know successively. Therefore), the earth-bound devas (bhumma devas) residing in the Mahāvana forest saw that transgression and—
156:
—shouted and proclaimed so loudly that it was heard by the higher and higher devas and Brahmās successively:

“Friends, the Saṅgha of monks was (formerly) free from the thief of immorality, free from the fault of immorality. But now, Sudinna, the son of the Kalanda merchant, has brought about the theft of immorality, has brought about the fault of immorality!”

Hearing the voice of the earth-bound devas, the sky-bound devas—the Cātumahārājikā devas, Tāvatiṃsa devas, Yāma devas, Tusita devas, Nimmānarati devas, Paranimmitavasavatti devas, and the Brahmās—likewise shouted and proclaimed successively. In this manner, within that moment, the tumultuous sound of blame and reproach spread up to the Brahma realm.

Thereafter, Venerable Sudinna’s former wife reached the end of her pregnancy and gave birth to a son. At that time, Venerable Sudinna’s friends named the child Bījaka (because it was well-known that the grandmother had requested, “Sudinna, dear son, if that is so, please give us the seed (bīja),” not allowing any other name to be given). They named Venerable Sudinna’s former wife Bījakamātā (Bījaka’s mother). They named Venerable Sudinna Bījakapitā (Bījaka’s father).

After seven or eight years had passed, the mother and son, Bījaka and Bījakamātā, left the lay life and entered the monkhood. Having become a monk and a nun respectively, and having found good teachers—
157:
—and noble friends (kalyāṇamitta), they attained the Fruit of Arahantship.

Thus, (later on), the monkhood of the mother and son became a fruitful monkhood. As for the father (Venerable Sudinna), he lived on, being severely oppressed by remorse.

(In this matter, the Commentary states: “Pitā pana vippaṭisārābhibhūto vihāsi = But the father (Venerable Sudinna) lived on, being severely oppressed by remorse.” Because of this explanation, it should be understood that for Venerable Sudinna, there was no attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship in that very life. From Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Vol. 2, p. 15).

In the Commentary, although the section where Sudinna, the son of the Kalanda merchant, went to listen to the Dhamma (Vinaya Commentary, Vol. 1, p. 168) describes him as “babbakulaputtassa = a noble son capable of attaining the Path and Fruit,” the teachers say that even though he was one endowed with past merit for attaining the Path and Fruit, because he committed a wrong act (sexual intercourse with his former wife), he was severely oppressed by remorse based on that evil deed, which became an obstacle to the Path and Fruit, just as it was for King Ajātasattu.

Here, a question may arise: Can an obstacle to the Path and Fruit occur for those endowed with past merit even in the presence of the Blessed One during His lifetime?

The answer is: Yes, it can. Specifically, it is not that the obstacle occurs because of the Buddhas. Indeed, the Buddhas always strive appropriately for others to attain the Path and Fruit as they exert effort. Therefore, because of the Buddhas, an obstacle to the Path and Fruit cannot occur for those endowed with past merit.
158:
In fact, the obstacle to the Path and Fruit occurs due to these reasons: (1) deficiency in performance/effort, and (2) association with bad friends.

Regarding those two, (1) deficiency in performance/effort is further divided into two types: (a) the lack of effort by the preacher that is conducive to the Path and Fruit, and (b) the lack of practice by the person endowed with past merit that is conducive to the Path and Fruit.

Among them, (a) deficiency in performance on the part of the preacher can only happen with disciples (sāvakas); it cannot happen with the Buddhas. To elaborate: (In the Dhanañjāni Sutta of the Brāhmaṇa Vagga, Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, Majjhima Nikāya, it is mentioned that the Venerable Sāriputta preached the four Brahma-vihāras, which lead to the Brahma realm, to the Brahmin Dhanañjāni when he was near death. Thus, when the Brahmin died, he reached the Brahma realm. For details, one should refer to that Sutta in the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka). If the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, had known the Brahmin Dhanañjāni’s underlying disposition (āsayānusaya) and preached accordingly, the Brahmin would have become a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). But since it was not so, he did not become an Ariya. Thus, the failure to attain the Path and Fruit occurred due to deficiency in performance on the part of the preacher.

Regarding (b) deficiency in performance on the part of the person endowed with past merit: (In the Kandaraka Sutta of the Gahapati Vagga, Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, Majjhima Nikāya, it is mentioned that a wanderer named Kandaraka and a man named Pessa, the son of an elephant-driver, came to the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One preached to Pessa about the four types of persons, such as the 'self-tormentor' (attantapa). After the Blessed One had preached only the brief outline (uddesa mātika), and before He could preach the detailed exposition (niddesa padabhājanī), Pessa, the son of the elephant-driver, left, being satisfied with just that much.
159:
If Pessa had listened until the detailed exposition (niddesa padabhājanī) was finished, he would have become a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). But because he left after hearing only the brief outline, he only gained two benefits: faith in the Saṅgha and a new method of establishing mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). For details, one should refer to that Sutta in the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka). If Pessa, the son of the elephant-driver, had waited just a moment while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One until the Blessed One had finished analyzing and preaching the four types of persons in detail, he would have become a Stream-enterer. But since he did not wait that long, he did not become a Stream-enterer. Thus, the failure to attain the Path and Fruit occurred due to deficiency in performance on the part of the person endowed with past merit.

(2) Regarding the occurrence of an obstacle to the Path and Fruit due to association with bad friends: If King Ajātasattu had not committed matricide by following the words of the bad friend (pāpamitta) Devadatta, he would have become a Stream-enterer on the day he listened to the Sāmaññaphala Sutta preached by the Buddha. But because he committed the wrong of killing his father by following the words of the bad friend Devadatta, he did not become an Ariya Stream-enterer. Thus, the obstacle to the Path and Fruit occurred due to association with bad friends.

Now, regarding Venerable Sudinna, it should be understood that the obstacle to the Path and Fruit occurred because he associated with bad friends. If Venerable Sudinna had not followed his parents' words and had not committed sexual intercourse with his former wife, there would have been no obstacle to the Path and Fruit due to remorse based on that act. But because he followed his parents' words and committed sexual intercourse with his former wife, he suffered remorse based on that act. Because he was severely oppressed by that remorse, the obstacle of not attaining the Path and Fruit occurred. (From Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Vol. 2, pp. 1-2).
160:
## Venerable Sudinna’s Remorse and Regret

At that time, remorse and regret arose in Venerable Sudinna’s mind, thinking: “Alas, I have not attained the virtues such as jhāna! Alas, the life of a monk is not well-attained by me! I have poorly attained this Dispensation! I have not well-attained this Dispensation! (The reason being) that although I have ordained in this well-proclaimed Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation, I was unable to practice the noble holy life of the three trainings with complete purity until the end of my life.” Due to that remorse and regret, Venerable Sudinna became thinner day by day; his skin became thin and dry, his appearance deteriorated, and he became pale like a withered leaf. With a body where veins stood out like a spread-out net, and with a mind that was constantly decaying and shrinking within, he lived in distress, severely oppressed by remorse, being unhappy in both body and mind.

Then, Venerable Sudinna’s fellow monks said to him: “Friend Sudinna, formerly you were handsome, with full faculties, a clear and bright face, and a very clear complexion. But now, you have become thinner day by day; your skin is thin and dry, your appearance has deteriorated, and you are pale like a withered leaf. With a body where veins stand out like a spread-out net, and with a mind that is constantly decaying and shrinking within, you live in distress, severely oppressed by remorse, being unhappy in both body and mind. Why is it so, friend Sudinna? Are you—”
161:
"Are you, friend, living the holy life of the threefold training dissatisfied in the Dispensation?" When they spoke thus, the Venerable Sudinna replied:
"Friends, I am not living the holy life of the threefold training dissatisfied in the Dispensation. However, I have committed a wrong deed; I have indulged in sexual intercourse with my former wife. Friends, within my mind, there is remorse and unhappiness, thinking: 'Alas, I have not attained the distinctions such as jhāna; alas, I have not gained the state of a monk; alas, I have poorly attained the Dispensation; I have not well attained the Dispensation, (because) having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation, I was unable to practice the holy life of the threefold training perfectly and purely for the rest of my life.'"

Then the monk friends of the Venerable Sudinna said to him:
"Friend Sudinna, since you were unable to practice the holy life of the threefold training perfectly and purely for the rest of your life after having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation, it is indeed fitting for you to have remorse and unhappiness.

Friend Sudinna, has not the Blessed One in many ways taught the Dhamma for the fading of passion, and not for the sake of passion?"
162:
"Has He not taught the Dhamma for detachment, and not for the sake of attachment? Has He not taught the Dhamma for the sake of non-clinging, and not for the sake of clinging with craving and views? Friend Sudinna, while the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma for the fading of passion, you strive for the sake of passion. While He has taught the Dhamma for detachment, you strive for attachment. While He has taught the Dhamma for non-clinging, you strive for clinging with craving and views.

Friend, has not the Blessed One in many ways taught the Dhamma for the fading of passion, for the subduing of pride, for the removal of the thirst of defilements, for the uprooting of the attachment of craving, for the cutting off of the cycle of rebirth, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for the cessation of craving, and for the cooling of defilements?

Friend, has not the Blessed One in many ways taught the abandonment of sensual pleasures? Has He not taught the full understanding of the perceptions of sensual pleasures? Has He not taught the removal of the thirst of craving for sensual pleasures? Has He not taught the cutting off of thoughts related to sensual pleasures (kāma-vitakka)?"
163:
"Has He not taught the cooling of the heat and fever of sensual pleasures?

Friend, this bad deed you have committed does not lead to the faith of the unfaithful, nor to the increase of faith in the faithful. Friend, indeed, this bad deed you have committed leads only to the lack of faith in the unfaithful and to the turning away of some who already have faith."

Having rebuked him in many ways, they reported this matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on this account, had the Saṅgha of monks assembled and questioned the Venerable Sudinna: "Sudinna, is it true that you indulged in sexual intercourse with your former wife?" When the Venerable Sudinna replied, "It is true, Blessed One," the Blessed One rebuked him in this manner:

"Worthless man (mogha purisa), who has not attained the Path or Fruition and has failed in his purpose! (This act you have committed) is not suitable for monks, not becoming, not proper, not the act of a recluse, not allowable, and should not be done. Worthless man, why were you unable to practice the holy life of the threefold training perfectly and purely for the rest of your life after having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation?"
164:
"Worthless man, has not the Buddha in many ways taught the Dhamma for the fading of passion, and not for the sake of passion? Has He not taught the Dhamma for detachment, and not for attachment? Has He not taught the Dhamma for non-clinging, and not for clinging with craving and views? Worthless man, while I have taught the Dhamma for the fading of passion, you strive for passion. While I have taught the Dhamma for detachment, you strive for attachment. While I have taught the Dhamma for non-clinging, you strive for clinging with craving and views.

Worthless man, has not the Buddha in many ways taught the Dhamma for the fading of passion, for the subduing of pride, for the removal of the thirst of defilements, for the uprooting of the attachment of craving, for the cutting off of the cycle of rebirth, for the destruction of craving, for dispassion, for the cessation of craving, and for the cooling of defilements?

Worthless man, has not the Buddha in many ways taught the abandonment of sensual pleasures? Has He not taught the full understanding of the perceptions of sensual pleasures? Has He not taught the removal of the thirst of craving for sensual pleasures? Has He not taught the cutting off of thoughts related to..."
165:
"...sensual pleasures (kāma-vitakka)? Has He not taught the cooling of the heat and fever of sensual pleasures?

Worthless man, it would be better for you to put your male organ into the mouth of a snake with swift and fierce poison than to put your male organ into the female organ.

Worthless man, it would be better for you to put your male organ into the mouth of a cobra than to put your male organ into the female organ.

Worthless man, it would be better for you to put your male organ into a heap of glowing coals, burning, blazing, and radiant, than to put your male organ into the female organ.

Why is that? Worthless man, because of putting the male organ into the mouth of that snake or into that heap of glowing coals, one might reach death or deadly suffering; however, because of that, one would not, after the breaking up of the body, after death, reach the four states of woe: hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the host of asuras. Worthless man, because of putting one's male organ into this female organ..."
166:
"...one would, after the breaking up of the body, after death, fall into the four states of woe: hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the host of asuras.

Worthless man, despite this, you have indulged in sexual intercourse, which is not the practice of the virtuous, but the practice of common villagers, which is coarse, which ends in washing (unbecoming to see), which is to be done only in private, and which is performed by pairs of men and women. Worthless man, you are the first-doer of many unwholesome states, the pioneer and the leader.

Worthless man, this bad deed you have committed does not lead to the faith of the unfaithful, nor to the increase of faith in the faithful. Worthless man, indeed, this bad deed you have committed leads only to the lack of faith in the unfaithful and to the turning away of some who already have faith."

Thus He rebuked him.

Then the Blessed One, after rebuking the Venerable Sudinna in many ways, spoke in dispraise of being difficult to support, difficult to maintain, of great desires, of discontent, of fondness for company, and of laziness. In many ways, He spoke in praise of being easy to support..."
167:
"...easy to maintain, of fewness of wishes, of contentment, of effacement of defilements, of shaking off defilements, of being inspiring, of destroying defilements, and of the exertion of energy. Then, having given a Dhamma talk to the monks suitable and appropriate to that incident, He addressed the monks:

## 10 Reasons for Laying Down the Vinaya

"Monks, if that is so, I shall lay down a training rule for the monks based on these ten reasons:
(1) For the excellence of the Saṅgha,
(2) For the comfort of the Saṅgha,
(3) For the restraint of the ill-behaved,
(4) For the ease of well-behaved monks,
(5) For the restraint of the special sufferings (taints) in the present life,
(6) For the warding off of the special sufferings (taints) in the future life,
(7) For the faith of the unfaithful,
(8) For the increase of faith in the faithful,
(9) For the long endurance of the three True Dhammas (the three Dispensations),
(10) For the support of the Vinaya rules.

Based on these ten excellent reasons, I shall lay down the training rule for the monks."
169:
In Sāvatthī, five hundred lay followers (upāsakas) entrusted all their household and family responsibilities to their wives and children, and traveled together as a group to listen to the Buddha's teachings. Among these five hundred lay followers, some were Stream-enterers (Sotāpannas), some were Once-returners (Sakadāgāmis), and some were Non-returners (Anāgāmis); not a single one among them was an ordinary worldling (puthujjana). Those who invited the Buddha also included these five hundred lay followers in the invitation list for the Saṅgha.

The five hundred young servants who attended to these five hundred lay followers by providing hot and cold water lived on the leftovers of their masters. After eating the morning leftovers, these five hundred scavengers had no other work; after waking from sleep, they went to the Aciravatī River and, shouting and clamoring so loudly that it echoed along the riverbank, they engaged in wrestling and boxing. Their masters, the five hundred noble (ariya) lay followers, remained silent without any shouting at all, dwelling in solitude and entering the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).

The Blessed One, hearing the loud shouting of those five hundred scavengers, asked the Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, what is this loud shouting I hear?" The Venerable Ānanda replied, "Magnificent Buddha, it is the sound of the five hundred scavengers."

Then the Blessed One said, "Ānanda, it is not only now that these five hundred scavengers eat leftovers and shout loudly;
170:
in the past also, they shouted loudly. And it is not only now that these five hundred lay followers dwell in peace; in the past also, they dwelt in peace." At the request of the Venerable Ānanda, he related a story of the past:

Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers and, upon reaching maturity, became a wise minister who advised the King on what is beneficial and what is not.

One day, King Brahmadatta heard news of a rebellion in the border regions. He had five hundred Sindh horses fully harnessed and, accompanied by the fourfold army, went to the border, pacified the region, and returned to Bārāṇasī. He then commanded his attendants, "Friends, the Sindh horses are exhausted. Give them a drink made from fresh grapes (mudara-rasa) to nourish them." The attendants did as the King commanded and gave the five hundred Sindh horses the fresh grape juice.

After drinking the fragrant and flavorful grape juice, the five hundred Sindh horses went to their stables and remained calm in their respective places.

After preparing the grape juice for the five hundred Sindh horses, a large amount of flavorless grape pulp remained. The attendants asked the King,
171:
"What shall we do with this grape pulp?" The King commanded, "Friends, knead that grape pulp with water, strain it through coarse cloth woven from hemp, and give it to the donkeys that carry the provisions for the Sindh horses." The attendants did as commanded and gave the strained dregs-water to the pack-donkeys.

After drinking the strained dregs-water, the pack-donkeys became intoxicated and, braying loudly, began jumping and running about playfully in the palace courtyard. The King opened the palace window and, looking out at the courtyard, asked the wise minister Bodhisatta who was standing nearby, "O wise one, look! These five hundred donkeys, having drunk the strained dregs-water, have become intoxicated and are braying and jumping about playfully. But the Sindh horses, born of the Sindh breed, having drunk the fragrant and flavorful fresh grape juice, remain silent and do not behave in a frivolous or boisterous manner, but stay calm. What is the reason for this?" Desiring to ask this, he recited the first verse:

Having drunk the dregs-water (vālodakaṃ), weak in flavor and inferior,
Intoxication arises in the donkeys.
But having drunk this superior juice,
Intoxication does not arise in the Sindh horses. (1)

(O wise one). Apparasaṃ = having little flavor. Nihīnaṃ = inferior. Vālodakaṃ = the grape pulp water strained through coarse hemp cloth. Pitvā = having drunk. Gadrabhānaṃ = of the donkeys. Mado = intoxication.
172:
Jāyati = arises. Paṇītaṃ = excellent. Imaṃ ca rasaṃ = this fresh grape juice. Pitvāna = although having drunk. Sindhavānaṃ = of the Sindh horses. Mado = intoxication. Na sañjāyati = does not arise. (Kāraṇam = the root cause of this happening. Kinnu kho = what is it?)

Thus he asked by reciting this first verse.

Then the Bodhisatta, wishing to explain the reason to the King, recited the second verse:

Having drunk even a little, one of low birth
Becomes intoxicated by it, O King.
But one of noble birth, accustomed to bearing burdens,
Does not become intoxicated even after drinking the finest juice. (2)

Janinda = O noble King. Yo = that donkey which. Nihīnajacco = is of low birth. Tena = because of being of low birth. Phuṭṭho = being affected and oppressed. So = that donkey. Appaṃ = even a little insignificant strained dregs-water. Pivitvāna = having drunk. Mazzati = becomes intoxicated. Kulahmī = in a noble family. Jāto-jātattā = because of being born. Dhorayhasīlī ca = the Sindh horse, who is accustomed to putting forth effort to bear the burdens of the state. Aggarasaṃ = the sweet and delicious juice that first comes from the fresh grapes. Pivitvā = although having drunk. Na mazzati = does not become intoxicated.
173:
Thus he answered by reciting this second verse. (The meaning is: Donkeys, being of low birth, become intoxicated even by drinking strained dregs-water of little flavor. Sindh horses, being of noble birth, do not become arrogant or intoxicated even after drinking the finest juice.)

Having heard the Bodhisatta's words, the King had the donkeys driven out of the palace courtyard. Thereafter, the King, established in the Bodhisatta's advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) and passed away according to his kamma.

The Blessed One, having delivered this Dhamma teaching of the Vālodaka Jātaka, identified the birth: "At that time, the five hundred donkeys became the five hundred scavengers of today. The five hundred Sindh horses became the five hundred noble lay followers. The King of Bārāṇasī became Ānanda. And the wise minister was I, the Buddha."

Thus ends the account of the Vālodaka Jātaka.

**********

## On Account of Venerable Rāhula
## The Preaching of the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta

While the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī, his son, the novice (sāmaṇera) Rāhula, had reached the age of eighteen and had completed eleven years as a novice.
174:
One day, in the morning, the Blessed One entered Sāvatthī for alms. The Venerable Rāhula followed closely behind the Blessed One, step for step.

As the Blessed One and the Venerable Rāhula walked one behind the other, the Blessed One appeared as magnificent as a great elephant in rut emerging from a forest to reach a pleasant plain, like an elephant emerging from a grove of fully blooming sal trees. The Venerable Rāhula appeared as magnificent as a young elephant following closely behind the great bull elephant. In the evening, the Blessed One was as magnificent as a king of lions emerging from a ruby cave to seek food. The Venerable Rāhula was as magnificent as a young lion following closely behind the king of lions. The Blessed One was as magnificent as a king of tigers emerging from a forest as beautiful as a mountain of emerald. The Venerable Rāhula was as magnificent as a young tiger following closely behind the king of tigers.

The Blessed One was as magnificent as a king of Garuḍas emerging from a forest of silk-cotton trees, and the Venerable Rāhula was like a young Garuḍa following closely behind the king of Garuḍas. The Blessed One was as magnificent as a king of golden swans (haṃsa) flying into the sky from Mount Cittakūṭa, and the Venerable Rāhula was like a young golden swan flying closely behind the king of golden swans. The Blessed One was like
175:
a great golden boat entering the Chaddanta Lake, and the Venerable Rāhula was like a small golden boat following steadily behind the great golden boat. The Blessed One was as magnificent as a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) traveling through the sky by the power of the Wheel-treasure, and the Venerable Rāhula was like the eldest son (the heir-apparent) traveling together with the Universal Monarch. The Blessed One was as magnificent as the moon, the lord of stars, moving through a cloudless sky, and the Venerable Rāhula was like the morning star (Venus) shining brightly and following closely behind the moon.

The Blessed One was born into the pure Okkāka dynasty of the Mahāsammata lineage; so too was the Venerable Rāhula. The Blessed One was born into the noble Khattiya caste, as pure as milk poured into a conch shell; so too was the Venerable Rāhula. The Blessed One renounced royal splendor to become a monk; so too did the Venerable Rāhula. The Blessed One's body was adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa), as captivating to the heart as a jeweled ceremonial archway well-planted at the gate of a celestial city, or like a great coral tree (pāricchattaka) in full bloom; so too was the body of the Venerable Rāhula.

Thus, both were born of royal lineage, fulfilled by special past aspirations, and endowed with the refinement of kings who have become monks, their complexions shining like liquid gold...
176:
The Buddha, endowed with the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa), and his son, the noble Rāhula, also a Great Man, walked together on the same path. Like two moons or two suns following one another, they were exceedingly magnificent, their splendor surpassing that of Sakka, Suyama, Santusita, Sunimmita, Vasavatti, and Mahābrahmā. 

As they walked, Venerable Rāhula followed closely behind the Buddha, step for step. Looking at the Buddha from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair, he beheld the Buddha's glory and thought: 

"My father, the Buddha, possesses a physical body (rūpakāya) adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. Surrounded by rays of light, he is like a golden mountain amidst falling gold dust, or a golden mountain encircled by lightning, or a golden portal adorned with seven kinds of jewels. Though clad in a reddish rag-robe, he is like a golden mountain wrapped in red blankets, or a golden portal decorated with coral, or a sacred golden stupa honored with vermilion powder, or a golden sacrificial pillar anointed with lac. He is as beautiful as the full moon rising suddenly from behind red clouds."
177:
"The splendor of his noble body, perfected by the power of the thirty perfections (pāramī), is truly wondrous beyond words." 

Thus he thought. Then, looking at himself, he thought: "I, too, am beautiful. If the Buddha were to become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) ruling the four continents, he would surely grant me the position of the eldest son and heir (orasa-pariṇāyaka). If that were so, the island of Jambudīpa would be even more magnificent." Thus, based on his own person, he gave rise to household-related craving (gehassita-taṇhā). 

The Buddha, walking ahead, reflected: "Now, the physical form (attabhāva) of my son Rāhula has become full of skin, flesh, and blood. It is a time when the mind wanders incessantly toward various attractive forms and objects. What kind of thoughts is Rāhula dwelling on as he passes the time?" At that very moment of reflection, the Buddha clearly saw Rāhula's mental process associated with household-related craving and greed, as clearly as seeing a fish in clear water or a reflection in a clean mirror. 

Seeing this, he thought: "This novice Rāhula, though my son and following behind me, is giving rise to household-related greed based on his own body, thinking 'I am beautiful, my appearance is pure and clear.' He has descended where there is no landing place..."
178:
"...wandering on a wrong path and dwelling on improper objects. Like a traveler who has lost his way, he is going where he should not. If this greed and defilement (lobha-kilesa) currently arising in Rāhula is allowed to continue and grow within him, it will not allow him to see the welfare of himself and others as it truly is. It would cause him to be reborn in the four lower realms—hell, the animal kingdom, the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), and the asura—and in the narrow confines of a mother's womb. Thus, it would cast him into the cycle of Saṃsāra, which has no known beginning. 

Indeed—this greed brings about harm. Greed destroys the wholesome mind. Based on this greed, a great and terrifying danger can arise within the mental continuum. People in general do not see this. 

One who is lustful cannot clearly see what is beneficial or not. When a being is overwhelmed by greed, there is only great darkness. 

Just as one should not neglect for even a moment a great ship laden with jewels into which water is seeping through cracks, but should quickly plug the leaks, so too should I not neglect this novice Rāhula. I shall suppress this defilement before it destroys the treasures of virtue (sīla) and other qualities arising in Rāhula's continuum." Thus he made his decision. 

Especially in such a situation, the Buddhas perform what is called the 'Elephant Look' (Nāgavilokana)..."
179:
...turning the whole body to look. Thus, like a golden statue turned by a mechanical device, the Buddha turned his entire body, stood still, and said to Venerable Rāhula: 

"Rāhula, any kind of form (rūpa) whatsoever—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self (attā)'." 

Then Venerable Rāhula asked: "Exalted Buddha, should only form be viewed in this way? O Buddha of auspicious speech, should only form be viewed in this way?" 

The Buddha replied: "Rāhula, form should be viewed in this way; feeling (vedanā) should be viewed in this way; perception (saññā) should be viewed in this way; mental formations (saṅkhāra) should be viewed in this way; and consciousness (viññāṇa) should be viewed in this way." 

(In this context, the reason Venerable Rāhula asked "Should only form be viewed in this way?" is as follows: 

As soon as he heard the teaching that all eleven types of form should be seen as "This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self..."
180:
...not my self,' a thought arose in his mind: 'The Buddha has taught that all form should be viewed with wisdom. How should the other four aggregates, such as feeling, be viewed and practiced? It must be that they should be viewed and practiced just like the aggregate of form.' This was the arising of his 'skill in methods' (nayakusala-ñāṇa), and based on that, he asked the question. 

Indeed, Venerable Rāhula was one who possessed 'skill in methods' (the wisdom to see a fathom when shown a span). If one thing was taught as 'this should not be done,' he could infer by hundreds and thousands of methods that 'this also should not be done, and this also should not be done.' If one thing was taught as 'this should be done,' he could similarly infer by hundreds and thousands of methods that 'this also should be done, and this also should be done.' 

Furthermore, Venerable Rāhula was one who dearly loved the three trainings (sikkhā). Every morning, in the precinct of the Gandhakuṭī where the Buddha resided, he would scatter a handful of sand and say: "Today, may I receive from the Buddha and from my preceptor, Venerable Sāriputta, as many words of advice and instruction as there are grains of sand." (It was because he was skilled in methods and loved the three trainings that he asked this question, wishing to practice fully.)
