When he asked thus, the Buddha, because all five aggregates (pañca-kkhandha) must be viewed in the same way, answered: "Rāhula, form should be viewed in this way; feeling should be viewed in this way;"
181:
"perception should be viewed in this way; mental formations should be viewed in this way; and consciousness should be viewed in this way." 

Upon hearing the Buddha's answer, Venerable Rāhula thought: 

"The Buddha, having known the greed and craving associated with my body, did not give me advice indirectly by saying 'A monk should not think such thoughts.' Nor did he send another monk as a messenger to say 'Monk, go and tell him not to think such thoughts again.' Instead, he stood facing me and gave me direct instruction, just as one might catch a thief by the hair along with the stolen goods. Such direct instruction from a Buddha is hard to obtain even in an aeon (kappa) or an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya). Having received such direct instruction from the Buddha, who among the wise would go into the village for alms today?" 

After this thought, Venerable Rāhula abandoned the matter of alms-food. From the very spot where he received the direct instruction, he turned back (instead of following further) and sat down at the foot of a tree. 

Although the Buddha saw Venerable Rāhula turning back, he did not say, "Rāhula, do not turn back yet; it is time for you to go on your alms-round."
182:
For the reason was: a thought arose in the mind of the Blessed One, "For today, let Rāhula consume the food of the Deathless, which is the meditation on mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati)."

## Duties of Venerable Sāriputta
The duties and routines of Venerable Sāriputta were of one kind when he lived alone, and of another kind when he lived together with the Blessed One.

To elaborate: When the two Chief Disciples lived in solitude (ekacārī), they would sweep the monastery grounds early in the morning, perform their personal ablutions, and then sit quietly after entering into meditative attainments. Afterwards, they would enter for alms according to their own wish. However, when they lived together with the Blessed One, the two Chief Disciples did not act in this way. To clarify: when living together, the Blessed One would enter for alms first, surrounded by the assembly of monks. After the Blessed One had entered for alms, the Venerable Sāriputta would leave his own dwelling and reflect, "In a place where many monks reside, there are those who can conduct themselves in a way that inspires faith, and there are those who cannot." He would then go to various monastery precincts, sweeping areas that had not yet been swept. If there was refuse that had not been discarded, he would discard it. If there was no drinking water pot where one should be, he would place one there. He would visit the sick (gilāna) and ask, "Friends, what kind of food should I bring for you?"
183:
"What kind of food do you require?" he would ask. He would go to the young monks who had not yet spent a rainy season (vassa) and admonish them, saying, "Friends, find delight in the Dispensation; do not be lazy. The Dispensation of the Buddha has the essence of practice (paṭipatti)." Having performed all that should be done within the monastery, he would enter for alms after everyone else.

For example, when a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), the ruler of the four continents, wishes to go to a certain place, he sets out first, surrounded by a fourfold army. The eldest legitimate son, the Counselor-gem (Pariṇāyaka-ratana), then manages the military units and sets out afterwards. Similarly, the Blessed One, who is the King of the True Dhamma (Saddhamma-cakkavatti) who turns the Wheel of Dhamma, sets out first surrounded by the assembly of monks. The Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati), who is like the eldest legitimate son and Counselor-gem, performs these aforementioned duties and enters for alms after all the monks.

On that day, Venerable Sāriputta completed the aforementioned duties within the Jetavana monastery and was entering for alms after all the monks when he saw Venerable Rāhula sitting at the foot of a tree, having crossed his legs, keeping his body erect, and establishing mindfulness directed towards his meditation subject. He said:

"Rāhula, develop the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati). Rāhula, when mindfulness of breathing is developed,
184:
and practiced frequently, it is of great fruit and great benefit."

Thus, he spoke words of encouragement to develop the meditation on mindfulness of breathing.

(In this matter, one might ask: Why did Venerable Sāriputta encourage Venerable Rāhula to develop mindfulness of breathing?

The answer is: He gave this encouragement because that posture of Venerable Rāhula was highly suitable for the meditation on mindfulness of breathing. To elaborate: Venerable Sāriputta, without considering the fact that the Blessed One had already taught the meditation on form (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) to Rāhula, thought, "Mindfulness of breathing is most suitable for the way Rāhula is sitting, motionless and composed," and thus he spoke in this manner.)

Regarding the statement "when mindfulness of breathing is developed and practiced, it is of great fruit and great benefit," the greatness of the benefit is as follows:

A monk who develops mindfulness of breathing can reach the Fruit of Arahantship in a single sitting. If he cannot reach it then, he can become a 'Same-Headed' Arahant (samasisī) at the time of death. If he cannot do that, he can be reborn in the celestial realm and reach Arahantship after hearing the Dhamma from a Dhamma-preaching deity. If he cannot reach it then, he can become a Paccekabuddha during a time when no Buddha has appeared. If he cannot do that, he can become an Arahant with swift intuition (khippābhiññā), like Venerable Bāhiya Dārucīriya, during the time of future Buddhas. Thus, mindfulness of breathing is of great fruit and great benefit.

Seeing such great benefits, Venerable Sāriputta encouraged his resident pupil (saddhivihārika),
185:
Venerable Rāhula, in the meditation of mindfulness of breathing.

In this way, the Blessed One taught the meditation on form, and Venerable Sāriputta taught the meditation on mindfulness of breathing, and then they both departed. Venerable Rāhula was left behind at the monastery.

Although the Blessed One knew that Rāhula was left behind, he did not personally bring food for him, nor did he have it sent through Venerable Ānanda, nor did he inform lay devotees such as King Pasenadi of Kosala or the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. (Indeed, if they had only known, they would have sent pots of alms-food carried on poles.)

Just like the Blessed One, Venerable Sāriputta also did nothing. On that day, Venerable Rāhula missed his meal, receiving no alms-food. Even though he did not get to eat, not even a single thought arose in Rāhula's mind such as: "The Blessed One knows I am left at the monastery, yet he did not personally bring the alms-food he received, nor did he send it through someone else, nor did he inform the people. My preceptor (upajjhāya) also knows I am left behind, yet he likewise did nothing." Because of that non-sending of food, how could he ever give rise to low pride or high pride (disparagement or conceit)? He certainly did not. In fact, he spent the morning and the afternoon focusing on the meditation on form taught by the Blessed One,
186:
reflecting without interruption, like one vigorously stirring a fire: "Form is surely impermanent because of this reason and that reason. Form is surely suffering because of this reason and that reason. Form is surely foul because of this reason and that reason. Form is surely non-self because of this reason and that reason."

In the evening, he thought: "My noble preceptor has admonished me to 'develop mindfulness of breathing.' I shall follow and practice the advice and instruction of that noble preceptor. Indeed, one who does not follow the advice and instruction of teachers and preceptors is called a person difficult to admonish (dubbaca). For me, if Rāhula were to be one difficult to admonish, there is no harsher oppression than the reproach of fellow monks (sabrahmacārī) for not even following the preceptor's instruction." Having thus reflected, and wishing to ask for the method of developing mindfulness of breathing, Venerable Rāhula rose from his seclusion in the evening, approached the Blessed One, paid respect most reverently, and sat in a place free from the six faults. He then asked the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, how is mindfulness of breathing developed, and how is it practiced frequently, so that it is of great fruit and great benefit?"

Then, the Blessed One, to Venerable Rāhula:
187:
(1)
(a) The twenty parts of the Earth element (pathavī-dhātu),
(b) The twelve parts of the Water element (āpo-dhātu),
(c) The four parts of the Fire element (tejo-dhātu),
(d) The six parts of the Air element (vāyo-dhātu) = thus, the meditation on the Great Primary Elements (mahābhūta-rūpa),
(e) And the meditation on the Space element (ākāsa-dhātu), which is derived form (upādā-rūpa);

(2)
The characteristic of equanimity (tādibhāva), which describes developing meditation similar to earth, water, fire, air, and space;

(3) Loving-kindness (mettā) meditation,
(4) Compassion (karuṇā) meditation,
(5) Appreciative joy (muditā) meditation,
(6) Equanimity (upekkhā) meditation,
(7) Foulness (asubha) meditation,
(8) The meditation on the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) (encouraging these by showing their benefits);

(9)
And the detailed method of developing mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), which was Venerable Rāhula's original question, along with its benefits—

All these were taught in detail. (The details of this teaching should be noted from page 91 of the Burmese translation of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa Pāḷi.)
189:
(5) Furthermore, the Buddha reflected: "Children are fond of speaking untruths. They say 'We have seen' even when they have not seen, and 'We have not seen' even when they have seen. Therefore, I shall give an exhortation to Rāhula in advance." Having thus reflected, for the sake of making it easy to understand and remember through visual observation, He first presented four similes of the water bowl, then two similes of the great war elephant, and one simile of the mirror—making a total of seven similes in succession—and preached the Ambalaṭṭhikā-rāhulovāda Sutta (found in the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa Pāḷi, Bhikkhu Vagga, page 77).

Moreover, He preached the Rāhula Sutta (found in the Sutta Nipāta, Khuddaka Nikāya, Vol 1, page 328) to prevent the arising of craving (taṇhā) that clings to the four requisites, to abandon sensual desire (chandarāga) and craving for the five cords of sensual pleasure, and to show the great benefit of associating with good friends. (This Rāhula Sutta is also called the Abhiṇha-rāhulovāda Sutta).

(2) He preached the Rāhula Saṃyutta (found in Saṃyutta Nikāya, Vol 1, page 439, etc.) to show that one should not have craving or desire for the three realms of existence wherever one may be.

(3) He preached the Mahā-rāhulovāda Sutta (found in Majjhima Paṇṇāsa Pāḷi, page 83) to show that one should not harbor house-dependent sensual desire (gehassita-chandarāga) based on the physical body, thinking, 'I am beautiful, my appearance is very pure and clear.'
190:
(4) Later, during the Buddha's 14th vassa (at a time when the Venerable Rāhula had just become a monk but had not yet completed a vassa), He preached the Cūḷa-rāhulovāda Sutta (found in Upari Paṇṇāsa Pāḷi, page 324) for the sake of his attainment of the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala).

Among these, the time of preaching the Rāhula Sutta (= Abhiṇha-rāhulovāda Sutta) cannot be specifically determined. Indeed, the Buddha preached this Rāhula Sutta (= Abhiṇha-rāhulovāda Sutta) as a constant and repeated instruction.

(2) The Rāhula Saṃyutta was preached as occasion permitted during the period from when the Venerable Rāhula was a seven-year-old novice (sāmaṇera) until he was a young monk who had not yet completed a vassa.

(3) The Mahā-rāhulovāda Sutta was preached when the Venerable Rāhula was eighteen years of age.

(4) The Cūḷa-rāhulovāda Sutta was preached at the time when the Venerable Rāhula had just become a monk and had not yet completed a vassa.

(1-5) The Sāmaṇerapañhā and the Ambalaṭṭhikā-rāhulovāda Sutta were preached when the Venerable Rāhula was a seven-year-old novice.

Among those discourses, (1) the Rāhula Sutta (= Abhiṇha-rāhulovāda Sutta) was preached for constant instruction. (2) The Rāhula Saṃyutta was preached for the Venerable Rāhula to acquire the essence of insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa). (3) The Mahā-rāhulovāda Sutta was preached to dispel house-dependent sensual desire (gehassita-chandarāga—the craving and greed dependent on the 'house' of the five cords of sensual pleasure). (4) The Cūḷa-rāhulovāda Sutta was preached when the Venerable Rāhula's fifteen qualities that ripen towards liberation (vimuttiparipācanīya-dhamma)...
191:
...were matured (at the time he had just become a monk and had not yet completed a vassa), for the sake of attaining the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala). Referring to this point, the Venerable Rāhula, wishing to praise the virtues of the Buddha in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, spoke these words:

Kikīva bījaṃ rakkheyya, camarī vālamuttamaṃ.
Nipako sīlasampanno, mamaṃ rakkhi tathāgato.

Just as the kikī bird protects its egg; just as the camarī yak protects its most excellent tail; even so, the Tathāgata, who is possessed of mature and sharp wisdom and endowed with incomparable virtue, has protected me, His beloved son Rāhula, until I reached the Fruit of Arahatship, like the protection of the kikī bird and the camarī yak.

(1) The Sāmaṇerapañhā was preached to abandon improper speech. (5) The Ambalaṭṭhikā-rāhulovāda Sutta was preached so that he would not tell a lie even knowingly.

In this way, the Buddha preached many Dhamma discourses on account of the Venerable Rāhula.

## Here ends Chapter 31.
192:
## Chapter 32
## Observing the Thirteenth Vassa at Cālika Mountain

In this way, while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī during the rainy season, He liberated and exhorted humans, devas, and brahmas through Dhamma discourses such as the Mahā-rāhulovāda Sutta. While traveling on a journey by stages, He arrived at the city of Cālika and was residing at the great monastery on Cālika Mountain near that city, observing the thirteenth (terasama) vassa.

(In this regard: Except for the gate area of that city, the city was surrounded by shimmering, moving quagmires. Because the city was built in the midst of such shimmering quagmires, to the eyes of those looking at the city from afar, the great city appeared to be shimmering and quivering. Therefore, the name of that city was called Cālika.

Near that city of Cālika, there was a mountain. That mountain was also entirely white, and to the eyes of those looking at it on the Uposatha day of the waning moon, it appeared to be shimmering and quivering. Thus, the name of the mountain was also famous as Cālika Mountain.

On that Cālika Mountain, many lay devotees (dāyakas and dāyikās) among the city dwellers built and offered a great monastery for the Buddha. It means that the Buddha, during the time of the thirteenth vassa, made that city of Cālika His alms-resort village and was residing in the great monastery on Cālika Mountain.)
194:
Because it had trees that were not sparse and lush green leaves, it was delightful. Because it had thick shade and the ground was excellent, it was very pleasant. It was a large mango grove that could make the hearts of those who entered it joyful and happy. Upon seeing it, the thought arose in the mind of Venerable Meghiya:

"This mango grove is delightful. It is very pleasant and can make the heart joyful and happy. This mango grove is indeed suitable for a son of good family who wishes to strive in the Dhamma. If the Buddha grants me permission, I shall return to this mango grove to strive in the Dhamma."

(As for that mango grove, it was a place where the Venerable Meghiya, in many previous lives, had been a king for five hundred consecutive lives and had enjoyed royal luxury. Therefore, as soon as he saw that grove, the desire to live there arose within the Venerable Meghiya.)

Then, the Venerable Meghiya approached the Buddha, paid homage, and sat down. He reported in detail everything from his entry for alms-food until the thought of returning to the mango grove to strive in the Dhamma. He then made a request: "Exalted Buddha, if the Lord Buddha grants me permission, I wish to go to that mango grove to strive in the Dhamma."
195:
When he had spoken thus, the Buddha forbade the Venerable Meghiya, saying: "Wait, Meghiya. Since I am alone now, wait until some other monk arrives."

(In this regard: The Buddha, having heard the Venerable Meghiya's request, investigated and reflected, and knowing that "the wisdom of this monk Meghiya has not yet reached maturity," He wished to refuse him and thus said, "Wait, Meghiya." As for the words "Since I am alone now," He reflected: "If I speak thus, even if this monk Meghiya goes to that mango grove and his meditation work is not fulfilled, he will return to Me without any hesitation or fear, out of affection for Me." Having thus reflected, He spoke to soften the mind of the Venerable Meghiya.)

A second time, the Venerable Meghiya addressed the Buddha: "Exalted Buddha, for the Lord Buddha, the sixteenfold functions of the Path (magga-kicca) have been completed, so there is nothing further to be done. There is no need to further develop what has already been done. But for me, Exalted Buddha, there is still much to be done (the sixteenfold functions of the Path). There is still a need to further develop what has been done. If the Lord Buddha grants me permission, I wish to go to that mango grove to strive in the Dhamma." A second time, the Buddha said to the Venerable Meghiya:
196:
“Wait, Meghiya. I am currently alone. Wait until at least one other monk arrives,” the Buddha replied, forbidding him as before.

For the third time, the Venerable Meghiya appealed to the Blessed One: “Exalted Buddha, for the Blessed One, the sixteen tasks of the Path (Magga) have been completed, so there is nothing further to be done, nor is there anything already done that needs to be further developed. But for me, Exalted Buddha, there are still many things to be done (the sixteen tasks of the Path), and there are things already done that must be further developed. Therefore, if the Blessed One would permit me, I wish to go to that mango grove to practice meditation.” (On this occasion, the Blessed One did not forbid him, saying: “Meghiya, how can We speak words of prohibition to one who says ‘to practice meditation’? Meghiya, you know the time for going; let it be according to your will.”)

Then the Venerable Meghiya rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and after performing the respectful circumambulation, went to the mango grove. Entering the grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree to spend the day in meditation.

## The Arising of Unwholesome Thoughts
## in the Mind of Venerable Meghiya

The stone slab at the foot of the tree where the Venerable Meghiya was now sitting was the very place where, in a continuous succession of five hundred past lives, he had sat as a sovereign king enjoying himself in the garden, surrounded by various...
197:
...dancers and enjoying great delight. 

As he sat there, from the moment he took his seat, it was as if his state as a monk vanished from the Venerable Meghiya’s mind. Taking on the appearance of a king, he felt as if he were sitting on a royal throne fit only for the noble, under a white parasol, surrounded by many dancers (like a dream).

When this occurred, for the Venerable Meghiya who was delighting in that royal luxury, unwholesome thoughts of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka) associated with the objects of pleasure arose incessantly.

At that moment, the Venerable Meghiya also saw (as if in a dream) two thieves who had been captured with their stolen goods being brought before him. Out of the intent to order the execution of one of those two thieves, thoughts of ill-will (byāpāda-vitakka) arose incessantly. Out of the intent to order the imprisonment of the other, thoughts of cruelty (vihiṃsā-vitakka) arose incessantly.

In this way, just as a mass of creepers entwines a tree, or as bees swarm around a honey-gatherer, the three types of unwholesome thoughts—sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty—surrounded the Venerable Meghiya so that he could not escape.

Then, in the mind of Venerable Meghiya, the thought arose: “Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how extraordinary! We...
198:
...have truly gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith (saddhā). Yet, despite this, we are being beset by these three evil, unwholesome thoughts: sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty.”

Thus, as the Venerable Meghiya was surrounded by these three unwholesome thoughts, he was unable to perform the work suitable for meditation. Realizing, “Surely the Blessed One, who sees the long-term, foresaw this and forbade me,” he regained mindfulness and thought, “I shall report these matters to the Blessed One.” He rose from his seat and went to the monastery on Cālika Mountain where the Blessed One was staying. Having paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, he sat in a suitable place and said to the Blessed One:

“Exalted Buddha, while I was staying in that mango grove, these three evil, unwholesome thoughts—sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty—arose in me frequently. Exalted Buddha, (when those three unwholesome thoughts arose frequently), the thought occurred to me: ‘Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how extraordinary! We have truly gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith. Yet, despite this, we are being beset by these three evil...
199:
...unwholesome thoughts: sensual thoughts, thoughts of ill-will, and thoughts of cruelty.’” Thus he reported what had happened to him.

(In this regard, one might ask: Why did the Blessed One permit the Venerable Meghiya to go to that mango grove? The answer is: The Blessed One foresaw that “Even if not permitted, this monk Meghiya will certainly go, leaving Me alone. (If I continue to forbid him), a distorted and mistaken thought might arise in Meghiya’s mind: ‘The Blessed One probably does not want to let me go because He only desires my service.’ Such a mistaken thought would lead to the lack of welfare and to suffering for this monk Meghiya for a long time.” Therefore, He permitted him to go.)

When the Venerable Meghiya had thus reported his experience and was sitting there, the Blessed One, wishing to preach a suitable Dhamma to him, spoke the words (found in the Pali): “Aparippakkāya Meghiya cetovimuttiyā pañca dhammā paripākāya saṃvattanti = Meghiya, five things lead to the maturing of the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) that is not yet mature,” and so forth. (The full Burmese translation of this Dhamma teaching can be found starting from page 107 of the Udāna Pali, Burmese Translation. In this Chronicle of the Buddhas, only the essential meaning will be presented):

“Dear Meghiya, these five things lead to the maturing of the liberation of mind (cetovimutti) that is not yet mature. What are the five?
201:
Then the Blessed One, knowing this matter, at that time uttered these two verses of Udāna (inspired utterances):

(1) Khuddā vitakkā sukhumā vitakkā,
Anugatā manaso uppilāvā.
Ete avidvā manaso vitakke,
Hurā huraṃ dhāvati bhantacitto.

Lowly thoughts and subtle thoughts follow the mind and cause it to be uplifted (agitated). One who does not understand these mental thoughts wanders from one object to another with an unsteady mind.

(2) Ete ca vidvā manaso vitakke,
Ātāpiyo saṃvaratī satīmā.
Anugate manaso uppilāve,
Asesamete pajahāsi buddho.

Knowing these mental thoughts, the noble disciple (suta-buddha) who is energetic and mindful restrains the thoughts that follow the mind and cause it to be uplifted. That noble disciple, knowing the Four Noble Truths, abandons those sensual thoughts and others without remainder.

(The above is an excerpt from the Udāna Commentary.)

(I shall now continue with the explanation from the Dhammapada Commentary):
202:
The Blessed One said to the Venerable Meghiya, who had returned to His presence because he was unable to practice meditation in that mango grove due to being beset by the three types of thoughts:

“Dear Meghiya, you have done a heavy thing by leaving Me alone, even though I appealed to you, saying: ‘Wait, Meghiya. I am currently alone. Wait until at least one other monk arrives.’ It is not proper for one called a monk to be a follower of the mind’s desires in this way. This mind is very light and swift; it is only proper to make that mind follow one’s own will.”

Having said this, He preached these two verses of Dhamma:

Phandanaṃ capalaṃ cittaṃ, dūrakkhaṃ dunnivārayaṃ.
Ujuṃ karoti medhāvī, usukārova tejanaṃ.

(Meghiya = Dear Meghiya). Usukārova = Just as a skilled fletcher. Tejanaṃ = takes a crooked arrow that is not smooth and. Ujuṃ karoti iva = straightens it by heating it in fire and drawing it according to his wish. (Evaṃ = In the same way). Medhāvī = the wise person who has penetrative insight. Phandanaṃ = [straightens] the mind which trembles among the six objects such as forms and sounds. Capalaṃ = which is fickle and does not remain steady on a single object. Dūrakkhaṃ = which is difficult to guard as it will not stay on a suitable object. Dunnivārayaṃ = which [wanders] among unsuitable objects...
203:
...which is difficult to restrain. Cittaṃ: The mind, which is diverse and wondrous. Ujuṃ karoti: One can make it straight, guiding it according to one's will, just as an arrow is straightened by heat, through the twofold effort of body and mind.

Vārijo va thale khitto, okamokatā ubbhato.
Paripphandatidaṃ cittaṃ, māradheyyaṃ pahātave.

(Meghiya: Dear Meghiya...) Okamokato: From its home, the water, which is its dwelling place. Ubbhato: Being drawn out. Thale: On dry land. Khitto: Being thrown. Vārijo: A fish born in water. Paripphandati iva: Just as it quivers and thrashes about without staying still. (Evaṃ: In the same way.) Idaṃ cittaṃ: This consciousness, which delights in pursuing the five sense-objects. Māradheyyaṃ: The internal enemy, the Mara of defilements. Pahātave: In order to abandon and cut off through the abandonment of eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). (Ubbhataṃ: Being drawn out from the vast waters of the realm of sensual pleasures. Khittaṃ: When placed upon the dry land of the practice of Vipassanā meditation.) Paripphandati: Being separated from the waters of the five sense-objects, it quivers and thrashes as if dying under the heat of the fourfold effort of intense exertion.

At the conclusion of the teaching of these verses, the Venerable Meghiya was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala); many others also became Stream-enterers and so forth.

The account of the teaching given to the Venerable Meghiya ends here.
204:
## The Fourteenth Vassa in Sāvatthī
## Observing the Vassa

As previously mentioned, the Buddha spent the thirteenth (terasama) Vassa at the great monastery on Cālikā Mountain near the city of Cālikā. After liberating those beings worthy of liberation through various teachings such as the Meghiya Sutta, he remained at that monastery on Cālikā Mountain as long as there were beings to be liberated. After that, he wandered through the regions, providing the deathless medicine of the cool Dhamma to humans, devas, and brahmas. Upon reaching Sāvatthī, he observed the fourteenth (cuddasama) Vassa at the Jetavana Monastery.

## The Teaching of the Story of Sāriputta Thera

At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta Thera, together with five hundred disciple monks, went to a large monastery in a country district to observe the Vassa. The people of that district, having seen the Venerable Sāriputta, made a formal promise to offer many rainy-season robes (vassika-sāṭika).

When the Vassa ended and the Pavāraṇā ceremony was completed, the Venerable Sāriputta wished to go and pay respects to the Buddha even before all the rainy-season robes had arrived. He addressed the monks, saying, "Friends, if the lay donors bring the rainy-season robes for the junior monks and novices, please accept them and send them to me; or else, store them well and send word to me."
205:
Having given these instructions, he departed for the presence of the Buddha.

When he arrived at Sāvatthī, many monks whispered among themselves, saying, "Friends, it seems that craving and greed (taṇhā-lobha) still exist within the Venerable Sāriputta. Because such craving and greed still exist, he gave instructions to the remaining monks, saying, 'If the lay donors bring and offer rainy-season robes, send the robes for my disciples to me, or else store them well and send word to me,' before coming to the Buddha."

The Buddha came to where those monks were and asked, "Monks, for what purpose are you gathered here now?" When the monks replied that they were gathered to discuss such a matter, the Buddha said, "Monks, in the heart of my eldest son Sāriputta, there is not even a trace of craving or greed. In truth, he gave those instructions out of consideration, thinking, 'May the lay donors not lose the opportunity for merit, and may the junior monks and novices not lose the gain of robes obtained rightfully.'" He then spoke this verse:

Āsā yassa na vijjanti, asmiṃ loke paramhi ca.
Nirāsāsaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.

(Bhikkhave: O monks...) Yassa: In which Arahant who has exhausted the taints (āsavas). Asmiṃ loke: In this present world. Paramhi ca: And in the next world. Āsā: Desires and longings. Na vijjanti: Do not exist, having been cut off and destroyed at the root by the abandonment of eradication through the fourfold Path-knowledge. Nirāsāsaṃ: One who is clearly liberated from the 108 types of craving. Visaṃyuttaṃ: One who is detached from all defilements. Taṃ: That Arahant who has exhausted the taints. Ahaṃ: I, the Teacher of the three worlds. Brāhmaṇaṃ: Call a true Brahmin. Brūmi: I declare so according to the true nature of things.
206:
At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

This is the story of Sāriputta Thera (from Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 2, 26-Brāhmaṇavagga, page 421).

Just as the monks had the misconception that "craving and greed seem to exist" in the Venerable Sāriputta, a similar misconception had also occurred regarding the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. The circumstances of the story were similar to those of the Sāriputta Thera story. Specifically, in the story of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Buddha preached that there was absolutely no craving in the heart of the Venerable Moggallāna, as in the previous case, and then spoke this verse:

Yassālayā na vijjanti, aññāya akathaṃkathī.
Amatogadhamanuppattaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.
207:
(Bhikkhave: O monks...) Yassa: In which Arahant who has exhausted the taints. Ālayā: Attachments of craving. Na vijjanti: Do not exist, having been cut off and destroyed at the root by the abandonment of eradication through the fourfold Path-knowledge. Aññāya: Having clearly seen and understood the Three Jewels, the Three Trainings, and the cycle of Dependent Origination from the beginning of Saṃsāra according to reality. Akathaṃkathī: One who is free from doubts and hesitations. Amatogadhaṃ: Having entered the city of Nibbāna, the Deathless, through wisdom. Anuppattaṃ: One who has reached the Fruit of Arahantship in due course. Taṃ: That Arahant who has exhausted the taints. Ahaṃ: I, the Teacher of the three worlds. Brāhmaṇaṃ: Call a true Brahmin. Brūmi: I declare so according to the true nature of things.

At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. (From Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 2, page 422).

## Preaching the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta
## Establishing Venerable Rāhula in the Fruit of Arahantship

As mentioned, the Buddha observed the fourteenth Vassa in Sāvatthī and was still residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. At that time, the Venerable Rāhula had reached the age of twenty and was a newly ordained monk who had not yet spent a Vassa as a bhikkhu.

Then one day, at dawn, while the Buddha was surveying the world of beings, the following thought arose in his mind:
208:
"In Rāhula's heart, the fifteen qualities that ripen liberation (vimuttiparipācanīya-dhammā) have matured. It would be well if I were to further guide and discipline Rāhula so that he reaches the Path and Fruit of Arahantship."

(In this context, the fifteen qualities that ripen liberation are:)
(1) Avoiding those who lack faith,
(2) Associating with those who have faith,
(3) Reflecting on Suttas that inspire confidence (three regarding Faith);
(4) Avoiding those who are lazy,
(5) Associating with those who are energetic and diligent,
(6) Reflecting on Suttas related to Right Effort (three regarding Energy);
(7) Avoiding those who are unmindful,
(8) Associating with those who are mindful,
(9) Reflecting on Suttas related to the Foundations of Mindfulness (three regarding Mindfulness);
(10) Avoiding those who lack concentration,
(11) Associating with those who have concentration,
(12) Reflecting on Suttas related to Jhanas and Liberations (three regarding Concentration);
(13) Avoiding those who are unwise,
(14) Associating with those who are wise,
(15) Reflecting on profound Suttas (three regarding Wisdom).
These are the fifteen.
209:
Furthermore, there are the five faculties (indriya): faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; the five perceptions leading to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya-saññā): perception of impermanence, perception of suffering, perception of non-self, perception of abandonment, and perception of dispassion; and the five factors mentioned in the Meghiya Sutta (Udāna): having good friends, being endowed with virtue, hearing and reflecting much on the ten subjects of talk (kathāvatthu), having exerted energy, and being endowed with wisdom regarding the rise and fall of phenomena. In this way, there are fifteen qualities that ripen liberation.

After this thought arose, the Buddha entered Sāvatthī for alms in the morning. After finishing his meal and departing from the alms-round, he addressed the Venerable Rāhula, saying, "Rāhula, take your sitting cloth (nisīdana). Let us go to the Andhavana forest for the day's abiding." The Venerable Rāhula replied, "Very well, Bhante," and taking his sitting cloth, he followed closely behind the Buddha.

At that time, thousands of devas and brahmas (who had made aspirations together with the future Venerable Rāhula when he was the Naga King Pālita in the presence of the Buddha Padumuttara a hundred thousand aeons ago) thought, "Today, the Buddha will further guide and discipline the Venerable Rāhula so that he reaches the Path and Fruit of Arahantship," and they followed the Buddha.

(In this context: The thousands of devas and brahmas who had made aspirations together a hundred thousand aeons ago were waiting, thinking, "When will the Buddha guide and discipline the Venerable Rāhula to reach the Fruit of Arahantship?")
210:
210
Because the faculties (indriya) such as faith (saddhā) and others had matured, when the Blessed One reflected, as previously mentioned, "Today, I shall discipline and lead Rāhula to the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship," thousands of devas and brahmas, who shared the same aspiration and had been waiting for the very moment the Blessed One would so reflect, perceived that the conditions were now met and gathered together in the single forest of Andhavana.

## About Andhavana Forest
In this regard, I shall first present a summary of the account of Andhavana forest near the city of Sāvatthī, as extracted from the commentary on the Vammika Sutta in the second volume of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa Aṭṭhakathā (pages 28, 29):

That forest was well-known as "Andhavana" (the Blind Men's Forest) during the eras of both the Blessed One Kassapa and our own Blessed One. To elaborate: the bodily relics (sarīrika-dhātu) of Blessed Ones with short lifespans do not remain as a single mass; according to their resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), they disperse into many fragments. For this reason, our Blessed One (whose lifespan was short), reflecting, "I shall not remain for long; because my lifespan is so short, only a few beings will have the opportunity to behold me. Those who do not behold me will be many. May those beings who do not behold me take my relics, worship them in various places, and thereby attain the heavenly realms (sugati)," made a resolution near the time of His Parinibbāna: "May my bodily relics be dispersed into many fragments." (Thus, the relics of our Blessed One were indeed fragmented).

However, the bodily relics of Blessed Ones with long lifespans remain as a single mass, like a block of gold. Therefore, (during the era of the twenty-thousand-year lifespan,
211:
211
when the Blessed One Kassapa appeared), the bodily relics of the Blessed One Kassapa, being a Buddha with a long lifespan, remained as a single mass. At that time, the people gathered and consulted: "The relics remain as a single mass; they cannot be divided. What shall we do?" They agreed to build a single solid stupa (cetiya). They unanimously decided to build a stupa with a height and circumference of one yojana. When they further consulted regarding the bricks and mortar, they decided to use gold bricks worth one hundred thousand for the outer layers, gold bricks worth fifty thousand for the inner layers, cinnabar (manosilā) and orpiment (haritāla) powder for the earth/mortar, and oil for the water. They then divided the four gates into four shares: (1) The King took responsibility for one gate; (2) Prince Pathavindhara took responsibility for another gate; (3) The General (Senāpati), acting as the leader of the royal officials, took responsibility for another gate; (4) The Great Merchant (Setthi), acting as the leader of the citizens, took responsibility for the remaining gate.

Among these four groups, (1) the King, (2) Prince Pathavindhara, and (3) the General were wealthy, so they brought out their own gold bullion and began work at their respective gates.

As for the gate for which the Great Merchant was the leader, the work was delayed because the citizens were not wealthy. At that time, an Anāgāmī lay devotee named Yasorata, who was a bearer of the Tipiṭaka, learned of the delay. He organized five hundred carts and traveled throughout the countryside, saying:

"O citizens and people! The Blessed One Kassapa stood firm like a great golden mountain for twenty thousand years and has now entered Parinibbāna. For that Blessed One,
212:
212
a jewel stupa of one yojana in size is being built to enshrine His single mass of bodily relics. Please donate whatever you can—gold, silver, the seven kinds of jewels, cinnabar, or orpiment."

Thus, he exhorted and proclaimed, establishing them in meritorious deeds. The citizens and people donated gold, silver, and so on according to their ability. Those who could not afford gold or silver also participated by donating rice, oil, and other provisions.

The Anāgāmī lay devotee Yasorata sent the rice, oil, beans, and other items as provisions for the workers. He had the remaining donations exchanged for gold and sent that as well. In this manner, he traveled throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa to collect and send donations.

When the great stupa was completed, the leaders at the construction site sent a message: "The work of building the great stupa is finished. We wish for the Great Teacher to come and worship the stupa." Yasorata, the Anāgāmī lay devotee, sent back a message: "I have exhorted and established the entire island of Jambudīpa in this meritorious deed. Complete the great stupa using only what is already there." The two messages crossed paths on the road. Notably, the message from the construction site reached the Great Teacher before his own message reached them.

After reading the message, the Great Teacher thought, "I shall worship the great stupa," and set out alone toward the site of the stupa. Along the way, five hundred robbers were creating unrest within a forest. When some of those robbers saw the Great Teacher, they said to the others, "This Great Teacher has collected gold and silver from the entire island of Jambudīpa. Great pots of gold are rolling and rolling
213:
213
toward us!" and they captured the Great Teacher.

## The Fate of Lay Devotee Yasorata
Then, when the Great Teacher asked, "Friends, why have you captured me?" the robbers spoke overbearingly, saying, "Great Teacher, you have collected all the gold and silver from the entire island of Jambudīpa. You must give us a portion of that gold and silver."

Then the Great Teacher said, "Friends, do you not know? The Blessed One Kassapa has entered Parinibbāna. A great jewel stupa of one yojana in size is being built to enshrine the bodily relics of that Blessed One. I have exhorted the citizens to perform this meritorious deed for that great stupa. It was not for myself. All the donations I received from various places have already been sent to the site where the stupa is being built. As for me, I have no wealth other than the clothes I am wearing, not even a grain's weight."

When he said this, some robbers said, "What this Great Teacher says is exactly the truth. Therefore, release the Great Teacher." However, other robbers argued against releasing him, saying, "This Great Teacher is one honored by kings and ministers. If he sees any of us in the middle of the city, he will tell the king and his ministers about this, and we will come to ruin and destruction."

Then the Anāgāmī lay devotee Yasorata said, "Friends, I will not do as you say." (He said this out of compassion for those robbers, not because of any attachment to his own life). Then, as the robbers disputed—some saying he should be kept captive and others saying he should be released—those who held the view that
214:
214
he should be kept captive were in the majority, and they eventually killed the Great Teacher.

At that very moment, because of the crime they had committed by going so far as to kill a great Anāgāmī noble one of such high virtue, the eyes of those robbers went blind, just as the flame of a lamp is extinguished. When those five hundred robbers wept and lamented, groping about and crying, "Friends, where are my eyes? Where are my eyes?" some robbers who had relatives were taken home by them. Other robbers, being without relatives or refuge, had to live miserably in huts roofed with leaves at the foot of trees within that forest.

People coming to the forest, out of compassion, gave those blind robbers rice, packets of food, and other provisions. When people who went to that forest to collect firewood or green leaves returned and were asked, "Friends, where did you go?" they would reply, "We went to the forest of the blind (Andhavana)."

Thus, even during the eras of the two Buddhas' dispensations (sāsanā), that forest became famous as "Andhavana" (the Blind Men's Forest). Specifically, during the era of the Blessed One Kassapa's dispensation, that forest was situated near a large, abandoned district. In the time of our Blessed One, however, that forest was located near the city of Sāvatthī, behind the Jetavana monastery, serving as a great meditation center for sons of good family who desired seclusion from the five strands of sensual pleasure. This is the account of Andhavana, the Blind Men's Forest.

Then the Blessed One entered Andhavana and sat down at the foot of a certain tree on a seat prepared by Venerable Rāhula. Venerable Rāhula, having respectfully

paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down at a respectful distance. To Venerable Rāhula, who was seated at a respectful distance, the Blessed One spoke these words:

## The Discourse on the Six Groups of Six

(This Dhamma teaching, which was asked and taught in three rounds to clearly reveal the points of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, is called the "Teparivaṭṭadhammadesanā").

(Conclusion) "Dear Rāhula, seeing thus, the well-taught disciple of the Buddha becomes disenchanted with the sensitive material called the eye; becomes disenchanted with various forms; becomes disenchanted with eye-consciousness; becomes disenchanted with eye-contact; and becomes disenchanted with the four mental aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that arise with eye-contact as a condition. He becomes disenchanted with the sensitive material called the ear; becomes disenchanted with various sounds; (Pe-yāla). He becomes disenchanted with the sensitive material called the nose; becomes disenchanted with various smells. He becomes disenchanted with the sensitive material called the tongue; becomes disenchanted with various tastes. He becomes disenchanted with the sensitive material called the body; becomes disenchanted with various tangibles. He becomes disenchanted with the mental faculty called the mind; becomes disenchanted with mental objects; becomes disenchanted with mind-consciousness; becomes disenchanted with mind-contact; and becomes disenchanted with the four mental aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that arise with mind-contact as a condition. Being disenchanted,
221:
he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated from the defilements. When he is liberated, the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) arises: 'I am liberated from defilements.' He understands through successive knowledge of reviewing: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done (the task of the Path) has been done, there is no more to be done for the sake of the Path.'"

When this Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta was taught by the Blessed One, Venerable Rāhula was established in the fruit of Arahantship. Many thousands of those devas and brahmas also respectively attained the stages of Stream-entry, Once-returning, Non-returning, or Arahantship according to their perfections (pāramīs).

## Points for Reflection and Practice
(When observing or listening to any Sutta, it is very important to note the Dhamma points that one must follow and practice. In this Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, while the Blessed One was teaching these six sets of five (Chappañcaka Dhamma)—the Five of the Eye, the Five of the Ear, the Five of the Nose, the Five of the Tongue, the Five of the Body, and the Five of the Mind—by the method of the three-round Dhamma teaching, Venerable Rāhula practiced the Dhamma in his heart while answering the Blessed One's questions and listening to the teaching, thereby reaching the state of a Noble One upon attaining the fruit of Arahantship.

Therefore, if one wishes to meditate and reflect upon the meditation subject through which Venerable Rāhula attained Arahantship, one should reflect upon and meditate on these very points of the six sets of five. The way to reflect is as follows:

If one wishes to reflect in Pali (for the Five of the Eye): Cakkhuṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā; netaṃ mama, neso hamasmi, na meso attā. Rūpā aniccā dukkhā anattā; netaṃ mama, neso hamasmi, na meso attā. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā; netaṃ mama, neso hamasmi, na meso attā. Cakkhusamphasso anicco dukkho anattā; netaṃ mama, neso hamasmi, na meso attā. Yamidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedanāgataṃ saññāgataṃ saṅkhāragataṃ viññāṇagataṃ,

227: ## (6) For the Mind Pentad (a) What is called the mind, the clear mental state, does not last for a long time; it arises for a moment and ceases in a moment. By the dual oppression of arising and ceasing, it is constantly and greatly suffering. It has no solid core or essence. When looking with the eye of wisdom, its nature is impermanence, suffering, and non-self. (b) What is called mental objects, both physical and mental, also do not last for a long time; they do not stay (recite as before). (c) What is called mind-consciousness also does not last for a long time; it does not stay (recite as before). (d) The contact that depends on the mind also does not last for a long time; it does not stay (recite as before). (e) Conditioned by mind-contact, the four groups of aggregates that often arise—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—also do not last for a long time; they arise for a moment and cease in a moment. By the dual oppression of arising and ceasing, they are constantly and greatly suffering. They have no solid core or essence. When looking with the eye of wisdom, its nature is impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Noble people who wish to practice the meditation on the five aggregates by following this 'Six Pentads Dhamma Verse' should also: 'What is called form, the aggregate... does not last for a long time' (and so on), 'What is called feeling, the aggregate... does not last for a long time' (and so on), 'What is called perception, the aggregate... does not last for a long time' (and so on), 'What is called mental formations, the aggregate... does not last for a long time' (and so on), 'What is called the six types of consciousness, the aggregate... does not last for a long time' (and so on). One should practice and contemplate the three characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self as before. This is to be extracted and practiced from the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta.
228: ## The Story of Māra Frightening Venerable Rāhula One day at dusk, many senior elders entered the Jetavana monastery and went to the place of Venerable Rāhula and stayed there. Venerable Rāhula, being a junior monk with few years of seniority, could not forbid the senior elders from staying in his place. When he searched for another place and could not find one, he had to lie down at the porch of the Buddha's Gandhakuṭī (Fragrant Chamber). At that time, Venerable Rāhula was a young monk who had just attained the fruit of Arahantship and had not yet completed a single vassa (rains retreat). Māra, while staying in the Vasavatti heaven, saw Venerable Rāhula lying down at the porch of the Gandhakuṭī and thought: 'The little finger of the recluse Gotama, which would be painful if touched (referring to Venerable Rāhula), is lying outside the Gandhakuṭī, while the recluse Gotama himself is lying inside the Gandhakuṭī. If the little finger is oppressed, it will be as if the recluse Gotama himself is oppressed.' Having thought thus, Māra transformed himself into the form of a great king elephant, approached Venerable Rāhula, wrapped his trunk around Rāhula's head, and trumpeted loudly like a crane. The Blessed One, while sitting inside the Gandhakuṭī, knew it was Māra and said: 'O Māra! Not to mention a single Māra like you, even a hundred thousand Māras...'
229:
“You are unable to cause fear in my son. Indeed, my son is entirely without dread, free from craving, great in effort, and great in wisdom.”

Having said this, and wishing to seal the truth of the Dhamma, the Buddha spoke these verses:

Niṭṭhaṅgato asantāsī,
vītatannho anaṅgaṇo.
acchindi bhavasallāni,
antimoyaṃ samussayo.

(Māra, you who have come to disturb me!) My son, Rāhula, has reached the goal (the end of the holy life known as the Fruition of Arahatship). He is entirely without fear or dread. He is also truly free from the one hundred and eight types of craving. He is free from the fifteen hundred defilements (kilesas). He has uprooted and cut off the thorns of existence—namely, the sensual, fine-material, and immaterial spheres of existence. This physical body currently possessed by my son Rāhula is his final body, the body of his last existence.

Vītatannho anādāno,
niruttipadakovido.
akkharānaṃ sannipātaṃ,
janyā pubbāparāni ca.
sa ve antimasārīro,
mahāpañño mahāpurisoti vuccatī.
230: (He who) is truly free from the one hundred and eight types of craving. He is one who has no grasping through craving, conceit, or wrong view—thinking 'I', 'mine', or 'my soul'—regarding the five aggregates of mind and matter. He is skilled and proficient in the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā): Attha, Dhamma, Nirutti, and Paṭibhāna. He knows the collection of words that form the natural language (sabhāva-nirutti) according to the truth. (This means that if someone who does not know natural language mispronounces the term for the mental factor of contact as 'Phusso', he knows the correct natural term as 'Phasso'). He also clearly and correctly knows the preceding and succeeding syllables, discerning the preceding syllable based on the succeeding one, and the succeeding one based on the preceding one. (In a natural Pali word like 'Cetanā', which has three syllables, even if only the initial syllable 'Ce' is apparent and the middle 'ta' and final 'nā' are not, he correctly knows the middle and final syllables based on the initial one. The same applies if only the middle or only the final syllable is apparent). Such a person, who possesses his final body, is indeed called one of great wisdom and a Great Man (Mahāpurisa) who is free from the fifteen hundred defilements.
231:
The Buddha preached these two verses. At the conclusion of the discourse, many people attained the Fruition of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and other stages. 

Māra, realizing that the Buddha had recognized him, vanished from that very spot.

The account of Māra's attempt to frighten the Venerable Rāhula ends here.
