## The Preaching of the Suciloma Sutta

(This Suciloma Sutta appears in the Sutta Nipāta and the Saṃyutta Nikāya (Sagāthā-vagga). Here, it will be described according to the commentary on the Sutta Nipāta.)

One day, at the approach of dawn, the Buddha arose from the Attainment of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) and surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye (consisting of the knowledge of the inclinations and latent tendencies of beings, and the knowledge of the faculties of beings). He saw that two yakkha friends, Suciloma and Kharaloma, possessed the merit from the past to attain the Fruition of Stream-entry. Therefore, taking his bowl and robes, he traveled within the dawn and sat upon the stone couch named Taṅkita, the dwelling place of Suciloma Yakkha near the village of Gayā.

(The Taṅkita stone couch is a seat made by placing a large stone slab on top of four smaller stones.)

At that time, the two friends, Suciloma Yakkha and Kharaloma Yakkha, were out searching for food and were walking not far from the Buddha.
232:
## The Story of Kharaloma Yakkha

Between these two yakkhas, one had in a past life taken oil belonging to the Saṅgha without permission and rubbed it on his body. Due to that unwholesome kamma, he suffered in hell and was later reborn among the yakkhas near the landing place of the Gayā lake. As a remaining result of that unwholesome kamma, his limbs and body had a terrifying and deformed appearance. His skin was extremely rough to the touch, like a tiled roof (appearing in scales like fish scales).

When this yakkha wished to frighten others, he would make his scale-like skin stand up to cause terror. Thus, because he had a rough body touch, he received the name Kharaloma (Rough-hair/Rough-skin).

## The Story of Suciloma Yakkha

The other yakkha, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, was a lay devotee (upāsaka) who used to go to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma on every eight-day Uposatha day of the month. One day, while the call for the Dhamma talk was being made, he was clearing his field near the gate of the monastery. Hearing the call, he thought, "If I take a bath, it will take too long." So, without bathing and with a dirty body, he entered the Uposatha hall and lay down disrespectfully on a very costly rug.
233:
Due to that kamma and other deeds, that devotee suffered in hell and was later reborn among the yakkhas near the landing place of the Gayā lake. As a remaining result of that unwholesome kamma, he was extremely ugly and unpleasant to look at. The hairs on his body were as sharp and stiff as needles. When he wished to frighten beings, he would terrify them as if piercing them with needle points. Thus, because he had hair like needles, he received the name Suciloma (Needle-hair).

These two yakkha friends had left their dwellings to search for food. After traveling for some time, they returned along the same path and, while heading elsewhere, were walking not far from the Buddha.

Then Kharaloma Yakkha said to Suciloma Yakkha, according to his honest impression, "That person is a monk." Suciloma Yakkha replied to Kharaloma, "That person is not a true monk; he is a fake monk. I will investigate to find out whether he is a true monk or a fake monk."

(In this context: Kharaloma, seeing the appearance of a monk, spoke honestly, "That person is a monk." Suciloma, however, held the view that "If he is one who gets frightened, he is not a true monk, but a fake one." Thinking that the Buddha would be someone who gets frightened, he spoke hastily, saying, "That person is not a true monk; he is a fake monk." Then, wanting to investigate further, he said again, "I will investigate to find out whether he is a true monk or a fake monk.")
234:
After saying this, Suciloma Yakkha went to where the Buddha was and leaned his ugly body, with its bristling hair, toward the Buddha. Then the Buddha moved his body away. Suciloma Yakkha then asked the Buddha, "Monk, are you afraid of me?" The Buddha replied, "Layman Yakkha, I am not afraid of you; however, your touch is indeed rough and evil."

Then, seeing the Buddha who was not in the least bit afraid, Suciloma Yakkha thought: "Although he is touched by my yakkha-touch which is this rough, this person, though a mere human, is not afraid. Now I will ask this monk a question within the domain of an Omniscient Buddha. Surely this monk will not be able to answer this question of the Buddha's domain completely. Then I will torment and oppress this monk in such and such a way." Having planned this, he spoke rudely: "Monk, I will ask you a question. If you cannot answer my question satisfactorily, I will scatter your mind and make you mad, or I will split your heart, or I will grab you by your two feet and hurl you to the other side of the river."

Then the Buddha, with a joyful face governed by great compassion, invited him with the invitation of Omniscient Buddhas: "Layman Yakkha, in this entire world including the devas, Māras, and Brahmās, and among the generation of humans including monks, brahmins, kings, and commoners, I do not see anyone who can scatter my mind or make me mad, or split my heart,
235:
or grab me by my two feet and hurl me to the other side of the river. Nevertheless, Layman Yakkha, ask whatever question you wish to ask (I shall answer your question without leaving anything out)." Being thus invited, Suciloma Yakkha addressed the Buddha with a verse:

Rāgo ca doso ca kuto-nidānā,
arati rati lomahaṃso kutojā.
kuto samuṭṭhāya mano vitakkā,
kumārakā dhaṅkamivossajanti.

(Ascetic!) From what cause do lust and hatred arise? From where do boredom (with wholesome deeds in solitary dwellings) and delight (in the five sensual pleasures) arise? From where do the terrors that make one's hair stand on end arise? From where do the nine types of thoughts arise and agitate the wholesome mind, just as boys (having caught a crow and tied its legs with a string) toss it up and play with it? (1)

Then the Buddha answered the question and preached the Dhamma to Suciloma Yakkha with these three following verses:
236: Lust and hatred have their origin here (in this body); aversion, delight, and horripilation are born from here. Thoughts arising from here toss the mind, just as young boys toss a crow (tied with a string). (2) Born of affection, produced from the self, like the aerial roots of a banyan tree. Defilements such as lust and hatred, which arise due to the moisture of craving, are produced within this individual existence (attabhāva)...
237: ...like the Māluva creeper spreading in the forest. Manifold defilements cling to the various objects of sense pleasure. (3) O Yakkha, listen! Those who clearly understand this (body of the Truth of Suffering) and its origin (the Truth of Craving), dispel that evil origin—the craving—with the Eightfold Path. Those noble ones who dispel craving with the Eightfold Path cross this flood (of defilements), so difficult to cross, which they had never crossed before in the long round of rebirths, for the sake of non-becoming (or for the sake of the Truth of Cessation). (4)
239:
## Chapter 33
## In Kapilavatthu
## Observing the Fifteenth (Pannarasama) Vassa
As previously mentioned, after the Blessed One observed the fourteenth Vassa in Sāvatthī and the retreat ended, He remained in Sāvatthī for as long as there were beings to be liberated. Then, He set out on a journey to provide the nectar of Dhamma to humans, devas, and brahmās, eventually arriving at the royal city of Kapilavatthu. (During the Blessed One's first visit to Kapilavatthu, the Sakyan prince Nigrodha had built a large monastery in his own park and offered it to the Blessed One. This monastery became known as the Nigrodhārāma.) There, surrounded by a company of monks, He observed the fifteenth Vassa at the Nigrodhārāma monastery.

## Teaching Mahānāma the Sakyan
## On the Definition of a Lay Follower and Other Matters
While the Blessed One was staying at the Nigrodhārāma monastery in Kapilavatthu, in the Sakyan country, one day Mahānāma the Sakyan prince went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. He then asked the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, to what extent is one a lay follower (upāsaka)?"

Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed Mahānāma the Sakyan prince:
240: 'Mahanāma, in so far as one (1) goes to the Buddha for refuge, (2) goes to the Dhamma for refuge, and (3) goes to the Saṅgha for refuge—to that extent, Mahanāma, one is a lay follower.' (This means that one who is established in the Three Refuges is called an Upāsaka.) (1) Again, Mahanāma the Sakyan asked the Buddha: 'Venerable Sir, to what extent is a lay follower one who is accomplished in virtue (sīla)?' The Buddha said to the Sakyan prince Mahanāma: 'Mahanāma, in so far as a lay follower (1) abstains from taking life, (2) abstains from taking what is not given, (3) abstains from sexual misconduct, (4) abstains from false speech, and (5) abstains from intoxicating drinks and drugs which cause heedlessness—to that extent, Mahanāma, a lay follower is accomplished in virtue.' (This means an Upāsaka established in the Refuges who fulfills the Five Precepts is a virtuous Upāsaka.) (2) Again, Mahanāma the Sakyan asked the Buddha: 'Venerable Sir, to what extent is a lay follower one who is accomplished in faith (saddhā)?'
241: The Buddha said to the Sakyan prince Mahanāma: 'Mahanāma, here a lay follower has faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Buddha thus: "The Blessed One is an Arahant because He is worthy of special offerings... (etc.)... He is the Bhagavā because He is endowed with supreme glory." To this extent, Mahanāma, a lay follower is accomplished in faith.' (Here, teaching only the nine qualities of the Buddha is merely an illustrative method. A lay follower who believes in the nine qualities of the Buddha will naturally believe in the six qualities of the Dhamma and the nine qualities of the Saṅgha. Therefore, it means that a lay follower who has deep faith in the qualities of the Triple Gem is one accomplished in faith.) (3) Again, Mahanāma the Sakyan asked the Buddha: 'Venerable Sir, to what extent is a lay follower one who is accomplished in generosity (cāga)?' The Buddha said to the Sakyan prince Mahanāma: 'Mahanāma, here a lay follower dwells at home with a heart free from the stain of stinginess (macchariya). He is open-handed, having hands ready for giving (literally, wet hands).
242:
"...he delights in generosity. Because he does not keep a stern face, he is approachable for those who wish to ask for donations; he delights in giving and sharing. Mahānāma, to this extent, a lay follower is one accomplished in generosity (cāga)." (4)

Again, Mahānāma the Sakyan asked the Blessed One:

"Venerable Sir, to what extent is a lay follower accomplished in wisdom (paññā)?"

When he asked this, the Blessed One said to Mahānāma the Sakyan prince:

"Mahānāma, in this Dispensation, a lay follower is wise; he is possessed of wisdom that is pure and noble, capable of destroying the mass of defilements, leading to Nibbāna where suffering ends, and knowing the rise and fall of mental and physical phenomena (udayabbaya-ñāṇa). Mahānāma, to this extent, a lay follower is one accomplished in wisdom." (5) (From Mahāvagga Saṃyutta Pāḷi, page 344). (The story of Mahānāma the Sakyan will be described in detail in the chapter on the Saṅgha-ratana).

## The Uncle King Suppabuddha the Sakyan
## The Cause of Being Swallowed by the Earth
While the Blessed One was staying at the Nigrodhārāma monastery in Kapilavatthu, in the Sakyan country, on account of His uncle King Suppabuddha the Sakyan—
243: To elaborate: The maternal uncle, King Suppabuddha the Sakyan, harbored a grudge against the Buddha for two reasons: 'This Prince Siddhattha, my nephew, now the Buddha Gotama, abandoned my daughter Yasodharā and went to the forest; and after ordaining my son Devadatta, He has also become an enemy to him.' One day, he thought, 'Now, I will not give my nephew, Prince Siddhattha the Buddha, the opportunity to go to the place where He has been invited for a meal.' Intentionally blocking the path the Buddha would take, he sat in the middle of the road drinking alcohol. Then, when the Buddha arrived at that place surrounded by a company of monks, the king's men reported to King Suppabuddha, 'The Buddha has arrived.' King Suppabuddha said to his men, 'Friends, tell that nephew of mine, Prince Siddhattha, to go by another way. This Prince Siddhattha is not older than me. Therefore, we cannot give the way for my nephew Siddhattha to pass.' He spoke harshly. Even though the men repeatedly informed him, he said the same thing and continued drinking alcohol as before. Since the Buddha did not get the path to pass from His uncle, He turned back from that very spot. King Suppabuddha also sent a spy, saying, 'Friend, go! My nephew, Prince Siddhattha...'
244: "Listen to what he says and come back," he instructed and sent him. While the Buddha was returning, he showed a smile. Venerable Ānanda asked, "Exalted Buddha, what is the reason for clearly showing this smile?" The Buddha asked, "Ānanda, did you see my uncle, King Suppabuddha?" Ānanda replied, "I saw him, Bhante." Then the Buddha said to Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, King Suppabuddha, who did not give way to a Buddha like me, has committed a very grave unwholesome deed. On the seventh day from today, at the foot of the stairs below the palace, King Suppabuddha will enter the earth (be swallowed by the earth)." The Buddha thus gave this prophecy. The spy heard this and went to King Suppabuddha. When the King asked, "What did my nephew say upon his return?", the spy reported everything he had heard. Upon hearing the spy's report, King Suppabuddha thought, "Now, there is no fault in my nephew's words; indeed, whatever he says usually happens. Even so, I will now defeat my nephew with a lie. Indeed, that nephew of mine, Prince Siddhattha who is a Buddha, did not just say 'he will enter the earth on the seventh day' without specifying the place, but he specified the location, saying 'he will enter the earth at the foot of the stairs below the palace.' From now on, I will not go to the foot of those stairs. If I do not go there, I will not be swallowed by the earth at that spot. When the seven days have passed and I have not been swallowed by the earth, I will defeat my nephew, the Buddha, with a lie."
245: Having thought thus, Suppabuddha the Sakyan had all his belongings moved to the highest floor of a seven-story palace. He had the stairs removed and the doors locked. He stationed two wrestlers at each door and instructed them, "If I should forget and try to go down, you must stop me." He then stayed in the royal chamber on the seventh floor. The Buddha heard about this and said, "Monks, whether my uncle King Suppabuddha stays on the palace roof, or flies into the sky and stays in the air, or descends into the ocean by boat, or enters a mountain cave, there is no such thing as the word spoken by the Buddhas being untrue or having two different meanings. (It is only the truth). At the very place I mentioned, at the foot of the stairs, King Suppabuddha will enter the earth." Having said this, wishing to connect the preceding and following words to preach the Dhamma:
246:
Na antalikkhe na samuddamajjhe,
Na pabbatānaṃ vivaraṃ pavissa.
Na vijjati so jagatippadeso,
Yattha ṭhitaṃ nappasaheyya maccu.

Monks, one who stands in the sky is not free from death. One who stands in the midst of the sea is not free from death. One who enters and stands within a mountain cave is not free from death. There is no place on this earth where death cannot overcome and oppress the one who stands there. Not even a space as small as the tip of a hair exists.

He taught this verse. At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and so on.

## The Time for King Suppabuddha to be Swallowed by the Earth Arrives
On the seventh day, at the time when the path where the Blessed One would go for His alms-meal was blocked, the auspicious royal steed of King Suppabuddha the Sakyan, kept below the palace, broke its tether, neighed loudly, and began kicking the walls here and there. No one could frighten or catch it. While King Suppabuddha the Sakyan was still in the palace, he heard the neighing of his auspicious royal steed—
247: He asked, "What is happening?" and the attendants replied, "Your Majesty's auspicious state horse has broken free from its tether." That auspicious state horse would stand still as soon as it saw King Suppabuddha. At that time, King Suppabuddha, unable to resist catching the horse, rose from his seat and headed toward the door. The doors opened by themselves. The stairs that had been removed also reappeared in their original places. The wrestlers stationed at the doors did not push him back into the palace but grabbed him by the neck and threw him down. In this manner, the doors on all seven floors opened by themselves, the stairs were in their places, and the wrestlers at each door grabbed him by the neck and threw him down to the lower levels. Then, when he reached the foot of the stairs below the palace, the great earth roared loudly, split open, and received Suppabuddha the Sakyan. King Suppabuddha entered the earth and was reborn in Avīci Hell. The story of the earth swallowing the uncle, Suppabuddha the Sakyan, ends.
249: In fact, one deva would ask another, and that one would ask yet another, and so they went on asking each other without finding a decision or answer. They wandered through the ten thousand world systems for twelve years. Even after twelve years, they could not understand the meaning of the questions. Then, all the devas living in the ten thousand world systems gathered and went to the Four Great Kings. When the Four Great Kings asked, "Friends, why has this great assembly of devas gathered?", the devas replied, "We have raised four questions and are unable to decide them; therefore, we have come to you, the Four Great Kings." The Kings asked, "Friends, what are these four questions?" The devas replied, "Among many gifts, many tastes, and many delights, which gift, which taste, and which delight is the most excellent? And why is the Fruit of Arahantship at the end of craving called the most excellent? Being unable to decide these four questions, we have come before you, Great Kings." Then the Four Great Kings said, "Friends, we also do not know the meaning of these questions. However, our lord,
250: Sakka, the King of Devas, can understand in an instant the meanings that a thousand people might think about. That Sakka is superior to us in knowledge, wisdom, and merit. Come, let us go to him." Saying this, they took the host of devas and went to Sakka. Sakka also asked, "Friends, why has such a great assembly of devas gathered?" and the devas explained the reason. Sakka said, "Friends, no one else (besides a Buddha) can know the meaning of these questions. Indeed, these four questions are within the domain of the Buddha. Where is the Buddha dwelling now?" Upon hearing that he was at Jetavana Monastery, he said, "Come, let us go and ask the Buddha." Together with the host of devas, he went at night, illuminating the entire Jetavana Monastery. After approaching the Buddha, paying respectful homage, and standing in a suitable place, the Buddha asked, "Sakka, why have you come with such a large host of devas?" Sakka replied, "Exalted Buddha, the devas have raised these four questions. Besides you, there is no one else who can know the meaning of these questions. May the Exalted One explain the meaning of these four questions."
251:
"Please answer us clearly," he requested.

The Buddha replied, "Very well, Sakka. I have fulfilled the Perfections and courageously renounced the five great sacrifices in order to attain and realize Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) specifically to sever the doubts of persons like you. Sakka, the answers to the four problems you asked are:

(1) Of all gifts, the gift of Dhamma is the most excellent.
(2) Of all tastes, the taste of Dhamma is the most excellent.
(3) Of all delights, delight in the Dhamma is the most excellent.
(4) The Fruition of Arahantship (Arahattaphala), which occurs at the end of the destruction of craving, is certainly the most excellent because it leads to the exhaustion and cessation of all suffering."

Having preached this in prose (cuṇṇiya), he then spoke this verse:

Sabbadānaṃ dhammadānaṃ jināti,
Sabbarasaṃ dhammaraso jināti.
Sabbaratiṃ dhammarati jināti,
Taṇhakkhayo sabbadukkhaṃ jināti.

(Sakka, King of Devas), Sabbadānaṃ = all kinds of gifts; dhammadānaṃ = the gift of Dhamma, such as preaching, teaching, and listening to the Dhamma; jināti = excels and conquers with greatness and stability.

* For this fourth answer, the meaning is expressed based on the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) which explains it later.
252:
Sabbarasaṃ = all kinds of tastes; dhammaraso = the taste of Dhamma, consisting of the thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) and the nine Supramundane States (Lokuttara-dhamma); jināti = excels and conquers with greatness and stability.

Sabbaratiṃ = all kinds of delights; dhammarati = delight in the Dhamma; jināti = excels and conquers with greatness and stability.

Taṇhakkhayo = the Fruition of Arahantship (Arahattaphala) which occurs at the end of the destruction of craving; sabbadukkhaṃ = all the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭadukkha); jināti = dominates and conquers completely.

He preached this verse of Dhamma.

## Explanation of Meaning
(1) Even if one were to offer robes as delicate and soft as a banana-leaf sheath to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants sitting without any space between them throughout the entire universe up to the Brahma realm, the sharing of Dhamma (anumodanā) performed with a four-line verse of Dhamma in that assembly is more noble. Indeed, that vast offering of robes is not worth even one two-hundred-and-fifty-sixth part of that verse of Dhamma appreciation. Thus, preaching the Dhamma, teaching it, and listening to it are most noble.
253:
In particular, the merit and benefits for a person who organizes and strives to enable many people to hear the Dhamma are immense.

Compared to the offering of alms-food where every single alms-bowl is filled with excellent food and offered to the assembly of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Arahants sitting without space throughout the entire universe as mentioned; compared to the offering of medicine where every single alms-bowl is filled with ghee, oil, etc.; compared to the offering of monasteries where hundreds of thousands of great monasteries like Mahāvihāra and hundreds of thousands of palatial buildings like Lohapāsāda are constructed and offered; and compared to the various offerings made by donors like Anāthapiṇḍika in relation to monasteries like Jetavana—the gift of Dhamma, even in the form of preaching a verse of appreciation (anumodanā) consisting of at least four lines, is more praiseworthy and noble.

Why is this? The answer is: those who perform the meritorious deeds of offering the four requisites—robes, alms-food, monasteries, and medicine—do so only because they have heard the Dhamma; they do not do so without hearing it. Indeed, if these beings did not hear the Dhamma, they would not even give a spoonful of gruel or a morsel of food. For this reason,
254:
the gift of Dhamma alone is more praiseworthy and noble than all other gifts.

To illustrate further, excluding the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, even great beings like Ven. Sāriputta—who possessed the wisdom to count every single drop of rain if it were to fall continuously for an entire aeon (āyukappa)—were unable to reach or attain the Noble Path and Fruition, such as the Fruition of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala), by themselves through natural intuition (without hearing the Dhamma). In fact, they realized Sotāpattiphala only after hearing the Dhamma preached by Ven. Assaji and others. They realized the Wisdom of a Disciple's Perfection (Sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) by hearing the Buddha's Dhamma teachings (such as the Dīghanakha Sutta). Sakka, for this reason also, the gift of Dhamma (Dhammadāna) is more praiseworthy and noble than all gifts of material requisites (paccayadāna). Therefore, the Buddha preached, "The gift of Dhamma excels and conquers all material gifts."

(2) All kinds of tastes, such as the taste of fruits, flowers, and perfumes (and even the taste of celestial ambrosia of the devas), only lead to falling into the round of rebirths (saṃsāra) and are causes for experiencing the sensation of suffering. The taste of Dhamma, which is the nine Supramundane States including the thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment, the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, is
255:
more superior, noble, and praiseworthy than all kinds of worldly tastes. Therefore, the Buddha preached, "The taste of Dhamma excels and conquers all tastes."

(3) Various kinds of delight and joy in worldly matters and possessions—such as delight in sons, delight in daughters, delight in wealth, delight in women, and joy in dancing, singing, and music—only lead to falling into the round of rebirths and are causes for experiencing the sensation of suffering. However, the joy and delight (pīti) that arises in the internal continuum of a person who preaches, teaches, or listens to the Dhamma by taking the Dhamma as an object, causes upliftment and exhilaration; it even causes tears to flow and the hair to stand on end with joy. Such delight in the Dhamma (dhamma-pīti) which arises from focusing on the Dhamma and causes exhilaration, tears, and goosebumps, is more superior, noble, and praiseworthy than all kinds of worldly delights because it can bring an end to the round of rebirths and bestow benefits up to the Fruition of Arahantship. Therefore, "Delight in the Dhamma
256:
(dhamma-rati) excels and conquers all kinds of delights," the Buddha preached.

(4) At the moment of the Path of Arahantship (Arahattamagga), all cravings are exhausted. Immediately after the Path of Arahantship, the Fruition of Arahantship (Arahattaphala) arises. Thus, Arahattaphala is called the destruction of craving (taṇhakkhaya) because it occurs at the end of the exhaustion of craving. That Arahattaphala, known as taṇhakkhaya, is a state more superior, noble, and praiseworthy than all dhammas because it overcomes and conquers all suffering of the round of rebirths. Therefore, the Buddha preached, "Taṇhakkhayo sabbadukkhaṃ jināti = The Fruition of Arahantship at the end of the destruction of craving dominates and conquers all suffering of the round of rebirths."

## Eighty-four Thousand Beings
## Attaining Liberation
While the Buddha was thus preaching the meaning of this verse in detail, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation.

Sakka, having heard the Buddha's detailed Dhamma teaching, paid homage to the Buddha with deep respect and said:

"Greatly Glorious Buddha, while the gift of Dhamma is so great, noble, and praiseworthy,
257:
why have You not allowed us to be given a share of the merit of Dhammadāna? From this time forward, please let the merit of that Dhammadāna be shared with us after the Dhamma has been preached to the Sangha of monks."

The Buddha, hearing Sakka's request, convened the assembly of monks and said:

"Monks, starting from today, whether it be a great Dhamma ceremony, an ordinary Dhamma talk, a discussion of Dhamma with those who visit you, or (at the very least) a Dhamma appreciation (anumodanā), after preaching, share the merit with all beings."

(From Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā, Vol. 2, page 350).

Here ends the account of answering the four problems asked by Sakka.
