## The Account of Taming and Disciplining the Ogre Āḷavaka
King Āḷavaka, the ruler of Āḷavī, renounced all the enjoyments of the golden palace along with his various royal attendants and dancers. In order to eliminate the danger of rebels and thieves, to prevent the encroachment and attacks of rival kings, and to exercise his royal vigor, he used to go out to the deer forest for hunting once every seven days.
258: One day, as King Āḷavaka was about to go hunting, he made a pact with his soldiers: "If a deer escapes through the station of any person, that person shall be held responsible." While they were in the deer forest, a deer escaped right through the King's station. Being a man of great speed, strength, and vigor, the King, armed with his bow, pursued the deer on foot for three yojanas without stopping. Creatures known as Eṇī deer can only run at full speed for three yojanas; thus, after three yojanas, the deer's momentum was spent, and it stood in a pond. The King shot and killed it with his bow, cutting it into two pieces. Although he had no desire for the meat, he carried it on a shoulder pole to avoid the ridicule and accusations of his soldiers that he was unable to catch the deer. As he was returning, not far from the city, he saw a large banyan tree with thick, lush foliage and pleasant shade. He approached the foot of that banyan tree to rest. In that large banyan tree lived the Yakkha Āḷavaka, who had received a boon from the Great King Vessavaṇa to rule over and eat any creatures that entered the area touched by the tree's shadow at the time the sun passed the meridian. (In this regard, it should not be understood that he ate only those who entered under the banyan tree at noon; rather, it should be understood that he ate those who entered the boundary of the banyan tree's shadow, whether by day or by night, at the time the sun passed the meridian). Then, the Yakkha Āḷavaka, seeing the King who had entered under his banyan tree, approached him to eat him.
259: The Yakkha revealed himself and approached. (The King wished to be released by offering the two pieces of deer meat, but the Yakkha Āḷavaka did not release him, saying, "From the moment you fell into my hands, does the deer meat not belong to me already? O King, how can you secure your release by giving me what is mine?" This passage in parentheses appears only in some versions). Then the King made a pact with the Yakkha Āḷavaka, saying, "Release me, and I will send you one human and a pot of cooked rice every single day." The Yakkha Āḷavaka replied, "You, O King, might become intoxicated with royal power and be negligent. As for me, I cannot eat anyone who does not come to my abode or who is not given to me with consent. If I release you, O King, how shall I live?" and he did not release him. The King then gave his full consent, saying, "On the day I do not send them, you may catch and eat me." Having thus secured his release from the Yakkha's hands, he headed toward the city of Āḷavī. While the army of soldiers was waiting for the King in temporary leaf-huts built along the way, they saw the King returning and went to meet him, saying, "Great King, why did you exert yourself so much, fearing what insignificant power?" The King did not mention the incident and, upon reaching the city and eating his morning meal, summoned the City Manager and secretly told him about the pact made with the Yakkha.
260: The City Manager asked, "Great King, how is it? Did you set a time limit?" When the King replied, "I did not set one, friend," the City Manager said, "Great King, you have made a mistake in this matter. Indeed, Yakkhas can only take what is specifically defined. Since no limit was set, it will bring danger and disease to the entire province. Great King, let it be; even though you have made such a mistake, enjoy your royal happiness without anxiety. I myself will carry out whatever needs to be done in this matter." Having said this, the City Manager rose early, went to the prison, and addressed the death-row inmates, saying, "Let those who wish to live come forth." He took the first prisoner who came out to his house, gave him a bath and food, and then sent him off, saying, "Go and deliver this pot of rice to the Yakkha." As soon as that prisoner entered the shade of the banyan tree, the Yakkha manifested a terrifying form and chewed and ate him noisily, like the stalk or root of a lotus. It is particularly noted that due to the supernatural power of Yakkhas, the entire body of a human, starting from the hair, becomes like a solid mass of butter or ghee. The King's men who accompanied the prisoner to take the food for the Yakkha Āḷavaka saw the Yakkha chewing and eating the prisoner in that manner. They were terrified and told their friends and loved ones about it. From that time on,
261: the news spread that "The King catches thieves and gives them to the Yakkha," and all the people abstained from theft. Later, because there were no new thieves and the old thieves were exhausted, the prisons became empty of thieves. The City Manager reported this to the King. The King thought, "Someone might take something out of desire," and ordered his gold and silver treasures to be placed on the city streets. However, not a single person touched that gold and silver, even with their feet. When King Āḷavaka could not obtain thieves even by this method, he revealed the matter and consulted with his ministers. The ministers suggested, "Let us send one old person from each household in order. An old person is naturally someone already at the mouth of Death." But the King forbade the proposal, saying, "O ministers, if we do that, the people will be shaken and distressed, saying, 'They are heartless enough to send our fathers and grandfathers to the Yakkha.' Do not favor such an arrangement to feed old people to the Yakkha." Then the ministers changed their approach and suggested, "Great King, if that is the case, let us send one infant who still sleeps on their back in a cradle every day. Indeed, such infants who sleep on their backs do not yet have affection, thinking 'This is my mother' or 'This is my father'." The King
262: agreed and gave his permission. The ministers arranged it accordingly. In the royal city, mothers took their children and fled, and pregnant women also fled to other countries to let their sons grow up. Only after they reached adulthood did they bring them back to the city of Āḷavī. In this way, the daily feeding of the Yakkha in Āḷavī continued for twelve years. Then one day, although they searched the entire city, they could not find a single child. The King's men reported to the King, "Great King, except for your son, Prince Āḷavaka, in the royal palace, there are no more children in the city." The King said, "Just as I love my son, so all people love their own children. However, there is no one dearer in the world than oneself. Go, my men, and give my son, Prince Āḷavaka, to the Yakkha to protect my life." At that time, the mother of Prince Āḷavaka, the Chief Queen, had bathed her son with scented water, adorned him, wrapped him in fine white cloth, and was sitting with him on her lap. By the King's command, the King's men went to the place where the Queen was sitting with her son on her lap. While the Queen and sixteen thousand concubines were weeping and lamenting, the men, along with the royal nurse,
263:
They took the young prince Āḷavaka and said, "Tomorrow, this prince shall become the food of the ogre," and then they departed.

## The Blessed One Journeys to the Country of Āḷavī
On that very day, at dawn, the Blessed One rose early and entered the attainment of Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) in the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭī) within the Jetavana monastery. Then, surveying the world of beings—devas, humans, and brahmās—who were worthy of liberation with His Buddha-eye (consisting of āsayānusaya-ñāṇa and indriyaparopariyatti-ñāṇa), He saw three special reasons:

(1) The past merit of the young prince Āḷavaka that would lead to the attainment of the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala);
(2) The past merit of Āḷavaka the Ogre that would lead to the attainment of the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala);
(3) The past merit of eighty-four thousand beings that would lead to the attainment of the Dhamma-eye (dhamma-cakkhu), the realization of the Four Noble Truths, at the conclusion of the teaching.

Having seen these three special reasons, when the night had ended and dawn broke, He performed the morning Buddha-duties. Before finishing the afternoon Buddha-duties, at sunset on the new moon day, He took His bowl and robes and traveled alone without a companion, journeying thirty yojanas on foot from Sāvatthī to enter the domain of Āḷavaka the Ogre's celestial mansion.
264: In this regard, did the Blessed One stay in the mansion of the Yakkha Āḷavaka, which is invisible to ordinary humans, near the banyan tree, or did he stay at the foot of the banyan tree? Where did he stay? He stayed in the Yakkha's mansion itself. To clarify further: just as the Yakkhas see their own mansions, so too did the Blessed One see it. Thus, the Blessed One went to the Yakkha Āḷavaka's mansion and stood at the mansion's gate. At that time, the Yakkha Āḷavaka had gone to an assembly of Yakkhas in the Himālaya mountains. Therefore, the Yakkha named Gadrabha, who was the gatekeeper for the Yakkha Āḷavaka, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and the following dialogue took place between Gadrabha and the Blessed One: (Gadrabha): "Exalted Blessed One, has the Lord Buddha arrived only at sunset?" (Buddha): "Yes, Gadrabha, I have arrived only at sunset. If it is not a burden to you, I wish to stay in the Yakkha Āḷavaka's mansion for just this one night." (Gadrabha): "Exalted Blessed One, it is no burden to me. However, that Yakkha Āḷavaka is extremely fierce and cruel. He does not even show respect, such as paying homage, to his own parents. Therefore, may the Lord Buddha not take pleasure in staying in this mansion of the Yakkha Āḷavaka."
265:
(The Buddha) "Gadrabha... I know the ferocity of this Āḷavaka Yakkha. No harm whatsoever will come to me. If it is not a burden to you, I wish to stay in Āḷavaka Yakkha's mansion for just this one night."

(Gadrabha) "Venerable Blessed One... Āḷavaka Yakkha is like a red-hot iron cauldron glowing with fire. He is one who knows nothing of parents, nor of recluses and brahmins, nor of the Dhamma. He is capable of causing the minds of those who arrive at this mansion to become distracted. He can even split their hearts. He is one who can seize them by their two legs and hurl them to the other side of the ocean or to the other side of the universe."

(The Buddha) "Gadrabha... I know these things. If it is not a burden to you, I wish to stay in Āḷavaka Yakkha's mansion for just this one night."

(Gadrabha) "Venerable Blessed One... for my part, it is not a burden. However, that Āḷavaka Yakkha might kill me for granting permission without informing him. Venerable Blessed One... (therefore) let me go and inform Āḷavaka Yakkha of the situation first."

(The Buddha) "Gadrabha... speak as you please."
266:
(Gadrabha) "Venerable Blessed One... if that is the case, may the Lord Buddha himself consider whether it is appropriate to stay or not."

Having spoken thus, Gadrabha paid homage to the Blessed One and departed toward the Himālaya. The door of Āḷavaka Yakkha's mansion opened of its own accord, without anyone having to open it. The Blessed One entered the mansion and sat upon the celestial jeweled throne where Āḷavaka Yakkha usually sat to enjoy celestial bliss on very prominent auspicious days, and he emitted a golden radiance of yellow light.

Beholding that golden radiance, the female attendants and retinues of the yakkha gathered together, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down surrounding him. The Blessed One preached a miscellaneous discourse on the Dhamma to those yakkhinīs, saying: "O yakkhinī devotees... you have attained and are enjoying this celestial bliss because in the past you gave gifts, observed virtue, and honored those worthy of honor. Now, in the same way as before, continue to do so. Do not live being overwhelmed and oppressed by the Dhamma of envy (issā) and stinginess (macchariya) toward one another."

The yakkhinīs, having heard the extremely sweet voice of the Dhamma from the Blessed One, gave thousands of cheers and remained sitting, surrounding the Blessed One as before.

Gadrabha Yakkha arrived at the Himālaya and respectfully addressed Āḷavaka Yakkha: "O free from suffering, Lord Āḷavaka, King of Yakkhas... I urge you;
267:
Please know, the Blessed One has arrived and is sitting in your mansion, O King of Yakkhas." Thus he informed him respectfully. At that time, Āḷavaka Yakkha made a sign to Gadrabha Yakkha, saying: "Be silent! (meaning, 'You keep quiet'). I will go right now and do what needs to be done."

(In this context: Āḷavaka Yakkha, because his unwise reflection (ayoniso manasikāra) was so intense, felt great pride and shame that the Blessed One had entered and was staying in his mansion. Thinking, "Let no one in this assembly of celestial yakkhas hear of this matter," he forbade him from speaking loudly.)

Then, the two friends, Sātāgira the Yakkha King and Hemavata the Yakkha King (who were noble/ariya devas), consulted and agreed: "Let us first pay homage to the Blessed One at the Jetavana monastery before going to the assembly of yakkhas." Accompanied by their celestial retinues, they rode various special vehicles and traveled through the sky.

In particular, there are no fixed paths everywhere in the sky for yakkhas; they travel only through areas that are suitable paths, avoiding the celestial mansions situated in the sky.

Āḷavaka Yakkha's mansion, however, was situated on the ground. It was well-secured, surrounded by walls, and fitted with properly arranged watchtowers and gateways. The top of the mansion was covered with a bronze net; it was like a box,
268:
and it was three yojanas in height. Above that mansion of Āḷavaka was the celestial path where yakkhas traveled.

As the two friends, Sātāgira the Yakkha King and Hemavata the Yakkha King (the noble devas), were coming through the sky to pay homage to the Buddha, they reached that spot (the sky path above Āḷavaka's mansion) and found themselves unable to proceed.

Indeed—no one is able to pass over the place where Buddhas are sitting, even as far up as the highest point of existence (Bhavagga).

Therefore, the two friends (the noble yakkha kings) reflected, "What is the reason for our being unable to proceed?" When they saw the Blessed One, they descended to the ground like a stone thrown into the air. After paying homage to the Buddha and listening to the Dhamma, they circumambulated him to the right and requested permission, saying: "Venerable Blessed One... we shall proceed to the assembly of yakkhas." Praising the virtues of the Triple Gem, they departed for the Himālaya where the yakkhas were assembled.

When Āḷavaka Yakkha saw the two friends (the noble yakkha kings), he invited them, saying: "Please sit here," and vacated a seat for them.

## Āḷavaka Yakkha's Intense Outburst of Anger

The two friends (the noble yakkha kings) informed Āḷavaka Yakkha: "Friend Āḷavaka... the Blessed One has arrived and is currently staying in your celestial mansion. Therefore, friend, you are truly fortunate.
269:
Friend Āḷavaka... go and attend upon the Blessed One."

(To one who lacks faith, talk of Dhamma related to faith is merely an irritation to the ears. To one who lacks virtue, talk of Dhamma related to virtue is merely an irritation to the ears. To one who lacks learning, talk of Dhamma related to learning is merely an irritation to the ears. To one who is stingy and unwilling to give, talk of Dhamma related to generosity (cāga) is merely an irritation to the ears. To one who lacks wisdom, talk of Dhamma related to wisdom is merely an irritation to the ears.)

The words concerning the Buddha, which were meant to inspire faith as spoken by the two friends (the noble yakkha kings), were merely an irritation to the ears of Āḷavaka Yakkha, who lacked faith. Thus, upon hearing the words of praise for the Buddha from the two yakkha kings, Āḷavaka Yakkha, lacking faith, felt intense anger rising within him like a lump of salt thrown into fire. With a heart that sizzled with rage, he spoke angrily: "What kind of person is this so-called 'Blessed One' who has entered and is staying inside my mansion?"

Then the two yakkha kings said: "Friend Āḷavaka... do you not know our teacher, the Blessed One? (He is a most distinguished and noble personage). While our teacher, the Bodhisatta, was still in the Tusita heaven, he made the five great observations..." (They continued to speak in this manner, describing everything up to the preaching of the Dhammacakka Sutta,
270:
and fully explained how the thirty-two great omens appeared at the time of his conception, etc.) "Friend Āḷavaka... did you not see these wonderful and extraordinary great omens?" they questioned and examined him. Although Āḷavaka Yakkha had seen those great omens, he followed the dictates of his anger and spoke evasively, saying: "I did not see them."

Then the two yakkha kings, feeling indignant, said: "Friend Āḷavaka... whether you saw them or not, what benefit is there in your seeing or not seeing? What could you possibly do to our teacher, the Blessed One? Compared to our teacher, the Blessed One, you appear like: (a) a calf born today near a great bull with a swaying dewlap; (b) a small newborn elephant near a great tusker with ichor flowing from three places—the trunk, the genitals, and the ears; (c) an old, wretched fox near a King of Lions with a majestic mane and powerful shoulders; (d) a small crow with broken wings near a King of Garudas with a body spanning a hundred and fifty yojanas. Go! Do what you have to do!"

When they spoke thus, Āḷavaka Yakkha became furious. He left his seat, stood firmly with his left foot on the Manosilā stone plateau, and shouted: "Is your teacher the Buddha greater in power and majesty, or am I? Look right now (to see who is greater in power and majesty)!"
271:
With a roar, he stamped his right foot on the peak of Mount Kelāsa, which was sixty yojanas in size. At that moment, just as sparks of iron fly off in layers when a red-hot iron mass from a smithy is placed on an anvil and struck with a hammer, so too did layers and slabs of rock break away from the peak of Mount Kelāsa.

Standing upon the peak of Mount Kelāsa, Āḷavaka Yakkha shouted loudly: "I am Āḷavaka!" That sound spread and overwhelmed the entire island of Jambudīpa.

## The Four Great Sounds

(1) The sound of the Yakkha General Puṇṇaka in the Vidhura Jātaka, who, after winning the dice game against King Dhanañjaya Koravya, clapped his hands and shouted: "I have won! I have won!"; (2) The sound of Sakka, King of Devas, who, when the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha was declining, made the deity Vissakamma take the form of a great black dog and shout: "I shall devour all wicked monks, wicked nuns, wicked laymen, wicked laywomen, and all those who speak contrary to the Dhamma!"; (3) The sound of the Bodhisatta King Kusa in the Kusa Jātaka, who, when the kings of seven kingdoms surrounded the city to claim Princess Pabhāvatī, mounted an elephant with the princess, exited the city, and shouted: "I am the Great King Kusa, the Lion-Voiced, whose voice is as bold and piercing as a King of Lions!"; (4) The sound of the one currently being described, who stood on the peak of Mount Kelāsa and shouted: "I am Āḷavaka!"
272:
The roar of the Yakkha general Āḷavaka: Thus, there are four great sounds that are heard throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. Indeed, when these four great sounds are uttered as shouts and cries, it seems as if they are being proclaimed while standing at every single gateway of all the cities and villages in the whole of Jambudīpa.

Due to the power and majesty of the Yakkha Āḷavaka, the Himavanta mountains, which are three thousand yojanas in extent, trembled and shook.

Thereafter, the Yakkha Āḷavaka (as described in the section on the victory over Māra the son of a deity in Volume II, page 287 of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas) harassed and attacked the Buddha with the nine types of great weapons (please refer back to Volume II, page 287). Although he harassed and attacked with these nine great weapons, he was unable to make the Buddha flee to another place. Therefore, he himself led and commanded a great fourfold army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, which was a terrifying and diverse mixture of various spirits and ghosts (bhūta and peta) holding various weapons, and marched towards the Buddha.

Those spirits and ghosts performed various kinds of transformations and terrors, shouting "Seize him! Kill him!" as if they were overwhelming the Buddha from the sky above. However, those spirits and ghosts...
273:
...just as flies do not dare to land on a red-hot iron ball, they did not dare to approach the Buddha.

Even though they did not dare to approach him, unlike Vasavatti Māra who retreated soon after arriving with his great army just before the Buddha attained Enlightenment at the Mahābodhi throne, they did not retreat in a short time but continued to harass him for half the night.

## The Final Throw with the Dussāvudha Weapon

Thus, because the Yakkha Āḷavaka was unable to make the Buddha tremble even by displaying various terrifying objects for half the night, he thought, "It would be well if I were to release the Dussāvudha celestial cloth weapon, which no one can conquer."

## The Four Great Weapons

There are four greatest weapons in the world. They are:
(1) The Vajira weapon of Sakka, King of Devas,
(2) The Gadā (iron club) weapon of the Great King Vessavaṇa,
(3) The Nayana (glance) weapon of King Yama,
(4) The Dussāvudha (celestial cloth) weapon of the Yakkha Āḷavaka.

(1) To elaborate: If Sakka, King of Devas, were to become angry and hurl the Vajira weapon at the summit of Mount Sineru, it would pierce through the Great Mount Sineru, which is 168,000 yojanas deep, and pass out through the bottom.
274:
(2) The Gadā weapon, which was hurled in the past when the Great King Vessavaṇa (while still a worldling) was angry, would cause the heads of thousands of Yakkhas to fall off like baskets and then return to Vessavaṇa's hand to rest in its original place.

(3) If King Yama, the lord of hell, were to look with a wrathful glance, thousands of Kumbhaṇḍa deities would perish, crackling like sesame seeds placed in a red-hot iron pan.

(4) If the Yakkha Āḷavaka were to become angry and hurl the Dussāvudha celestial cloth weapon into the sky, there would be a drought for twelve years. If he were to hurl it onto the ground, all grass, trees, and so forth would wither instantly and would not be able to grow again for twelve years. If he were to hurl it into the ocean, all the water in the ocean would dry up like a drop of water in a red-hot pan. If he were to hurl it at a mountain like Mount Sineru, the mountain would break into pieces and be destroyed.

(This is the account of the four great weapons).

After thinking thus, the Yakkha Āḷavaka took off the Dussāvudha celestial cloth weapon, which possessed such great power and was used as an upper robe, and stood holding it, thinking, "I shall now hurl it."

At that time, the deities living in the ten thousand world systems mostly thought, "Today the Buddha will discipline the fierce Yakkha Āḷavaka; we shall listen to the Dhamma at that place of discipline," and they quickly assembled. Besides the deities who wished to hear the Dhamma, those who wished to see the battle also assembled.
275:
In this way, the entire sky was filled with deities.

Then, the Yakkha Āḷavaka moved around, ascending higher and higher in the vicinity of the Buddha, and hurled the Dussāvudha celestial cloth weapon towards the Buddha. That Dussāvudha weapon hurled by the Yakkha Āḷavaka made a terrifying sound in the sky like a thunderbolt, emitting clouds of smoke and burning with bright flames. When it reached the Buddha, in order to break the pride of the Yakkha, it became a foot-wiping cloth (pādapuñchanī) and fell at the Buddha's feet.

Seeing that event, Āḷavaka became like a bull with broken horns, or like a poisonous cobra or king cobra whose fangs had been extracted. Deprived of his power and without any masculine pride, his banner of conceit fell. He wondered, "Even the Dussāvudha weapon cannot overwhelm or oppress the monk Gotama. What is the reason?" Then he realized, "The monk Gotama is one who dwells in Mettā (loving-kindness). This is the root cause. Now, I will speak provocative words to this monk Gotama and make him lose his Mettā." Having thought thus, he approached within earshot of the Buddha and said:

"O monk Gotama... why have you entered my palace without my permission and sat in the midst of my harem like the master of the house? To enjoy another's property that has not been given, and to sit mingled with women, is it not improper for one who is a monk? Therefore,
276:
if you, monk Gotama, are one who stands in the Dhamma of a monk, (O monk Gotama... leave my palace right now)."

(In this collection of words spoken by the Yakkha Āḷavaka, only the essential words in the parentheses ( ) were recited at the Council; the remaining words are the detailed explanation from the Commentary).

Then the Buddha (knowing the nature of the Dhamma that a fierce person cannot be disciplined by responding with fierceness—indeed, just as putting bear's gall on the nose of a fierce and wicked dog only makes it more fierce and wicked, so too a fierce and wicked person becomes more fierce and wicked when responded to with fierceness; in truth, a fierce person can only be disciplined with a gentle method) accepted Āḷavaka's words with very pleasant speech, saying, "Very well, friend Āḷavaka," and stepped out of the palace.

Then the Yakkha Āḷavaka thought, "This monk Gotama is indeed very easy to talk to; he left with just one word. I have been fighting all night for no reason against this monk Gotama who is so easy to make leave." He became one with a softened mind, but then thought again, "Even now, it is not certain. Did he leave because he is easy to talk to, or did he leave because he was angry? I shall test him again." Then he said, "O monk Gotama... come in."

Then the Buddha, in order to let the thought "He is a monk who is very easy to talk to" be firmly established in Āḷavaka's mind with a gentle
277:
disposition, again spoke pleasant words, saying, "Very well, friend Āḷavaka," and entered the palace again.

The Yakkha Āḷavaka, wishing to test repeatedly whether he was truly easy to talk to, said for a second and third time, "Go out," and "Come in." The Buddha, in order to make Āḷavaka's mind softer and softer, complied with everything he said. (How great is His Great Compassion!) If He had not complied with what the Yakkha said, the naturally fierce mind of the Yakkha would have become increasingly fierce and would not have been a fit vessel for the Dhamma teaching. Therefore, just as in a worldly example, a naughty little child who is crying and behaving badly is cared for and encouraged to be good by giving him what he wants and following his preferences, so too the Buddha (the Great Mother of the three worlds) wished to care for and encourage the Yakkha Āḷavaka (the naughty, fierce child) who was crying with the 'crying' of the defilement of anger, and thus complied with all that the Yakkha said.

To use another example: Just as a nurse coaxes a naughty child who will not suckle by giving him something and then feeds him sweet, cool milk, so too the Buddha (the Great Nurse of the three worlds), in order to feed the Yakkha Āḷavaka (the naughty child) the sweet, cool milk of the Supramundane Dhamma (Lokuttara Dhamma), wished to coax him by
278:
complying with what the Yakkha Āḷavaka (the naughty child) desired, and thus He complied with all that he said.

To use another example: Just as a man who wishes to fill a crystal jar with Catumadhu (the fourfold sweet) first wipes and washes the inside of the crystal jar to make it clean, so too the Buddha, wishing to fill the crystal jar of the Yakkha's mind with the Catumadhu of the Supramundane Dhamma, and wishing to wipe and wash away the stain of anger from within the crystal jar of the Yakkha's mind, complied with the Yakkha's words up to three times by leaving and entering the palace. (It was not out of fear that He complied).

Thereafter, the Yakkha Āḷavaka thought, "This great monk is truly easy to talk to. When I say 'Go out,' he leaves with one word; when I say 'Come in,' he enters with one word. It would be well if I were to make this great monk exhausted all night in this way (by making him go out and come in) and then, seizing him by his feet, hurl him to the other side of the Ganges River." Having formed this wicked intention, he said for the fourth time, "O great monk... go out."

Then the Buddha, knowing the wicked thought of the Yakkha Āḷavaka, and knowing that if He spoke as follows, the Yakkha, seeking what to do next, would think of asking questions, and that such asking of questions would be an excellent reason for preaching the Dhamma, said: "Friend Yakkha... in your mind, such..."
279:
“Because of your evil intent, I shall not leave the mansion. Do whatever you must do,” the Buddha said.

At that time, before meeting the Buddha, the yakkha Āḷavaka used to think whenever he saw ascetics or wanderers with psychic powers traveling through the sky, “Is this mansion made of gold, or is it one of silver or rubies? I shall go and see that mansion now.” When they arrived at his mansion, he would ask them questions. If they could not answer, he would torment them by making them distracted and insane, by splitting their hearts, or by seizing them by their feet and flinging them to the other side of the river Gaṅgā. How did he torment them?

The answer is: Yakkhas make people distracted and insane in two ways: (1) by showing terrifying forms, and (2) by crushing the heart-base (hadayavatthu). Among these two methods, the yakkha Āḷavaka knew that ascetics and wanderers who possessed psychic powers and attainments would not be frightened by terrifying forms. Therefore, he did not use the first method. Instead, using his celestial power, he created a subtle form, entered the bodies of those ascetics and wanderers (possessors of psychic power), and crushed their heart-base. At that time, the mental continuum of those possessors of psychic power could not remain stable. When their mental continuum could not remain stable, they became distracted and insane. He also split the hearts of those distracted and insane ascetics and wanderers. Saying, “Let these ascetics and wanderers who cannot answer the questions never come to my mansion again,” he would seize those possessors of psychic power...
280:
...by their two feet and fling them to the other side of the river Gaṅgā.

Therefore, remembering the questions he had asked in the past, he thought, “I shall now ask this ascetic Gotama questions in the same way. If he cannot answer, it would be good if I torment him by making him distracted and insane, splitting his heart, and seizing him by his two feet to fling him to the other side of the Gaṅgā.” Having thought so, he spoke rudely:

“O Great Ascetic Gotama, I shall ask you a question. If you cannot answer that question thoroughly, I will make your mind distracted and insane, or I will split your heart, or I will seize you by your two legs and fling you to the other side of the river.”

(If one asks where the questions that the yakkha Āḷavaka would ask originated from, the answer is: The parents of the yakkha Āḷavaka, who were celestial yakkhas, had attended upon the Buddha Kassapa and had learned eight questions along with their answers. Those parents had taught the eight questions along with the answers to the yakkha Āḷavaka since his childhood.

As a long time passed, the yakkha Āḷavaka forgot the answers. Then, Āḷavaka thought, ‘Let these questions (not be lost as time goes by).’ He had them written on a gold plate with pure cinnabar and kept them at the front of his mansion. Thus, these questions to be asked by the yakkha Āḷavaka were questions originating from a Buddha, being within the domain of a Buddha (buddha-visaya), which only Buddhas could answer.)
281:
When the Blessed One heard the words of that yakkha, since no one can cause harm to the gains offered to the Buddhas, the life of the Buddhas, their Omniscient Knowledge, or their physical radiance, and wishing to demonstrate the Buddha-power that is incomparable to anyone in the world, He said:

“Friend yakkha, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmas, and among the generation of mankind with its ascetics, brahmins, kings, and men, I see no one who could make my mind distracted and insane, or split my heart, or seize me by my two legs and fling me to the other side of the river. (Having thus restrained the yakkha's desire to torment Him, and wishing to encourage him to ask the questions, the Buddha continued:) Friend yakkha, nevertheless, ask whatever question you wish. (I shall answer your questions without leaving anything out.)”

Thus, He invited him with the invitation of the Omniscient Buddhas.

(In this regard, there are two types of invitations: the invitation of the Omniscient Buddhas and their Bodhisattas, and the invitation of other persons. Among them, the Omniscient Buddhas and their Bodhisattas invite boldly, saying, “Ask whatever you desire; I shall answer your questions without leaving anything out.” Other persons, however, invite more modestly, saying, “Ask, friend; having heard your question, if I know it, I shall answer.”)
282:
## The Questions of the Yakkha Āḷavaka and the Answers of the Blessed One

When the Blessed One had thus invited him with the invitation of the Omniscient Buddhas, the yakkha Āḷavaka then questioned the Blessed One with this verse:

Kiṃsūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭhaṃ,
Kiṃsu suciṇṇāṃ sukhamāvahāti.
Kiṃsu have sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ,
Kathaṃ jīviṃ jīvitamāhu seṭṭhaṃ. (1)

(O Ascetic, known by the lineage name Gotama!) Idha = In this world. Purisassa = Of a man. Seṭṭhaṃ = The most excellent and praised. Vittaṃ = Wealth. Kiṃsu = What is it? Suciṇṇāṃ = Well-practiced for a long time. Kiṃsu = What Dhamma. Sukhaṃ = The three types of happiness: human, celestial, and Nibbāna. Āvahāti = Can bring about great benefit? Rasānaṃ = Among all tastes that are pleasant. Kiṃsu = What kind of Dhamma. Have = Indeed. Sādutaraṃ = Is the most delicious and superior, pleasant to beings? Kathaṃ jīviṃ jīvitaṃ = What kind of living. Seṭṭhaṃ = Is called the most excellent and praised. Āhu = Have the virtuous ones, starting with the Buddhas, spoken of in sweet and gentle tones?

In this verse, in the first question, the inquiry “What is a man’s best wealth?” uses the method of excellence (ukkaṭṭha-naya), focusing only on the superior. Therefore,
283:
it should be specifically understood as meaning, “What is the best wealth of all beings, both men and women?” Thus, with this verse, he asked these four questions:

(1) What is the most excellent wealth in the world?
(2) What Dhamma, when practiced and developed for a long time, can lead to the three types of happiness: human, celestial, and Nibbāna?
(3) Among all tastes, what is the sweetest?
(4) Living by what Dhamma is the most excellent?

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to answer in the same way as the Buddha Kassapa had answered, spoke this verse of reply:

Saddhīdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭhaṃ,
Dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahāti.
Saccaṃ have sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ,
Paññājīviṃ jīvitamāhu seṭṭhaṃ.

(Āvuso = O yakkha named Āḷavaka!) Idha = In this world. Purisassa = Of all beings, men and women. Seṭṭhaṃ = The most excellent and praised. Vittaṃ = Wealth. Saddhā = Is indeed faith, both mundane and supramundane.

Suciṇṇo = Well-practiced for a long time. Dhammo = The ten wholesome courses of action,
284:
the meritorious Dhamma. (Or) the three types of merit: generosity (dāna), virtue (sīla), and mental development (bhāvanā). Sukhaṃ = The three types of happiness: human, celestial, and Nibbāna. Āvahāti = Can bring about great benefit.

Rasānaṃ = Among all tastes that are pleasant. Saccaṃ = The Dhamma of Nibbāna, known as the ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca). (Or) the truthful speech of verbal auspiciousness, which is speaking the truth and abstaining from false speech (virati-sacca). Have = Indeed, truly. Sādutaraṃ = Is the most delicious and superior, pleasant to beings.

Paññājīviṃ jīvitaṃ = The kind of living of one who lives by completing the noble practice of right conduct (sammā-paṭipatti) through wisdom. Seṭṭhaṃ = Is called the most excellent and praised. Āhu = Have the Noble Ones (ariyas), starting with the Buddhas, spoken of in sweet and gentle tones.

(In this regard, the meaning should be understood neither too briefly nor too extensively as follows: (1) Just as mundane wealth such as gold and silver brings about physical and mental happiness (kāyika-sukha and cetasika-sukha) through the use of various utilities, prevents suffering such as hunger, calms the distress of poverty, is the cause for obtaining jewels like pearls and rubies, and brings the praise of people; so too, the two types of faith, mundane and supramundane, bring about their respective mundane and supramundane resultant happiness. For those who practice correctly with faith as the forerunner, it removes and prevents various types of
285:
sufferings in the round of rebirths (saṃsāra), such as the suffering of conception and the suffering of aging. It calms the poverty of being devoid of virtues and reputation. It is the cause for obtaining the seven jewels of Dhamma, such as the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (sati-sambojjhaṅga).

“One who has faith, is endowed with virtue, and is possessed of fame and wealth, is honored in whatever place he frequents.” Because the Buddha taught this (in the Dhammapada, Verse 303, Pakinnaka-vagga, Story of Citta the Householder), faith can also bring the praise of all humans and devas. Therefore, the Blessed One taught the two types of faith, mundane and supramundane, as wealth.

This wealth of faith is the cause of the three types of prosperity—human, celestial, and Nibbāna—and is a type of treasure or wealth that is not shared with others. Furthermore, it is the root cause for obtaining mundane wealth and treasures like gold and silver. Indeed, only a person with faith can perform meritorious deeds such as generosity and obtain mundane wealth and treasures. The wealth of a person without faith only leads to disadvantage. Therefore, this wealth of faith is taught as the “most excellent and praised wealth.”

(2) When the ten wholesome courses of action (or the three Dhammas of dāna, sīla, and bhāvanā) are practiced and developed for a long time, they can bring human happiness, as they did for the sons of wealthy men like Soṇa and Raṭṭhapāla; celestial happiness, as for Sakka, the king of devas; and ultimately Nibbānic happiness, as for King Mahāpaduma and others.

(3) That which is licked and enjoyed is called a taste (rasa). Various tastes such as the taste of roots or the taste of stems cause the physical body to grow and flourish; they can only bring mundane happiness. The truth of abstinence (virati-sacca) and the truth of speech (vacī-sacca)...
286:
The tastes [of Dhamma] nourish and develop the mind through tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), and they also lead to supramundane happiness. The Fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala), known as the taste of liberation (vimutti-rasa), is exceedingly sweet and noble because it is infused with the peaceful taste of Nibbāna, the ultimate truth. Therefore, these three kinds of tastes—the ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca), the truth of abstinence (virati-sacca), and the truth of speech (vacī-sacca)—are the most excellent among all tastes.

(4) A person who lacks both the eye of mundane worldly wisdom and the eye of Dhamma wisdom is called a blind person (andha-puggala). A person who possesses only the eye of mundane worldly wisdom but lacks the eye of Dhamma wisdom is called a one-eyed person (eka-cakkhu-puggala). A person who possesses both types of wisdom eyes mentioned above is called a two-eyed person (dvi-cakkhu-puggala).

Among these three types of persons, the two-eyed (dvi-cakkhu) layperson lives by accomplishing household duties, taking refuge in the Triple Gem, practicing charity and sharing, observing the precepts, and practicing the Uposatha through wisdom. Similarly, a monk lives by accomplishing monastic duties such as purification of virtue (sīla-visuddhi) and purification of mind (citta-visuddhi) through wisdom. The Buddha and other Noble Ones (ariyas) declare that only the life of one who lives through such wisdom is praiseworthy and noble. (They do not declare the life of one who merely lives by breathing to be praiseworthy or noble). In this way, the meaning of the first verse should be understood in a balanced manner.

Having heard these four problems answered by the Blessed One, the yakkha Āḷavaka was greatly delighted and, wishing to ask the remaining four questions, recited this verse:
287:
Kathaṃsu tarati oghaṃ, kathaṃsu tarati aṇṇavaṃ.
Kathaṃsu dukkhamacceti, kathaṃsu parisujjhati.

(Venerable Sir, the Blessed One...) How [or by what Dhamma] does one cross the flood (ogha) of the fourfold torrents? How does one cross the ocean (aṇṇava) of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra)? How does one overcome suffering (dukkha) of the round? How is one purified (parisujjhati) from the defilements?

When he asked thus, the Blessed One, wishing to answer in the same manner as before, spoke this verse:

Saddhāya taratī oghaṃ, appamādena aṇṇavaṃ.
Vīriyena dukkhamacceti, paññāya parisujjhati.

(O Āḷavaka...) By faith (saddhā), one crosses the flood (ogha) of the fourfold torrents. By heedfulness (appamāda)—which is the repeated and continuous practice of the ten types of wholesome deeds—one crosses the ocean (aṇṇava) of the round of rebirths. By energy (vīriya), one overcomes the suffering (dukkha) of the round. By wisdom (paññā), one is purified from the defilements.
288:
(In this context: Although one who crosses the four floods can also cross the ocean of saṃsāra, overcome the suffering of the round, and be purified from defilements, (1) a person without faith (saddhā) cannot perform the 'crossing' which is the practice of meditation (bhāvanā) because they lack conviction in the good practice that leads across the four floods; thus, they cannot cross or overcome the four floods. (2) A person who is heedless by letting the mind wander among the five cords of sensual pleasure cannot cross the ocean of saṃsāra because they remain attached to those very sensual pleasures. (3) A person without effort (vīriya) who is lazy lives miserably, entangled only in unwholesome states. (4) A person without wisdom (paññā) does not know the right path of practice for purification from defilements and thus cannot be purified. Therefore, the Blessed One taught this answering verse by highlighting faith as the opposite of lack of faith, heedfulness as the opposite of heedlessness, energy as the opposite of laziness, and wisdom as the opposite of delusion.

Furthermore, in these four lines of the answering verse:

The faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is the fundamental root cause of the four factors for stream-entry (sotāpattiyanga), namely: (a) association with superior persons (sappurisa-saṃseva), (b) hearing the true Dhamma (saddhamma-savana), (c) wise reflection (yoniso-manasikāra), and (d) practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhamma-ppaṭipatti), which is the practice of tranquility and insight meditation leading to the nine supramundane states. (Only when there is faith can these four factors for stream-entry arise; only when these four factors arise can the Path of Stream-entry be attained). Therefore, by the first line of the answer, "Saddhāya taratī oghaṃ" (By faith one crosses the flood), the Buddha showed the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) and the Stream-winner (sotāpanna) who crosses the flood of views (diṭṭhogha).
289:
The Noble Stream-winner, being endowed with heedfulness (appamāda)—the constant practice of developing wholesome states—completes the second path. Except for one more rebirth in this human world, they cross the ocean of saṃsāra rooted in the flood of existence (bhavogha) which was not yet crossed by the Path of Stream-entry. Therefore, by the second line of the answer, "Appamādena aṇṇavaṃ" (By heedfulness one crosses the ocean), the Buddha showed the Path of Once-returner (sakadāgāmi-magga) and the Once-returner (sakadāgāmī) who crosses the flood of existence (bhavogha).

The Noble Once-returner, through energy (vīriya), completes the third path and overcomes the suffering of the sensual realm (kāma-dukkha) associated with the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha), which was not yet overcome by the Path of Once-returner. Therefore, by the third line of the answer, "Vīriyena dukkhamacceti" (By energy one overcomes suffering), the Buddha showed the Path of Non-returner (anāgāmi-magga) and the Non-returner (anāgāmī) who crosses the flood of sensual desire (kāmogha).

The Noble Non-returner, being free from the mire of sensual desire, completes the wisdom of the fourth path, which is absolutely pure from defilements, through the extremely pure wisdom of insight (vipassanā-paññā). They abandon the great impurity of ignorance (avijjā) which was not yet abandoned by the Path of Non-returner. Therefore, by the fourth line of the answer, "Paññāya parisujjhati" (By wisdom one is purified), the Buddha showed the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga) and the Arahat (arahant) who crosses the flood of ignorance (avijjogha).

At the conclusion of this answering verse, which culminated in the Fruit of Arahatship, the yakkha Āḷavaka was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
290:
## After becoming a Stream-winner
## Questions asked by Āḷavaka Yakkha

Now, the yakkha Āḷavaka, taking up the term 'wisdom' (paññā) taught by the Blessed One in the fourth line of the answer, "Paññāya parisujjhati" (By wisdom one is purified), and acting as a Noble Stream-winner, wished to ask questions through his own intellectual intuition concerning both mundane and supramundane matters. Thus, he recited this six-line verse:

Kathaṃsu labhate paññaṃ, kathaṃsu vindate dhanaṃ.
Kathaṃsu kittiṃ pappoti, kathaṃ mittāni ganthati.
Asmā lokā paraṃ lokaṃ, kathaṃ pecca na socati.

(Venerable Sir, the Blessed One...) By what cause does one gain (labhate) both mundane and supramundane wisdom (paññā)? By what cause does one obtain (vindate) both mundane and supramundane wealth (dhana)? By what cause does one attain (pappoti) fame and a good reputation (kitti)? By what Dhamma does one bind or acquire (ganthati) friends (mittāni)? When one has passed (pecca) from this present world (asmā lokā) to the next world (paraṃ lokaṃ),
291:
by what Dhamma does one not grieve (na socati) or become distressed?

(With this verse, Āḷavaka Yakkha asked these five questions:
1. The cause for gaining wisdom,
2. The cause for obtaining wealth,
3. The cause for attaining fame and reputation,
4. The cause for acquiring friends,
5. The cause for not grieving after passing from this life to the next).

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to clearly show Āḷavaka Yakkha that both mundane and supramundane wisdom can be obtained through four causes (wishing to answer the first question), spoke this verse:

Saddahāno arahatāṃ, dhammaṃ nibbānapattiyā.
Sussūsaṃ labhate paññaṃ, appamatto vicakkhaṇo.

(O Āḷavaka...) One who has faith (saddahāno) in the Dhamma of the Arahats—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples—which consists of the ten types of righteous conduct and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that lead to the direct attainment of Nibbāna; who is attentive (sussūsaṃ), listening and recording with respect in the presence of the wise; who is heedful (appamatto), possessing intense and constant mindfulness; and who is discerning (vicakkhaṇo), being able to distinguish between
292:
well-spoken and ill-spoken words—such a person gains (labhate) both mundane and supramundane wisdom (paññā).

(By this verse, the Blessed One intended to answer that these four factors are the causes for gaining wisdom:
(1) Faith (saddhā),
(2) Attentiveness/Desire to learn (sussūsā),
(3) Heedfulness (appamāda),
(4) Discernment (vicakkhaṇā).

To clarify further: The Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples reached Nibbāna through the ten types of righteous conduct (sucarita) in the initial stage and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) in the later stage. Therefore, these ten righteous conducts and thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are called the good Dhamma for reaching Nibbāna. Only a person who has unwavering faith (saddhā) in this collection of Dhamma can gain both mundane and supramundane wisdom.

However, such gain is not possible through faith alone. Indeed, a person who has developed faith must further cultivate the factor of attentiveness (sussūsā)—which includes approaching the wise, performing major and minor duties for them, and listening attentively to the Dhamma they teach—in order to gain both mundane and supramundane wisdom. (The meaning is: after believing in the Dhamma that leads to Nibbāna, one must approach teachers and preceptors at appropriate times and serve them with major and minor duties. By doing so, the teachers and preceptors will be pleased, and when they teach the Dhamma, one must listen with focused attention. The aforementioned acts of approaching teachers and performing duties...)
293:
Listening attentively to the Dhamma taught by teachers and preceptors = these are briefly called 'sussūsā' (the desire to hear/attentive listening). It means that only a person with such sussūsā can attain the two types of wisdom: mundane and supramundane.

A person who has faith and listens attentively must also be endowed with two further qualities: 'appamāda' (heedfulness/mindfulness) and 'vicakkhaṇā' (discernment/investigation between blameless 'subhāsita' speech and blameworthy 'dubbhasita' speech). Only then can they attain mundane and supramundane wisdom. Without these four—saddhā, sussūsā, appamāda, and vicakkhaṇā—one cannot attain these two types of wisdom.

The causal connection between these four qualities and supramundane wisdom is as follows: (1) Through faith (saddhā), one practices the conduct that leads to wisdom; (2) through attentive listening (sussūsā), one respectfully hears the good Dhamma that causes wisdom; (3) through heedfulness (appamāda), one does not lose or forget the Dhamma that has been heard and noted; (4) through discernment (vicakkhaṇā), one notes the Dhamma without excess or deficiency and without distortion, thereby expanding one's intellectual wisdom. (Alternatively: (2) through sussūsā, one respectfully listens to the good Dhamma; (3) through appamāda, one retains the heard Dhamma without forgetting; (4) through vicakkhaṇā, one contemplates the profound meaning of the retained Dhamma). When these four qualities are repeatedly cultivated, one gradually realizes the ultimate truth of Nibbāna, reaching the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala). Thus, it should be well noted that supramundane Path-wisdom and Fruit-wisdom arise because of these four qualities.

Having thus answered the first question, the Blessed One, wishing to answer the second, third, and fourth questions in order, spoke this verse:
294:
Wishing to answer the three questions in order, He spoke and taught this verse:

Patirūpakārī dhuravā, uṭṭhātā vindate dhanaṃ.
Saccena kittiṃ pappoti, dadaṃ mittāni ganthati.

(O friend Āḷavaka...) One who acts appropriately (patirūpakārī) to acquire both mundane and supramundane wealth according to the place and time; one who is responsible (dhuravā) and does not abandon his duty through mental energy; and one who is industrious (uṭṭhātā) and exerts physical effort—such a person can surely acquire (vindate) both mundane and supramundane wealth (dhanaṃ). (With the first half of this verse, He answered that through these three causes—acting suitably for the time and place, having mental energy, and having physical energy—one can obtain both types of wealth). Through the auspicious word of verbal truth (saccena), one can attain (pappoti) fame (kittiṃ) as "This person is a speaker of truth, a speaker of reality." Through the truth of the ultimate goal, Nibbāna (saccena), one can attain fame as "This person is a Buddha, this person is a Paccekabuddha, this person is a Noble Disciple." (With this third line of the verse, He taught the answer to the third question). One who gives (dadaṃ) what others need without stinginess, with a clear and joyful heart, binds (ganthati) friends (mittāni).
295:
One can fulfill this. (With this fourth line of the verse, the answer to the fourth question was taught).

(In this regard, how mundane wealth is obtained through appropriate action and being endowed with both physical and mental energy can be understood through the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka, where a man became wealthy with two hundred thousand in four months starting from a dead mouse.

How supramundane wealth is obtained can be understood through the story of Mahā Tissa Thera. To clarify: In Sri Lanka, the elderly Mahā Tissa Thera resolved to live only in three postures—sitting, standing, and walking. While performing his duties, when sloth and torpor (thina-middha) approached, he would soak a straw head-rest in water, place it on his head, and enter water up to his neck to dispel the sloth and torpor. Practicing the Dhamma in this way, he reached the fruit of Arahatship after twelve years).

Having thus answered the first four questions by a method combining both mundane and supramundane aspects concerning both laypeople and monks, the Blessed One now wished to answer the fifth question specifically for laypeople and spoke this verse:

Yassete caturo dhammā, saddhassa gharamesino.
Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, sa ve pecca na socati.

For a faithful (saddhassa) householder seeking the welfare of the home (gharamesino), in whom (yassa) these four qualities exist: truthfulness (saccaṃ), wisdom (dhammo), both physical and mental energy (dhiti), and generosity/liberality (cāgo).
296:
These four qualities (ete caturo dhammā) exist (santi). That person (sa/so) who is endowed with these four qualities, indeed (ve), after passing away (pecca) and reaching the next world, does not grieve (na socati), does not worry, and does not fade away.

Having thus answered the fifth question, the Blessed One, wishing to encourage the ogre Āḷavaka, spoke this verse:

Ingha aññepi pucchassu, puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe.
Yadi saccā damā cāgā, khantyā bhiyyodha vijjati.

(O Āḷavaka, the ogre...) I, the Buddha, encourage you. If you think there exists (yadi vijjati) in this world (idha) any quality superior (bhiyyo) to the two truths taught by me (saccā) that leads to fame; or superior to the wisdom of self-control and discernment (damā) that leads to mundane and supramundane wisdom; or superior to generosity (cāgā) that leads to gaining friends; or superior to the quality of patience consisting of physical and mental energy (khantyā) that leads to mundane and supramundane wealth; or any quality superior to these four—Sacca, Dama, Cāga, and Khantī—that prevents grief in the next life; then go and ask (pucchassu) other (aññepi) numerous (puthū) recluses and brahmins (samaṇabrāhmaṇe) such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others who falsely claim, "I am the All-knowing Buddha."
297:
"Go and ask other recluses and brahmins like Pūraṇa Kassapa, who falsely claim to be enlightened, to satisfy your mind."

When the Blessed One spoke thus, Āḷavaka the Ogre, having already removed the doubt that would lead him to ask Pūraṇa Kassapa and others (by means of his own Path of Stream-entry), spoke the half-verse: "Kathaṃ nu dāni puccheyyaṃ, puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe." Then, wishing to let those who did not know the reason for his not asking understand, he continued with the latter half-verse: "Yohaṃ ajja pajānāmi, yo attho samparāyiko."

Kathaṃ nu dāni puccheyyaṃ,
puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe.
Yohaṃ ajja pajānāmi,
yo attho samparāyiko.

(Venerable Sir... I, who am called Āḷavaka...) Now that I have removed all doubts with the sword of the Knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry, how could I ask (kathaṃ nu puccheyyaṃ) many other recluses and brahmins (puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe) like Pūraṇa Kassapa, who falsely claim "I am an Omniscient Buddha"? (I shall certainly not ask, as I am free from the defilement of doubt). I, Āḷavaka, starting from this very day, clearly understand (pajānāmi) through Your teaching the entire Dhamma that leads to wisdom,
298:
the Dhamma that leads to wealth, to fame, and to the binding of friends; and the entire Dhamma that ensures one need not worry upon reaching the next world (samparāyiko). (Therefore, I shall not ask others for satisfaction).

Now, Āḷavaka the Ogre, wishing to show clearly that the Blessed One is the source and origin of the knowledge and wisdom he has obtained, spoke this verse in address:

Atthāya vata me buddho,
vāsāyāḷavimāgamā.
Yohaṃ ajja pajānāmi,
yattha dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ.

The Buddha, the Supreme One of the world known as the Omniscient One, has indeed come (āgamā vata) to the royal city of Āḷavī to dwell (vāsāya) for the benefit (atthāya) and growth of mundane and supramundane happiness for me, Āḷavaka. I, Āḷavaka, now know that a gift given (dinnaṃ) to the Omniscient Buddha (yattha) yields great fruit (mahapphalaṃ), leading to prosperity in the human realm, the deva realm, and all the way to Nibbāna. That most excellent recipient of offerings, the Master of Omniscience—
299:
to the Buddha. 'Ajja' = Now. 'Pajānāmi' = I have come to know clearly.

Thus, the ogre Āḷavaka, having expressed through this verse that he had attained his own great benefit, now wished to clearly state how he would practice for the benefit of others, and he spoke this further verse:

'So ahaṃ vicarissāmi, gāmā gāmaṃ purā puraṃ.
Namassamāno sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammataṃ.'

(Bhante = O Blessed One, who shines like the sun...) 'So ahaṃ' = I, who am called Āḷavaka. (Ajja paṭṭhāya = From this day forth, having met the Buddha.) 'Sambuddhaṃ-sambuddhabhāvañca' = The true state of being a Buddha, endowed with the vast and glorious attributes of the Lord of the Three Worlds. 'Dhammassa' = Of the Dhamma, the ten-fold teaching consisting of the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna. 'Sudhammatañca' = The quality of being the excellent Dhamma that leads out of the cycle of suffering. 'Namassamāno' =

"The Lord of the Three Worlds, our supreme head, the Omniscient One whose wisdom is sovereign, the glorious Buddha is truly so... The Great Conqueror, the Inconceivable One, has clearly taught the ten-fold Dhamma, which is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, and endowed with the three-fold goodness... The eight-fold Noble Saṅgha also perfectly practices the three-fold training which is worthy of praise; I delight in these practices with a renewed heart"—

Thus, praising the various and wondrous qualities of the Three Jewels, with hands joined in reverence above his head, and becoming one who proclaims the way to Nibbāna with joyful devotion. 'Gāmā' = From one celestial village to another.
300:
gāmaṃ = to a celestial village; purā = from a celestial city; puraṃ = to a celestial city; vicariṣṣāmi = I shall wander and proclaim, O Lord.

In this manner—
(1) The conclusion of this verse spoken by the ogre Āḷavaka,
(2) The clearing of the night's darkness and the breaking of dawn,
(3) The emergence of the tumultuous sound of 'Sādhu' in applause,
(4) The arrival of the royal messengers at the ogre's mansion to deliver Prince Āḷavaka—
these four events occurred at the same time.

When the royal messengers heard the shouts of 'Sādhu', they reflected, "Such a sound of 'Sādhu' cannot occur for anyone else except the Buddhas; has the Exalted One perhaps arrived?" Upon looking, they saw the radiance of the Exalted One's body. No longer standing outside as before, they entered the mansion boldly. Inside the ogre's mansion, they saw the Exalted One seated and the ogre Āḷavaka standing with his hands joined in reverence.

Having seen this, the royal messengers said to the ogre Āḷavaka, "O Great Ogre, we have brought this Prince Āḷavaka to be offered as a sacrifice for you. If you wish to devour him now, devour him; if you wish to eat him, eat him;
301:
do as you see fit according to the circumstances," and they boldly handed the prince over into the hands of the ogre. At that time, because the ogre Āḷavaka had already become a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer), and especially because such words were spoken in the presence of the Exalted One, he felt great shame.

Then, the ogre Āḷavaka tenderly took the prince in both hands and said:

"Exalted Buddha, this prince has been delivered to me. I offer this prince to the Exalted One. The Buddhas protect the world of beings for their welfare. Exalted Buddha, may the Lord Buddha accept this Prince Āḷavaka for his welfare and happiness."

Thus he requested and offered him to the Exalted One. He also recited this verse:

Imaṃ kumāraṃ satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ,
sabbaṅgupeṭaṃ paripuṇṇabyañjanaṃ.
udaggacitto sumano dadāmi te,
paṭiggaha lokahitāya cakkhuma.

Cakkhuma = O Exalted One endowed with the five eyes. (Ahaṃ = I, your disciple named Āḷavaka). Udaggacitto = with an exultant and joyful heart. Sumano = with a happy mind. Satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ = endowed with the complete signs of a hundred merits from the past.
302:
Sabbaṅgupeṭaṃ = endowed with all limbs, large and small. Paripuṇṇabyañjanaṃ = having a perfect and complete physical form. Imaṃ kumāraṃ = this prince named Āḷavaka. Te = to You, Lord. Dadāmi = I give with faith and clarity. (Tvaṃ = You, Lord). Lokahitāya = for the increase of the welfare of the world of beings. Paṭiggaha = please accept out of compassion.

The Exalted One accepted the young Prince Āḷavaka with His hands. While accepting him, wishing to perform an act of blessing for the longevity, health, and welfare of both the ogre and the prince, He preached a verse with one line missing (intended to be completed). The ogre Āḷavaka completed that verse by adding a fourth line three times to establish the young prince in the Refuges. The verses preached and recited by the Exalted One and the ogre Āḷavaka in this manner of completion are as follows:

(Buddha)
Dīghāyuko hotu ayaṃ kumāro,
tuvañca yakkha sukhito bhavāhi.
abyādhitā lokahitāya tiṭṭhatha,
(Yakkha)
ayaṃ kumāro saraṇamupeti buddhaṃ. (1)

(Buddha)
Dīghāyuko hotu ayaṃ kumāro,
tuvañca yakkha sukhito bhavāhi.
abyādhitā lokahitāya tiṭṭhatha,
(Yakkha)
ayaṃ kumāro saraṇamupeti dhammaṃ. (2)

(Buddha)
Dīghāyuko hotu ayaṃ kumāro,
tuvañca yakkha sukhito bhavāhi.
abyādhitā lokahitāya tiṭṭhatha,

ayaṃ kumāro saraṇamupeti saṅghaṃ. (3)

(Buddha) Ayaṃ kumāro = may this prince named Āḷavaka. Dīghāyuko = be long-lived. Hotu = may it be so. Yakkha = O lay disciple ogre named Āḷavaka. Tuvañca = you also, lay disciple ogre. Sukhito = be endowed with both physical and mental happiness. Bhavāhi = may it be so. (Tumhe = may both of you, the prince and the ogre). Abyādhitā = being free from all ninety-six kinds of diseases. Lokahitāya = for the welfare of many people. Tiṭṭhatha = remain for a long time.

Sukhito = be endowed with both physical and mental happiness. Bhavāhi = may it be so. (Tumhe = may both of you, the prince and the ogre).
