305:
The Exalted One said, "Nurture this young prince until he grows up, and then you must give him back to me," and He handed the young prince back into the hands of the royal messengers.

## Becoming Known as Hatthaka-āḷavaka
The prince's original name was "Āḷavaka". As mentioned, on the day the ogre Āḷavaka was tamed, the young prince passed successively from the hands of the messengers to the hands of the ogre, from the hands of the ogre to the hands of the Exalted One, and from the hands of the Exalted One back to the hands of the messengers. Therefore, he became known by the name "Hatthaka-āḷavaka". (He is also called Hatthakāḷavaka).

Seeing the royal messengers returning carrying the young prince, all the people they met, such as farmers and forest workers, asked in fear, "How is it? Did the ogre Āḷavaka not want to eat the prince because he was too small?" and so on. The royal messengers replied, "Friends, do not be afraid; the Exalted One has made him safe," and recounted the entire event.

Then, shouting "Sādhu! Sādhu!", the entire city of Āḷavī was filled with a single tumultuous roar, saying, "The Exalted One has made him safe! The Exalted One has made him safe!" while facing towards the direction of the ogre Āḷavaka's dwelling.
306:
When it was time for the Exalted One to enter for alms, the ogre Āḷavaka took the bowl and robes and accompanied the Exalted One halfway before returning to his celestial mansion.

## The Great Festival of Realizing the Dhamma
Afterwards, the Exalted One wandered for alms within the city of Āḷavī. When the meal was finished, He sat on a noble Buddha-seat prepared at the foot of a quiet tree near the city gate. At that time, King Āḷavaka along with his ministers and army, as well as the citizens of Āḷavī, went together to the presence of the Exalted One. After paying homage and sitting around Him, they asked, "Exalted Buddha, by what means did You tame and liberate such a fierce and cruel ogre?"

To the king and the citizens of Āḷavī, the Exalted One began the discourse from the start of the ogre Āḷavaka's attack, saying, "In this way, he caused nine kinds of weapon-showers to fall; in this way, he performed terrifying acts; in this way, he asked me questions; and in this way, I answered the questions and preached the Dhamma to that ogre." He explained the details and preached the aforementioned Āḷavaka Sutta, which consists of twelve (12) verses, once again. At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths and were liberated.
307:
## Constant Offerings to the Deity
Thereafter, King Āḷavaka and the citizens of Āḷavī built a new mansion for the ogre Āḷavaka near the existing shrine of King Vessavaṇa, and they established constant offerings to the deity (devatā-bali) complete with flowers, scents, and other offerings.

When Prince Āḷavaka reached the age of discretion, they told him, "Prince, you obtained your life because of the Exalted One. Go and serve only the Exalted One; serve also the Order of Monks (Saṅgha)," and they sent him to the presence of the Exalted One. The prince served the Exalted One and the Saṅgha, practiced the Dhamma, and before long, he was established in the Fruit of Anāgāmī (Non-returner). He mastered the entire Tipiṭaka and became a leader of five hundred lay followers. Later, when the Exalted One held an assembly to appoint disciples to titles of pre-eminence (Etadagga), He praised and conferred upon the Anāgāmī prince Hatthakāḷavaka the title of Etadagga for being the foremost in winning over an audience through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu).

## Here ends Chapter 33.
310:
she paid homage to the Buddha at Uttarā's house after He and the Sangha had finished their meal. On that very day, after listening to the Buddha's discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), specifically at the conclusion of the verse beginning with "Akkodhena jine kodhaፃ" (Conquer anger with non-anger), she attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). (This is just a summary; the detailed account will be provided in the section on the Sangha-ratana, specifically in the chapter on the laywomen Nandamātā and Uttarā).

The day after attaining the Fruit of Stream-entry, Sirimā invited the Sangha led by the Buddha and offered a great donation. From that day forward, she provided regular alms (nibaddha-dāna) to eight monks daily. Every day, eight monks whose turn it was would go to Sirimā's house for alms. The donor Sirimā would say, "Venerable sirs, please accept this ghee; please accept this milk," and with words of faith and devotion, she would fill the bowls of the eight monks. Consequently, the food received by a single monk from Sirimā's house was enough for three or four monks. Sirimā spent sixteen kahāpaፇas every day on these alms.

One day, a certain monk, who was one of the eight whose turn it was to receive alms at Sirimā's house, arrived at a monastery more than three yojanas away from Rājagaha after finishing his meal. Later in the evening, while this visiting monk was sitting in the place where he performed duties for the senior elder,
311:
his fellow monks asked him in a friendly manner, "Friend, where did you have your meal before coming here?" The visiting monk replied, "Friends, I have come after eating the regular alms-food provided by Sirimā to eight monks." When the monks asked again, "Friend, does Sirimā offer the food in a pleasing manner?" the visiting monk replied, "Friends, I cannot fully describe Sirimā's alms-food; it is prepared most excellently and exquisitely. The food received by one monk is enough for three or four. Moreover, seeing Sirimā herself is even more sublime than her offerings. Indeed, that woman Sirimā is endowed with such and such beautiful features and graceful limbs."

Upon hearing these words regarding Sirimā's virtues, a certain monk fell in love with her without even seeing her. Thinking, "I must go and see Sirimā," he told the visiting monk his seniority rank and asked about the current rotation of the Sangha for the meal. When the visiting monk replied, "Friend, if you go now, you will be the senior monk at Sirimā's house tomorrow and will receive the alms-food for eight," the monk immediately took his bowl and robes and departed. Although he could not reach Rājagaha that night, he traveled with great effort and arrived at the lottery hall (salāka-agga) just as dawn was breaking.
312:
Being the senior monk, he drew the lot for the alms-food for eight at Sirimā's house.

Notably, at the very time the monk who had eaten Sirimā's food the previous day was departing, a fatal illness had struck Sirimā's body. Thus, Sirimā had removed her usual ornaments and was lying on her bed. When Sirimā's maids saw the eight monks arriving after drawing the lots, they informed Sirimā. Since Sirimā was no longer able to take the bowls with her own hands, provide seats, or serve the monks as she had done before, she instructed her maids from her bed, "Dear ones, go and receive the venerable ones' bowls, provide them with seats, serve them rice gruel first, then offer them sweets, and when it is time for the main meal, fill their bowls to the brim."

The maids replied, "Very well, mistress," and invited the monks inside. They first served them rice gruel, then sweets, and when it was time for the meal, they filled the bowls with rice and curry. They then informed Sirimā. Sirimā said, "Dear ones, lift me up and carry me near the venerable ones; I wish to pay them homage." The maids lifted her and carried her to the monks. Because she could not stand normally, she paid homage to the monks with a trembling body.
313:
The monk who had fallen in love with Sirimā without seeing her stared intently at her and thought, "Even while ill, Sirimā's appearance is this beautiful. What must her beauty and splendor be like when she is free from illness, healthy, and adorned with all her ornaments?" At that moment, lust (rāga) arose and overwhelmed him, as if it had been accumulated for millions of years. He became oblivious to everything, unable even to eat his food. He took his bowl back to the monastery, covered it and set it aside, spread out his robe, and lay down flat. Even when his fellow monks pleaded with him, he could not be persuaded to eat; he remained there, fasting.

That very evening, Sirimā passed away. King Bimbisāra sent a message to the Buddha, saying, "Magnificent Buddha, Sirimā, the younger sister of the physician Jĩvaka, has passed away." Upon hearing this, the Buddha sent a message back to the King, saying, "Do not cremate Sirimā's physical remains yet. Have her body placed on its back in the cemetery where corpses are discarded, and have it guarded so that crows, dogs, jackals, and other animals cannot eat it." The King did exactly as the Buddha instructed.
314:
In due course, three days passed, and on the fourth day, Sirimā's physical remains became bloated and swollen. Maggots began to swarm and ooze from the nine openings of the body. The entire body cracked and began to seethe like a pot of boiling rice. Then, King Bimbisāra had a drum sounded throughout Rājagaha, announcing, "Except for children left to guard the houses, all people must come to view Sirimā's remains. Those who do not come will be fined eight kahāpaፇas." He also sent an invitation to the Buddha, saying, "I wish for the Buddha and the entire Sangha to come and view Sirimā's remains."

The Buddha addressed the monks, saying, "Let us go to view Sirimā's remains." The young monk who was infatuated with Sirimā had been lying there for four whole days, refusing to listen to anyone and fasting. The food in his bowl (received four days ago) had become rotten and the bowl was covered in filth. Then, a friend told the young monk, "Friend, the Buddha is about to depart to view Sirimā's remains." Although he was severely oppressed by hunger, as soon as the name "Sirimā" was mentioned, the monk afflicted by his mind jumped up quickly and asked, "Friend, what did you say?" When his friend replied, "Friend, the Buddha is about to go see Sirimā; will you also come?"
315: "Alright, I will go," he said, discarding the stale food, washing his bowl, and placing it in its bowl-bag, then followed along with the community of monks. The Blessed One, surrounded by the assembly of monks, stood to one side at the cemetery. The assembly of bhikkhunīs, the royal retinue, the male lay followers, and the female lay followers each took their places and stood to one side. When the assembly was complete, the Blessed One asked King Bimbisāra, "Great King, who is this woman?" The King replied, "Venerable Sir, she is the young woman named Sirimā, the sister of the physician Jīvaka." The Blessed One asked again to confirm, "Great King, is this Sirimā?" The King confirmed, "Yes, Venerable Sir." Then the Blessed One said: "Great King, if that is so, have it proclaimed throughout the city by beat of drum: 'Let those who desire Sirimā take her for a thousand kahāpaṇas.'" The King did as the Buddha instructed. Not a single person said "Yes" or "I will." The King reported, "Venerable Sir, there is no one who will take her." The Blessed One said, "Great King, if there is no one to take her for a thousand, then reduce the price." The King then had it proclaimed, "Let those who desire her take her for five hundred kahāpaṇas." Still finding no one who wanted her, he proclaimed, "For..."
316: "...two hundred and fifty, (etc.), two hundred, one hundred, fifty, twenty-five, ten, five, one kahāpaṇa, half a kahāpaṇa, a quarter, a mace, or even a single red bean; let those who desire Sirimā take her." Yet, there was still no one who wanted her. He then had it proclaimed, "Let those who desire her take her for free," but still, not a single person said "Yes" or "I will." The King reported, "Venerable Sir, even for free, there is no one to take her." Then the Blessed One said: "Monks, look at this woman (Sirimā) who was once so beloved and desired by many. In this very city of Rājagaha, people previously had to pay a thousand kahāpaṇas just to spend one day in her company. Now, even for free, there is no one to take her. Such a beautiful and valuable form has now reached a state of decay and destruction. Monks, look with the eye of wisdom at this physical body (attabhāva), which is constantly afflicted and unbearable." After saying this, he recited the following verse of Dhamma: "Passa cittakataṃ bimbaṃ, arukāyaṃ samussitaṃ. Āturaṃ bahusaṅkappaṃ, yassa natthi dhuvaṃ ṭhiti."
317: (Bhikkhave = O monks). Yassa = for such a physical body. Dhuvaṃ = a nature of stability or firmness. Ṭhiti = a nature of lasting endurance. Natthi = there is not even a bit. Cittakataṃ = adorned and prepared strangely and attractively with clothes, ornaments, flowers, and perfumes. Bimbaṃ = a collection of various large and small limbs, some long and some short, which leads to the delusion of beauty. Samussitaṃ = erected and held upright by three hundred bones. Āturaṃ = constantly afflicted and unbearable. Bahusaṅkappaṃ = much thought of and wrongly imagined as beautiful, worthy, or auspicious by the blind worldlings who lack the Dhamma and wisdom. Taṃ arukāyaṃ = that physical body which is like a great sore, unattractive and covered in loathsomeness, oozing from the nine openings. Passa—passatha = look at it repeatedly with the eye of wisdom. At the end of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation. That young monk who was infatuated with Sirimā also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). (This account is extracted from the Dhammapada Commentary, Volume 2, page 66, 11-Era Vagga, 2-Sirimā Vatthu. Regarding this story of Sirimā, what is mentioned in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, Volume 1, page 235, 1-Uraga Vagga, in the explanation of the 11-Vijaya Sutta, is also very inspiring and will be further presented).
318:
While that young monk was fasting and starving himself, Sirimā passed away and was reborn in the Yāma heaven as the chief queen of Suyama, the king of gods. Subsequently, the Buddha requested King Bimbisāra not to cremate Sirimā's body but to leave it in the cemetery where corpses are discarded. The Buddha, accompanied by a company of monks, including that infatuated young monk, went to view the physical remains. Likewise, the townspeople and King Bimbisāra also arrived there.

At the cemetery, the people said, "Friends, in the past, even with one thousand and eight kahāpaṇas, it was very difficult to get a turn to see and enjoy Sirimā. Now, there is no one who wants to look at her even for free."

The celestial queen Sirimā also arrived at the cemetery, escorted by five hundred celestial chariots. At that cemetery, the Buddha preached the Vijaya Sutta to the assembled humans and monks, and for the sake of disciplining that young monk, He preached this verse from the Dhammapada, beginning with "Passa cittakataṃ bimbaṃ" (Behold this adorned body).

(At this point, as the Dhamma essence is very profound, I shall present the Burmese translation of the Vijaya Sutta so that the devout readers of the Buddha's life may practice and reflect upon it in their hearts):—

## Burmese Translation of the Vijaya Sutta

(1) Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the body moves and stretches; this is the movement of the body.
319: Caraṃ vā = walking. Yadi = or. Tiṭṭhaṃ vā = standing. Nisinno vā = sitting. Uda = or. Sayaṃ vā = lying down. Samiñjeti = bending the various joints. Pasāreti = stretching them out. Esā = all these various movements and postures—walking, standing, sitting, lying, moving forward or backward, bending, and stretching. Kāyassa = of the physical body. Iñjanā = are merely movements. (This verse expresses the following meaning: In this body, there is no other person or being who walks, stands, (etc.), or stretches. In reality: (a) Know the mind that wants to walk, stand, sit, or sleep. (b) Because of the mind, the air element (vāyo-dhātu) pervades and fills the body. (c) When the air element is full, new matter (rūpa) appears, and the matter walks. (d) No person walks, "I" do not walk; know with wisdom that matter walks. (e) No person stands, "I" do not stand; know with wisdom that matter stands. (f) No person sits, "I" do not sit; know with wisdom that matter sits. (g) No person sleeps, "I" do not sleep; know with wisdom that matter sleeps. (h) No person bends, "I" do not bend; know with wisdom that matter bends. (i) No person stretches, "I" do not stretch; know with wisdom that matter stretches. According to this: (1) When the intention to walk arises, the air element born of that mind pervades the entire body. Because the air element pervades the body, the movement of the body toward the desired direction occurs. This means that distinct material phenomena (rūpa) appear in the form of walking toward another place. Such a succession of material phenomena...
320: ...occurring through the movement of walking is what is called "walking" by worldly designation (loka-paññatti). (2) Similarly, when the intention to stand arises, the air element born of that mind pervades the entire body. Because the air element pervades the body, the upright posture of the body occurs; this means the successive arising of distinct material phenomena in an upward position. Such a succession of material phenomena occurring through the movement of standing is what is called "standing" by worldly designation. (3) Similarly, when the intention to sit arises, the air element born of that mind pervades the entire body. Because the air element pervades the body, the lower part of the body bends and the upper part remains upright; this means distinct material phenomena appear through the bending of the lower body and the uprightness of the upper body. Such distinct material phenomena occurring through the movement of sitting are what is called "sitting" by worldly designation. (4) Similarly, when the intention to lie down or sleep arises, the air element born of that mind pervades the entire body. Because the air element pervades the body, the horizontal stretching of the body occurs; this means distinct material phenomena appear through the horizontal stretching movement. Such distinct material phenomena occurring through the horizontal stretching movement—the movement of lying down—are what is called "lying down" or "sleeping" by worldly designation. Likewise, regarding "bending" and "stretching," when the intention to bend or stretch arises, the air element born of that mind pervades the respective joints. Because the air element pervades them, the movement of bending or stretching the joints [occurs]...
321:
321
...comes into being; it means that specific material phenomena (rūpa-visesa) manifest through the modes of bending and stretching. Because these specific material phenomena occur through the modes of bending and stretching, they are referred to by the worldly convention (loka-paññatti) as "bending" or "stretching."

Therefore, the collection of all modes mentioned as worldly conventions—going, standing, sitting, lying down (sleeping), bending, and stretching—is merely the movement of this body. It means it is only the manifestation of specific material phenomena through those various modes. In this body, there is no other person, being, self, or soul (atta-jīva) who is capable of going, standing, sitting, lying down, bending, or stretching. This body is empty of any person, being, self, or soul who can go, stand, sit, lie down, bend, or stretch. In reality:

Cittanānatta-māgamma, nānattaṃ hoti vāyuno.
Vāyunānatta-to nānā, hoti kāyassa iñjanā.

Due to the diversity of the mind, the diversity of the air element (vāyo-dhātu) arises. Due to the diversity of the air element, various and diverse movements of this body occur. This is the ultimate (paramattha) meaning of this verse.

In this way, the Blessed One, through this first verse, clearly demonstrated the three characteristics: the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), the characteristic of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa), and the characteristic of non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa). The manner of demonstration is as follows:

Among the four postures (iriyāpatha)—going, standing, sitting, and lying down—bodily pain and suffering arise from remaining in one posture for a long time. To remove that bodily pain and suffering, one must change to another posture. (Bodily pain and suffering, which is the characteristic of dukkha, is concealed by the postures; or rather, it is covered by changing from one posture to another so that the characteristic of dukkha cannot manifest. Therefore, the wise have said, "Postures conceal the characteristic of suffering.")
322:
322
Thus, with the three lines of the verse beginning with "Caraṃ vā yadi vā tiṭṭhaṃ," the Blessed One showed the characteristic of suffering which is concealed by the changing of various postures. (Because of bodily suffering, one must change postures; thus, by describing the effect, which is the changing of various postures, the cause, which is bodily suffering or the characteristic of dukkha, becomes known.)

Similarly, because there is no standing, etc., at the time of going, the Blessed One, by teaching "Esā kāyassa iñjanā = All these various modes and collections of going, standing, sitting, lying down, moving forward, retreating, bending, and stretching are merely the movement of the body," showed the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa) which is concealed by continuity (santati).

To clarify further: the uninterrupted occurrence of mental and material phenomena is called continuity (santati). Because of this uninterrupted occurrence of mind and matter—continuity—the characteristic of impermanence, which is the cessation and destruction of those mental and material phenomena at their respective moments, is not seen. Based on this reason, the wise have said, "Continuity conceals the characteristic of impermanence." By teaching "Esā kāyassa iñjanā = All these various modes and collections of going, standing, sitting, lying down, moving forward, retreating, bending, and stretching are merely the movement of the body," He made the following meaning known:

"In each mode of posture, groups of similar mind and matter arise continuously. When one posture or mode changes, those mental and material phenomena also change in groups—that is, they cease and pass away."

Therefore, it should be understood that with this final fourth line, the Blessed One clearly showed the characteristic of impermanence which is concealed by continuity.

As stated previously, in the ultimate sense (paramattha-sabhāva), due to the mind that wishes to go, stand, sit, or lie down,
323:
323
the mind-born air element (cittaja-vāyo-dhātu) arises. Because that air element spreads throughout the entire body, specific material phenomena (rūpa-visesa) arise through the modes of going, standing, sitting, and lying down. It is only this occurrence that is called "going," "standing," "sitting," "lying down," "moving forward," "retreating," "bending," or "stretching" by way of worldly convention (loka-paññatti). In the ultimate sense, it is merely the arising of specific material phenomena due to the convergence of various causes. It means it is only the arising of specific material phenomena through the modes of going, standing, etc., due to the convergence of relevant causes of the body, which consists of both mind and matter.

Because they do not understand this point deeply, proponents of the self-doctrine (atta-vāda) say, "The soul-self itself goes, stands, sits, and lies down." According to their view, they speak of "the going, standing, sitting, and lying down of the soul-self." Regarding this, the Blessed One taught, "It is not the going, standing, sitting, or lying down of a soul-self; Esā kāyassa iñjanā = all these actions are merely the movement of the body, the mere manifestation of specific material phenomena through various modes due to the convergence of various causes."

## The Four Types of Compactness (Ghana)
In this context, there are four types of compactness: (1) Santati-ghana, (2) Samūha-ghana, (3) Kicca-ghana, and (4) Ārammaṇa-ghana.

(1) Among these four, the occurrence of preceding and succeeding mental and material phenomena in a way that they appear as a single solid entity, without any perceived gap or interval, being joined, connected, and massed together, is called Santati-ghana (compactness of continuity).

Here, "occurring without interval" means the succeeding phenomenon arises while the preceding phenomenon is at its moment of dissolution (bhaṅga-khaṇa), or (alternatively) the succeeding phenomenon arises immediately after the cessation of the preceding phenomenon. The great commentators (Ṭīkā-teachers) refer to this as "purima-pacchimānaṃ nirantaratā" (the state of being without interval between the preceding and succeeding phenomena). By occurring in such a way that no gap or interval is perceived,
324:
324
the aspect of arising is powerful and acts as if concealing, and because the aspect of passing away is not apparent, people collectively fall into delusion, misconception, and wrong perception, thinking, "The phenomenon seen now is the very same phenomenon seen before." This nature is evidenced by the "illusion of a circle of fire when a single burning stick is whirled around." (This is Santati-ghana).

(2) The occurrence of mental phenomena such as contact (phassa) and material phenomena such as the earth element (pathavī) within their respective mental and material clusters (kalāpa) in a way that they appear as a single ultimate reality, being joined, connected, and massed together as a single group, is called Samūha-ghana (compactness of grouping).

When mental and material phenomena occur, they do not arise as a single entity (nature/potency) alone. On the mental side, at least eight types arise (referring to eye-consciousness and the seven universal mental factors); on the material side, at least eight types also arise (referring to the octad-cluster of matter). The occurrence of at least eight such natural potencies joined, combined, and massed together so that they are perceived as a single natural potency is called Samūha-ghana. (This is Samūha-ghana).

(3) The various mental and material phenomena contained within each mental cluster and material cluster occur while performing and completing their respective functions. In such occurrence (for those without the eye of Abhidhamma wisdom), it is very difficult to know the specific functions, such as "this is the function of contact," "this is the function of feeling," "this is the function of perception," etc., or "this is the function of the earth element," "this is the function of the water element," "this is the function of the air element," "this is the function of the fire element," etc. The occurrence of mental and material phenomena massed together so that they appear as a single entity because their specific functions are difficult to distinguish is called Kicca-ghana (compactness of function). (This is Kicca-ghana).
325:
325
(4) The occurrence of various mental phenomena within a single mental cluster massed together in the mode of taking a single object, or the occurrence of various material phenomena within a single material cluster as a single object, so that they appear as a single ultimate reality (natural potency), being joined, connected, and massed together, is called Ārammaṇa-ghana (compactness of object). (This is Ārammaṇa-ghana).

In brief, the occurrence of numerous mental and material phenomena, which arise as causes and effects, in a way that they appear as a single entity because their distinctions in terms of time, nature, function, and object are difficult to know, is called respectively Santati-ghana, Samūha-ghana, Kicca-ghana, and Ārammaṇa-ghana. (This information regarding the four Ghana is extracted from the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Mūla-ṭīkā, page 60, and the Dhammasaṅgaṇī Anu-ṭīkā, page 66).

"Just as one looks for the spiciness within a chili seed as a distinct mental experience, so too must one look for the potency (satti) in ultimate reality (paramattha)."

According to this, only when one can see the natural potency (sabhāva-satti) of those various mental and material phenomena with the eye of wisdom does the vision reach ultimate reality. Only when the vision of wisdom reaches ultimate reality is compactness (ghana) broken. Only when compactness is broken can the wisdom of non-self (anatta) be obtained. If one does not see the natural potency with the eye of wisdom, the vision does not reach ultimate reality; if the vision of wisdom does not reach ultimate reality, compactness is not broken; if compactness is not broken, the wisdom of non-self cannot be obtained. Therefore, the wise have said, "Compactness conceals the characteristic of non-self."

In this first verse, the Blessed One, by teaching the fourth line, "Esā kāyassa iñjanā = All these actions are not the actions of a person, being, or soul-self; in truth, they are merely the occurrence or movement through the performance and completion of the respective functions of those various groups of mental and material phenomena," showed the nature of the characteristic of non-self which is concealed by compactness. (This subject matter is extremely profound and cannot be known by ordinary wisdom).

The first verse is finished.

326
In this way, the Blessed One, by demonstrating the three characteristics, taught the meditation on emptiness (suññata-kammaṭṭhāna) which is empty of the nature of permanence, happiness, and self. Then, to show the two kinds of foulness—saviññāṇaka-asubha (animate foulness) and aviññāṇaka-asubha (inanimate foulness)—He continued to teach the subsequent verses:

(2) Aṭṭhi-nahāru-saṃyutto,
taca-maṃsāvalepano.
Chaviyā kāyo paṭicchanno,
yathābhūtaṃ na dissati.

Kāyo = This body, called animate (saviññāṇaka), aṭṭhi-nahāru-saṃyutto = is bound, entwined, and connected with (three hundred) bones, (nine hundred) sinews that bind the bones, and (seven thousand) nerves that carry flavors. Taca-maṃsāvalepano = It is plastered with the thick inner skin of white color and (nine hundred) pieces of flesh. (Parama-duggandha-jeguccha-paṭikūlo = It is extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive). Kāyo = This body, called animate, chaviyā = by the outer skin (cuticle) of various colors, paṭicchanno = is covered and decorated, just as a house wall is painted with blue or other colors; yathābhūtaṃ = the true nature of foulness, na dissati = is not seen at all by the foolish who are blind to wisdom.

(The nature of this body is as follows: Just as the beams, rafters, crossbeams, and supports of a house are tied and bound with rattan vines so they do not move, so too the three hundred and sixty bones, which are the supports, are bound with nine hundred sinews, which are like rattan vines, so they remain stable without moving.)
327: It is bound and tied together. Just as a wall called bitti is plastered and smeared with cow dung and fine clay, it is smeared and plastered with nine hundred pieces and lumps of flesh. Over that, it is again wrapped and bound with thick skin, like a smooth plaster finish. These bones, nerves, lumps of flesh, and thick skin are naturally foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive. However, just as a house wall is painted and covered with various colors like blue, yellow, green, and red to make it look beautiful, these bones, nerves, flesh, and thick skin are covered by a very delicate outer thin skin, similar in color to a fly's wing (which, if peeled off and rolled up, would be only about the size of a jujube seed), having various hues like dark, golden, red, and white, resembling dyes. Therefore, those without the eye of wisdom do not see the true nature of impurity (asubha). This means that because it is wrapped and bound with thick skin stained with the dye of thin skin, the various internal impure parts (koṭṭhāsa), which are not apparent to people and are extremely unclean, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive, should be seen and scrutinized with the eye of wisdom. To show this, the Buddha continued to preach these verses: (3) Antapūro udarapūro, yakanapeḷassa vatthino. Hadayassa papphāsassa, vakkassa pihakassa ca. Through these two verses, the Blessed One showed that just as when cooking rice, the impurities of the rice-water rise with the foam, smear the rim of the pot, and slide down the outside, so too when the consumed food is cooked by the fire of the karma-born heat element (kammaja-tejo-dhātu), the impurities of the food rise and exit as eye-wax, etc., from the eyes and other openings, flowing outwards.) Now, there is that which is designated in the world as the noblest limb, the head. Wishing to show the impurity of this body again by the fact that even that head has no essence and is unclean, he preached this verse:

(7) Moreover, this head is hollow and filled with the brain. The fool, obscured by ignorance, regards it as beautiful.

'Atha' means moreover. 'Assa kāyassa' means of this body, called the animate body. 'Susiraṃ sīsaṃ' means the head is hollow. The section on Animate Impurity (Saviññāṇaka Asubha) is finished.
