Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the section on animate impurity, now speaks this verse to show inanimate (aviññāṇaka) impurity; (alternatively) even the body of a Universal Monarch is filled with such foulness. Therefore, having shown impurity in the state of success (sampatti-bhava), He now speaks this verse to show impurity in the state of failure or decay (vipatti-bhava):
335:
(8) And when it lies dead, swollen and discolored, cast away in the cemetery, even relatives lose their regard for it.

'Yadā ca' means and at which time. 'So kāyo' means that body (being devoid of the three things: life, heat, and consciousness). 'Mato' means having passed away and died. 'Uddhumāto' means being swollen like a leather bag filled with air after death. 'Vinīlaka' means having a discolored, blue-black appearance, the original complexion having faded. 'Susānasmiṃ' means at the edge of the cemetery where corpses are discarded. 'Apaviddho' means being cast away. 'Seti' means it must lie in the coffin. 'Tadā' means at that time. 'Ñātayo' means the close relatives and friends who loved the person before death. 'Anapekkhā' means they become devoid of regard, thinking, 'Truly, this person will never return to life again.' 'Honti' means they become so.

(In this verse: By the word 'Mato' (dead), the Buddha shows the nature of impermanence (anicca). By the word 'Seti' (lies), He shows that the person no longer has any effort or volition. By these two, He encourages the removal of the pride of life (jīvita-māna) and the pride of strength (bala-māna).

By the word 'Uddhumāto' (swollen), He shows the destruction of the physical form. By the word 'Vinīlaka' (discolored), He shows the destruction of the original skin complexion. By these two,
336:
He encourages the removal of pride based on the beauty of complexion and pride based on the beauty of physical form.

By the word 'Apaviddho' (cast away), He shows that there is nothing left to take or gain. By the word 'Susānasmiṃ' (in the cemetery), He shows the state of loathsomeness, such that it is not even fit to be kept inside a house. By these two, He encourages the removal of attachment as 'mine' and the removal of the perception of beauty (subha).

By the words 'Anapekkhā honti ñātayo' (relatives lose their regard), He shows that the relatives and friends who previously cherished the person no longer do so. By showing this, He encourages the removal of pride based on having many followers (parivāra-māna).

Thus, with this verse, the Blessed One shows inanimate (aviññāṇaka) impurity while the corpse is still intact).

Now, wishing to show inanimate impurity when the corpse is decaying, He spoke this verse:

(9) Dogs eat it, and jackals, wolves, and worms; crows and vultures also eat it, and whatever other living creatures there are.

'Naṃ kāyaṃ' means that body cast away at the edge of the cemetery. 'Suvānā ca' means domestic dogs. 'Siṅgālā ca' means jackals (wild dogs). 'Vakā' means hyenas or small leopards. 'Kimī' means worms and maggots. 'Khādanti' means they bite and eat. 'Kākā ca' means crows. 'Gijjhā ca' means vultures.
337:
'Khādanti' means they bite and eat. 'Aññေ' means others besides those mentioned. 'Ye ca pāṇino' means whatever other carnivorous creatures such as leopards, tigers, hawks, and kites. 'Santi' means they exist. 'Te ca pāṇino' means those creatures also. 'Khādanti' means they bite and eat.

The section on Inanimate Impurity (Aviññāṇaka Asubha) is finished.
**********
Thus, having shown the nature of this body through the power of the meditation on emptiness (suññata-kammaṭṭhāna) with the first verse 'Caraṃ vā yadi vā tiṭṭhaṃ', through the power of animate impurity with the six verses starting with 'Aṭṭhīnahārusamyutto', and through the power of inanimate impurity with the two verses starting with 'Yadā ca so mato seti'; and having shown the state of the fool by saying 'The fool obscured by ignorance regards it as beautiful' regarding this body which is truly devoid of permanence, happiness, and self, and is indeed impure—thus showing the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) led by ignorance—the Blessed One now speaks these verses to show the state of the wise person regarding such a body, and to show the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) led by the three full understandings (pariññā):

(10) Having heard the Buddha's word, the wise monk here understands it; for he sees it as it really is.

'Idha' means in this Dispensation of eight wonderful qualities. 'Buddhavacanaṃ' means this teaching of the Vijaya Sutta (otherwise known as the Kāyavicchandannika Sutta), which is the word of the Buddha. 'Sutvāna' means because of hearing it appropriately. 'Paññāṇavā' means endowed with the wisdom of insight (vipassanā).
338:
'So bhikkhu' means that monk, whether a worldling (puthujjana) or a trainee (sekha) practitioner. 'Hi yasmā' means because. 'Yathābhūtaṃ' means as it really is. 'Passati' means he sees with the eye of insight wisdom. 'Tasmā' means therefore. 'Naṃ kāyaṃ' means that body. 'Parijānāti' means he understands it distinctly through the three full understandings: full understanding of the known (ñāta), full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa), and full understanding by abandoning (pahāna).

In this context, the manner of knowing this body through the three full understandings is as follows:
Just as a clever merchant, after carefully examining various goods he intends to buy, first calculates with wisdom, 'If I buy at this price, the profit will be this much,' and after acting according to that calculation, then takes the capital along with the profit and sells or relinquishes those goods; in the same way, when a worldling or trainee practitioner observes and reflects with the eye of wisdom, 'The things truly existing in this body are only bones, sinews, etc. (explicitly mentioned in the Pali) and hair, body hair, etc. (not explicitly mentioned in the Pali),' he understands this body through full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā). When he observes, investigates, and decides with the eye of insight wisdom that 'The things in this body are only impermanence, suffering, and non-self,' he understands this body through full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā). When, after such investigation, he reaches the Noble Path and abandons the attachment and lust (chandarāga) for this body, he understands this body through full understanding by abandoning (pahāna-pariññā).

(In this regard: Although this body is obvious to everyone,
339:
if one does not hear the Buddha's word, one cannot understand aspects such as emptiness through the three full understandings; only by hearing the Buddha's word can one know them. To show the cause for knowing aspects like emptiness through the three full understandings, and to show that those with external (bāhiraka) views outside this Dispensation are unable to see in this way, He spoke these words: 'Sutvāna buddhavacanaṃ idha'.

Because this teaching of the Vijaya Sutta (or Kāyavicchandannika Sutta) was taught concerning the bhikkhunī Nandā Therī and a monk whose mind was corrupted by infatuation with the beauty of Sirimā; and because among the four assemblies, the assembly of monks is the most noble; and because only the assembly of monks stays constantly near the Buddha; and because He wished to show that anyone, whether monk or layperson, who reaches the practice of observing impurity and the practice of observing impermanence, suffering, and non-self is called a 'bhikkhu', He used the term 'bhikkhu'. He did not say 'bhikkhu' because only monks should know through the three full understandings. This meaning should be specifically noted).

Now, the Blessed One, wishing to show the manner of seeing 'as it really is' according to the words 'yathābhūtañhi passati', spoke this verse:

(11) As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this. Internally and externally, one should discard desire for the body.

'Idaṃ saviññāṇakāsubhaṃ' means this animate foul body (because it is not devoid of the three things: life, heat, and consciousness; just as it walks, stands, sits, and lies).
340:
'Tathā' means in the same way. 'Etaṃ' refers to that inanimate foul body now lying in the cemetery (which previously, before death, because it was not devoid of those three things, had the nature of walking, standing, sitting, and lying).

'Etaṃ' refers to that inanimate foul body now dead (which, because of the cessation and absence of those three things, does not have the nature of walking, standing, etc.). 'Tathā' means in the same way. 'Idaṃ saviññāṇakampi' means this animate foul body also (because of the cessation and absence of those three things, will not have the nature of walking, standing, etc. It will become so).

('Evaṃ' means in this way. 'Paṭipanno bhikkhu' means the wise one who, seeing the danger of the round of rebirth and the nature of the aggregates, practices). 'Ajjhattañca kāye' means in the internal body. 'Bahiddhā ca kāye' means and in the external body. 'Chandaṃ' means the desire and lust (chandarāga) of attachment. 'Virājaye' (or virājeyya) means one should be able to discard and become detached from it through the abandoning by cutting off (samuccheda-pahāna) of the fourfold Noble Path wisdom.

(In this verse, by reflecting on oneself and the dead corpse as being the same—'As this animate body of mine is, so that inanimate corpse was in the past'—one abandons the defilement of anger/lust (that would arise) regarding the external body.
341:
“As that is, so this will be” — by contemplating and comparing this living, conscious body of mine with that dead corpse, one abandons sensual lust (rāga) in the internal body.

By knowing through wisdom the manner in which both internal and external bodies, or in another way, both animate and inanimate bodies, can be viewed as equal, one abandons the lack of understanding of the nature of these two bodies, which is the defilement of delusion (moha).

(In this way, even during the stage of preliminary insight (vipassanā), by knowing and seeing according to reality, the three unwholesome roots — greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), and delusion (moha) — can be abandoned through substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna). Subsequently, through the sequence of the four paths (magga) above that insight, all desire and lust (chandarāga) can be abandoned without remainder through the abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). This is the intended meaning to be understood.)

Having thus shown the plane of the trainee (sekha), the Buddha now wished to show the plane of the non-trainee (asekha) and spoke this verse:

(12) Chandarāgaviritto so,
bhikkhu paññāṇavā idha.
ajjhagā amataṃ santiṃ,
nibbānaṃ padamaccutaṃ.

Idha = In this Dispensation (Sāsana) of eight wonders. Or — in this body which is conscious or unconscious, internal or external. Chandarāgaviritto = One who has abandoned, uprooted, and cleared away every single trace of desire and lust (taṇhā-chanda). Paññāṇavā = Possessing the wisdom of the Path of Arahantship. So bhikkhu = That Arahant who has reached the Fruit immediately following the Path (maggānantara-phala). Amataṃ = Free from death. Or — the most excellent taste of the deathless nectar. Santiṃ = The state where all formations (saṅkhāra) are stilled. Or — the most peaceful state characterized by peace. Nibbānaṃ = The state of liberation from craving (taṇhā).
342:
Accutaṃ = Having no falling away or death whatsoever. Padaṃ = Nibbāna, which is to be reached through the path-knowledge and so forth. Ajjhagā = Has reached.

(By this verse, it is shown that one who practices as described abandons this desire and lust (the group of defilements headed by chanda-taṇhā) and attains the two elements of Nibbāna.)

Thus, having taught the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) by way of the animate and inanimate, ending with the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna, the Buddha then wished to censure the dwelling in heedlessness (pamāda-vihāra), which acts as an obstacle to such a great and fruitful meditation, and spoke the final two verses with a concise teaching:

(13) Dvipādako'yaṃ asuci,
duggaṇdho parihārati.
nānākuṇapaparipūro,
vissavanto tato tato.

(14) Etādisena kāyena,
yo maññe uṇṇametave.
paraṃ vā avajāneyya,
kimanyatra adassanā.

Dvipādako = Having two legs. Ayaṃ kāyo = This human body. Asuci = Being full of impurities and utterly loathsome. Duggaṇdho = Being foul-smelling and having an unpleasant odor. Parihārati = Must be maintained daily by bathing, applying perfumes, and so forth. (Atha = Even though it is maintained daily in such a way). Nānākuṇapaparipūro = It is constantly filled with various and numerous kinds of carcasses.
343:
It remains filled with filth. Tato tato = From those nine openings, the pores of the skin, and the roots of the hair. Vissavanto = Even though one attempts to cover it by applying perfumes, wearing flowers, and repeatedly grooming, the effort is fruitless; saliva, eye-wax, sweat, snot, and earwax flow out in abundance and loathsomeness.

Etādisena = With such a body that is full of impurities and loathsomeness. Kāyena = With the body. Or — because of the body. Yo = Any foolish person, male or female, who does not take heed. Uṇṇametave = To be conceited, thinking proudly, "It is I." Maññe-maññeyya = One might think through craving as "my body," through conceit as "I am," and through wrong view as "my body is permanent." Paraṃ vā = And towards others. Avajāneyya = One might look down on them with contempt based on birth, name, clan, and such qualities. (Atra = In such uplifting of oneself and disparaging of others). Adassanā = Not seeing the Four Noble Truths as they really are. Anyatra = Apart from this. Kāraṇaṃ = Another cause. Kiṃ siyā = What else could there be?

(The meaning is that it is only because of not knowing the Four Noble Truths that one uplifts oneself and disparages others in such a way.)

At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths and were liberated. The celestial queen Sirimā attained the fruit of Non-Returning (Anāgāmi-phala). The monk who was attached to Sirimā was established in the fruit of Stream-Entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

The Burmese translation of the Vijaya Sutta is finished.
**********
344:
## Appendix to the Translation of Vijaya Sutta
## The Three Names
This sutta is known by three names: (1) Vijaya Sutta, (2) Kāyavicchandannika Sutta, and (3) Nanda Sutta. The reasons are:

(1)(2) It is called the Vijaya Sutta because it is the means to conquer (vijaya) the desire and lust (taṇhā-lobha) attached to the body. It is called the Kāyavicchandannika Sutta (or Kāyavicchindannika Sutta) because it is the means to cut off (vicchindana) the desire and lust attached to the body.

(3) The life story of the courtesan Sirimā is the occasion for the second preaching of this sutta. For the first occasion, the Buddha preached this sutta in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā. Therefore, this sutta is also called the Nanda Sutta.

To elaborate: This Vijaya Sutta was preached for the first time in Sāvatthī concerning the nun Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā. It was preached for the second time in Rājagaha concerning the courtesan Sirimā. The account of the second preaching has already been described. The background story (uṭṭhappatti) of the first preaching is as follows:

After the Buddha first visited the royal city of Kapilavatthu in due course, disciplined the Sakyan princes, and ordained Prince Nanda and others, he later (in the 5th vassa) granted permission for women to ordain.
345:
(1) Nandā, the sister of the Venerable Ānanda,
(2) Abhirūpanandā, the daughter of the Sakyan King Khemaka,
(3) Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā, the betrothed of Prince Nanda —
these three Sakyan princesses named Nandā also became nuns.

When these princesses became nuns, the Buddha was still residing in Sāvatthī. Among them, (2) Abhirūpanandā was so called because she was exceedingly beautiful. (3) Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā also saw no one equal to herself in beauty. Because both of these bhikkhunīs were intoxicated with the pride of their beauty, they thought, "The Buddha censures beauty; he shows the faults of beauty in many ways," and so they did not go to attend upon the Buddha, nor did they wish to see him.

(One might ask: why then did they become nuns? The answer is that they became nuns because they had no other refuge to rely on in the lay life.

To clarify further: The Sakyan prince who was the husband of the Sakyan princess Abhirūpanandā died on their wedding day. Then, her parents made her a bhikkhunī even though she did not wish it.

As for Janapadakalyāṇī Nandā, when the Venerable Nanda attained Arahantship, her hopes were cut off. She thought, "My lord Prince Nanda, my mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, and my other Sakyan relatives have all ordained. To live in the lay life as a householder apart from my relatives is very miserable." Finding no comfort in the life of a householder, she became a nun. Neither of them became nuns out of faith.)
346:
Thereafter, the Buddha, knowing the maturity of the wisdom of these two bhikkhunīs, said to the Great Mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, "All bhikkhunīs must come in turn to receive instruction." When their turn arrived, those two bhikkhunīs sent others to represent them. Then the Buddha had to say again, "When the turn comes, one must come in person. One must not send another."

Then one day, the nun Abhirūpanandā came to the Buddha to receive instruction. The Buddha caused her to feel spiritual urgency (saṃvega) by means of a created image of a woman, and said:

Aṭṭhīnaṃ nagaraṃ kataṃ, maṃsalohitalepanaṃ.
yattha jarā ca maccu ca, māno makkho ca ohito.

(Nande = Dear daughter Abhirūpanandā. Yathā = Just as. Karonti = People build. Nagaraṃ = A granary for storing grain. Ussāpetvā = By erecting. Kaṭṭhāni = Timbers. Vallibaddhaṃ = Bound with rattan. Mattikālepanaṃ = And plastered with mud. Tathā = So too). Nagaraṃ = This granary of a body. Kataṃ = Has been built by the carpenter of craving. Aṭṭhīnaṃ = By erecting three hundred bones. (Ussāpetvā = By erecting. Nhāruvinaddhaṃ = Bound and wrapped with nine hundred tendons). Maṃsalohitalepanaṃ = Plastered and adorned with nine hundred pieces of flesh and about a measure of blood.
347:
Yattha = In which house of the body. Jarā ca = Decay, the state of being old, worn out, and ripened. Maccu ca = Death, the falling away and passing. Māno ca = Conceit, the pride of thinking "It is I." Makkho ca = Hypocrisy, the erasing of others' gratitude. Ohito = Are stored and kept within. By this verse from the Dhammapada, and also:

Āturaṃ asuciṃ pūtiṃ,
passa nande samussayaṃ.
ugharantantṃ paggharantaṃ,
bālānam abhipatthitaṃ. (*)
animittañca bhāvehi,
mānānusayamujjaha.
tato mānābhisamayā,
upasantā carissasi.

Nande = Dear daughter Abhirūpanandā. Passa-passāhi = Look closely with the eye of wisdom. Samussayaṃ = At this body. Āturaṃ = Which is incessantly afflicted and painful. Asuciṃ = Which is impure. Pūtiṃ = Which is putrid. Uggharantaṃ = Which oozes and flows upwards. Paggharantaṃ = Which oozes and flows downwards. (Taṃ = That body). Abhipatthitaṃ = Is greatly desired and craved. Bālānaṃ = By fools.

(*) In the latter half of this verse in the Therīgāthā, it says "Asubhāya cittaṃ bhāvehi..."
348:
The text states: “Ekaggaṃ susamāhitaṃ.” According to the meaning of this passage: “Nandā (dear daughter Abhirūpanandā), behold (passa) with the eye of wisdom this body (samussayaṃ), which is afflicted (āturaṃ) by constant suffering and pain, impure (asuciṃ), and putrid (pūtiṃ). Develop (bhāvehi) the mind (cittaṃ) in the meditation on the foul (asubha) of a conscious body, which is one-pointed (ekaggaṃ) through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and well-concentrated (susamāhitaṃ) through attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi).

Nandā, also develop (bhāvehi) without ceasing the meditation on impermanence, suffering, and non-self, known as the ‘signless’ (animitta). Abandon (ujjhaha) the latent tendency of conceit (mānānusaya)—the notion of ‘I’ that has remained latent throughout the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra—by means of the path of eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). Then, because you have completely uprooted and abandoned the latent tendency of conceit through eradication, you shall live (carissasi) in peace (upasantā), with all the heat of the defilements extinguished.”

By giving this instruction and advice through these verses of the Therīgāthā, the Buddha established the bhikkhunī Abhirūpanandā in the Fruit of Arahantship. (This concludes the account of the Elder Nun Abhirūpanandā).
350:
(3) The group of devas and humans who take austerity as their measure (lūkhappamāṇika), placing great weight on the scarcity of the four requisites and the thinning of defilements, feel devotion upon learning how the Buddha, despite being a noble prince of the pure Sakyan kshatriya lineage, practiced extreme austerities (dukkara-cariyā) and lived with such meager requisites.

(4) The group of devas and humans who take Dhamma as their measure (dhammappamāṇika), placing great weight on virtues such as morality, concentration, and wisdom, feel devotion by investigating and reflecting on any one of the Buddha’s five peerless qualities: morality (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana).

In this manner, everywhere people were constantly praising the Buddha’s virtues, their mouths never tiring of the subject.

(A special note here: (1) If all beings are divided into three parts, two parts are those who take form as their measure (rūpappamāṇika)—that is 66 out of 100. (2) If all beings are divided into five parts, four parts are those who take sound as their measure (ghosappamāṇika)—that is 80 out of 100. (3) If all beings are divided into ten parts, nine parts are those who take austerity as their measure (lūkhappamāṇika)—that is 90 out of 100. (4) If all beings are divided into one hundred thousand parts, only one part consists of those who take Dhamma as their measure (dhammappamāṇika)—meaning only one in a hundred thousand people is a dhammappamāṇika.)
351:
No matter how many beings there are, they all fall into these four categories when divided this way.

Among these four groups of beings, those who lack devotion to the Buddha are few, while those with devotion are many. To further clarify: (1) For the rūpappamāṇika individuals, there is no form more conducive to devotion than the Buddha’s appearance. (2) For the ghosappamāṇika individuals, there is no sound more conducive to devotion than the Buddha’s natural voice and the sound of his fame. (3) For the lūkhappamāṇika individuals, there is no austerity more conducive to devotion than that of the Buddha, who abandoned soft Kāsi robes, golden bowls, and golden palaces suited for the three seasons to rely on refuse-heap robes (paṃsukūla), a stone bowl, and dwellings at the foot of trees. (4) For the dhammappamāṇika individuals, there is no virtue more conducive to devotion than the Buddha’s morality and other qualities, which are peerless in the entire world. Thus, the Buddha holds the entire world of beings (catuppamāṇika) as if grasping it in his hand. (These bracketed remarks are from the Abhidhamma Commentary, Vol. 3, pp. 80-81. The remaining text is from the Suttanipāta Commentary, Vol. 1, p. 234).

When the Elder Nun Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā arrived at the nunnery, she heard the people praising the Buddha’s virtues for many reasons. She thought, “These people praise my elder brother’s (the Buddha’s) virtues incessantly. Even if the Buddha were to preach to me about the faults of beauty all day long, how much could he possibly say?
352:
It would be good if I go with the other nuns, without showing myself, to behold the Buddha, listen to the Dhamma, and then return.” Having thought this, she told the other nuns, “Today, I too shall go to listen to the Dhamma.” The nuns were delighted, thinking, “This desire of Bhikkhunī Rūpanandā to visit the Buddha has arisen after a long time. Today, the Buddha will surely preach a diverse and wonderful Dhamma discourse on account of her.” They then took Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā with them.

The Buddha, knowing in advance that the Elder Nun Rūpanandā was coming, decided to remove her pride in her beauty using beauty itself—just as a man might use a thorn to extract a thorn, or use a cricket to lure out a cricket. By his psychic power, he created a vision of a young woman about fifteen or sixteen years old, exceedingly beautiful, standing near him and appearing to fan him.

Rūpanandā approached the Buddha with the other nuns, paid homage, and sat among the assembly of bhikkhunīs. As she gazed at the splendor of the Buddha’s physical form from his feet to his hair, and then saw the created figure of the woman fanning him, she thought, “Oh, how beautiful this young woman is!” She abandoned her own pride in her beauty and felt a strong attachment to the beauty of that created woman.
353:
Then, while preaching the Dhamma, the Buddha transformed that created woman to appear twenty years old. Indeed, a woman is only truly beautiful at sixteen; beyond that, she is not as beautiful. Thus, as she saw the beauty of the created woman decline through this transformation, Rūpanandā’s previous lustful attachment (chandarāga) toward the figure began to fade.

Thereafter, the Buddha successively transformed the vision into the appearance of a woman who had not yet given birth, one who had given birth once, a middle-aged woman, an old woman, and finally a hundred-year-old woman, grey-haired, toothless, leaning on a staff, and covered in moles. While Rūpanandā watched, he showed the death of that created old woman, followed by the body becoming a bloated corpse, and finally reaching a state of putrefaction that was utterly loathsome and repulsive.

Seeing this sequence of created forms, Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā reflected: “This process I have just seen is the same nature that applies to all beings, including myself.” Thus, the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) became established in her. Following this perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering (dukkha-saññā) and the perception of non-self (anatta-saññā) also became established and clear. The three realms of existence appeared to her as being without refuge, like a house engulfed in flames.

The Buddha, knowing that “Bhikkhunī Nandā’s mind has now entered into the practice of meditation,”
354:
preached these Dhamma verses to the Elder Nun Nandā in a way that was suitable and beneficial for her:

“Āturaṃ asuciṃ pūtiṃ, passa nande samussayaṃ.
Uggharantaṃ paggharantaṃ, bālānaṃ abhipatthitaṃ.
Yathā idaṃ tathā etaṃ, yathā etaṃ tathā idaṃ.
Dhātuto suññato passa, mā lokaṃ punarāgami.
Bhave chandaṃ virājetvā, upasantā carissasi.”

(For the meaning of the first verse, see page 347).

“Nandā (dear daughter Rūpanandā), just as (yathā) this internal body of yours has the nature of impermanence and so on, so too (tathā) does that (etaṃ) external body you see. Just as (yathā) that external body you see has reached the state of a bloated corpse, abandoning the various stages of youth and maturity, so too (tathā) will this (idaṃ) internal body of yours certainly become (bhavissati) a bloated corpse, abandoning all stages of youth and maturity. Behold (passa) the collection of these two bodies—internal and external—as consisting of elements (dhātuto) such as the earth element, and as being empty (suññato) of a self or anything belonging to a self. Do not come (mā āgami) again to the world (lokaṃ) of the aggregates of clinging. By relinquishing desire (chandaṃ) for the three realms of existence—the sensual, fine-material, and immaterial—
355: ...having removed craving and desire (taṇhā-chanda) by means of abandonment through eradication (samuccheda-pahāna)... you will live in peace and coolness. At the end of the verse, Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā Therī was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Thereafter, the Blessed One, wishing for Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā Therī to attain the higher paths and fruits, preached this Vijaya Sutta (as previously mentioned) accompanied by meditation on emptiness (suññata-kammaṭṭhāna). (The Blessed One preached this Vijaya Sutta to Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā Therī for the first time around the 5th or 6th Vassa. The second time he preached this Vijaya Sutta was in the 17th Vassa, concerning a monk who was infatuated with Sirimā). At the conclusion of the first preaching of this Vijaya Sutta, Janapadakalyāṇī Rūpanandā Therī was deeply moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "Oh, how foolish I have been! I did not come to attend upon my elder brother (the Buddha), who, out of great compassion, has preached such various Dhamma teachings specifically for me." Having been thus moved, she repeatedly contemplated that very Vijaya Sutta and diligently practiced the meditation on emptiness (suññata-kammaṭṭhāna), attaining the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahatta-phala) within two or three days. The supplement to the Burmese translation of the Vijaya Sutta is finished.
356:
## The Story of a Certain Lay Disciple (Ekaupāsaka-vatthu)
As previously mentioned, the Blessed One spent the 17th Vassa at the Veluvana Monastery in the city of Rājagaha. After converting and liberating devas, humans, and Brahmas who were ready for liberation through various Dhamma teachings such as the Vijaya Sutta, he traveled by stages at the end of the Vassa and arrived at the city of Sāvatthī, where he resided at the Jetavana Monastery. Then one day, while sitting in the Gandhakuṭī of the Jetavana Monastery, the Blessed One surveyed the world at dawn and saw a poor man from the city of Āḷavī. Knowing that this poor man possessed the merit from the past to attain the Path and Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga-phala), he traveled to the city of Āḷavī accompanied by five hundred monks. The people of Āḷavī, being civilized Buddhists with right view, respectfully invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for a meal. That poor man also heard the news that "The Buddha has arrived" and thought with joy, "I shall get to hear the Dhamma from the Buddha." However, a peculiar event occurred: on the very day the Buddha was to enter the city, one of the poor man's oxen broke its tether and ran away. The poor man thought, "What should I do? Should I search for the ox first, or should I listen to the Dhamma first?"
357: He decided, "I will search for the ox first and then listen to the Dhamma with a settled mind," and left home early to find the lost ox. The people of Āḷavī provided seating for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, offered the meal, and made arrangements for the preaching of the Dhamma of appreciation (anumodanā). The Blessed One thought, "I have traveled a journey of thirty leagues for the sake of this poor man. That poor man has gone into the forest to find his lost ox. I will preach the Dhamma only when that poor man arrives," and remained silent. The poor man found the lost ox only when the sun was high. After putting it back into the herd, he thought, "Even if there is no other service or meritorious deed of giving to perform at this time, I will at least pay homage to the Buddha." Although he was severely oppressed by hunger and thirst, he did not even think of going home but quickly came to the Buddha, paid homage with deep respect, and stood in a suitable place. When that man arrived and stood there, the Blessed One asked the steward of the offerings, "Layman, is there any leftover food or provisions after offering to the Saṅgha?" The steward replied, "Magnificent Buddha, there is plenty." The Blessed One then instructed, "Layman, if that is so, feed this man."
358: The steward seated the poor man in the very place designated by the Buddha and served him respectfully with rice porridge, snacks, and food. After eating the meal with relish, the poor man washed his mouth thoroughly. (Aside from this instance, there is no other place in the Tipiṭaka where the Blessed One himself gave instructions to "feed" a specific layperson). Having eaten the meal with relish, the poor man's hunger and distress were calmed, and his mind became tranquil and concentrated on a single object. Then, the Blessed One preached the gradual discourse to him: the talk on giving (dāna-kathā), the talk on virtue (sīla-kathā), the talk on heaven (sagga-kathā), the talk on the danger of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnavakathā), and the talk on the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma-ānisāṃsakathā). After that, he preached the Four Noble Truths. At the end of the discourse, the poor man attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and became a Stream-winner (Sotāpanna). The Blessed One, after preaching the Dhamma of appreciation, rose from his seat and departed. The crowd of people followed the Buddha to see him off and then returned to Āḷavī. While walking along with the Blessed One, the monks said: "Friends, look at the Buddha's action! In other places, there has never been such an instruction to feed a layperson. Today, however, as soon as he saw a poor man, he himself spoke and arranged for rice porridge and so on to be given."
359:
They spoke words of criticism and mockery. The Blessed One turned back and, while standing, asked, "Monks, what are you talking about?" Upon hearing the reason, he said, "Yes, monks, I have traveled the difficult journey of thirty leagues because I saw the past merit (upanissaya) of this poor lay disciple for attaining the Path and Fruit of Stream-entry. That poor man was extremely hungry; he had been wandering in the forest searching for his lost ox since early morning. I considered that if I were to preach the Dhamma (without feeding him), he would not be able to penetrate and understand the Dhamma due to the suffering of hunger. Therefore, I acted thus. There is no other disease like the disease of hunger." He then preached this verse:
Jighacchā paramā rogā, saṅkhāra-paramā dukhā.
Etaṃ ñatvā yathābhūtaṃ, nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ.
"Bhikkhus, monks! Among diseases that oppress and cause pain, hunger is the greatest. (This means that among all diseases, hunger is the most severe. Indeed, other diseases may be completely cured with one treatment, or they may subside after days, months, or years. But the disease of hunger is not completely cured by eating once; one must give food and treat it every single day."
360: "Therefore, it means hunger is a more severe disease than others). Among the painful sufferings that are hard to endure, the five aggregates of conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are the greatest. (This means that as long as the five aggregates of conditioned things exist, suffering cannot cease; therefore, the collection of the five aggregates is the most severe suffering among all sufferings). Nibbāna, the unconditioned element (asaṅkhata-dhātu), is the highest bliss. (The bliss of feelings (vedayita-sukha) that worldly people enjoy is pleasant only while it exists and lasts; when it reaches the moment of dissolution, it is no longer pleasant. The bliss of peace (santi-sukha) which is Nibbāna, however, never has the nature of destruction and is always peaceful; therefore, it is the highest among all blisses). The wise person, knowing this matter as it truly is, realizes and attains the bliss of Nibbāna for himself." At the conclusion of the discourse, many beings attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. (From Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 2, Sukhavagga, page 169). The Story of a Certain Lay Disciple is finished.
361:
## The 18th Vassa: Residing at the Cāliya Mountain Monastery
## Residing for the Vassa
As mentioned, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma and liberated many people who were ready for liberation, such as the poor man from Āḷavī who searched for his lost ox, according to their temperaments. He spent the 18th (aṭṭhārasama) Vassa at the Cāliya Mountain Monastery, providing the medicine of the Deathless (Amata), the cool water of the Dhamma, to those ready for liberation. After the 18th Vassa at the Cāliya Mountain Monastery, he traveled by stages and arrived at Sāvatthī, where he was residing at the Jetavana Monastery.
## Preaching the Dhamma to the Weaver's Daughter
## The Story of the Weaver's Daughter (Pesakāradhītu-vatthu)
Three years before his current residence at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī after the 18th Vassa, the Blessed One arrived at the city of Āḷavī. The people of Āḷavī invited the Buddha and performed a great act of giving. When the meal was finished, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma of appreciation: "Laymen and laywomen! Develop the mindfulness of death (maraṇassati) thus: 'My life is not permanent; my death is certain. I must surely die. My life ends in death. Life is unstable; death is certain.'"
362:
362
The benefit of practicing mindfulness of death (maraṇassati) is this: Those who do not practice mindfulness of death, at their final hour, die in terror and lamentation, like a man who sees a snake and, having no stick or weapon, is filled with fear. Those who have practiced mindfulness of death, however, die courageously without fear or trembling at their final hour, like a man who sees a snake from afar, pins it down with a stick, catches it, and throws it away to a safe place, remaining at ease. Therefore, one should reflect and practice mindfulness of death as described."

Thus did he give this word of advice.

Upon hearing that Dhamma teaching, while other people went about their business with interest, the sixteen-year-old weaver's daughter thought, "Oh, how wonderful are the words of the Buddhas! It is proper for me to practice mindfulness of death." Thus, she practiced mindfulness of death alone, day and night. The Blessed One then departed from the city of Āḷavī and returned to the Jetavana monastery. The weaver's daughter continued to practice mindfulness of death constantly for a period of three years.

After three years had passed (while the Buddha was residing at the Jetavana monastery), one day at dawn, as the Blessed One surveyed the world of sentient beings, the young girl appeared within the net of his divine knowledge.
363:
363
Seeing the young girl, the Buddha further reflected, "What will happen?"

He perceived: "This young girl has practiced mindfulness of death for three years since the day she heard my teaching on maraṇassati. Now, I shall go to the city of Āḷavī and ask her four questions. When she answers, I will say 'Sādhu' (Well done) at each of the four points and then preach this Dhamma verse beginning with 'Andhībhūto ayaṃ loko'. At the conclusion of the verse, she will attain the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). Based on her, the Dhamma teaching will also be beneficial for the multitude of people."

Having thus determined, he departed from the Jetavana monastery accompanied by five hundred monks and, traveling by stages, arrived at the great monastery named Aggāḷava in the city of Āḷavī.

The people of Āḷavī, hearing the news that the Blessed One had arrived, went joyfully to the Aggāḷava monastery and invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for a meal.

At that time, the weaver's daughter also heard that the Blessed One had arrived. With a joyful heart, she thought, "My father in the Dhamma, my teacher, the Great Sage of the Gotama lineage, whose face is as beautiful as the full moon, has arrived!"
364:
364
"Three years ago, I had the opportunity to pay homage to the Blessed One, whose complexion is as radiant as pure gold. Now I shall have the good fortune to behold the golden body of my Father-Buddha again and to listen to the sweet and essence-filled sublime Dhamma."

Thus she reflected.

In particular, as her father was about to leave for the weaving workshop, he instructed her: "Daughter, I have set the cloth belonging to another on the loom. About a span's length remains unfinished. I shall finish that cloth today. Dear daughter, quickly wind the weft-thread and bring it to me."

The young girl thought: "I wish to listen to the Dhamma of the Blessed One. But my father has given me this urgent instruction. What should I do? Should I first listen to the Blessed One's Dhamma, or should I wind the weft-thread and deliver it to my father?" Then she further thought: "If I do not deliver the weft-thread, my father might strike or beat me. Therefore, I will wind the weft-thread, give it to my father, and only then listen to the Dhamma." She then sat on a small stool and began winding the thread.

The people of Āḷavī, having served and attended to the Blessed One with alms-food, held their water-vessels for the libation.
365:
365
They prepared to listen to the Anumodanā (thanksgiving) discourse. The Blessed One reflected: "I have traveled a journey of thirty yojanas for the sake of this young woman, the weaver's daughter. Even until now, she has not yet found the opportunity to listen to the Dhamma. Only when she has the opportunity to listen will I preach the Anumodanā discourse." Thus, he remained silent.

(Notably, when the Blessed One remained silent in this manner, no one in the world of beings, including the devas, dared to say anything such as "Please preach the Dhamma.")

The young girl, after winding the weft-thread and placing it in a basket, went toward her father. On the way, she stood at the edge of the assembly, gazing at the Blessed One. The Blessed One raised his neck and looked at her. By the manner of the Blessed One's gaze, she understood: "Even while sitting in the midst of such a large assembly, the Blessed One looks at me; he desires me to come into his presence."

She set down the basket containing the weft-thread and approached the Blessed One.

(Here, one might ask: Why did the Blessed One raise his neck to look at the young girl?

The answer is: The Blessed One reflected: "If this young girl goes to her father
366:
366
without hearing the Dhamma even from the edge of the assembly, she will die as a worldling (puthujjana) and her future destination will be uncertain. But if she comes to me and goes only after hearing the Dhamma, she will attain the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and, with a certain happy destination, will be reborn in the Tusita heaven-mansion." Furthermore, for that young girl, there was no escape from death on that day. Therefore, the Blessed One raised his neck and looked at her even from the midst of the assembly.)

Recognizing the Buddha's intent by that sign, she approached the Blessed One, entering within the range of his six-colored rays. She paid homage with deep respect and stood in a suitable place. When she stood there, the sequence of the Buddha's questions and the girl's answers was as follows:

(The Buddha)
"Young girl, where do you come from?"
(The girl)
"I do not know, Bhante."
(The Buddha)
"Where will you go?"
(The girl)
"I do not know, Bhante."
(The Buddha)
"Young girl, do you not know?"
(The girl)
"I know, Bhante."
(The Buddha)
"Young girl, do you know?"
(The girl)
"I do not know, Bhante."

In this way, the Blessed One asked the young girl four questions. The young girl, understanding the Blessed One's intention with her own deep meaning, gave her answers.
367:
367
The people, not understanding the meaning, spoke words of blame: "Look, friends, this weaver's daughter speaks whatever she likes with the Blessed One. Truly, when the Blessed One asked 'Where do you come from?', she should have answered 'I come from the weaver's house'. When asked 'Where will you go?', she should have answered 'I am going to the weaving workshop'."

The Blessed One silenced the people and asked:

"(1) Young girl, when I asked 'Where do you come from?', why did you answer 'I do not know, Bhante'?"

The young girl replied: "Exalted Buddha, you know that I have come from the weaver's house. However, when you asked 'Where do you come from?', you intended to ask 'From what state of existence did you come to be born as this weaver's daughter?' I do not know from what state of existence I came to be born here. Therefore, I answered 'I do not know, Bhante'."

When she explained thus, the Blessed One said, "Sādhu, Sādhu, young girl! You have indeed answered the question I asked." Having given the first 'Sādhu', he proceeded to the next level:
368:
368
"(2) Young girl, when I asked again 'Where will you go?', why did you answer 'I do not know, Bhante'?"

The young girl replied: "Exalted Buddha, you know that I am going to the weaving workshop carrying the weft-thread. However, you intended to ask 'When you pass away from this human world, in what state of existence will you be reborn?' I do not know in what state of existence I will be reborn after passing away from this life. Therefore, I answered 'I do not know, Bhante'."

When she explained thus, the Blessed One said, "You have indeed answered the question I asked," and gave the second 'Sādhu'. He then proceeded to the next level:

"(3) Young girl, that being so, when I asked 'Do you not know?', why did you answer 'I know, Bhante'?"

The young girl replied: "Exalted Buddha, I know the fact that I must die. Therefore, I answered 'I know, Bhante'."

When she explained thus, the Blessed One said, "You have indeed answered the question I asked."
369: "You have answered correctly, young girl," He said, giving the third "Sādhu." Then, proceeding further, He asked again: "(4) Young girl, if that is so, why did you say 'I do not know, Bhante' when I asked 'Do you know?'" The young girl replied, "Exalted Buddha, I only know that I must die; however, I do not know at what time—whether by night, day, morning, or so on—I shall die. Therefore, I answered 'I do not know, Bhante.'" When she had explained and answered thus, the Buddha said, "Young girl, you have indeed answered the very question I asked," and gave the fourth "Sādhu." Then, addressing the assembly, He said: "You do not understand even this much of the meaning of what this young girl has answered; you only know how to criticize. Indeed, those without the eye of wisdom are but blind (even if they possess physical eyes); those with the eye of wisdom are those who truly see." Having said this, He preached this verse: Andhībhūto ayaṃ loko, tanukettha vipassati. Sakuṇo jālamuttova, appo saggāya gacchati.
370:
Sādhavo = O virtuous assembly... Ayaṃ loko = This world of many beings. Andhībhūto = Is like a blind person who cannot see clearly due to the lack of the eye of wisdom. Ettha = Among this world of many beings. Tanuko = Only a few with sharp wisdom. Vipassati = Can contemplate and see the conditioned phenomena of mind and matter through the three characteristics (Anicca, Dukkha, Anatta). Jālamutto = Like a bird escaped from a hunter's net. Sakuṇo = A quail. Appo iva = Just as only a few escape. Tathā = Similarly. Appo = Only a few people with sharp wisdom. Saggāya = Reach the celestial realms and the bliss of Nibbāna. Gacchati = Arrive there through the support of merit.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the weaver's daughter was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). The discourse was also beneficial to the great multitude of people.

## The Fate of the Young Girl

That young girl then took the shuttle and went to her father. Her father was sitting at the loom, nodding off to sleep. When the girl inadvertently pushed the shuttle, it struck the edge of the loom, made a sound, and fell down.

The father, the weaver, woke up from his slumber and, following his habitual movement, pulled the shuttle. The shuttle, moving with excessive force, struck the young girl directly in the chest.
371: The young girl died right there and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. When the father, the weaver, looked at his daughter, he saw her lying dead, covered in blood. At that moment, great grief and sorrow arose in the father's mind. Then, the father thought, "No one other than the Buddha will be able to quench this fire of grief currently burning within me." Weeping bitterly, he went to the presence of the Buddha, reported the matter, and pleaded, "Exalted Buddha, please extinguish my fire of grief." The Buddha consoled the father, saying, "Lay disciple, do not grieve. Indeed, throughout the beginningless round of rebirths (Saṃsāra), the mass of tears you have shed when a daughter died is far greater than the drops of water in the four great oceans." He then preached the Anamataggiya Dhamma discourse. The father's grief diminished, and he requested the Buddha to ordain him as a monk. After receiving ordination, he practiced the Dhamma and soon attained the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahatta-phala). (From Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 2, 13-Lokavagga, page 111). The Story of the Weaver's Daughter ends. **********
373: ...Kukkuṭamitta, who made his living by killing deer using five hundred snares and five hundred stakes. He had killed five hundred animals, loaded a cart full of their meat, and was driving the cart into the city to sell the meat, sitting at the front of the cart. Upon seeing him, she felt a sense of attachment to the hunter. She handed over gifts to her maidservant and sent her with instructions: "Lady, go; give these gifts to that hunter, find out the time he will return, and then come back." The maidservant went, gave the gifts to the hunter, and asked, "At what time will you return?" The hunter replied, "I will sell the meat today and leave through such-and-such a gate early tomorrow morning to return." The maidservant, having heard the hunter's words, returned to the merchant's daughter and informed her of the matter. The merchant's daughter prepared the clothes, ornaments, and wealth she should take, and early the next morning, dressed in soiled clothes and carrying a water pot on her head as if going to the watering place with the other servants, she left the house. She went to the place mentioned by the hunter and stood waiting for his arrival. The hunter also drove his cart out of the city early in the morning. The merchant's daughter followed closely behind the hunter's cart. When the hunter saw her, he said, "O lady, I do not know whose daughter you are; do not follow me." The merchant's daughter replied, "You did not call me; I am following of my own accord. You just drive your cart quietly."
374:
When he spoke thus, the hunter repeatedly forbade the merchant's daughter as before. Then, the merchant's daughter said to the hunter, "O Lord, one should not forbid the arrival of fortune to oneself." At that moment, the simple hunter, realizing without doubt that the merchant's daughter was following him steadfastly, took her onto his cart and drove away.

The merchant's daughter's parents had people search for her here and there, and when she could not be found, they thought, "She must have died," and performed the ritual of offering food for the dead (matakabhatta) in her memory.

The merchant's daughter, living in union with the hunter Kukkaṭamitta, gave birth to seven sons. When those seven sons reached adulthood, she bound them in marriage.

## The Time for the Hunter Kukkaṭamitta's Family to Attain Liberation

Then one day, when the Blessed One surveyed the world of beings at dawn, he saw the hunter Kukkaṭamitta along with his seven sons and seven daughters-in-law entering the net of his knowledge. Considering "What is the reason?", he investigated further and saw the past merit (upanissaya) of those fifteen people for attaining the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). Early in the morning, he took his bowl and robes and went alone to the place where the hunter Kukkaṭamitta had set his snares. On that day, not even a single animal was caught in the snares.
375: The Buddha left His footprint near the hunter's snares and sat in the shade under a bush nearby. The hunter Kukkuṭamitta took his bow and arrows early in the morning and went to the place where he set his snares. As he inspected the snares one by one from the first, he did not find a single animal caught, but saw only the Buddha's footprint. At that moment, a thought arose in the hunter Kukkuṭamitta's mind: "Who could be wandering around, releasing the animals caught in my snares?" Even before seeing Him, he harbored ill-will toward the Buddha. As he went along, he saw the Buddha sitting under a bush ahead and thought, "This person must be the one releasing the deer caught in my snares. I shall kill him by shooting him with an arrow." He notched an arrow and pulled the bow with all his might. The Buddha allowed him only to notch and pull the bow, but not to release it. (He used His psychic power so that the hunter could only pull the bow but could not release the arrow). The hunter was unable to release his arrow, nor could he put it back down. He stood there like a stone statue, feeling as if his ribs were about to break, with saliva dripping from his mouth, in a state of extreme exhaustion. Then, the hunter's seven sons arrived at their father's place and said to their mother, "Our father is taking a very long time; what could be the reason for this delay?" The mother said, "Sons, to your father..."
376:
Having been ordered, "Go and follow them," the seven sons each took their bows and followed. They found their father, the hunter, standing still like a stone statue. Thinking, "This person (the Buddha sitting in the shade of a bush) must be our father's enemy," the seven sons each raised their bows and pulled the strings. However, by the psychic power of the Blessed One, they remained standing as if they were great stone statues, just like their father Kukkuṭamitta, exhausted and frozen.

Then their mother thought, "Why are my sons taking so long?" and followed them together with her seven daughters-in-law. When she saw the eight men, father and sons, standing like stone statues, she looked here and there, wondering, "At whom are these eight men aiming their bows?" She then saw the Blessed One. Raising both her arms, she cried out loudly, "Sons, do not kill my father!"

When the hunter Kukkuṭamitta heard his wife's voice, he thought, "Oh, I am ruined! This person is my father-in-law. Oh, I have committed a grave mistake!" The seven sons also thought, "This person is our grandfather. Oh, we have committed a grave mistake!" Then, Kukkuṭamitta, thinking, "This person is my father-in-law," developed a mind of loving-kindness. The seven sons also—
377:
—developed a mind of loving-kindness, thinking, "He is indeed our grandfather."

At that time, the mother of those seven sons, the treasurer's daughter, said to the eight men, "Quickly, discard your bows and pay homage to my father." Knowing that the minds of those eight people had become supple, the Blessed One allowed them to lower their bows. (This means that whereas he had previously used his psychic power to prevent them from lowering their bows, he now withdrew that power.) Those eight people paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Exalted Buddha, please forgive us," and sat down in a suitable place.

When they were all seated together, the Blessed One preached the graduated discourse (ānupubbīkathā) to the sixteen members of the hunter Kukkuṭamitta's family, namely: the talk on giving (dāna-kathā), the talk on virtue (sīla-kathā), the talk on heaven (sagga-kathā), the talk on the danger of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnavakathā), and the talk on the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma-ānisamsakathā). At the conclusion of the teaching, the hunter Kukkuṭamitta, along with his seven sons and seven daughters-in-law—fifteen people in total—were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Having assisted the hunter, his sons, and daughters-in-law in reaching the fruit of Stream-entry, the Blessed One went for alms in the city of Rājagaha and returned to the monastery after noon.

Then, the Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One, "Exalted Buddha, where did you go?" The Blessed One replied, "Ānanda, I went to the hunter Kukkuṭamitta."
378:
Venerable Ānanda asked again, "Exalted Buddha, have you made that hunter Kukkuṭamitta refrain from the evil deed of killing living beings? Have you disciplined and liberated him?" The Blessed One replied, "Yes, Ānanda, I have. That hunter Kukkuṭamitta, being the fifteenth member (along with his seven sons and seven daughters-in-law), has become established in unshakable faith, has completely abandoned doubt regarding the Triple Gem, and has become one who no longer commits the evil deed of killing living beings."

Then the monks interrupted and asked, "Exalted Buddha, does the hunter Kukkuṭamitta not also have a wife?" The Blessed One replied, "Yes, monks, he does. That housewife had already attained the fruit of Stream-entry while she was still a young maiden in her parents' house."

The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall:

"Friends, the wife of the hunter Kukkuṭamitta (the treasurer's daughter) attained the fruit of Stream-entry while she was still a young girl in her parents' house. She then followed that hunter to his home and had seven sons. When her husband, the hunter, commanded her, saying, 'Bring the bow, bring the arrows, bring the spear, bring the iron spit, bring the net,' she would bring and give those bows, arrows, and so on. The hunter, taking the bows and arrows given by his wife—a Stream-enterer—
379:
carried them out and committed the evil deed of killing living beings for many days. Friends, how is it? Do noble disciples who are Stream-enterers also commit the evil deed of killing living beings?"

Thus, the discussion arose. The Blessed One came to the Dhamma Hall and asked, "Monks, what subject are you discussing now that I have arrived?" When the monks replied, "We are discussing this matter (concerning the treasurer's daughter, the wife of the hunter Kukkuṭamitta)," the Blessed One said:

"Monks, noble disciples who are Stream-enterers do not commit the evil deed of killing living beings. The treasurer's daughter, the wife of the hunter Kukkuṭamitta, thinking, 'I have a duty to obey the words of my husband,' performed her duty and gave the bows, arrows, and so on that the hunter requested. That treasurer's daughter did not have even the slightest intention or thought such as, 'Let this hunter take these bows and arrows, go to the forest, and commit the evil deed of killing living beings.'

To illustrate with a simile: if there is no wound on the palm of the hand, the poison cannot burn the person who holds it. Similarly, for one who does not commit evil because there is no unwholesome intention, even if they bring and give bows, arrows, and so on, it cannot be called an evil deed."
380:
After saying this, the Blessed One, wishing to connect the preceding and following parts of the discourse, spoke this verse:

If there is no wound on the palm,
one may carry poison in one's hand.
Poison does not affect one without a wound;
there is no evil for one who does no evil.

Monks (bhikkhave), if there is no open wound or cut on the palm (pāṇimhi), poison (visaṃ) cannot burn, harm, or infect the hand that has no wound (abbaṇaṃ). Therefore (tasmā), one is able to carry poison with a hand that has no wound. In the same way (evaṃ), for one who does not commit (akubbato) a collection of evil deeds because of the absence of unwholesome intention, there is not even a trace of evil (pāpaṃ) merely by the act of giving a bow and so on (dhanu-ādi-dāna-mattena).

(Just as poison cannot burn or harm a hand without a wound, so too, even if one brings and gives bows, arrows, and so on, no evil can occur for one who does not commit evil due to the absence of unwholesome intention. It means that just as poison cannot infect or burn a hand without a wound, evil cannot follow the mind of such a person.)

At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth.

## The Past Merits of the Hunter Kukkuṭamitta's Family

At another time, the monks in the Dhamma Hall—
381:
—started a discussion: "(1) Friends, what was the past merit—the supporting condition (upanissaya)—of the hunter Kukkuṭamitta, along with his seven sons and seven daughters-in-law, for attaining the Path of Stream-entry? (2) For what reason were they born into a family of hunters?"

Then the Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, what subject are you gathered here discussing now?" When the monks reported the matter, the Blessed One preached the past karma of the hunter's family as follows:

Monks, in the distant past, when arrangements were being made to build a great relic stupa (dhātu-cetiya) for the Blessed One Kassapa, the people consulted one another, saying, "For this great relic stupa, what shall we use as mortar and what shall we use as water?"

Then, the thought arose in the minds of the people in that assembly to use orpiment and realgar as the mortar and sesame oil as the water. They agreed, and the group of people ground the orpiment and realgar into powder, mixed it with sesame oil, and used it as mortar to bind the bricks. They then gilded the interior of the stupa. For the exterior layer of bricks, they used only bricks made of solid gold. Each brick was worth one hundred thousand (kyat/units of currency).
382:
## Selecting the Chairman for the Enshrinement Ceremony

When the great stupa was completed enough to enshrine the relics, those people consulted one another, saying, "A large amount of money is needed for the enshrinement of the relics. Whom shall we appoint as the leader and chairman?"

Then, a treasurer living in a country village thought, "I shall be the leader and chairman," and donated ten million (one crore) for the relic enshrinement ceremony. Seeing the generous faith of that country treasurer, the citizens of the city mocked the city treasurer, saying, "This city treasurer is like a hidden termite, only collecting wealth. He is unable to become the leader and chairman in the building and worship of such a great relic stupa. The country treasurer, however, has generously donated ten million and has become the leader and chairman of the enshrinement ceremony."

When the city treasurer heard the words spoken by the people, he thought, "I shall donate twenty million and become the leader and chairman," and he donated twenty million.

The country treasurer then thought, "I alone shall be the leader and chairman of the enshrinement ceremony," and donated thirty million. In this manner, they continued to donate more and more, one-upping each other, until the city treasurer donated eighty million.

Notably, the country treasurer had only ninety million in his house. The city treasurer, however, had four hundred million in his house. Therefore—
383:
383
The village treasurer thought and reflected, "If I donate nine crores, this city treasurer will say, 'I shall donate ten crores.' At that time, (since I cannot keep up with him), my state of being penniless will become evident." He then said, "I will also contribute this much wealth, and together with my seven sons, seven daughters-in-law, and my wife, I will also accept the status of being servants to the great stupa." He then brought his seven sons, seven daughters-in-law, and his wife, the treasurer's lady, and donated the sixteen of them, including himself, to the great stupa.

The citizens and the general public unanimously decided and reached a consensus, saying, "Wealth can be acquired again in the future. However, this village treasurer is one who has surrendered himself along with his sons, daughters-in-law, and wife to the great stupa. Therefore, let this village treasurer be the chairman and head of the enshrinement ceremony." Thus, they appointed the village treasurer as the chairman.

In this way, those sixteen family members became the servants of the great stupa (servants of the Buddha). However, the citizens and the general public agreed to release those sixteen family members from servitude. Even though they were released, those sixteen family members continued to clean the great stupa and remained there until the end of their lives. After passing away from that life, they were reborn in the celestial realm.

While those sixteen people lived happily in the celestial realm throughout the interval between Buddhas (Buddhantara)—the period between Kassapa Buddha and our Buddha—
384:
384
When the era of the current Buddha's appearance arrived, the treasurer's lady passed away from the celestial realm and became a treasurer's daughter in the city of Rājagaha. Even as a young girl, that treasurer's daughter attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

(Adiṭṭhasaccassa pana paṭisandhi nāma bhāriyā. — Commentary) = The rebirth of a worldling (puthujjana) who has not realized the Four Noble Truths is a heavy burden. (Because they are not yet free from the danger of falling into lower realms, even if they are to be a person in their final birth (pacchimabhavika), they may still be reborn in a low-born family). Thus, when the celestial being who was the husband and master of that treasurer's daughter was reborn in the human world, he was reborn in a family of hunters. As soon as she saw that hunter, the element of love based on past craving (taṇhā-pema) arose and overwhelmed the treasurer's daughter. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke this verse:

Pubbe va sannivāsena, paccuppanna-hitena vā.
Evaṃ taṃ jāyate pemaṃ, uppalaṃ va yathodake.

Pubbe = In previous lives. Sannivāsena vā = Because of having lived together in close affection. Paccuppanna-hitena vā = Or because of performing beneficial services in this present life. Evaṃ = Through these two causes of association. Pemaṃ = The element of love, in its two forms as craving-love and metta-love. Jāyate = Arises and becomes manifest. (Kimi va = In what manner?). Uppalaṃ vā = Like a lotus. Aññaṃ vā = Or other...
385:
385
...flowers that grow in water. (Dve kāraṇāni = Depending on the two causes: water and silt. Nissāya = Relying on). Jāyate yathā = Just as they arise.

Because of that very love that had existed in the past, the treasurer's daughter followed him to the hunter's house. The sons also passed away from the celestial realm and took rebirth in the womb of that treasurer's daughter (their former mother). The seven daughters-in-law were also born in various families, and when they reached of age, they also arrived at the house of that hunter's family because of the love that had existed in the past.

In this way, those sixteen members of the hunter's family had together cleaned the great relic stupa of Kassapa Buddha in the past. By the power of that wholesome kamma, they attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) in this Dispensation.

This is the past kamma of the family of Kukkuṭamitta the hunter.
The Story of Kukkuṭamitta the Hunter ends.

## The Story of Ānanda the Treasurer
As previously mentioned, while the Blessed One was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery in the city of Rājagaha, having nourished and liberated those worthy of liberation, such as the family of Kukkuṭamitta the hunter, with the deathless medicine of the cool Dhamma, He departed from the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha surrounded by a company of monks. While traveling by stages on a Dhamma tour, He arrived at the city of Sāvatthī. While staying and residing at the Jetavana Monastery, He spoke the Dhamma teaching beginning with "Puttā matthi dhanaṃ matthi" concerning the treasurer Ānanda of Sāvatthī. The detailed account is as follows:

In the city of Sāvatthī, there was a treasurer named Ānanda who possessed a fortune of forty crores and was extremely stingy and miserly. Once every fortnight, that treasurer would summon his relatives and, in their midst, would advise his son named Mūlasiri at the three times of the day: "Dear son, do not think that this wealth of forty crores is much. One should not give one's existing property to others. One must cause new wealth to arise. Indeed, the wealth of a person who spends even a single kyat (kahāpaṇa) until it is gone will surely be exhausted one day. Therefore:

Añjanānaṃ khayaṃ disvā, upacikānañca ācayaṃ.
Madhūnañca samāhāraṃ, paṇḍito gharamāvase.

Tāta = Dear son. Añjanānaṃ = Of eye-ointments. Khayañca = The exhaustion through frequent rubbing. Upacikānaṃ = Of termites. Ācayañca = The anthill that grows large through frequent accumulation. Madhūnaṃ = Of bees. Samāhārañca = The honeycomb that grows large through frequent carrying. Disvā = Seeing these as examples. Paṇḍito = A wise person. Gharam = The household. Āvase—āvaseyya = Should live and strive so that old wealth does not fade and new wealth increases."
386:
He preached the Dhamma teaching beginning with "Putta matthi dhanaṃ matthi." The detailed account is as follows:

In the city of Sāvatthī, there was a millionaire named Ānanda who possessed forty crores of wealth but was extremely stingy and miserly. Every fortnight, he would have his relatives assemble, and in their presence, he would advise his son named Mūlasiri at the three times of the day: "Dear son, do not think this forty crores of wealth is much. You should not give your existing property to others; you must increase it with new wealth. Indeed, the wealth of one who spends even a single coin will surely be exhausted one day. Therefore:

Anjanānaṃ khayaṃ disvā, upacikānañca ācayaṃ.
Madhūnañca samāhāraṃ, paṇḍito gharamāvase.

Dear son, seeing the exhaustion of collyrium stones through frequent rubbing, the growth of anthills through the accumulation of termites, and the growth of honeycombs through the collection of bees, a wise man should dwell in a house, striving to prevent old wealth from fading and to increase new wealth."

Thus he gave counsel. Later, that millionaire Ānanda died while being attached to his wealth with greed and stained with the impurity of stinginess, without telling his son Mūlasiri about the five large pots of gold he had buried. He was reborn at the gate of that city of Sāvatthī...
387:
387
...thus he gave advice. At a later time, that treasurer Ānanda, without telling his son Mūlasiri about the five large jars of gold he had buried, died with his mind attached to wealth and stained by the defilement of stinginess. He took rebirth in the womb of an outcast (caṇḍāla) woman in a village of outcasts consisting of a thousand households at the gate of that city of Sāvatthī.

King Pasenadi of Kosala, having heard of the death of treasurer Ānanda, had the son Mūlasiri summoned to his presence and appointed him to the position of treasurer in his father's place.

Those thousand households of outcasts (laborers) had lived by working together for daily wages. From the time the former treasurer Ānanda, the miser, took rebirth, they no longer received their daily wages. They did not even get enough rice to be satisfied. Those outcast laborers said, "Now, even though we work, we do not get even a morsel of rice. There must be an unlucky, base person among us." They divided themselves into two groups and continued dividing until they reached the single house of the parents of that former miserly treasurer Ānanda. When it came to that single house, they said, "An unlucky, base person has arisen in our house," and they drove the mother of the former miserly treasurer Ānanda out of the house.

That mother, as long as the son was in her womb, obtained even a meager amount of food with great difficulty and hardship, and she gave birth to the son with great pain. The hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, and mouth—these body parts of the child—did not stay in their proper places but were distorted. Because the child was thus physically deformed, he was extremely ugly and difficult to look at, like a small mud-goblin. Even though this was so, the mother...
388:
388
...could not bear to abandon him. Indeed, a mother's love for the child who dwelt in her womb is very strong.

While the mother was raising the child with great hardship, on the days she took the child with her, she received nothing at all. On the days she left the child at home and went alone, she received her daily wages.

Later, when the child was old enough to be able to seek food on his own, the outcast mother placed a small bowl in the child's hand and said, "Dear son, because of you, we have reached great misery. Now, we are no longer able to continue raising you. Inside this city of Sāvatthī, there is rice arranged to be given to the destitute, travelers, and so on. Go and wander to beg for food where that rice is and support your life." Saying this, she abandoned the young son.

As the boy wandered from house to house begging for rice, he reached the place where he had lived when he was the treasurer Ānanda. Gaining the knowledge of recollecting past lives (jātissara-ñāṇa), he boldly entered his own house. When he entered through the first, second, and third gates, no one noticed or paid attention to him. At the fourth gate, however, the young children of the treasurer Mūlasiri saw the boy and, being terrified, wept loudly.

Then, the servants of the treasurer Mūlasiri, saying "You unlucky, base person," struck the boy and threw him out of the gate onto a rubbish heap. At that time, the Blessed One, while wandering for alms with the Elder Ānanda as his attendant monk...
389:
389
...arrived at that place. He looked at the Elder Ānanda, and when the Elder Ānanda asked about the matter, the Buddha revealed and spoke the entire sequence of the treasurer Ānanda's past and present circumstances.

The Elder Ānanda had the treasurer Mūlasiri summoned. At that time, a great crowd of people gathered. The Blessed One asked the treasurer Mūlasiri, "Lay disciple Mūlasiri, do you know this boy?" When he replied, "I do not know him, Bhante," the Buddha said, "This boy is your father, the treasurer Ānanda." When the treasurer Mūlasiri showed disbelief, the Buddha commanded, "Treasurer Ānanda, tell your son Mūlasiri about the five large jars of gold you buried." He had him reveal the five large jars of gold and thus made the treasurer Mūlasiri believe.

The treasurer Mūlasiri approached the Blessed One as his refuge (took the Three Refuges). Wishing to preach the Dhamma to the treasurer Mūlasiri, the Blessed One spoke this verse:

Puttā matthi dhanaṃ matthi,
iti bālo vihaññati.
Attā hi attano natthi,
kuto puttā kuto dhanaṃ.

Me = My. Puttā = Sons and daughters. Atthi = Exist. Me = My. Dhanaṃ = Wealth and property. Atthi = Exists. Iti = Thinking thus. Bālo = The fool. Vihaññati = Suffers and is exhausted by craving for sons and craving for wealth. Hi = Indeed. (Or) In truth. Attano = For oneself. Attā-attāpi = Even oneself...
390:
“Dukkhaparittāṇaṃ kātuṃ” = To provide protection from suffering. “Natthi” = It is not possible. “Puttā” = Children. “Kuto atthi” = How can they exist? “Dhanaṃ” = Wealth. “Kuto atthi” = How can it exist?

(The meaning is: Thinking, “I have children, I have wealth,” the fool suffers, becoming exhausted by the two types of craving—craving for children and craving for wealth. It means one suffers because of these two: putta-taṇhā and dhana-taṇhā. How does one suffer? One suffers by thinking, “My children have perished.” One suffers by thinking, “They are perishing.” One suffers by planning and thinking, “They will perish.” The same applies to wealth. Thus, one suffers through these six modes: three regarding children and three regarding wealth. Because of craving for children, one suffers by making various efforts day and night on water and land, thinking, “I shall support my children.” Because of craving for wealth, one suffers by engaging in farming, trade, and so on, thinking, “I shall acquire wealth.”)

In truth, for oneself who has reached such suffering due to craving for children and wealth, it is not possible to provide protection or defense to escape that suffering during one's lifetime. It is not within one's power. At the time of death, when oppressed and scorched by the pains of death (maraṇantikavedanā) like flames of fire, with the joints of the bones breaking and the skeletal structure falling apart, with eyes flickering, closing them to look at the next world and opening them to look at this world—for oneself lying on the deathbed in such misery, even the self, who was nurtured for a lifetime by being bathed twice a day, fed three times a day, and adorned with perfumes and flowers, is unable to...
391:
...provide protection or defense to escape from the suffering that has arrived as a close companion.

In such times of great suffering, whether during the course of life or at the moment of death, how can one's children or one's wealth provide protection? They simply cannot.

Regarding the millionaire Ānanda, he did not wish to give even a small amount to anyone and only accumulated wealth for his son Mūlasiri. When he lay on his deathbed in his previous life, and in this life when he faced the suffering of hunger, poverty, and being mistreated by others, what suffering could his beloved children or the wealth he had accumulated remove? (They could not remove any). What kind of happiness could they produce? (They could not produce any). This is the intended meaning of the teaching.

At the conclusion of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation. Thus, the teaching was beneficial to many people. (From Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 1, p. 297).

The Story of the Millionaire Ānanda ends.
