## The Twentieth Vassa (Rainy Season Retreat) in Rājagaha
## Observing the Vassa
In this way, the Blessed One, constantly and without fail carrying out the five great Buddha-duties, and offering the deathless medicine of the cool Dhamma to the devas and humans who were ready for liberation, departed from the city of Sāvatthī...
392:
...and while traveling by stages with a company of monks, he arrived at the city of Rājagaha in the Magadha country and observed the twentieth (vīsati-ma) vassa, residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery.

## Special Note on Anibaddha-vassa and Others
Among the forty-five years of the Buddha's vassa, the first twenty years from the time of his Enlightenment are called Anibaddha-vassa (non-fixed retreats) or Aniyata-vassa (uncertain retreats) because he stayed in various towns and villages for one, two, or three years without a fixed residence. They are also called Paṭhama-bodhi-vassa or Purima-bodhi-vassa because they were the years in the first part of his career when he enabled devas and humans to penetrate the Bodhi, the four paths of knowledge.

The remaining twenty-five years are called Nibaddha-vassa (fixed retreats) or Niyata-vassa (certain retreats) because he resided permanently and regularly at the Jetavana Monastery and the Pubbārāma Monastery in the city of Sāvatthī in the Kosala country. They are also called Dutiya-bodhi-vassa or Pacchima-bodhi-vassa because they were the years in the second or latter part of his career when he enabled devas and humans to penetrate the Bodhi, the four paths of knowledge.

(To elaborate: For twenty years during the Paṭhama-bodhi, the Blessed One had no fixed residence and stayed in various cities as he pleased. From the twenty-first vassa onwards, he made Sāvatthī his resort village and resided regularly...
393:
...at the great monasteries of Jetavana and Pubbārāma. — From Buddhavamsa Commentary, p. 4).

(In the commentary to the Samacitta Sutta, Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 30, it is specifically explained:

From the twenty-first vassa onwards, he made regular use of these two great monasteries: Jetavana and Pubbārāma. Why? Because the millionaire Anāthapiṇḍika and the great laywoman Visākhā were of great service to the Sāsana. Indeed, out of gratitude to Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā, the Blessed One made use of Jetavana and Pubbārāma as his permanent residences.

Specifically, even when he went on tour to various towns and villages during the non-vassa period, he would return to spend the vassa alternating between these two great monasteries. While residing in this manner, the Blessed One would stay at the Jetavana Monastery during the night, and the next morning, surrounded by a company of monks, he would enter Sāvatthī through the South Gate for alms. After collecting alms, he would exit through the East Gate and spend the day at the Pubbārāma Monastery. After staying at the Pubbārāma Monastery that night, the next morning, surrounded by a company of monks, he would enter Sāvatthī through the East Gate for alms, and after collecting alms, he would exit through the South Gate to spend the day at the Jetavana Monastery. For the Pali text, one should refer to those commentaries.)

## Appointment of Venerable Ānanda
## as the Permanent Attendant (Nibaddha-upaṭṭhāka)
(From Theragāthā Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 414). During the twenty years of the Paṭhama-bodhi, there were no permanent monks to attend to and serve the Blessed One. Sometimes Venerable Nāgasamāla would follow him, carrying the Blessed One's bowl and robes and attending to him.
394:
Sometimes Venerable Nāgita, sometimes Venerable Upavāna, sometimes the Licchavī prince Sunakkhatta, sometimes Venerable Cunda (the younger brother of Venerable Sāriputta), sometimes Venerable Sāgata, and sometimes Venerable Meghiya would follow him and attend to him. These venerable ones, for the most part, were unable to serve in a way that fully satisfied the Blessed One's mind.

One day, while the Blessed One was seated surrounded by a company of monks on the noble Buddha-seat prepared within the precinct of the Gandhakuṭī, he addressed the monks:

“Monks, I am now advanced in age (at that time, the Blessed One was 55 years old). Some attendant monks, when told, ‘Let us go by this path,’ leave me and go by another path. Some attendant monks act as if they would drop my bowl and robes on the ground. Consider and select a monk who will attend to me permanently.”

Hearing these words, a sense of spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose within the monks. Then, Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One with joined palms, and said, “Venerable Sir, I will attend to the Blessed One.” The Blessed One rejected Venerable Sāriputta’s offer. In the same manner, starting from Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, all the great Arahant disciples except Venerable Ānanda rose one by one and said, “Venerable Sir, I will attend to you; Venerable Sir, I will attend to you.”
396:
(4) [Note: The text ends here, but the 4th request usually involves the Buddha repeating any Dhamma taught in Ānanda's absence].

“...If I receive these permissions, I will attend to the Blessed One,” he requested.

(The reason for requesting these boons was to ensure he could fulfill his duties effectively and maintain his knowledge of the Dhamma while serving the Buddha.)
397:
(4) If the Lord Buddha preaches a teaching in my absence, may he preach that teaching to me again.

If it is thus (if these four points are allowed), I will attend to and serve the Lord Buddha."

(Venerable Ānanda requested these four boons to avoid the danger of others accusing him, saying, "Although Venerable Ānanda serves the Blessed One day and night, he receives no such honor from the Blessed One," and to fulfill the merit and perfections of being known by gods and men as the Treasurer of the Dhamma.)

In this way, Venerable Ānanda requested these eight boons—four to be rejected and four to be accepted. The Blessed One granted those eight boons requested by Venerable Ānanda. Thus, Venerable Ānanda, having received the eight boons, became the permanent attendant (nibadda-upaṭṭhāka). On that day, he attained the fruit of the perfections he had fulfilled for a period of one hundred thousand aeons for that very position of attendant (upaṭṭhāka).

## A Brief Account of His Service

Starting from the day he received the position of attendant, Venerable Ānanda served the Blessed One with both hot and cold water, with three types of tooth-sticks (short, long, and medium), by massaging his hands and feet, by rubbing his back when he bathed, and by sweeping the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī)...
398:
...serving with such duties, thinking, "At this time, the Blessed One should have this; at this time, this should be done," he spent the whole day moving about near the Blessed One. At night, holding a large torch, he would walk around the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) nine times so that if the Blessed One called him, he could respond easily, and to dispel sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha). This is a brief account of Venerable Ānanda's service. The remaining stories of Venerable Ānanda will be written and described when reaching the section on the Jewel of the Saṅgha.

## Here ends Chapter 34.
399:
## Chapter 35
## The Story of Māra (Māra Vatthu)

(From this Chapter 35 onwards, only a portion of the noteworthy events from the many occurrences during the Buddha's latter period of enlightenment (pacchima-bodhi), within the 25 years of his ministry, will be described.)

At one time, the Blessed One, seeing the past merit (upanissaya) of five hundred brahmin maidens of the village named Pañcasālā in the Magadha country for attaining the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), stayed near that village of Pañcasālā as his resort for alms. Those five hundred brahmin maidens of Pañcasālā village, on a festival day, went to the riverbank to bathe, and after dressing and adorning themselves well, they headed back toward Pañcasālā village.

The Blessed One also entered that village to wander for alms. At that time, Māra the Evil One possessed the bodies of all the villagers and made it so that not even a single person gave a spoonful of alms-food. Standing at the village gate, he saw the Blessed One coming out of the village with his bowl as clean as it was washed and asked, "O monk, did you receive alms?" Then the Blessed One said, "O Evil Māra, was it not you who made it so that I, the Buddha, did not receive alms?" Thereupon, Māra said, "Glorious Blessed One, if that is so, please enter for alms again."

(Māra did not say this out of sincerity; in truth, he plotted wickedly, thinking, "If he enters for alms again because I asked, I will possess the bodies of all the villagers and have them clap their hands and laugh in front of this great monk to mock and ridicule him.")
400: The Buddha, knowing Māra's intent, thought, "If this Māra were to carry out the harassment he has planned against me, his head would split into seven pieces." Out of compassion for Māra, He did not enter for alms again. At the very moment Māra was speaking, the five hundred maidens arrived at the village gate, paid homage to the Buddha, and stood in a suitable place. Māra then said to the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, will the suffering of hunger not severely oppress You who have received no alms?" The Buddha replied, "O Evil One, even if we receive no food today, we shall spend the time with the rapture and bliss (pīti-sukha) associated with meditative absorption (jhāna), just like the Great Brahmas of the Ābhassara realm." He then spoke this verse: Susukhaṃ vata jīvāma, yesaṃ no natthi kiñcanaṃ. Pītibhakkhā bhavissāma, devā ābhassarā yathā. (O Māra, we live very happily indeed, we who have no impediments such as lust or hatred. Like the Ābhassara Brahmas, we shall surely be nourished by rapture.)
401:
...having the joy and bliss (pītisukha) as their sustenance. Bhavissāma = they shall certainly be.

At the end of the teaching, the five hundred maidens were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). (From Dhammapada Commentary, Vol 2, 15-Sukhavagga, page 167).

The Story of Māra ends.

## About King Kosala's Incomparable Alms-giving (Asadisa-dāna)

At one time, the Blessed One, after wandering on a journey, entered the great Jetavana Monastery surrounded by five hundred monks. King Pasenadi Kosala went to the monastery, invited the Blessed One, and on the next day, prepared a grand alms-giving for the newly arrived monks (āgantuka-dāna). He invited the citizens, saying, "Come and see my alms-giving."

The citizens came and saw the King's alms-giving, and not wanting to be outdone, they invited the Blessed One for the next day. After preparing the offerings completely, they invited the King, saying, "May the Sovereign King (Sammuti-deva) also come and witness our alms-giving."

The King, seeing the citizens' alms-giving, thought, "These citizens have performed an alms-giving superior to mine. I shall perform an alms-giving superior to theirs again." On the next day, he prepared a great alms-giving, invited the citizens, and gave. The citizens also, seeing the King's...
402:
...seeing that alms-giving, and not wanting to be outdone, they prepared a greater alms-giving for the next day, invited the King, and gave again. In this manner, the King could not defeat the citizens, and the citizens could not defeat the King.

Then, in the sixth round of alms-giving, the citizens increased their efforts a hundredfold and a thousandfold, preparing the offerings so that no one could say, "This particular item is missing from the citizens' alms-giving." The King, seeing that alms-giving, thought, "If I cannot perform an alms-giving that excels and surpasses that of these citizens, what is the use of my living?" Thinking of a way to surpass the citizens' alms-giving, he lay down on his royal couch. Then, Queen Mallikā approached the King and asked, "Great King, why do you lie down like this? Why do your faculties, such as your eyes, appear to be withered?" When the King asked, "O Queen, do you not know the reason?", Queen Mallikā replied, "I do not know, Great King." The King then told Queen Mallikā the reason.

## Queen Mallikā
## Arranging the Items for the Incomparable Alms-giving

Then Queen Mallikā spoke back to the King thus:

"Great King, do not be troubled with various thoughts. Where can the citizens get what the King, who rules the land..."
403: ruler of the land being defeated by his subjects? I, your servant, shall organize Your Majesty's almsgiving." To organize the King's Incomparable Almsgiving (Asadisa Dāna), she spoke these encouraging words: "Great King, have a pavilion built within the palace grounds for the five hundred monks to sit, using planks of Sāla-kalyāṇī sandalwood. The rest of the people will stay outside the palace grounds. Have five hundred white umbrellas made. Five hundred elephants will stand, each holding a white umbrella with its trunk over the head of one of the five hundred monks. Have eight or ten golden boats made of red gold. These golden boats will be placed in the center of the pavilion to hold scented water. Between every two monks, a princess will sit and grind or rub perfumes. Each princess will hold a fan and constantly fan the two monks. The remaining princesses will take the ground perfumes and put them into the golden boats. Some of those princesses, holding bunches of blue lotuses,
404: will stir the perfumes already placed in the golden boats to release the fragrance. It is true—the citizens have no princesses, no white umbrellas, and no elephants. For these reasons, the citizens will be defeated. Great King, please arrange and act exactly as I have now suggested." The King agreed, saying, "Very well, Queen. You have given excellent advice," and he had everything done according to Queen Mallikā's instructions. In particular, as she had advised, one tame elephant was needed for one monk. The King asked Queen Mallikā, "Queen, one tame elephant is missing for one monk. What shall we do?" She asked, "Great King, are there not five hundred elephants?" "Queen, there are, but the remaining ones are wild elephants. They become very violent like a Veramba wind as soon as they see monks," the King said. Queen Mallikā replied, "Great King, I have thought of a place where a young wild elephant should stand, holding a white umbrella with its trunk." When the King asked, "Where shall we place that young wild elephant?" she replied, "Beside the Elder Aṅgulimāla—"
405:
“They must be placed nearby,” she replied in her suggestion.

The King acted according to Queen Mallikā's advice. The fierce young elephant tucked its tail between its legs, lowered its ears, closed its eyes, and stood perfectly still. The multitude of people looked at the elephant in amazement, saying, “Even such a fierce elephant has become so disciplined, gentle, and calm.”

The King, having served the community of monks headed by the Buddha, paid homage to the Blessed One with great respect and devotion, saying:

“Venerable Sir, in this alms-pavilion, I donate to you both allowable items (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) and unallowable items (akappiya-bhaṇḍa) for the monks.”

Specifically, in that Great Incomparable Alms-giving (Asadisa Dāna), the wealth distributed in a single day was worth one hundred and forty million (140,000,000). The four items offered specifically for the Buddha—(1) a white umbrella, (2) a throne, (3) a bowl-stand, and (4) a footstool to step on after washing the feet—were of priceless value. It is impossible to organize such alms-rituals and offer such gifts to the Buddhas again; therefore, this alms-giving of King Kosala became famous in the Dispensation as the Asadisa Dāna—the Incomparable Alms-giving.

Furthermore, this Asadisa Dāna is a natural occurrence that happens only once for every Buddha.
406:
It is a natural occurrence that happens only once for every Buddha, and these Incomparable Alms-givings are always managed and organized only by a wise woman.

## The Story of the Ministers Junha and Kāla

King Pasenadi Kosala had two advisory ministers named Junha and Kāla. Between these two, the minister Kāla reflected thus:

“Alas, the decline and loss of the King’s palace has come to pass. In just one single day, wealth amounting to one hundred and forty million has reached exhaustion. These monks, after receiving and consuming the King’s alms, will return to the monastery and simply sleep soundly. Alas, the King’s golden palace is being ruined in an unlovely way.”

Thus he planned and reflected. The minister Junha, however, reflected thus:

“Oh, the King has successfully performed a truly excellent alms-giving. Indeed, one who does not possess the status of a King cannot give such an alms-giving. There is no donor who does not share the portion of merit from the alms with all beings. I joyfully express my appreciation (sādhukāra) for the King’s most noble and great Incomparable Alms-giving. Sādhu, sādhu, sādhu!”

In this way, the minister Junha reflected and rejoiced. When the Buddha’s meal was finished, King Pasenadi Kosala took the water vessel and prepared to listen to the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā). The Blessed One—
407:
—reflected: “The King has given a great alms-giving, like letting a great torrent of water roll and flow. Is the multitude of people able to gladden their minds, or are they not?”

Knowing the state of the minds of the two ministers, He further knew: “If I were to preach a detailed discourse of appreciation in accordance with the King’s alms-giving, the minister Kāla’s head would split into seven pieces. The minister Junha, however, would be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).” Based on compassion for the minister Kāla, He preached only a single four-line verse (catuppadika gāthā) to the King who stood having given such a great alms-giving, and then rose from His seat and returned to the monastery.

## The Courageous Mind of Venerable Aṅgulimāla Thera

When they arrived at the monastery, the venerable monks asked Venerable Aṅgulimāla Thera, “Friend, were you not afraid when you saw the fierce elephant holding the umbrella over you?” When Venerable Aṅgulimāla Thera replied, “Friends, I was not afraid,” the monks approached the Blessed One and reported disparagingly, “Venerable Sir, Venerable Aṅgulimāla Thera is claiming the Fruit of Arahantship.”

The Blessed One said, “Monks, Aṅgulimāla is truly not afraid. Indeed, monks who are like my son, who are great and noble among the noble Arahants, do not fear.” He then preached this verse from the Brāhmaṇa Vagga:
408:
Usabhaṃ pavaraṃ vīraṃ, mahesiṃ vijitāvinaṃ.
Anejaṃ nhātakaṃ buddhaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.

(Bhikkhave = Monks). Usabhaṃ = like a bull-king, fearless and unshakable. Pavaraṃ = noble. Vīraṃ = endowed with the energy of Right Effort (Sammappadhāna). Mahesiṃ = who has sought and practiced special virtues such as the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha). Vijitāvinaṃ = who has conquered and dispelled the three Maras: Devaputta Mara, Kilesa Mara, and Abhisaṅkhāra Mara. Anejaṃ = in whom all cravings (ejā) for existence have been extinguished. Nhātakaṃ = who has washed away the impurities of defilements with the pure water of the Path. Buddhaṃ = who has realized the Four Noble Truths. Taṃ = that Arahant whose taints are exhausted. Ahaṃ = I, the Buddha. Brāhmaṇaṃ = as a true Brahmin (paramattha brāhmaṇa). Brūmi = declare according to reality.

## The Outcome for the Two Ministers

King Pasenadi Kosala, becoming displeased, thought: “To me, who stands having given a great alms-giving in such an assembly, the Buddha did not preach a discourse of appreciation in accordance with the great gift, but preached only a single four-line verse and then rose from His seat and departed. I must have performed an unsuitable alms-giving instead of a suitable one for the Buddha. I must have offered unallowable items instead of allowable ones. The Buddha might be angry with me. Indeed, this alms-giving I have now offered is called the Asadisa Dāna; therefore, a discourse of appreciation suitable and—
409:
—fitting for the Asadisa Dāna should have been preached.” Thinking thus, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One with respect, and asked:

“Venerable Sir, did I not offer an alms-giving that should be offered? Or did I offer unallowable items instead of allowable items (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) that are suitable for donation?”

When the Blessed One asked, “Great King, why do you ask this?”, King Kosala replied, “Venerable Sir, you did not preach a discourse of appreciation that is fitting and suitable for my great Asadisa Dāna.” Then the Blessed One said to King Kosala:

“Great King, you have indeed offered an alms-giving that is suitable to be offered. Indeed, the alms-giving you have now given is called the great Asadisa Dāna. This great Asadisa Dāna can be offered only once to each Buddha. It is not easy to perform such an Asadisa Dāna again.”

When He said this, King Kosala asked the Blessed One, “Venerable Sir, if that is so, why did you not preach a discourse of appreciation to me that is fitting for the great Asadisa Dāna?” The Blessed One stated the reason, saying, “Great King, because the assembly was not pure.” Then King Kosala—
410:
—asked, “Venerable Sir, what was the fault of the assembly?”

Then the Blessed One informed the King about the thoughts of the two ministers and explained that He did not preach a detailed discourse of appreciation out of compassion for the minister Kāla. Then King Kosala asked, “Kāla, is it true that you thought in this way?” When the minister Kāla replied, “It is true,” the King said:

“While I am giving my own wealth together with my wife and children, without taking even a single penny of your wealth, what harm does it do to you? Go, minister Kāla! Let the wealth I have already given you remain yours (meaning he would not seize it back), but you must leave my kingdom this very day.”

After banishing the minister Kāla, he summoned the minister Junha and asked, “Junha, is it true that you thought in this way?” When the minister Junha replied, “It is true,” the King said:

“Sādhu, sādhu, Uncle! I have faith in you. Take my attendants and perform alms-giving for seven days in the same manner that I have given.”

Saying this, he handed over the kingship to the minister Junha for seven days. Then he said to the Blessed One, “Venerable Sir, please look at the way of the fool.
411:
He is one who has insulted and criticized the alms-giving I have offered in this way.” The Blessed One said, “Yes, it is so, Great King. Those who are fools cannot rejoice in the alms-giving of others and they criticize it; therefore, they have only the states of deprivation (apāya) and unhappy destinations (duggati) as their final end. The wise and virtuous, however, cultivate the merit of appreciation (anumodanā) by rejoicing in the alms-giving of others, and they have only the human realm and celestial worlds—the happy destinations (sugati)—as their final end.” He then preached this verse of Dhamma:

Na ve kadariyā devalokaṃ vajanti,
Bālā have nappasaṃsanti dānaṃ.
Dhīro ca dānaṃ anumodamāno,
Teneva so hoti sukhī parattha.

(Mahārāja = Great King). Ve = Indeed. Kadariyā = those who are harsh misers. Devalokaṃ = to the celestial world. Na vajanti = do not go. Bālā = fools who do not know both this world and the next. Have = indeed. Dānaṃ = alms-giving. Nappasaṃsanti = cannot praise or rejoice in. Dhīro ca = only the wise person who considers the consequences. Dānaṃ = in alms-giving. Anumodamāno = can perform joyful appreciation (sādhukāra). So = that wise person. Teneva = because of that merit of joyfully appreciating the gifts offered by others. Parattha = in the celestial world after death.
412:
Sukhī = enjoying celestial bliss, being very happy. Hoti = is.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the minister Juṇha was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (became a Sotāpanna). The Dhamma teaching also became beneficial for the assembled audience who had arrived.

After becoming a Sotāpanna, the minister Juṇha received royal favor and, for seven days, performed a great alms-giving in the same manner as the King had given.

The account of King Kosala's Incomparable Alms-giving (Asadisa-dāna) ends.
**********
## The Preaching of the Sivi Jātaka and Āditta Jātaka
## Concerning King Kosala's Incomparable Alms-giving

When the Blessed One preached the Dhamma with this verse beginning with "Na ve kadariyā devalokaṃ vajanti," King Pasenadi of Kosala was greatly inspired. He offered an upper robe made in the Sivi kingdom, worth one hundred thousand, to the Blessed One and then entered the city.

The next day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks began a discussion: "Friends, after giving the great Incomparable Alms-giving, King Kosala was still not satisfied with such a gift. When the Blessed One preached the Dhamma, he again offered an upper robe from the Sivi kingdom worth one hundred thousand. Friends, the King is indeed extremely insatiable in his giving."

The Blessed One arrived and, having asked about the subject of their discussion,
413:
was informed of the matter. The Blessed One said:

"Monks, it is easy to give what is called external wealth (bāhira-vatthu). In the past, wise Bodhisattas, while giving alms by spending six hundred thousand daily and plowing the entire island of Jambudīpa to its limits, were not satisfied with external giving. Believing firmly that 'one who gives what is dear to oneself attains a special benefit that is dear,' they even plucked out their own eyes and gave them to the recipients who came before them."

Having said this, at the request of the monks, he preached the Sivi Jātaka (found in the Vīsati Nipāta) concerning the events of the past.

## The Preaching of the Āditta Jātaka

On the day after King Kosala had given the great Incomparable Alms-giving, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised a discussion: "Friends, King Kosala, having personally recognized the good field in which to sow the seeds of merit after careful selection, has given the great Incomparable Alms-giving to the community of Noble Monks (Ariya Saṅgha) headed by the Buddha."

The Blessed One arrived and, having asked about the subject of their discussion, was informed of the matter. The Blessed One said:

"Monks, it is not surprising that King Kosala has now sown the seeds of the Incomparable Alms-giving in the good field of the Sāsana, where one sows the most excellent and incomparable merit after careful selection. In the past, wise ones and Bodhisattas also gave great alms only after careful selection."

Having said this, at the request of the monks, he preached the Āditta Jātaka (found in the Aṭṭhaka Nipāta) concerning the past events.
414:
(The detailed accounts of the Sivi Jātaka in the Vīsati Nipāta and the Āditta Jātaka in the Aṭṭhaka Nipāta should be taken from the 550 Jātaka prose texts.)

The account of the preaching of the Sivi Jātaka and Āditta Jātaka ends.
**********
## The Story of the Two Friends:
## Garahadinna, a Follower of Heretics, and
## Sirigutta, a Follower of the Blessed One
## The Story of Garahadinna

In the city of Sāvatthī, there were two friends named the householder Sirigutta and the householder Garahadinna. Of these two, the householder Sirigutta was a disciple of the Blessed One, while the householder Garahadinna was a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas (naked ascetics). Garahadinna's teachers, the Nigaṇṭhas, constantly said to him:

"Go to your friend Sirigutta and say, 'Friend, why do you attend upon the ascetic Gotama? What will you gain from that ascetic Gotama?' If he is exhorted in this way, Sirigutta might come to us
415:
and give offerings to us as well. Is it not proper to exhort him in this manner?"

Having heard the words of his teachers, the Nigaṇṭhas, repeatedly, the householder Garahadinna went to his friend Sirigutta at his place of standing or sitting and exhorted him, saying:

"Friend, what benefit is there for you with the ascetic Gotama? What benefit will you get by attending upon that ascetic Gotama? Is it not proper for you to attend upon my lords, the Nigaṇṭhas, and give alms to them?"

Although Sirigutta heard Garahadinna's words, he remained silent for many days without replying. However, because Garahadinna spoke so frequently that it became annoying, Sirigutta one day said to him:

"Friend, you constantly come to me at my place of standing or sitting and say, 'What benefit will you get by attending upon the ascetic Gotama? Attend upon my lords, the Nigaṇṭhas, and give alms to them.' Before discussing giving, please tell me first: what Dhamma do your lords, the Nigaṇṭhas, know?"

Then the friend Garahadinna said to the friend Sirigutta:
416:
"Oh, how wonderful, my dear householder! Do not speak like that. For my lords, the Nigaṇṭhas, there is nothing that is not known. They know all things of the three periods of time—past, present, and future. They know everything that is done, said, or thought—all bodily, verbal, and mental actions. They know everything completely, saying, 'This will happen, this will not happen.'"

When he said this, the friend Sirigutta pressed him, "Friend, is this what you say?" The friend Garahadinna boldly confirmed, "Yes, that is what I say."

Then the householder Sirigutta said to his friend Garahadinna:

"Friend, if that is the case, you have done a very burdensome thing by not telling me this for so long. Only today do I know the power of the knowledge and wisdom of your lords, the Nigaṇṭhas. Friend, go and invite your lords, the Nigaṇṭhas, to come for a meal tomorrow."

The householder Garahadinna, feeling very joyful, went to the Nigaṇṭhas, paid his respects, and informed them, "Lords, my friend the householder Sirigutta invites you to come for a meal tomorrow." When the senior Nigaṇṭhas asked, "Did the householder Sirigutta tell you himself?", Garahadinna replied firmly, "Lords, yes, the householder Sirigutta himself spoke and invited you."

The senior Nigaṇṭhas
417:
were filled with joy and said, "Lay disciple Garahadinna, the matter is accomplished. From the time the householder Sirigutta gains faith in us, what kind of wealth will we not acquire?"

## The Preparations at Sirigutta's House

The householder Sirigutta's house was very spacious. Between two buildings within his compound, Sirigutta had a long, deep pit dug, and he had it filled with liquid filth and sewage.

He had stakes driven into the ground at both ends of the pit and had ropes tied to those stakes. He then arranged the couches so that their front legs rested on the edge of the pit and their back legs rested on the ropes. He did this with the intention: "When they arrive and sit down, they will sit like this, and when they sit, they will fall head-first into the pit."

After that, to hide the pit from view, he had rugs spread over the couches, with the edges of the rugs reaching down to the ground.

He had many large pots placed at the back of the house, with their mouths covered and tied with banana leaves and cloth. These empty pots were smeared on the outside with gruel, rice, ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and flour.

The next day, the householder Garahadinna went quickly to Sirigutta's house early in the morning and
418:
asked, "Have the offerings and preparations for the lords been made?" When Sirigutta replied, "Yes, friend, they have been made," Garahadinna asked again, "Where are these offerings?"

Sirigutta pointed to the pots and the places and said, "These many pots are filled with gruel. These many pots are filled with rice. These many pots are filled with ghee, molasses, and cakes. The seats have also been prepared." The friend Garahadinna said, "Good, friend," and departed. After Garahadinna left, the five hundred Nigaṇṭhas arrived at Sirigutta's house.

## Sirigutta's Admonition to the Nigaṇṭhas

The householder Sirigutta went out from his house, paid respectful homage to the Nigaṇṭhas with the five-point prostration, and stood before them with joined palms, thinking to himself:

"It is said that you, lords, know all things, including the past and so forth. This is what your attendant and disciple Garahadinna told me.

If it is true that you, lords, know everything, then do not enter my house. For indeed, there is no gruel for you who enter my house, nor is there any rice or other food."
419:
“If you venerable ones enter the house unknowingly, I will have you thrown into the cesspit and beaten.”
Thinking thus, Sirigutta gave a signal to his workmen, saying, “Knowing that these naked ascetics will be sitting here, you men must stand behind them. Before they sit, remove the coverings spread over the couches. Do not let those coverings be soiled with filth.”
Then Sirigutta addressed the naked ascetics, “Venerable ones, please come this way.” The naked ascetics entered between the two houses and prepared to sit on the arranged seats. At that moment, Sirigutta’s men said to the naked ascetics, “Wait a moment, venerable ones! Do not sit yet.” The naked ascetics asked, “For what reason?” Sirigutta’s men replied, “Venerable ones, you should sit only after knowing the proper etiquette for those entering our house.” The naked ascetics asked again, “Laymen, what should we do?” Sirigutta’s men replied, “Venerable ones, you should all stand near your respective seats and sit down all at once.”
(The purpose of this request was to prevent any single ascetic from falling into the pit and then being able to warn the others, saying, ‘Friends, do not sit in the remaining places.’)
420:
The naked ascetics agreed, saying, “Very well,” and thinking, “We should follow what these people say.” All five hundred naked ascetics stood in order near their respective seats. Then, Sirigutta’s men said to the naked ascetics, “Venerable ones, please sit down quickly and all at once!” Knowing that the naked ascetics were about to sit, they removed the coverings spread over the couches. As the naked ascetics sat down simultaneously, the legs of the couches, which were merely placed over ropes, slipped away. The naked ascetics fell headlong into the pit.
When the naked ascetics fell into the pit, the householder Sirigutta closed the house doors. As each ascetic tried to climb out, he beat them to his heart's content with sticks, saying, “Why do you not know all things of the past, future, and present, as your lay-follower Garahadinna claimed?” Then, saying, “This much should be enough for these naked ascetics,” he ordered the doors to be opened.
The naked ascetics attempted to flee from the house. However, along the path within the compound where they had to go, the ground had been previously prepared with slippery slime and smoothed over. Consequently, the naked ascetics could not maintain their balance on that slippery surface and fell down one after another. Each time they fell, he had the naked ascetics beaten again.
421:
Saying, “This much should be enough for you,” he released them.
The naked ascetics lamented, saying, “Sirigutta, you have ruined and disgraced us! You have ruined and disgraced us!” and went to the door of their supporter Garahadinna’s house.
## Garahadinna Sues Sirigutta
When the householder Garahadinna saw his teachers, the naked ascetics, in such a disgraced and disfigured state, he became violently angry.
“My friend Sirigutta has ruined me! (Not to mention those who give), even to those who merely extend their hands in salutation, my masters, the naked ascetics, are like a fertile field for sowing merit, capable of granting desired blessings in the world including the devas. Yet he has dared to have them beaten and brought to ruin!”
Lamenting thus, he went to the golden palace of King Pasenadi of Kosala and filed a lawsuit against the householder Sirigutta, seeking a fine of one thousand kahāpaṇas.
Then King Pasenadi sent a royal summons to the householder Sirigutta, calling him to the palace. Sirigutta went to the palace, paid respectful homage to the King, and pleaded, “Your Majesty, please investigate this matter to find the truth before
422:
imposing a fine. Please do not act without investigation.” King Pasenadi said, “Householder, I shall impose the fine only after investigation.” Sirigutta replied, “Very well, Your Majesty.”
“In that case, you, householder Sirigutta, state the facts of the case to me,” the King commanded, opening the proceedings. Sirigutta then said:
“Your Majesty, Garahadinna, who is a disciple of my friend’s teachers, the naked ascetics, came to me repeatedly. Whether standing or sitting, he would constantly say, ‘Friend, what benefit is there for you with the recluse Gotama? What benefit can you gain by attending on that recluse Gotama?’—starting with these words.”
Sirigutta then related the entire sequence of events to the King and concluded his testimony, saying, “Your Majesty, if it is appropriate to impose a fine based on these facts, then please do so.”
The King looked at the householder Garahadinna and asked, “Is it true that you spoke in this manner?” “It is true, Your Majesty,” Garahadinna admitted. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala said:
“Garahadinna, why did you speak to Sirigutta, a disciple of the Buddha, claiming, ‘My masters know all things that occur in the three periods of time—past, future, and present,’ while following these naked ascetics who did not even know this much (about the prepared cesspit) and regarding them as ‘Great Buddhas’? The fine of one thousand kahāpaṇas you proposed shall be yours to pay (you yourself shall bear it).”
423:
Having delivered this royal decree, the King imposed the fine of one thousand coins on Garahadinna himself. The naked ascetics (Garahadinna’s teachers) who had followed him to the palace as parties to the case were also beaten and driven away.
## Garahadinna’s Plan
The householder Garahadinna was furious with Sirigutta. From that time on, he did not speak to Sirigutta for about half a month (15 days). Later, he thought, “It is not proper for me to remain without speaking like this. I must also bring ruin to the teachers of this Sirigutta (in revenge).” He then went to Sirigutta and called out, “Friend Sirigutta!” When Sirigutta asked, “What is it, friend?” Garahadinna said:
“Friend, it is the nature of relatives and friends that quarrels and disputes may occur. Friend, why do you not speak any word to me? Why do you act in this way (not speaking or calling out)?”
When Sirigutta calmly replied, “Friend, because you did not speak with me, I also did not speak. (There is no other reason),” Garahadinna spoke words of reconciliation, saying, “Friend, let what is done be done.
424:
Let us not destroy our mutual affection.” From that time on, the two of them stood together and sat together in the same places (acting in companionship).
One day, the householder Sirigutta said to his friend Garahadinna, “Friend, what benefit is there for you with your teachers, the naked ascetics? What benefit will you gain by attending on those naked ascetics? For your sake, is it not proper to attend on my teacher, the Blessed Buddha, and offer alms to the noble ones?” (speaking just as Garahadinna had spoken before). Since Garahadinna was someone who had always longed for such an opportunity, it was to him like having an itch scratched with a fingernail.
Therefore, Garahadinna asked, “Friend Sirigutta, what does your teacher, the recluse Gotama, know?” Then the householder Sirigutta said:
“Friend Garahadinna, do not speak like that. For my teacher, the Blessed Buddha, there is no dhamma that is unknown. He knows all dhammas, including those of the past and so on. He knows the mental states of beings in sixteen ways.”
When he said this, his friend Garahadinna said, “Friend, I did not know this before. Why did you not tell me for so long? Friend, if that is so, go and invite your teacher, the Buddha, for tomorrow (to receive a meal at my house). I wish to offer alms. Please request him to accept my alms-food together with five hundred monks.”
425:
Sirigutta approached the Blessed Buddha, paid respectful homage, and said:
“Exalted Buddha, my friend the householder Garahadinna has asked me to invite you. He requests you to accept his alms-food tomorrow together with five hundred monks. There is a special circumstance: on a previous day, I did this certain thing to his teachers, the naked ascetics. I do not know if he wishes to take revenge for what I did, or if he truly wishes to offer alms to the Exalted One with a pure mind. Please consider this, and if it is appropriate, please accept; if it is not appropriate, please do not accept the invitation, Lord.”
The Blessed Buddha, contemplating, “What does this householder Garahadinna wish to do to us?” saw this: “He has had a great pit dug between two houses, had eighty cartloads of khadira (acacia) wood brought and filled the pit, and set it on fire. He intends to make me and the monks fall into the pit of glowing embers and thus oppress us.”
Contemplating further, “Will there be any benefit or not by going to Garahadinna’s house?” He clearly saw the following:
“I, the Buddha, shall extend my foot over the pit of khadira embers. At that very moment, the bamboo matting used to cover the pit will disappear.”
426:
“The charcoal pit will burst open, and a great Paduma lotus, the size of a chariot wheel or a cart wheel, will emerge. Then, I shall step upon the pericarp of the Paduma lotus and sit in my place; the five hundred monks will likewise step upon Paduma lotuses and sit in their respective places. A great multitude of people will gather. In that assembly, I shall deliver a discourse of appreciation with two verses of Dhamma. At the conclusion of the discourse of appreciation, eighty-four thousand beings will realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation. The two friends, the householder Sirigutta and the householder Garahadinna, will become Sotāpannas. Both friends will joyfully offer their wealth as a sacrifice in this Sasana of mine, which is endowed with the eight wonderful qualities. It is for the sake of this noble son Garahadinna that I should go.”

Clearly perceiving this matter, the Buddha accepted the invitation to the meal by remaining silent. The householder Sirigutta went to Garahadinna’s house and informed his friend Garahadinna that the Buddha had accepted the invitation, saying, “Friend, perform the act of offering and honor to the Buddha, the leader and chief of the three worlds, in peace.” Having said this, he returned to his home.

## The Arrangement at Garahadinna’s House
The householder Garahadinna, thinking, “Now I shall know what is fit to be done to that Sirigutta,”
427:
had a large pit dug between two houses. He had about eighty cartloads of acacia wood brought and filled the great pit with the wood. He set it on fire to create a mass of acacia charcoal and had it fanned all night. Over the pit, he had wooden planks laid, covered with mats, and smeared with cow dung. On one side, he had weak sticks laid to form a path. (This was done with the intention that: “When these weak sticks are stepped upon, they will break each time, and they will fall into the charcoal pit.”)

At the back of the house, he placed large pots in the same manner as Sirigutta had done, and the seats were also arranged in the same way.

Early in the morning, the householder Sirigutta went to Garahadinna’s house and asked, “Friend, have you prepared the offerings?” When Garahadinna replied, “Yes, friend, they are prepared,” Sirigutta asked, “Where are those offerings?” Garahadinna said, “Friend, come, let us go and see,” and he showed him around in the same manner that Sirigutta had shown him. Sirigutta expressed his joy, saying, “Excellent, friend.”

A great multitude of people gathered. Indeed, whenever a person of wrong view invites the Buddha, there is always a great assembly. Those with wrong views gathered, thinking, “We shall see the
428:
downfall and ruin of the ascetic Gotama with our own eyes.” Those with right view also gathered, thinking and encouraging one another, “Today the Buddha will deliver a great Dhamma discourse. We shall investigate and witness the range of the Buddha and the splendor of the Buddha.”

## The Emergence of Great Lotuses from the Fire
On the following day, the Buddha, together with five hundred monks, arrived at the door of Garahadinna’s house. Garahadinna came out of the house, paid homage with the fivefold prostration with respect and devotion, and stood before the Buddha with palms joined (not speaking aloud, but thinking in his mind):

“Venerable Sir, it is said that you know all things, such as the past and so forth. It is said that you can discern the mental states of beings through sixteen modes. Your disciple Sirigutta told me so. If it is true that you know as he says, then do not enter my house. For indeed, there is no rice-gruel for you who enter my house. There is no food or such things. In truth, I shall cause you all to fall into the acacia charcoal pit and subdue you.”

Having thus thought, he took the bowl from the Buddha’s hand and said, “Venerable Sir, please come this way.” Then he said, “Venerable Sir, those who come to our house
429:
should enter knowing the proper conduct.” When the Buddha asked, “Lay follower, what should be done?” the householder Garahadinna replied, “Venerable Sir, it is proper for each monk to enter the house one by one, and after the one in front has sat down, the next monk should come.” (The intention behind this request was: if all the monks entered together, they would see the monk in front falling into the charcoal pit; if they saw that, the remaining monks would not come. Therefore, he thought, “I shall throw the monks into the fire pit one by one and subdue them.”)

The Buddha said, “Very well, lay follower,” and proceeded alone. When the householder Garahadinna reached the vicinity of the acacia charcoal pit, he stepped aside and said, “Venerable Sir, please proceed ahead.” At that moment, as the Buddha extended his foot over the acacia charcoal pit, the mats vanished. Bursting through the charcoal pit, great Paduma lotuses, the size of chariot wheels or cart wheels, rose up in succession. The Buddha, stepping upon the pericarps of the Paduma lotuses, proceeded and sat upon the prepared seat. The five hundred monks likewise stepped upon the pericarps of the Paduma lotuses and sat in their respective seats.

## Garahadinna’s Great Distress
Seeing this extraordinary and unprecedented event, heat and vapor rose from Garahadinna’s body like a pot of hot ghee.
430:
Garahadinna went quickly to his friend Sirigutta and pleaded, “Noble Sirigutta, please be my refuge.” When Sirigutta asked, “Why do you speak thus?” Garahadinna said, “Friend, there is no rice-gruel in my house for the five hundred monks, nor is there any food. What shall I do?” The householder Sirigutta asked directly, “Friend, what have you done?” Then the householder Garahadinna said:

“Friend, (to speak plainly), between the two houses, I had a great pit filled with charcoal, intending to throw the five hundred monks, headed by the Buddha, into the charcoal pit and subdue them. Nevertheless, bursting through that charcoal pit, great Paduma lotuses have risen up in succession. The Buddha and all the monks have stepped upon the pericarps of the Paduma lotuses and are now sitting in the prepared seats. What should I do now, noble Sirigutta?”

Thus he confessed and asked for advice. Sirigutta then said, “Friend, did you not just recently show me yourself, saying, ‘These are the large pots for rice-gruel, and these are the large pots for food’?” Garahadinna replied, “Noble Sirigutta, those words I spoke were not true at all. The large pots do not contain rice-gruel or food; they are merely empty pots.”
431:
He confessed again. Then the householder Sirigutta (being one who had unwavering faith in the Buddha’s virtues and power) said, “Let it be, friend. Just go back to the house and look at the pots you mentioned for rice-gruel and food.”

## The Range of a Buddha is Inconceivable
At the very moment Sirigutta said this, all the large pots that Garahadinna had previously lied about, saying, “These are pots of rice-gruel,” were filled with rice-gruel. All the large pots he had described as “pots of food” and so forth were filled with food and other provisions. When Garahadinna reached the house, he saw all these wonders for himself. Upon seeing all this miraculous abundance, Garahadinna’s entire body was filled with joy and delight, and his mind became very clear.

The householder Garahadinna respectfully served the meal to the Sangha headed by the Buddha. After the meal, wishing for a discourse of appreciation, he took the bowl of the Buddha. The Buddha, intending to deliver the discourse of appreciation, said, “Because these beings lack the eye of wisdom, they do not perceive the virtues of the Buddha’s disciples or the virtues of the Sasana. Indeed, those without the eye of wisdom are called blind; those with the eye of wisdom are called those with sight.” Having said this, he spoke these two verses:
432:
Yathā saṅkāradhānasmiṃ, ujjhitasmiṃ mahāpathe;
Padumaṃ tattha jāyetha, sucigandhaṃ manoramaṃ. (1)
Evaṃ saṅkārabhūtesu, andhabhūte puthujjane;
Atirocati paññāya, sammāsambuddhasāvako. (2)

Just as in a heap of refuse discarded on the high road where many people travel, a hundred-petaled Paduma lotus, pure in fragrance and delightful to the mind, might grow and emerge as a wonderful marvel; (1)

Even so, among beings who are like discarded refuse, the disciple of the Fully Enlightened One, a noble person of great glory who has destroyed the taints, outshines the worldlings who are like the blind because they lack the power of wisdom. (2)

At the conclusion of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation. The two friends, the householder Garahadinna and the householder Sirigutta, also reached the Fruit of Stream-entry (i.e., they became Sotāpannas). Those two friends joyfully offered and donated all their personal possessions as a sacrifice in this Sasana of the Buddha, which is endowed with the eight wonderful qualities.
433:
## Ekaka Nipāta
## The Preaching of the Khadirangāra Jātaka
After the Blessed One had delivered the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), he rose from his seat and returned to the monastery. In the evening, the monks gathered in the Dhamma Hall and spoke in praise of the Buddha:

“Friends, the virtues of the Blessed One are truly worthy of praise and wonder! Out of such a terrifying mass of glowing acacia embers (khadirangāra), lotus flowers (paduma) the size of chariot wheels and cart wheels emerged and blossomed in succession.”

When the Blessed One arrived at the Dhamma Hall, he asked, “Monks, for what purpose are you gathered here now?” When the monks replied, “We are gathered here discussing this matter (concerning the virtues of the Buddha),” the Blessed One said:

“Monks, it is not surprising that lotus flowers emerged from a mass of embers for me to walk upon now that I have become the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Omniscient Buddha. In the past, when I was still a Bodhisatta and established in knowledge that was not yet mature, lotus flowers also emerged and blossomed for me.”

Having said this, at the request of the monks, he preached the Khadirangāra Jātaka (found in the 4th Kulāvaka Vagga of the Ekaka Nipāta) in detail.

(The detailed account of this Khadirangāra Jātaka should be extracted and noted from the prose versions of the 550 Jātaka stories.)
434:
In particular, in those 550 Jātakas, this was preached concerning the donation of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. It should be specifically noted that this Khadirangāra Jātaka was preached again in this story of the householder Garahadinna by connecting the sequence of events.

(This story of Garahadinna is extracted and described from the Dhammapadaṭṭhakathā, Book 1, 4-Puppha Vagga, 12-Garahadinnavatthu, page 275.)

The Story of Garahadinna ends.

## Giving Instructions to Venerable Moggallāna
## and Subduing the Naga King Nandopananda
On one occasion, after the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika had listened to the Dhamma discourse of the Blessed One, he invited him, saying, “Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One together with five hundred monks accept a meal at our house tomorrow.” He then departed for his home.

The Blessed One accepted the invitation of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. After the remainder of that day and night had passed, as dawn was approaching, he surveyed the ten thousand world systems with his divine eye. Then, the celestial Naga King named Nandopananda appeared within the range of his knowledge.

The Blessed One reflected, “This Naga King has appeared in my knowledge. Does he have the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of past merit?” He then saw, “This Naga is one without faith in the Triple Gem and holds wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi).” He further reflected, “Who can cause this Naga to be free from his wrong views?” and he saw the Elder Mahāmoggallāna.
435:
Then, when morning came, after performing his morning duties, the Buddha instructed Venerable Ānanda, “Dear Ānanda, tell the five hundred monks that the Blessed One will be traveling to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.”

On that particular day, the Nagas were preparing a banquet of food, drink, and intoxicants for the Naga King Nandopananda. The Naga King Nandopananda was sitting on a celestial jeweled throne under a white celestial umbrella, surrounded by three groups of Naga dancers—the elder, the younger, and the middle-aged—as well as his Naga retinue. He was looking at the celestial food and drinks served in celestial gold and silver vessels.

At that time, the Blessed One, making himself visible to the Naga King, traveled directly toward the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with the five hundred monks, passing right above the Naga King’s palace.

Then, a wicked wrong view arose in the mind of the Naga King Nandopananda: “These vile shaven-headed monks go above our palaces and enter and exit the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. From now on, I will not allow these vile shaven-headed monks to go by scattering the dust from their feet upon us.” Having formed this wrong view, the Naga King Nandopananda rose from his jeweled throne, went to the foot of Mount Sineru, abandoned his original form, and coiled himself seven times around Mount Sineru. Then, spreading his hood above, he covered the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with his inverted hood, causing it to disappear from sight.
436:
Then, Venerable Raṭṭhapāla asked the Blessed One, “Venerable Sir, in the past, standing in this place, we could see Mount Sineru, the seven surrounding mountain ranges, the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the Vejayanta Palace, and the banner of Sakka, King of Devas, hoisted atop the Vejayanta Palace. Venerable Sir, what is the reason why we cannot see Mount Sineru, the seven surrounding mountain ranges, the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the Vejayanta Palace, and the banner of Sakka now?”

The Blessed One replied, “Dear Raṭṭhapāla, this Naga King named Nandopananda is angry with you. He has coiled himself seven times around Mount Sineru and, covering it with his hood from above, has created darkness and remains there.” Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said, “Venerable Sir, let me subdue that Naga King.” The Blessed One did not grant him permission. Then, in succession, all the monks such as Venerable Bhaddiya and Venerable Rāhula stood up and requested as Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had, but the Blessed One did not grant them permission (the reason for which will become clear later).

Finally, when the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said, “Venerable Sir, let me subdue that Naga King,” the Blessed One granted permission, saying, “Subdue him, Moggallāna.”
437:
After receiving the Blessed One’s permission, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna abandoned his original form and, having manifested the form of a great Naga King, coiled himself fourteen times around the Naga King Nandopananda. He then placed his own hood over the hood of the Naga King and pressed him against Mount Sineru. The Naga King Nandopananda emitted smoke. The Elder also said, “It is not only in your body that there is smoke; there is also in mine,” and he emitted even more smoke. The Naga King’s smoke could not harm the Elder, but the Elder’s smoke harmed and afflicted the Naga King.

Then, the Naga King Nandopananda emitted a mass of flames. The Elder also said, “It is not only in your body that there is flame; there is also in mine,” and he emitted even greater masses of flames. The flames emitted by the Naga King could not touch or harm the Elder, but the flames emitted by the Elder touched and afflicted the Naga King.

The Naga King Nandopananda thought, “This person is crushing me against Mount Sineru, emitting smoke, and also emitting masses of flames.” He then asked the Elder, “O Noble One, who are you?” Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied, “Nanda, I am the Elder Moggallāna.” The Naga King said, “Venerable Sir, if that is so, please remain in your form as a monk.” Then the Elder abandoned that Naga form and, in his natural form as a monk, entered the Naga King Nandopananda’s right ear and exited through his left ear. Again, he entered through the left ear and exited through the right ear.
438:
Similarly, he entered through the right nostril and exited through the left nostril. Again, he entered through the left nostril and exited through the right nostril.

Then, the Naga King Nandopananda opened his mouth. The Elder entered through the mouth and walked back and forth in meditation (caṅkama) within the Naga's stomach. The Blessed One gave a warning, saying:

“Dear Moggallāna, apply your mind very firmly. This Naga King Nandopananda is one of great power.”

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied:

“Venerable Sir, I have already developed the four bases of power (iddhipāda) and mastered them through the five masteries (vasībhāva). Venerable Sir, let alone one Naga King Nandopananda, I can subdue hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of Naga Kings similar to Nandopananda.”

The Naga King Nandopananda thought, “Let it be that the Elder Moggallāna entered through my mouth. When he comes out now, I will place him between my fangs and chew him up.” He then said, “Venerable Sir, please come outside. Do not oppress me by walking back and forth within my stomach.” The Elder came out and stood outside.
439:
As soon as the Naga King saw him, thinking, “This is that Elder Moggallāna,” he blew a fierce blast of air from his nose. The Elder entered the fourth jhāna and blocked that air. Consequently, the air from the Naga King’s nose could not move even a single hair on the Elder’s body.

(It is specifically to be noted: Although other monks might have been able to perform all the previous miracles from the beginning, when reaching this stage of the nasal blast, they would not have been persons of quick intuition (khippanisantipuggala) like Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, able to enter the meditative attainment (samāpatti) so rapidly. For this reason, the Blessed One did not grant permission to those other monks to subdue the Naga King.)

Then, the Naga King Nandopananda thought, “I was not able to move even a single hair of this monk with my nasal blast. This monk is indeed one of great power.” While he was reflecting thus, the Elder abandoned his natural form, manifested the form of a Great Garuda (Garuḍa), and continuously pursued the Naga King while displaying the wind-force of a Garuda. The Naga King, finally unable to escape, abandoned his original Naga form, manifested the form of a young man, and said, “Venerable Sir, I take you as my refuge,” while respectfully prostrating at the Elder’s feet.

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said, “Nanda, the Blessed One has arrived. Come, let us go to the Blessed One.” Thus, he subdued the Naga King and removed his pride.
440:
After neutralizing the poison, he led the Naga king to the presence of the Blessed One. The Naga king paid homage to the Blessed One with great respect and devotion, saying, “Exalted Buddha, I take refuge in the Blessed One and recognize you as my guide,” and thus he took the Three Refuges. The Blessed One said, “Naga king, may you be endowed with both physical and mental happiness,” and then, surrounded by the assembly of monks, he proceeded to the house of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika.

Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant asked, “Exalted Buddha, why have you arrived so late in the day?” The Blessed One replied, “Lay disciple, today a great battle of ‘you lose, I win’ took place between Moggallāna and the Naga king Nandopananda. (Therefore, we have arrived late in the day.)” When Anāthapiṇḍika asked, “Exalted Buddha, whose was the victory and whose was the defeat? (=Who won and who lost, Bhante?)”, the Blessed One replied, “Lay disciple, it was Moggallāna’s victory and Nanda’s defeat (=Moggallāna won and Nandopananda lost).”

Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant was so delighted and overjoyed that he requested, “Exalted Buddha, may the Lord Buddha accept my alms-food together with the assembly of monks for seven consecutive days; for seven days, I shall perform offerings and honors to the Great Elder.” Having made this request, for seven days, he [honored] the Buddha and the...
441:
five hundred monks by celebrating a grand festival of victory through great offerings and honors.

(The account of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna taming the Naga king Nandopananda is extracted and presented from the Visuddhimagga Commentary, Volume II, 12-Iddhividhaniddesa, page 27, and the Theragāthā Commentary, Volume II, page 501, in the explanation of the Mahāmoggallānattheragāthā).

The account of taming the Naga king Nandopananda by giving instructions to the Elder Moggallāna ends here.

## Subduing and Taming Baka Brahmā

(These accounts of the Blessed One subduing and taming Baka Brahmā appear in the Baka Jātaka of the Sattakanipāta and the Kesava Jātaka of the Catukkanipāta, along with their commentaries; as well as in the Baka Brahmā Sutta of the Brahma Saṃyutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya and its commentary. Since the explanation in the Commentary to the Brahmanimantanika Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa encompasses the explanations in those Jātakas and the Saṃyutta Nikāya Commentary, this Mahā-Buddhavamsa will focus on the explanation from the Mūlapaṇṇāsa Brahmanimantanika Sutta Commentary).

At one time, while the Blessed One was dwelling in the Jetavana monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī, he addressed the monks, saying:

“Monks, once I was staying at the foot of a royal Sal tree in the Subhaga forest near the city of Ukkaṭṭhā. Monks, at that time, a view of Sassatamicchādiṭṭhi (Eternalist wrong view) of this nature arose in the mind of Baka Brahmā:

‘This Brahma world, together with this body, is permanent. It is stable. It is eternal. It is absolute. It is not subject to passing away. In this Brahma world, there is no one who is reborn, who ages, who dies, who passes away, or (after passing away, by way of being reborn again) who...
442:
reappears. Apart from this Brahma world, together with this body, there is no other superior escape.’

Such was the powerful Eternalist wrong view that had arisen.

(Specifically, this Baka Brahmā, because he himself had reached the realm of the First Jhāna, was effectively denying and rejecting the higher states such as the Second Jhāna Brahma realm, the Third Jhāna Brahma realm, the Fourth Jhāna Brahma realm (including the four Arupa realms), as well as the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna).

Monks, then I, knowing the thought in Baka Brahmā’s mind with my own mind, just as a strong man might stretch out his bent arm or bend his outstretched arm, even so, I vanished from the foot of the royal Sal tree in the Subhaga forest near Ukkaṭṭhā and appeared in that (First Jhāna) Brahma world.

Monks, Baka Brahmā saw me coming from afar and said:

“Come, Noble One! Welcome, Noble One! Noble One, it has been a long time since you made the turn to come to this Brahma world. Noble One, this Brahma world, together with this body, is permanent, stable, eternal, absolute, and not subject to passing away. In this Brahma world, there is no one who is reborn, who ages, who dies, who passes away, or (after passing away, by way of being reborn again) who reappears.
443:
Apart from this Brahma world, together with this body, there is no other superior escape.”

Monks, when this was said, I said to Baka Brahmā:

“Friends, Baka Brahmā is indeed mired in ignorance! Friends, Baka Brahmā is indeed mired in ignorance! This Baka Brahmā says that which is impermanent is ‘permanent.’ He says that which is not stable, not eternal, not absolute, and subject to passing away is ‘stable,’ ‘absolute,’ and ‘not subject to passing away.’ While there are those who are reborn, age, die, pass away, and reappear in that (First Jhāna) Brahma realm, he says of that (First Jhāna) Brahma world, ‘In this Brahma world, there is no one who is reborn, who ages, who dies, who passes away, or who reappears.’ While there clearly exist superior escapes such as the Second Jhāna Brahma world, the Third Jhāna Brahma world, the Fourth Jhāna Brahma world, and the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna, which are beyond this (First Jhāna) Brahma world, he says, ‘Apart from this Brahma world, together with this body, there is no other superior escape.’”

## Māra possessing a Brahma attendant

Monks, then the Evil Māra, having possessed a minor Brahmapārisajja attendant, spoke to me in this offensive manner:
444:
“Bhikkhu, bhikkhu! Do not offend this Baka Brahmā. Do not offend this Baka Brahmā. Bhikkhu, this Baka Brahmā is the Great Brahma, the Overlord, the Unconquered, the All-seeing, the Controller, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Disposer (who ordains: ‘You shall be a king, you shall be a brahmin, you shall be a merchant or a farmer, you shall be a poor man; you shall be a human, you shall be a monk, or (at the lowest) you shall be a camel, you shall be an ox’), the Master of Jhāna, and the Father of those who have been and those who are to be.*

Bhikkhu, there were ascetics and brahmins before you who criticized and loathed the earth element (as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, just as you do), who criticized and loathed the water element, the fire element, the air element,

* Regarding 'those who have been and those who are to be'—beings born from an egg or a womb are called 'those who are being born' while they remain inside the egg or womb, and from the moment they emerge from that egg or womb, they are called 'those who have been born.'
Beings born from moisture (=saṃsedaja) are called 'those who are being born' at the moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness, and thereafter they are called 'those who have been born.'
Beings of spontaneous birth (opapātika) are called 'those who are being born' during the first posture, and from the second posture onwards, they are called 'those who have been born.' (From Majjhima Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 303).
445:
beings, gods, Māra, and Brahma (criticizing them as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, just as you do). After the dissolution of the body and after death, they were reborn in a low (unhappy) realm.

Bhikkhu, there were ascetics and brahmins before you who praised and delighted in the earth element (as permanent, stable, eternal, unbreakable, indestructible, and inexhaustible), who praised and delighted in the water element, the fire element, the air element, beings, gods, Māra, and Brahma (as permanent, stable, eternal, unbreakable, indestructible, and inexhaustible). After the dissolution of the body and after death, they were reborn in a noble (Brahma) realm.

Bhikkhu, therefore I say this to you: Friend, I wish to urge you—follow only the words spoken by Brahma; do not transgress the words of Brahma. Bhikkhu, if you should transgress the words of Brahma, it will be just as if a man were to drive away good fortune that has come to him by beating it with a long stick (four cubits long), or as if a man falling down a precipice were to fail to grasp or support himself on the ground with his hands or feet. Even so will this simile be fulfilled for you. Friend, (therefore) I wish to urge you—follow only the words spoken by Brahma; do not
446:
transgress the words of Brahma. Bhikkhu, do you not see the assembly of Brahma gathered here?”

Thus he spoke offensively. Monks, in this way, the Evil Māra tried to draw me into the fold of Brahma’s assembly.

(In this matter, it may be asked: How did Māra see the Blessed One? The answer is: While staying in his own celestial mansion, Māra frequently reflects, “Where is the recluse Gotama dwelling now?” On this occasion, when he reflected, he knew, “He is dwelling in the Subhaga forest near Ukkaṭṭhā.” Then, looking further to see “Where is the recluse Gotama going?”, he saw the Blessed One proceeding to the Brahma world. He thought, “The recluse Gotama is now going to the Brahma world. He will preach the Dhamma there, and before he can lead the assembly of Brahmas beyond my domain, I shall go there and make them lose interest in hearing the Dhamma.” Thus, he followed the Blessed One closely without losing sight of him and stood with an invisible body in the midst of the Brahma assembly. He realized that the Blessed One had already rebuked Baka Brahmā, saying, “Friends, Baka Brahmā is indeed mired in ignorance!” and so on, and he stood there to provide support for Baka Brahmā.

That Māra was unable to possess the Great Brahma or the Brahmapurohita Brahmas; therefore, he entered into the body of a minor Brahmapārisajja attendant).

Monks, when the Evil Māra had spoken thus (through possession), I said to the Evil Māra:

“I know you, Evil One! Do not think, ‘The recluse Gotama does not know me.’ You, Evil One, are Māra.”
447:
447
"O Evil One, Mahābrahmā, the assembly of Brahmās, and the entire retinue of Brahmās have all fallen into your hands; they have all come under your influence. O Evil One, a wrong thought and a wrong intention have arisen in your mind: 'May this ascetic also fall into my hands; may this ascetic also come under my influence.' O Evil One, in truth, I have neither fallen into your hands nor have I come under your influence."
Thus did the Buddha refute and speak.
Monks, when I had spoken thus to Māra, Baka the Brahmā spoke to me in this way:
"Venerable Sir, I say that which is permanent is 'permanent'; I say that which is stable, constant, exclusive, and not subject to passing away is 'stable', 'constant', 'exclusive', and 'not subject to passing away'. I say that in this Brahmā realm, there is no one who is reborn, grows old, dies, passes away, or reappears. I say that 'in this Brahmā world, there is no one who is reborn, grows old, dies, passes away, or reappears.' Because there is no other superior liberation beyond this Brahmā world, I say, 'There is no other superior liberation beyond this Brahmā world.'"
448:
448
"O monk, the practices of the ascetics and brahmins who preceded you in the world were as long as your life. Those ascetics and brahmins would have known if there were another superior liberation beyond this Brahmā world, saying 'There is another superior liberation,' and they would have known if there were no other superior liberation beyond this Brahmā world, saying 'There is no other superior liberation.'
O monk, therefore, I say this to you—(meaning he speaks firmly and boldly)—you will not find another superior liberation beyond this Brahmā world; you will only experience weariness and suffering.
O monk, if you cling to the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), you will be one who dwells near me, one who dwells in my place, a subordinate whom I can treat as I wish. If you cling to the water element, the fire element, the air element, to beings, to devas, to Māra, or if you cling to Brahmā, you will be one who dwells near me, one who dwells in my place, a subordinate whom I can treat as I wish."
Thus did he speak. (The Blessed One replied and said):
"Brahmā, I also know this: 'If I were to cling to the earth element, I would be one who dwells near you,
449:
449
one who dwells in your place, a subordinate whom you can treat as you wish. If I were to cling to the water element, the fire element, the air element, to beings, to devas, to Māra, or if I were to cling to Brahmā, I would be one who dwells near you, one who dwells in your place, a subordinate whom you can treat as you wish.' This I also know.
Brahmā, indeed, I know your state: 'Baka the Brahmā has such great power, such great majesty, such great fame and retinue.' I also know your reach and ability."
Thus did the Buddha say. Then Baka the Brahmā replied and asked again:
"Venerable Sir, how do you know my state: 'Baka the Brahmā has such great power, such great majesty, such great fame and retinue'? How do you know my reach and ability?"
Then the Blessed One answered:
"Your authority extends over a thousand world systems (sahassī lokadhātu), as far as the sun and moon revolve, beautifying and illuminating the quarters. (The meaning is: the circular area where a pair of sun and moon revolve, beautifying and illuminating the quarters, is called one world system.
450:
450
In such a thousand world systems, your power and authority spread—this is the meaning.)
Within these thousand world systems, you know the assembly of superior and inferior beings, those with lust and those without lust, this world system and the other nine hundred and ninety-nine, and the rebirth and death of beings within them.
Baka Brahmā, I know your state: 'Thus Baka the Brahmā is one of great power, great majesty, and great fame and retinue.' I also know your reach and ability. (The Blessed One's discourse is not yet finished; some noteworthy points will be inserted here):
(The Blessed One, having spoken thus, rebuked him: "Baka Brahmā, you are one whose power and authority spread only within a thousand world systems; nevertheless, you think, 'I am a very great Brahmā.' You are only a Sahassī Brahmā who can see only a thousand world systems. In truth, there are countless others superior to you: Dvisahassī Brahmās who can see and rule two thousand world systems, and Satasahassī Brahmās who can see and rule three thousand, four thousand, five thousand, ten thousand, or even a hundred thousand world systems. Nevertheless, like one who tries to compare a long garment of many cubits with a four-cubit loincloth (simile from the Commentary), or like one who wishes to dive in water only ankle-deep (simile from the Sub-commentary), or like a small frog who mistakes a cow's footprint for a deep ocean (simile used by the wise), you are one who thinks highly of yourself, believing 'I am a very great Brahmā.'")
451:
451
"Baka Brahmā, there is yet another realm and existence beyond this first jhāna realm. You do not know or see that realm; I know and see it. Baka Brahmā, there is indeed a realm and existence called Ābhassara. Having passed away from that Ābhassara realm, you were reborn in this first jhāna realm. Because you have lived here (in this first jhāna realm) for a long time, your mindfulness and memory of that have faded. Therefore, you do not know or see that (Ābhassara) realm; I know and see that (Ābhassara) realm. Baka Brahmā, because I know thus (the Ābhassara realm which you do not know), I am not your equal in wisdom. How could I be inferior to you? In truth, I alone am superior to you in wisdom." (1) (The Blessed One's discourse is not yet finished. Some noteworthy points will be inserted here):
(This Baka Brahmā was one who passed away from higher Brahmā realms and was reborn in lower Brahmā realms. To elaborate: In a past world-cycle when no Buddha appeared, this Baka Brahmā became a hermit, practiced kasina meditation, and attained meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Passing away from that life without losing his jhāna, he was reborn in the Vehapphala realm of the fourth jhāna, where the lifespan is five hundred mahākappas. Having stayed there for the full lifespan of five hundred mahākappas, he desired rebirth in a lower realm and developed the superior third jhāna of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). Passing away from that (Vehapphala realm), he was reborn in the Subhakiṇṇa Brahmā realm of the third jhāna, where the lifespan is sixty-four mahākappas.
It is specifically to be noted: Just as when one has committed many ānantariya kammas (heinous crimes) such as killing one's mother, only the strongest and heaviest
452:
452
among those many ānantariya kammas gives the result of rebirth in the Great Avīci hell, while the remaining ānantariya kammas do not give rebirth but only support the kamma that gave rebirth; similarly, when all four rūpa-jhānas have been developed, only the jhāna developed specifically with the four predominants (adhipati) gives the result of rebirth in its corresponding rūpāvacara Brahmā realm. The other rūpa-jhānas, not having the opportunity to give rebirth themselves, do not give rebirth but only provide support to the rebirth-giving rūpa-jhāna so that it can yield its result for the full lifespan. (From the Sub-commentary).
Baka Brahmā stayed in that Subhakiṇṇa realm for the full lifespan of sixty-four mahākappas. Then, as before, he developed the superior second rūpāvacara jhāna and (passing away from that Subhakiṇṇa realm) was reborn in the Ābhassara Brahmā realm of the second jhāna, where the lifespan is eight mahākappas. Having stayed there for the full lifespan of eight mahākappas, he developed the superior first rūpāvacara jhāna as before and (passing away from that Ābhassara realm) was reborn in the Mahābrahmā realm of the first jhāna, where the lifespan is sixty-four antarakappas, which is one asankheyya-kappa.
In the early period of his current existence in the Mahābrahmā realm of the first jhāna, Baka Brahmā still knew his past jhāna-merit and his past existences and realms. As a long time passed, he forgot both and adopted the wrong view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi). Therefore, the Blessed One said to Baka Brahmā, "Because that mindfulness and memory have faded, you do not know or see that Ābhassara realm," and so on.
## The Story of Baka Brahmā's Past
When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Baka Brahmā thought, "The Ascetic Gotama [knows] my successive existences..."
453:
453
He knew his lifespan, the realms and abodes where he had previously existed, and the meritorious deeds of jhāna he had performed in the past. He thought, "Now, I will ask the ascetic Gotama about my own meritorious deeds performed in the past." Having reflected thus, he asked the Blessed One about his past meritorious deeds. The Blessed One answered and preached to him.

To elaborate: In the distant past, this Baka Brahmā was a man of noble birth. Seeing the faults in sensual pleasures, he thought, "I shall make an end to rebirth, aging, sickness, and death." He renounced the world to become an ascetic. He attained the mundane meditative attainments (jhāna) and, having gained the jhānas which are the basis for supernormal powers (abhiññā), he built a small leaf-roofed hut near the banks of the Gangā River and spent his time delighting in the practice of jhāna.

In particular, while he was living there, caravans of merchants with five hundred wagons would frequently cross the desert. In the desert, they could not travel by day and had to travel only at night. Once, as the merchants were crossing the desert at night, the oxen yoked to the front yoke of the lead wagon turned back while walking and, losing their way, headed back toward the path they had come from. The remaining wagons likewise turned back toward the way they had come. Only when dawn broke did the merchants realize they had turned back.
