For those merchants, that day was supposed to be the day they crossed the desert. All their firewood and water were exhausted. Consequently, they thought, "Now our lives are no more," unyoked the wagons, tied the oxen to the wheels, and the people went under the shade of the rear of the wagons to sleep.

Early in the morning, the ascetic who was the future Baka Brahmā, having attained jhāna, came out of his small leaf-roofed hut. While sitting at the door of the hut and looking at the Gangā River, he saw the entire expanse of the Gangā flowing with a great current of water, appearing as if a large block of emerald were rolling along.
454:
454
Seeing the water flowing, he reflected, "Are there beings in this world who are exhausted because they do not get such sweet water?" While contemplating thus, he saw the group of merchants in distress within the desert. With a strong wish, "May these beings not perish," he resolved with the mind of supernormal power (abhiññā), "May this great mass of water from the Gangā River break off and flow toward the merchants in the desert."

As soon as the mind of supernormal power arose, a great mass of water flowed into that desert as if flowing into a canal. When the people heard the sound of water and woke up, they saw the water and were exceedingly joyful. They bathed and drank, gave water to the oxen, and reached their desired destination in comfort.

The Blessed One, wishing to show that past meritorious deed of Baka Brahmā, spoke this verse:

"When you gave drink to many people,
Who were thirsty and oppressed by the heat in the desert,
I remember that ancient vow and virtue of yours,
Like one waking from sleep."

(O Brahma named Baka, in the past when you were an ascetic who had attained jhāna, you caused many people—merchants who were oppressed by the heat of the sun and thirsty in the desert—to drink, bathe, and use water through your supernormal power. I, the Teacher of the three kinds of beings, remember that ancient practice of virtue and vows you undertook and practiced, clearly and repeatedly through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa), just as a man who was sleeping wakes up.)
455:
455
At another time, that ascetic built a small leaf-roofed hut on a bank of the Gangā River and lived depending on a small forest village for alms. At that time, bandits attacked, struck, and looted that village, taking away precious gold and silver, as well as cattle and human captives. The cattle, oxen, dogs, and people made a loud, tumultuous noise. The noble ascetic heard that sound and, upon reflecting "What is this?", he knew that danger had befallen the villagers. With a strong wish, "May these beings not perish while I am watching," he entered the jhāna which is the basis for supernormal power. Emerging from that jhāna, he used his supernormal power to create a great fourfold army (consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry) that marched toward the bandits, making their respective sounds of shooting and drumming.

The bandits saw the great army and, thinking "The King has come out!", they abandoned all the looted property and fled. The noble ascetic resolved, "Whatever property belongs to whom, let that property belong only to that person." It happened exactly as the ascetic resolved. All the people attained safety.

The Blessed One, wishing to show this past meritorious deed of Baka Brahmā as well, spoke this verse:

"When at the bank of the Eṇī, the people who were captured,
And the property being carried away by the captors, you released,
I remember that ancient vow and virtue of yours,
Like one waking from sleep."

(O Brahma named Baka, in the past when you were an ascetic who had attained jhāna, at the landing of the Gangā River named Eṇīkūla—so named because of the abundance of deer called Eṇī—you caused the people of the village who were being led away as captives and the mass of property taken by the thieves to be completely released from the hands of the thieves by creating a fourfold army.)
456:
456
(I, the Teacher of the three kinds of beings, remember that ancient practice of virtue and vows you undertook and practiced, clearly and repeatedly through the knowledge of recollecting past lives, just as a man who was sleeping wakes up.)

Again, at another time, a family living upstream on the Gangā and a family living downstream on the Gangā formed an alliance through marriage, giving and taking a daughter. They joined boats together to form a raft and, loading it with many kinds of food, perfumes, and flowers, they traveled with the current of the Gangā. The many people on the boat were eating, drinking, dancing, and singing, being exceedingly merry and joyful as if traveling in a celestial mansion.

At that time, a Nāga king who ruled over the Gangā saw those people and became angry, thinking, "These people do not show any regard for me, thinking 'If we play and make merry like this, the Nāga king of the Gangā will be angry.' Now, I shall cause these people to reach the middle of the ocean." He created a massive body, split the water, emerged suddenly, and stood with a great hood raised, making a hissing sound as if about to strike and kill.

The people saw the Nāga king and, out of fear, made loud and frantic cries. The noble ascetic, while sitting in his leaf-roofed hut, heard that sound and reflected, "Earlier, these people were coming with great joy, dancing and singing. Now, they are crying out in fear because they have met with danger."
457:
457
"What is the reason?" When he reflected, he saw the Nāga king and thought, "May these people not perish while I am watching." He entered the jhāna which is the basis for supernormal power, gave up his natural form, and created the form of a great Garuḍa king, appearing as if he were about to swoop down and seize the Nāga king.

The Nāga king was terrified, withdrew his hood, and entered the water. All the people attained safety.

The Blessed One, wishing to show this past meritorious deed of Baka Brahmā as well, spoke this verse:

"When on the stream of the Gangā, the boat was seized,
By a fierce Nāga, and the people were in peril,
You released them by force and power,
I remember that ancient vow and virtue of yours,
Like one waking from sleep."

(O Brahma named Baka, in the past when you were an ascetic, a fierce and cruel water-deity Nāga, wishing to destroy the many people from the two villages on the stream of the Gangā, threatened and oppressed their boat. You, by the power of supernormal power known as vikubbana-iddhi, overcame him and released them from the danger of the Nāga. I, the Teacher of the three kinds of beings, remember that ancient practice of virtue and vows you undertook and practiced, clearly and repeatedly through the knowledge of recollecting past lives, just as a man who was sleeping wakes up.)

At another time in a past life, this future Baka Brahmā became a noble ascetic named Kesava. At that time, our
458:
458
Bodhisatta was a young man named Kappa, who was a resident pupil (antevāsika) always serving and attending to the teacher, the ascetic Kesava. He was one who always obeyed orders, asking what task he should perform for the teacher, doing only what pleased the teacher, endowed with wisdom, and acting for the teacher's benefit. The teacher, the ascetic Kesava, was unable to travel, stay, or eat without his primary disciple, the ascetic Kappa. Although he was supported by the King of Bārāṇasī, he left the King and lived depending only on his primary disciple, the ascetic Kappa. (The detailed story should be looked for in the Kesava Jātaka of the Catukka Nipāta.)

The Blessed One, wishing to show this past meritorious deed of Baka Brahmā as well, spoke this verse:

"And Kappa was your devoted companion,
Who regarded you as wise and virtuous.
I remember that ancient vow and virtue of yours,
Like one waking from sleep."

(O Brahma named Baka, I, the Teacher of the three kinds of beings, in a certain past life, was the noble ascetic named Kappa, who was the resident disciple always attending to you when you were the virtuous ascetic named Kesava. At that time, you cherished and praised me as one who possessed excellent and distinguished wisdom and as one who was fully endowed with virtuous conduct. I, the Teacher of the three kinds of beings, remember that ancient practice of virtue and vows you undertook and practiced, clearly and repeatedly through the knowledge of recollecting past lives, just as a man who was sleeping wakes up.)
459:
In this way, the Blessed One pointed out and preached the various meritorious deeds performed by Baka Brahmā in his previous existences. While the Blessed One was preaching, Baka Brahmā himself regained the memory of his past lives. In Baka Brahmā's knowledge, all his past kamma became clearly manifest, just as various forms appear clearly when a thousand lamps are lit. Baka Brahmā, filled with overflowing faith and devotion, addressed the Buddha with this verse:

"Addhā pajānāsi mametamāyuṃ,
Aññampi jānāsi tathā hi buddho.
Tathā hi tyāyaṃ jalitānubhāvo,
Obhāsayaṃ tiṭṭhati brahmalokaṃ."

(Mārisa = O Blessed One who has extinguished all suffering. Tvaṃ = You) Addhā = certainly and truly. Mama etaṃ āyuṃ = all the life spans I have had in past existences. Pajānāsi = You know with distinct penetration. Aññampi = All other things that should be known (besides my life span). Jānāsi = You know with distinct penetration. Tathā hi = For that very reason. Buddho = You are truly the Omniscient Buddha. Tathā hi = Because You are truly the Omniscient Buddha. Te ayaṃ jalitānubhāvo = this radiant majesty of Your physical body. Brahmalokaṃ = the entire Brahma realm. Obhāsayaṃ = shining and illuminating more than a thousand suns and moons. Tiṭṭhati = stands manifest.

(Thus he addressed the Buddha with this verse).

After the Blessed One had preached the events of the past lives as an interlude in response to Baka Brahmā's inquiry, He continued the original discourse in connection with the previous context as follows:

"Baka Brahmā, there are still the realms known as Subhakiṇha, Vehapphala, and Abhibhū..."
460:
"...realms still exist. You do not know or see those realms; I, the Buddha, know and see them. Baka Brahmā, because I know in this way (the Abhibhū realm which you do not know), I am not your equal in terms of wisdom. How could I be inferior to you? In fact, I alone am superior to you in wisdom."

Thereafter, the Blessed One, wishing to clearly demonstrate that He was not equal to the Great Brahma in wisdom and that He alone was superior to Baka Brahmā in wisdom, continued to preach as follows:

"Baka Brahmā, having known the earth element as the earth element through higher knowledge as being impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and having realized and known Nibbāna, which is the state not reached by the nature of the earth element of all earth elements, I do not cling to the earth element (through craving, conceit, and wrong view); I do not cling in the earth element (in the sense of a self residing there); I do not cling from the earth element (in the sense of a self emerging from it); I do not cling to the earth element as 'mine'. I do not assert the earth element (as 'I', 'mine', or 'my soul'). Baka Brahmā, because I know in this way (Nibbāna which you do not know), I am not your equal in terms of wisdom. How could I be inferior to you? In fact, I alone am superior to you in wisdom."

"Baka Brahmā, I [know] the water element, (p), the fire element, (p), the air element, (p),"
461:
"...beings, (p), devas, (p), Māra, (p), Brahmā, (p), the Ābhassara Brahmās, (p), the Subhakiṇha Brahmās, (p), the Vehapphala Brahmās, (p), the Abhibhū Brahmā, (p), the All (the mundane sakkāya-dhamma of the three planes). Having known the All as the All through higher knowledge as being impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and having realized and known Nibbāna, which is the state not reached by the nature of the All of all the All (the mundane sakkāya-dhamma), I do not cling to the All = the mundane sakkāya-dhamma (through craving, conceit, and wrong view); I do not cling in the All = the mundane sakkāya-dhamma; I do not cling from the All = the mundane sakkāya-dhamma; I do not cling to the All = the mundane sakkāya-dhamma as 'mine'; I do not assert the All = the mundane sakkāya-dhamma (as 'I', 'mine', or 'my soul'). Baka Brahmā, because I know in this way (Nibbāna which you do not know), I am not your equal in terms of wisdom. How could I be inferior to you? In fact, I alone am superior to you in wisdom."

Thus He spoke. (At that time, Baka Brahmā, wishing to suppress the Blessed One with falsehood, said):

"Venerable Sir, if there were a state not reached by the nature of the All of the All, then Your statement that You know such a state not reached (will become a void statement). Let not such a void statement occur; let Your statement not be..."
462:
"...(an empty statement). Let it not be an empty statement."

(At this point, I shall provide a brief explanation so that the devout readers of the Buddha's life story do not become confused:

The Burmese word 'Alon-son' and the Pali word 'Sabba' have the same meaning. This Pali word 'Sabba' (the All) is used to refer to all mundane things (= all sakkāya-dhamma). The Pali and Burmese word 'Sabba = the All' used in this sense, referring to all mundane things, is called 'Sakkāya-sabba = all sakkāya-dhamma'. It is with reference to this Sakkāya-sabba = all sakkāya-dhamma = all mundane things that the Buddha preached in the Ādittapariyāya Sutta: 'Sabbaṃ bhikkhave ādittaṃ' (All, O monks, is burning).

In this Pali text, when it says 'O monks, all things are burned by the fires of passion, etc.', it cannot be said that supramundane (lokuttara) dhammas are burned by the fires of passion, etc., because unwholesome states like passion, hatred, and delusion cannot take those supramundane dhammas as objects at all. Only mundane things = sakkāya-dhamma = the aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) can be taken as objects by unwholesome states like greed, hatred, and delusion; therefore, it is said that only those mundane things are burned by the fires of passion, etc. Thus, according to the words 'Sabbaṃ = all things', excluding the supramundane dhammas, one must take only all mundane things = all sakkāya-dhamma = all aggregates of clinging. Therefore, the 'Sabba' in that Ādittapariyāya Sutta is called 'Sakkāya-sabba = all sakkāya-dhamma'.

In the term 'Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa = the knowledge that knows the All', since the Blessed One knows all mundane things, all supramundane things, and all concepts (paññatti) through that Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa,"
463:
"...in the word 'Sabba = the All' contained in the term 'Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa', one must take all existing things—mundane, supramundane, and concepts. Therefore, the 'Sabba' in that term 'Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa' is called 'Sabba-sabba = all of the all'.

With this much said, the use and preaching of 'Sabba = the All' in the field of Dhamma literature is: (1) there is the use and preaching referring only to Sakkāya-sabba = all sakkāya-dhamma = all mundane things; (2) there is the use and preaching referring to Sabba-sabba = all existing things—mundane, supramundane, and concepts. In summary, the devout readers of the Buddha's life will understand that there are two kinds of 'Sabba = the All': (1) Sakkāya-sabba and (2) Sabba-sabba. Now, let us examine the meaning of 'Sabba' as used by the Blessed One and Baka Brahmā.

When the Blessed One demonstrated that He was superior to Baka Brahmā in wisdom:

(1) I know the earth element (which you know). I also know the Nibbāna-dhamma which is not reached by the nature of the earth element (which you do not know). (2) I know the water element (which you know). I also know the Nibbāna-dhamma which is not reached by the nature of the water element (which you do not know)... (and so on for) (3) fire element, (4) air element, (5) beings, (6) devas, (7) Māra, (8) Brahmā, (9) Ābhassara Brahmā, (10) Subhakiṇha Brahmā, (11) Vehapphala Brahmā, (12) Abhibhū Brahmā = meaning the Asaññasatta Brahmā... (13) I know the All (which you know) = referring to Sakkāya-sabba. I also know the (Nibbāna) dhamma which is not reached by the nature of the All (which you do not know).

Thus, thirteen points were presented. Baka Brahmā could find no fault to criticize in the first twelve points."
464:
"However, in the final thirteenth point—

(The Blessed One), referring to Sakkāya-sabba = all sakkāya-dhamma = all mundane things, said: 'Baka Brahmā, I know the All (sakkāya = mundane things) through higher knowledge as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. Having known thus (by the grace of that special insight knowledge, through path knowledge), I also know the (Nibbāna) dhamma which is not reached by the nature of the All (sakkāya = the collection of mundane things).' He spoke this meaning in cryptic and profound words: 'Having specially known the All through the nature of the All, I also know the dhamma which is not reached by the nature of the All of the All.'

In that statement, 'Having specially known the All through the nature of the All' means: 'I, the Buddha, have known all the tebhūmaka sakkāya-dhamma, the five mundane aggregates, distinctly through their nature of impermanence, suffering, and non-self (through insight knowledge).' Here, the Blessed One said 'the All through the nature of the All' referring only to Sakkāya-sabba. 'Knowing the dhamma not reached by the nature of the All of the All' means: 'Having realized and known through path knowledge the Nibbāna-dhamma which is not reached by the conditioned nature of all the tebhūmaka sakkāya-dhamma, the five mundane aggregates.'

(The conditioned nature of material things like the earth element and water element, such as hardness and cohesion, and the conditioned nature of mental things like contact and feeling, do not exist at all in Nibbāna, which is the unconditioned (Asaṅkhata) dhamma. In that unconditioned dhamma called Nibbāna, there is the nature of peace (santi-sabhāva), which is the opposite of conditioned natures. Referring to this very point, [it is said]: 'Nibbāna not reached by the nature of the earth element of the earth element; Nibbāna not reached by the nature of the water element of the water element; (p) [Nibbāna not reached] by the nature of the sakkāya of all sakkāya-dhamma.'"
465: (It should be specifically noted that the Buddha taught, "Nibbāna is not reached.") To this extent, the pious audience reading the Buddhavaṃsa can clearly understand that the Exalted One intended to say to Baka Brahmā: "I, the Buddha, fully understand the entire Sakkāya-dhamma, the five mundane aggregates (which you can know); I also know Nibbāna, which is not reached by the nature of the entire Sakkāya-dhamma (which you cannot know)." In this statement, the term "All" (Sabba) refers only to the five mundane aggregates, the Sakkāya-sabba, while Nibbāna should be understood as the "dhamma not reached by the nature of the All." Baka Brahmā, being a person who holds a fault-finding view (and completely failing to understand that the Exalted One was referring to the Sakkāya-sabba), misinterpreted "All" as "Sabba-sabba," meaning every single mundane, supramundane, and conceptual dhamma. He then attempted to trap the Exalted One with a charge of falsehood, saying: "Venerable Sir, if there is a dhamma that is not reached by the nature of the all of the All, then Your statement that You know such a dhamma which is not reached will become a statement devoid of meaning. Let Your statement not be a void statement. Your statement will become a futile statement; let it not be a futile statement." Baka Brahmā's intended meaning was: In Your statement, Venerable Sir, there are two sets of words: (1) I know all dhammas. (2) I also know the dhamma that is not reached by the nature of the all of those all dhammas. Between these two—
466: (1) In the statement "I know all," since the word "All" already includes and takes in every single existing dhamma (as all dhammas are exhausted in the first statement), (2) the designated "dhamma not reached by the nature of the all of those all dhammas" can no longer exist. If You say You know such a dhamma while it does not exist, Your statement regarding that second (2) dhamma will be like the terms 'sky-flower,' 'rabbit-horn,' 'tortoise-hair,' or 'crab-blood'—words that exist only as assertions but have no corresponding substance or reality. If You say that the second (2) "dhamma not reached by the nature of the all of that All" exists separately, then that dhamma is not included in the first (1) "all dhammas." Therefore, that first (1) dhamma cannot and should not be called "All." While it is not the All, Your statement "I know the All" would be a deviant and false statement. In this way, he intended to crush the Exalted One with a charge of falsehood. (Here, it should be summarized that since the Exalted One taught with reference to the Sakkāya-sabba, both types of dhamma exist; Baka Brahmā, however, erred in his attempt to crush the Buddha because he misunderstood it as Sabba-sabba.) Because the Exalted One is a Great Teacher (Vādī) who is superior to Baka Brahmā by hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands of times, He wished to bring forth the teaching to refute and crush Baka Brahmā's erroneous accusation of falsehood, saying: "I, the Buddha, shall indeed speak of the All, and I shall also speak of Nibbāna, the dhamma not reached by the nature of the all of the All. Listen!" "Baka Brahmā, there exists the dhamma of Nibbāna, which is known through the Knowledge of the Path, the Knowledge of Fruition, and the Knowledge of Reviewing as a dhamma that is exceptionally superior to all conditioned dhammas (saṅkhata-dhamma).
467: It is not visible and cannot be seen with the ordinary physical eye; (or) it is a dhamma for which there is no other comparable dhamma to point out. It is entirely without the extreme of arising (uppāda) or the extreme of passing away (bhaṅga). It has a radiance that is more brilliant than the All; (or) it is a Nibbāna-dhamma that is perpetually sparkling and radiant, where darkness never exists. (By this statement, it is boldly declared and shown that Nibbāna certainly exists, which is not reached by the nature of the entire collection of Sakkāya-dhammas belonging to the three planes of existence.) That Nibbāna-dhamma (1) is not reached by the nature of the earth element; (2) is not reached by the nature of the water element; (3) of the fire element; (4) of the air element; (5) is not reached by the nature of beings; (6) of the devas; (7) of Māra; (8) is not reached by the nature of the Brahmās; (9) of the Ābhassara Brahmās; (10) of the Subhakiṇha Brahmās; (11) is not reached by the nature of the Vehapphala Brahmās; (12) is not reached by the nature of the Abhibhū Brahmā (= Asaññasatta Brahmā); (13) is not reached by the nature of the All (the collection of Sakkāya-dhammas). (By this statement, it is made clear that the Exalted One also speaks of the All.) Thus, there exists the entire collection of Sakkāya-dhammas belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka), which is the domain of knowledge for persons like you, Baka Brahmā. By the nature of the Sakkāya-dhamma of that entire collection of tebhūmaka Sakkāya-dhammas,
469: it is not visible because it is too subtle. Therefore, to be seen by others, they remain only with (2) a created form, which is a coarse body. Thus, when the Exalted One gave him permission, Baka Brahmā inclined his mind to withdraw the current created coarse form and change into the subtle natural form. Knowing this, the Exalted One made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna): "Let this Baka Brahmā not remain in the subtle natural form, but let him remain only in the current created coarse form." Consequently, Baka Brahmā was unable to change into his natural form. Thus, his body remained without vanishing. Again, Baka Brahmā, being unable to change into his natural form, tried to create a great darkness to shroud his current form. The Exalted One, by His own power, dispelled the darkness created by Baka Brahmā. Therefore, he was again unable to hide. Since Baka Brahmā could not change into his natural form nor create darkness, and was thus unable to hide, he acted desperately, hiding inside his celestial palace, then hiding behind a Kalpavriksha (wishing-tree), and then sitting crouched down. At that time, the assembly of Brahmās mocked and ridiculed him, saying, "This Baka Brahmā is hiding in the palace! He is hiding behind the wishing-tree! He is sitting crouched down! O Baka Brahmā, do you even have the perception that 'I am hidden and vanished'?" Baka Brahmā felt humiliated as he was mocked by the assembly of Brahmās. Summarizing these events, it is taught in the Pāḷi: "Monks, then Baka Brahmā said, 'I will vanish before the eyes of the recluse Gotama, I will vanish before the eyes of the recluse Gotama,' yet he was unable to vanish before My eyes."
470: When Baka Brahmā was unable to hide in this manner, the Exalted One said to him: "Baka Brahmā, if you cannot hide, I shall now vanish before your eyes; I shall perform a psychic miracle so that you cannot see Me." Then Baka Brahmā replied to the Exalted One: "Venerable Sir, if that is so, if You are able, then vanish right now before my eyes." Then the Exalted One (following the sequence: base jhāna, resolution, then again base fourth jhāna, then abhiññā): (1) First, He entered the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere functional consciousness (rūpāvacara-kiriya), which is the base for resolution. (2) Then, emerging from that jhāna, He made a resolution with the process of great functional consciousness associated with knowledge (mahākiriya ñāṇasampayutta javana vīthi): "Let the Great Brahmā, the assembly of Brahmās, and the minor attendant Brahmās hear only My voice, but let them not see Me." This means the resolution process occurred. (3) Thereafter, He entered the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere functional consciousness, which is the base for direct knowledge (abhiññā). (4) After emerging from that jhāna, the process of psychic power direct knowledge (iddhividha-abhiññā vīthi) arose in the Exalted One's mental continuum. In that mental process, as soon as the iddhividha-abhiññā jhāna-javana occurred once, His great physical body vanished. Not a single Brahmā could see Him anymore. Then, while remaining vanished, the Exalted One, to make it known that He was still there, recited this verse:
471: "Bhavevāhaṃ bhayaṃ disvā, bhavañca vibhavesinaṃ. Bhavaṃ nābhivadiṃ kiñci, nandiñca na upādiyiṃ." (O Brahmās assembled here!) I, the Buddha, the Teacher of the three worlds, having clearly seen with the eye of wisdom the fearsome danger of rebirth, aging, sickness, and death within the three realms of existence—the sensual, the fine-material, and the immaterial—and having seen the continuous arising in the three levels of existence of those beings (like Baka Brahmā) who search for the wrong path to the end of existence, I no longer misperceive any existence as permanent, stable, or eternal through the power of craving and views. I have also not clung to the craving for existence, having severed it four times at the root with the axe of knowledge that has the radiance of the four Paths, so that it is completely vanished.
472: ## Ten Thousand Brahmas Becoming Ariyas  In this verse, the word 'bhavam' indicates the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The word 'nandiṃ' indicates the Truth of the Origin of Suffering (samudaya-sacca). The word 'vibhava' indicates the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (nirodha-sacca). The phrase 'nandiñca na upādiyiṃ' indicates the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca).  In this way, the Blessed One extensively expounded the Four Noble Truths according to the dispositions of the gathered Brahmas, leading them to the wisdom of insight (vipassanā-ñāṇa), and finally crowned the discourse with the Fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala). At the conclusion of the teaching, following the sequence of the Dhamma with their knowledge and grasping the essence of insight, ten thousand Brahmas were established: some in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), some in the Fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala), some in the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), and some in the Fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala). At that time, the assembly of Brahmas was greatly delighted and spoke words of praise in amazement. Therefore, it is stated in the Pali:  'Monks, then the Brahma, the Brahma's assembly, and the Brahma's retinue thought: "Friends, it is wonderful indeed, it is marvelous indeed, the great power and great majesty of the recluse Gotama! We have never before seen nor heard of any other recluse or brahmin of such great power and majesty as this recluse Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan. Friends, this recluse Gotama, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan, is able to uproot the existence..."'
474: "Venerable sir, if you know thus (the Four Noble Truths), if you have realized the Four Noble Truths through self-enlightened knowledge (sayambhū-ñāṇa), do not lead your disciples to that Dhamma; do not lead recluses and wanderers to that Dhamma. Do not teach the Dhamma to your disciples; do not teach the Dhamma to recluses and wanderers. Do not show affection for your disciples; do not show affection for recluses and wanderers.  Recluse, there were in the world before you recluses and brahmins who claimed to be Arahants and Fully Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas). Those recluses and brahmins led their disciples and recluses and wanderers to the Dhamma. They taught the Dhamma to their disciples and recluses and wanderers. They showed affection for their disciples and recluses and wanderers. Because those recluses and brahmins led their disciples and recluses and wanderers to the Dhamma, taught them the Dhamma, and had minds full of affection for them, after the breakup of the body, after death, they were reborn in a low state, in a realm of misery (apāya). (a)  Recluse, there were in the world before you recluses and brahmins who claimed to be Arahants and Fully Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas). Those recluses and brahmins did not lead their disciples and recluses and wanderers...
475: ...to the Dhamma. They did not teach the Dhamma to their disciples and recluses and wanderers. They did not show affection for their disciples and recluses and wanderers. Because those recluses and brahmins did not lead their disciples and recluses and wanderers to the Dhamma, did not teach them the Dhamma, and did not have minds full of affection for them, after the breakup of the body, after death, they were reborn in a superior Brahma realm. (b)  Recluse, therefore I say this to you: 'Venerable sir, I urge you. Strive to live happily in the present life and remain unconcerned. Venerable sir, it is better not to teach the Dhamma. Do not instruct others.' This is what I wish to say to you."  Monks, when he had spoken thus, I said to Mara the Evil One:  "Evil One, I know you. Do not think, 'The recluse Gotama does not know me.' Evil One, you are Mara. O Evil One, you do not speak thus to me out of a desire for my welfare; O Evil One, you speak thus to me out of a desire for my harm and ill-welfare. O Evil One, this thought has occurred to you: 'Those who hear the Dhamma taught by the recluse Gotama will transcend the three worlds of existence, which are my domain.'"
476: "O Evil One, those recluses and brahmins you mentioned, though they were not themselves Fully Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas), they claimed, 'We are Fully Enlightened Ones.' O Evil One, I, however, am truly a Fully Enlightened One who has personally realized all truths, and I claim the truth when I say, 'I am a Fully Enlightened One.'  O Evil One, whether the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to his disciples or not, he is endowed with the quality of equanimity (tādi-guṇa), being free from like or dislike. O Evil One, whether the Tathāgata leads his disciples to the Dhamma or not, he is endowed with the quality of equanimity, being free from like or dislike. Why is that?  O Evil One, the Tathāgata has abandoned the taints (āsavas) which cause defilement, which lead to renewed existence, which are accompanied by fever and result in suffering, and which lead to future birth, aging, and death. He has cut them off at the root like an anusaya, made them like a palm tree stump, done away with them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. (Thus, for the Tathāgata, those taints) have no nature to arise again in the future.  O Evil One, just as a palm tree, once its crown is cut off, is incapable of further growth, even so, the Tathāgata has abandoned the taints which cause defilement, which lead to renewed existence, which are accompanied by fever and result in suffering, and which lead to future...
478: "...upon his request."  When both of those friends reached adulthood, they each held the position of a great merchant in their respective cities. Later, on one occasion, the merchant Ugga arrived at the house of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika in the city of Sāvatthī with five hundred carts for trade. Anāthapiṇḍika called his daughter Cūḷasubhaddā and assigned her the task, saying, "Dear daughter, your father's friend, the merchant named Ugga, has arrived. All the major and minor duties to be performed for this merchant are your responsibility."  Cūḷasubhaddā agreed, saying, "Very well," and from the day the merchant Ugga arrived, she personally prepared and cooked the meals and dishes. She arranged flowers, perfumes, and scented pastes. When serving food, she arranged the bathwater for the merchant Ugga, and from the time he finished his bath, she respectfully supervised and performed all the necessary duties for the merchant herself.  The merchant Ugga, seeing that Cūḷasubhaddā was endowed with the conduct befitting a good housewife, felt affection and appreciation for her. One day, while sitting and conversing comfortably with the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, he reminded him, "Friend, we made such a promise in our youth," and requested Cūḷasubhaddā for his son. Notably, the merchant Ugga was by nature a person of wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). Therefore, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika did not yet make a decision (on his own), but [intended to ask] the Blessed One about this matter.
479:
479
Having made the request, the Buddha, seeing the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the merchant Ugga to attain the Path and Fruit of Stream-entry, gave his permission. After consulting with the Great Merchant’s wife, Puṇṇalakkhaṇadevī, Ugga accepted the proposal. On the appointed day, just as the Great Merchant Dhanañjaya had sent his daughter Visākhā, a grand marriage ceremony was arranged with all the necessary provisions. Calling his daughter Subhaddā close, he said:

“Dear daughter, a daughter-in-law living in her father-in-law’s house—
(1) Must not take the indoor fire outside. (This means one should not speak of the faults of the father-in-law or husband to those in other houses).
(2) Must not bring the outdoor fire inside. (This means if neighbors speak of the faults of the father-in-law or husband, one should not repeat those words to them).
(3) Must give only to those who return. (This means one should lend household items only to those who return them promptly).
(4) Must not give to those who do not return. (This means one should not lend items again to those who do not return what they have borrowed).
(5) Must give whether they return or not. (This means when poor relatives or friends come to the house, whether they are able to return the favor or not, one should certainly give to them).
480:
480
(6) Must sit happily. (This means upon seeing the father-in-law or husband, one must rise first. It is inappropriate to remain sitting when one should stand).
(7) Must eat happily. (This means one should not eat before the father-in-law or husband; after feeding them first and ensuring all members of the household have received their portion of food, only then should one eat).
(8) Must sleep happily. (This means one should not go to bed before the father-in-law or husband. Only after performing the major and minor duties for them should one sleep).
(9) Must tend the fire respectfully. (This means one should regard the father-in-law and husband as a great mass of fire or as a powerful king of serpents, looking upon them with respect and not with a disrespectful or frowning gaze).
(10) Must revere the household deities. (This means one should treat the father-in-law and husband as the primary deities of the home, relying on and respecting them).

In this manner, following the same method by which the Great Merchant Dhanañjaya gave advice to his daughter Visākhā, he gave these ten points of admonition and said:
481:
481
“If any fault arises in my daughter Cūḷasubhaddā where she goes, you must investigate and settle it according to the law.”

Having spoken thus, he sent eight wise householders as guarantors. On the day Cūḷasubhaddā was to be sent to the house of the merchant Ugga, he offered a great dāna to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha. To demonstrate clearly to the multitude the fruition of the meritorious deeds performed by his daughter in her past lives, he sent Cūḷasubhaddā to Ugga’s house with grand ceremony and provisions.

When the merchant’s daughter Cūḷasubhaddā eventually reached the city, the entire household of her father-in-law and the townspeople came out to welcome her. To make manifest the splendor of her merit and glory, Cūḷasubhaddā, like the merchant’s daughter Visākhā, showed herself to the entire city by standing upon a carriage as she entered. She accepted the gifts sent by the townspeople and, in return, gave gifts appropriate to their status, thus winning over the entire city with her wisdom and grace.

Furthermore, on the day Cūḷasubhaddā’s father-in-law, the merchant Ugga (who was of wrong view), held a festival at his house, he made offerings to the Acelakas (naked ascetics). He sent a messenger to call her, saying, “Let the daughter-in-law come and pay respects to our teachers, the recluses.” Cūḷasubhaddā, feeling ashamed, did not dare to look at the naked ascetics and, unwilling to go to the place of worship, refused the invitation.
482:
482
Although the merchant Ugga sent messengers to call his daughter-in-law Cūḷasubhaddā repeatedly, she continued to refuse and reject the invitation. Consequently, he became greatly incensed and said, “Friends, drag this Cūḷasubhaddā out of the house and expel her!” Cūḷasubhaddā thought, “He cannot blame me without cause; I will not accept this accusation.” She then called for the eight wise householders who had been sent as guarantors and presented the matter to them in person. Those eight householders, realizing that Cūḷasubhaddā was entirely without fault, informed the merchant Ugga of her innocence.

The merchant Ugga then said to his wife, “My lady, this Cūḷasubhaddā did not pay respects to my teachers, calling them ‘shameless ones.’” The merchant’s wife thought, “What kind of recluses are this daughter-in-law’s teachers? She praises her own teachers so excessively.” She then summoned Cūḷasubhaddā to her presence and asked:

“Kīdisā samaṇā tuyhaṃ,
bāḷhaṃ kho ne pasaṃsasi.
Kiṃ sīlā kiṃ samācārā,
taṃ me akkhāhi pucchitā.”

(Subhaddā, our daughter-in-law...) What are your recluses like, whom you take as your refuge and teachers? What noble qualities of practice do they possess? You speak so excessively in praise of that recluse Gotama and his disciples. What kind of special habits do they have? What kind of special conduct do they possess? Being asked by me, tell me the truth of that matter.”
483:
483
In response, Cūḷasubhaddā, wishing to clearly reveal the virtues of the Buddha and his disciples to the merchant’s wife, recited these following verses:

“Santindriyā santamānasā,
santaṃ tesaṃ gataṃ ṭhitaṃ.
Okkhibittacakkhū mitabhāṇī,
tādisā samaṇā mama.” (1)

(Noble Lady, my mother-in-law...) My teachers—the Buddha and his disciples who are my benefactors—possess senses that are perfectly calm, unlike the frivolous and agitated teachers you revere. They have minds that are peaceful, unburnt by the heat of defilements. Therefore, the walking of my teachers, the Buddha and his disciples...
484:
484
...and their standing are peaceful and steady, inspiring faith in those who behold them. They keep their eyes downcast, looking only a yoke’s length ahead, and are habituated to speaking measured words appropriate to the time and place. My teachers, the Buddha and his disciples, are endowed with such admirable conduct and virtues. (1)

“Kāyakammaṃ sucī nesaṃ,
vācākammaṃ anāvilaṃ.
Manokammaṃ suvisuddhaṃ,
tādisā samaṇā mama.” (2)

(Noble Lady, my mother-in-law...) All the bodily actions performed by my teachers, the Buddha and his disciples, are pure and free from the taint of unwholesome faults. All their verbal actions are clear and undisturbed by the impurities of unwholesome speech. All their mental actions are perfectly pure, far removed from the stains of misconduct. My teachers, the Buddha and his disciples, are endowed with such admirable conduct and virtues. (2)
485:
485
“Vimalā saṅkhamuttābhā,
suddhā antarabāhirā.
Puṇṇā suddhehi dhammehi,
tādisā samaṇā mama.” (3)

(Noble Lady, my mother-in-law...) My teachers, the Buddha and his disciples, are stainless like a conch or a string of pearls, free from the impurities of defilements. They are pure both within and without, without even a speck of fault. They are fully endowed with the three types of pure training (sikkhā). My teachers, the Buddha and his disciples, are endowed with such admirable conduct and virtues. (3)

“Lābhena unnato loko,
alābhena ca onato.
Lābhālābhena ekaṭṭhā,
tādisā samaṇā mama.” (4)

(Noble Lady, my mother-in-law...) The people of the world are uplifted and arrogant when they obtain gain due to their past merit and present effort. But when they do not obtain gain due to past demerit and lack of effort, they become dejected and downcast...
486:
486
...their minds become withered and they remain in a state of gloom. However, my teachers, the Buddha and his disciples, remain steady and unshaken by both gain and loss. My teachers, the Buddha and his disciples, are endowed with such admirable conduct and virtues. (4)

“Yasena unnato loko,
ayasena ca onato.
Yasāyasena ekaṭṭhā,
tādisā samaṇā mama.” (5)

(O Noble Lady, my mother-in-law...) The people of the world are uplifted and arrogant when they have many followers and fame due to their past merit and present effort. But when they have few followers and their reputation diminishes due to past demerit and lack of effort, they become dejected and downcast, their minds withering in gloom. My teachers, the Buddha and his disciples, remain steady and unshaken by both fame and obscurity (or having many or few followers).
487:
My ascetics (the Buddha and his disciples) are such; they are endowed with such admirable and inspiring qualities of conduct. (5)

Through praise, the world is uplifted,
And through blame, it is dejected.
But my ascetics are the same in both blame and praise;
Such are my ascetics. (6)

(O Lady, the wife of the merchant in the city of Ugga...) The people of the world are uplifted and become arrogant because of receiving praise, which results from the combination of two causes: their own successful efforts and the wholesome kamma they have performed. Because of receiving blame, which results from the combination of two causes: their own failed efforts and the unwholesome kamma they have performed, they become dejected, depressed, and downcast. (But my teacher, the Buddha, and his disciples) are exactly the same, without any wavering or agitation, in both blame and praise. My ascetics are such; they are endowed with such admirable and inspiring qualities of conduct. (6)

Through happiness, the world is uplifted,
And through suffering, it is dejected.
But my ascetics are unshaken in happiness and suffering;
Such are my ascetics. (7)
488:
(O mother-in-law, renowned as the wife of the merchant in the city of Ugga...) The people of the world are uplifted and become arrogant because of happiness, which results from the combination of two causes: their own successful efforts and the wholesome kamma they have performed. Because of suffering, which results from the combination of two causes: their own failed efforts and the unwholesome kamma they have performed, they become dejected, depressed, and downcast. (But my teacher, the Buddha, and his disciples) remain firm and unshaken, without any wavering or agitation, in both happiness and suffering. My ascetics are such; they are endowed with such admirable and inspiring qualities of conduct. (7)

The wise daughter-in-law, Cūḷasubhaddā, pleased her mother-in-law with these words of praise. Then, the mother-in-law asked her daughter-in-law, Cūḷasubhaddā, "Would you be able to show us your teacher, the Buddha, and his disciples?" When Cūḷasubhaddā replied, "I am able to do so," the mother-in-law gave her permission, saying, "If that is the case, then arrange it so that we may see your teacher and the monks."

Cūḷasubhaddā accepted, saying, "Very well," and prepared great offerings for the Sangha of monks led by the Buddha.
489:
After preparing the offerings, she stood on the upper terrace of the mansion, facing the direction of the Jetavana monastery. She paid homage respectfully with the fivefold prostration and, reflecting on the virtues of the Buddha such as 'Arahant' and so forth, she made offerings of jasmine flowers and incense sticks. 

She made a solemn resolution: "O Blessed One, I invite the Sangha of monks led by the Buddha for tomorrow's meritorious deed. May the Teacher of gods and men, the Blessed One, clearly know the invitation of me, Cūḷasubhaddā, by this sign of jasmine flowers now being sent."

Having made this resolution, she threw eight handfuls of jasmine flowers into the sky. The jasmine flowers flew through the air like little butterflies and remained as a floral canopy above the Blessed One, who was then preaching to the fourfold assembly in the midst of the Jetavana monastery.

At that moment, Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant, having finished listening to the Dhamma, invited the Blessed One for tomorrow's meritorious deed. The Blessed One said, "O householder, I have already accepted the meal for tomorrow's meritorious deed." Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant then asked, "O Blessed One, there was no one who arrived to invite you before me. Whose meal have you already accepted?" The Buddha replied, "O householder, I have already been invited by Cūḷasubhaddā." Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant then said, "O Blessed One,
490:
Does not my daughter Cūḷasubhaddā live in the city of Ugga, which is more than one hundred and twenty (120) yojanas away from this city of Sāvatthī?" When he asked this again, the Blessed One replied:

"Yes, it is so, householder. Indeed, the virtuous, even when living in a place many yojanas away, appear clearly as if they were standing in my presence."

Having said this, he preached this verse of Dhamma:

The virtuous shine from afar,
Like the Himalayan mountains.
The wicked are not seen here,
Like arrows shot in the night.

(O householder Anāthapiṇḍika, the donor of Jetavana monastery...) The virtuous ones, who are masters of great merit and have pure hearts, even though they stay (ṭhitāpi) in a place many yojanas distant (dūre), appear clearly (pakāsenti) in the Buddha's knowledge as if they were standing nearby. The foolish ones, both monks and laypeople, even though they stay (ṭhitāpi) here (ettha) in the presence of the Buddha, are not seen (na dissanti) like arrows (sarā yathā) shot (khittā) in the night (rattiṃ)—a night characterized by four factors: midnight, the new moon, the middle of a forest, and being covered by thick clouds. Because they are utterly lacking in the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of past kamma performed to attain the Path and Fruit,
493:
went to the presence of that Brahmin who was clearing his field. Although the Brahmin saw the Buddha, being one with wrong views, he did not show respect and remained silent without speaking. At that time, the Blessed One himself first greeted the Brahmin and asked, "O Brahmin, what are you doing?" "O Gautama, I am clearing the field," the Brahmin replied. The Blessed One said only this much on the first day and departed.

On the next day as well, the Blessed One went to the Brahmin who had come to plow the field and asked, "O Brahmin, what are you doing?" Hearing the Brahmin's reply, "O Gautama, I am plowing the field," he departed.

On subsequent days, he went there in the same manner and asked, "O Brahmin, what are you doing?" as before. Hearing the Brahmin's replies according to his work, such as "O Gautama, I am sowing the seeds; I am planting; I am weeding; I am guarding," he departed.

Because of these frequent visits, the Brahmin one day developed affection and devotion for the Blessed One and said, "O Gautama, you have been coming since the day I started clearing my field. If my crops are successfully completed and successful, I will share them with you. Without giving to you, I alone_"
494: "I will not eat; from today onwards, you are my friend," he spoke words of friendship. Later, on another occasion, the Brahmin's crops reached full maturity. The Brahmin thought and decided, "My crops have reached maturity; I shall have them harvested tomorrow or the day after." While he was making all the necessary arrangements for the harvest, a heavy rainstorm fell during the night and washed away all the crops. Thus, the Brahmin's entire field became as bare as a cleared threshing floor, looking as if it had been uprooted. The Buddha had already known from the very first day he visited the Brahmin that "those crops would not reach completion." However, knowing that the Brahmin would not listen if He preached and gave advice on the day the crops were destroyed, the Buddha had visited him since the day he was clearing the field to establish a bond of trust and intimacy, believing that the Brahmin might listen to the Dhamma on the day of the disaster. Early in the morning, the Brahmin went thinking, "I shall look at the field." When he saw the field cleared bare, he was struck with intense grief and sorrow. He thought: "The ascetic Gotama has been coming since the time I was clearing my field. I also told him, 'When these crops reach completion, I shall share and distribute them to you; I will not eat them alone without giving to you.' Now, from today..."
495: "...you have become my friend,' I had said. That wish of my heart has not reached its end." Thinking thus, he returned home, fasted, and lay down on a small couch. At that time, the Buddha went to the door of the Brahmin's house. The Brahmin, hearing that the Buddha had arrived, told his household, "Friends, bring my friend in and provide a seat inside this house." The household members did as the Brahmin said. After the Buddha was seated, He asked, "Where is the great Brahmin?" When the household members replied, "He is lying on a small couch in the inner room," the Buddha said, "Bring that great Brahmin here." When the Brahmin was brought before Him and sat in a suitable place, the Buddha asked, "O Brahmin, what has happened?" The Brahmin replied to the Buddha, "O Venerable Gotama, you have been coming since the day I cleared my field. I said, 'When the crops reach completion, I shall share them with you.' That heart's desire and longing of mine is now unfulfilled. Therefore, intense grief and sorrow have arisen in my mind. I do not even wish to eat my portion of rice." Then the Buddha asked the Brahmin, "O Brahmin, do you know based on what..."
496: "...this sorrow has arisen in your mind?" When the Brahmin asked, "O Venerable Gotama, I do not know. Does the Blessed One know?", the Buddha replied, "Yes, I know, Brahmin. All sorrow and all collections of fear that arise do so only based on craving and greed (taṇhā)." He then preached this verse of Dhamma: Taṇhāya jāyatī soko, taṇhāya jāyatī bhayaṃ. Taṇhāya vippamuttassa, natthi soko kuto bhayaṃ. (O Brahmin who is suffering from sorrow), Soko = the state of sorrow and unease of mind; jāyati = arises and becomes manifest; taṇhāya = because of the group of Dhamma known as craving and greed. Bhayaṃ = the collection of fears and mental terrors caused by weak anger; jāyati = arises and becomes manifest; taṇhāya = because of the group of Dhamma known as craving and greed. Vippamuttassa = For one who is liberated through the Fruit of Arahantship; taṇhāya = from the group of Dhamma known as craving and greed; soko = sorrow and unease of mind; natthi = does not occur even slightly. Bhayaṃ = the collection of fears and mental terrors; kuto atthi = how can it exist, since it was already destroyed and abandoned at the moment of the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga)?
498: The cowherds answered honestly, "In the place with such a name." The merchant, using the information given by the cowherds, rode a small carriage to the house of that mountain-foot worker. Descending from the carriage and entering the house, he called out the name of the mistress of the house. The mistress, thinking, "He must be one of our relatives," went quickly and prepared a seat. After the merchant sat down, he mentioned the name and asked, "Where has my friend gone now?" The mistress also replied honestly, "Sir, your friend has gone to the forest." Then the merchant mentioned the children's names and asked warmly, "Where have my son (Master So-and-so) and my daughter (Miss So-and-so) gone?" After asking for everyone by name, he said, "Please give these clothes and ornaments to my son and daughter. Also, give these clothes and ornaments to my friend when he returns from the forest," and he gave the clothes and ornaments as gifts. The mistress provided the merchant with excellent food and drink, fulfilling the duties of hospitality. When her husband returned from the forest, she told him what happened: "Sir, since this guest arrived, he greeted everyone in the house by name and gave these specific clothes and ornaments." The worker, becoming well-acquainted, performed all the necessary duties...
501:
501
(The emission of the brilliant glow was the result and power of the meritorious deed of offering red sandalwood powder in the shape of a moon at the stupa of Kassapa Buddha.)

The brahmins thought and consulted among themselves, "We can take this youth and travel around to deceive and live off the people of the world." They placed the youth on a vehicle and boasted, "A person who touches the body of this youth Sandābha with their hand can obtain such prosperity and happiness." They traveled throughout the island of Jambudīpa. Only those who could give a hundred or a thousand were allowed to touch and stroke the body of the youth Sandābha with their hands.

As the brahmins traveled continuously in this manner, they arrived at the city of Sāvatthī and took up a place to stay between Sāvatthī and the Jetavana monastery. In Sāvatthī, five crores of noble disciples (ariyas) would give alms in the morning, and in the afternoon, they would go to the Jetavana monastery to listen to the Dhamma, carrying perfumes, flowers, garments, medicinal requisites, and so on.

The brahmins saw those noble disciples and asked, "Where are you going?" When the noble disciples replied, "We are going to listen to the Dhamma from the Blessed One," those brahmins said, "Friends, come! What is the use of going to that Blessed One? There is no other power equal to the power of our Brahmin Sandābha. Indeed, those who touch the body of this Brahmin Sandābha receive such benefits..."
502:
502
...they obtain [these benefits]. Come, look at this Brahmin Sandābha."

## Taking Sandābha and Going to the Monastery
The noble disciples also said, "Friends, what kind of power is the so-called power of Brahmin Sandābha? Only our teacher, the Blessed One, is the most supreme in power in the world." Since the brahmins and the noble disciples were unable to reach a final decision among themselves, they finally agreed, "Let us go to the monastery and investigate to know the power of Brahmin Sandābha and the power of our teacher, the Buddha." Thus, they took Brahmin Sandābha and went to the monastery.

## Brahmin Sandābha Becoming a Monk
As soon as Brahmin Sandābha came near the Blessed One, the Buddha, by His psychic power of determination, made the moon-like glow from the brahmin's navel disappear. Near the Buddha, the brahmin became like a small crow in a basket of charcoal. Then, they took Brahmin Sandābha to another place away from the Blessed One; the glow from the brahmin's navel reappeared as it was originally. When they brought him back to the presence of the Blessed One, the glow from the brahmin's navel disappeared again as before. Having seen the glow disappear three times in this manner, Brahmin Sandābha thought, "This Venerable One must know the mantra that causes the glow to disappear." He then asked, "How is it, Venerable One? Do you know the mantra that causes the glow to disappear?"
503:
503
When the Blessed One replied, "Yes, I know it," the brahmin requested, "If that is so, please give that mantra to me." The Blessed One said, "I am unable to give it to one who is not a monk." Brahmin Sandābha encouraged his fellow brahmins, saying, "After learning this mantra, I will be the greatest in the whole of Jambudīpa. You all wait right here at our current lodging in Sāvatthī. I will learn the mantra within two or three days after becoming a monk." Having pleased them, he approached the Blessed One, requested the state of a novice, and then became a monk.

## Venerable Sandābha Becoming an Arahant
Thereafter, the Blessed One taught the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra) to Venerable Sandābha. When Venerable Sandābha asked, "What are these things like hair of the head, hair of the body, etc.?" the Blessed One replied, "This meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body, such as hair of the head and hair of the body, is the preliminary preparation (parikamma) for the mantra. You must recite and study this preparation."

The fellow brahmins also came at intervals and asked, "Have you learned the mantra yet?" Venerable Sandābha replied, "I have not yet learned the root mantra; (I am still reciting and studying the preparation)." In this way, Venerable Sandābha established concentration through the meditation on the thirty-two parts of the body, progressed further, and strove diligently in the practice of Insight (Vipassanā). Within two or three days, he reached the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). When the brahmins came and asked him, he spoke clearly and decisively, "You may go. Now, I have no nature of returning to the lay life."
504:
504
When the monks heard the words spoken by Venerable Sandābha, they reported to the Blessed One, "Exalted Buddha, this monk Sandābha speaks falsely and claims the Fruit of Arahantship." The Blessed One said, "Monks, now my son, the monk Sandābha, has exhausted the taints (āsavas) and become an Arahant. This monk Sandābha speaks only the truth." He then recited this verse of Dhamma:

Candaṃva vimalaṃ suddhaṃ, vippasannamanāvilaṃ.
Nandībhavaparikkhīṇaṃ, tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ.

(Bhikkhave = O monks, my dear sons). Vimalaṃ = free from the five kinds of stains. Or, because of being free [from them]. Suddhaṃ = pure without any perceived fault. Candaṃva = like the moon, the celestial vehicle. Vippasannaṃ = having a mind that is clear and without perceived fault. Anāvilaṃ = having become free from the turbidity of all defilements. Nandībhavaparikkhīṇaṃ = having exhausted the craving and greed that delights and clings to the three realms of existence. Taṃ = that person who is called a Khīṇāsava (one whose taints are exhausted), an Arahant. Ahaṃ = I, the Buddha, the teacher of the three types of beings. Brāhmaṇaṃ = as a true person called a 'Brahmin'. Brūmi = I declare and make known according to the reality of nature.

At the end of the discourse, many people reached the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and so forth. (From the Dhammapada Commentary, Volume 2, 26-Brāhmaṇavagga, page 423).

The Story of Venerable Sandābha (Sandābhattheravatthu) ends.
506:
506
"Exalted Buddha, may the Blessed One, the Lord, rule as king. May the Blessed One, who speaks good words, rule righteously, without killing oneself, without causing others to kill, without destroying others' property oneself, without causing others to destroy it, without causing others sorrow and grief oneself, and without causing others to do so."

Thus he spoke words of temptation and encouragement.

Then the Blessed One asked, "O Evil Māra, what Dhamma do you see in my continuity that you speak to me like this?" Māra replied, "Exalted Buddha, the Lord has fully and masterfully developed the four bases of power (iddhipāda). Indeed, if the Lord so desires and inclines His mind toward the great Himalayan mountain to 'become gold,' the great Himalayan mountain would become pure gold. If you, Venerable Sir, rule righteously, I shall also help and carry out various large and small matters that must be done with gold, silver, and wealth."

When Māra had spoken thus, the Blessed One said:

Pabbatassa suvaṇṇassa,
Jātarūpassa kevalo.
Dvittāva nālamekassa,
Iti vidvā samaṃ care.

Jātarūpassa = having the color that shines like the light of the sun. Suvaṇṇassa = of gold. Kevalo = pure, unmixed with earth or stone.
507:
507
Pabbato = a great mountain nearly as large as the Himalayas. (Or) Kevalo suvaṇṇassa pabbato = a great mountain of pure gold unmixed with copper, iron, lead, etc. Assa-bhaveyya = it might come to be by the support of meritorious kamma. (Tiṭṭhatu eko pabbato = let alone one great mountain of gold). Dvittāva = even if there were two great mountains of gold as high and solid as the Himalayas. Ekassa = for one single person. Na alaṃ = it is not enough to satisfy the desire of craving. Iti = thus. Vidvā = the wise one who discerns and knows the difficulty of satisfying craving and its rarity. Samaṃ = in the three doors of mind, speech, and body. Care-careyya = should practice, strive, and develop the ten types of good conduct (sucarita) in accordance with the Dhamma.

Yo dukkhamaddakkhi yatonidānaṃ,
Kāmesu so jantu kathaṃ nameyya.
Upadhiṃ viditvā saṅgoti loke,
Tasseva jantu vinayāya sikkhe.

Yo jantu = whatever being. Dukkhaṃ = various types of suffering. Yatonidānaṃ = seeing clearly that it has its root cause in the five objects of sensual pleasure (kāma). Addakkhi = sees clearly. So jantu = that being who knows and sees that "all suffering has its root cause in the acquisitions (upadhi) of sensual pleasure." Kāmesu = in the objects of sensual pleasure. Or, in the various collections of sensual objects. Kathaṃ nameyya = how and for what reason would they think it good and incline their mind toward it? Loke = in this current world of humans. Upadhiṃ = the acquisition of sensual pleasure, which is the collection of sensual objects. Saṅgoti = as a point of attachment through lust, hatred, delusion, pride, and wrong view...
508:
508
As Dhamma. Viditvā = having known distinctly. Jantu = a being. Tasseva = that very group of things, the objects of sensual desire. Vinayāya = for the sake of removal. Sikkhe-sikkheyya = one should train and practice in the three trainings.

After causing alarm with these Dhamma verses, the Buddha said, "O Evil Mara, your teaching is one thing. My teaching is another. (You teach to strive and acquire the two types of sensual desire, namely objects and defilements. I teach to remove those sensual desires). Any association with you in the Dhamma is impossible (in any way). Indeed, I teach in the following manner," and He preached these three Dhamma verses:

Atthami jātamhi sukhā sahāyā,
Tuṭṭhī sukhā yā itaritarena.
Puññaṃ sukhaṃ jīvitasaṅkhayamhi,
Sabbassa dukkhassa sukhaṃ pahānaṃ. (1)

(Loke = in this present world of humans). Atthami = when various matters, large and small, arise according to one's life. Sahāyā = relatives and friends are the source of happiness (a). Itaritarena = with whatever requisites are obtained. Yā tuṭṭhī = that which is easy contentment and delight. (Atthi = there is. Sā tuṭṭhī = that contentment with whatever is obtained) is the source of happiness (b). Jīvitasaṅkhayamhi = when life is ending and the time of death approaches.
509:
509
Puññaṃ = the various meritorious deeds performed according to one's noble intentions and wishes. Sukhā = is the source of happiness (c). Sabbassa dukkhassa = of all the sufferings of the round of rebirth without exception. Pahānaṃ = the Path of Arahantship, which is the abandoning of those sufferings. Sukhā = is the source of obtaining happiness (d). (In this context, the cause of happiness is preached as 'happiness' by way of metonymy of the effect; the same applies to the subsequent verses. Through this verse, the four causes of obtaining happiness are preached).

Sukhā matteyyatā loke,
Atho petteyyatā sukhā.
Sukhā sāmaññatā loke,
Atho brahmaññatā sukhā. (2)

Loke = in this present world of humans. Matteyyatā = dutifully caring for and serving one's graceful mother is the source of happiness (1). Atho = furthermore. Petteyyatā = dutifully caring for and serving one's graceful father is the source of happiness (2). Loke = in this present world of humans. Sāmaññatā = approaching, respecting, and offering to recluses and monks with delight is the source of happiness (3). Atho = furthermore. Brahmaññatā = approaching, respecting, and offering to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples who have abandoned evil is the source of happiness (4). (By this verse also...)
510:
510
...the four causes of obtaining happiness are preached).

Sukhaṃ yāva jarā sīlaṃ,
Sukhā saddhā patiṭṭhitā.
Sukho paññāya paṭilābho,
Pāpānaṃ akaraṇaṃ sukhaṃ. (3)

Sīlaṃ = the practice of virtue, such as the five, eight, or ten precepts, which are many. Yāva jarā = until one becomes old with white hair, lost teeth, and wrinkled skin. Sukhaṃ = is excellent and beautiful as a cause of happiness (I).

(Ornaments such as ruby earrings and bright red garments are beautiful only for those of a certain age. The ornaments of the young do not look good when one is old, and the ornaments of the old do not look good when one is young. If an old person wears the ornaments of the young, or a young person wears the ornaments of the old, it only causes blame and fault, as people might think, "This person seems to have gone mad." The practice of virtue, such as the five or ten precepts, is beautiful for both the young and the old at all three stages of life. It brings the joy of rapture and happiness by causing praise such as, "Oh, this person is indeed virtuous").

Patiṭṭhitā = well-established with unwavering faith. Saddhā = mundane and supramundane faith. Sukhā = is excellent and beautiful as a cause of happiness (II). Paññāya = of the two types of wisdom, mundane and supramundane. Paṭilābho = the acquisition through intense effort. Sukho = is excellent and beautiful as a cause of happiness (III). Pāpānaṃ = of the collection of unwholesome and evil deeds.
511:
511
Akaraṇaṃ = not committing them, including the removal of underlying tendencies (anusaya). Sukhaṃ = is excellent and beautiful as a cause of happiness (IIII). (By this verse also, the four causes of obtaining happiness are preached).

At the end of the teaching, countless multitudes of devas realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation. (From Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 2, page 324).

The Story of Mara ends.

## The Story of the Great Brahmin Pokkharasāti
## (From Dīgha Nikāya, 1, 3-Ambaṭṭha Sutta)
(The detailed account of this Brahmin Pokkharasāti should be noted from the Burmese translation of the Sīlakkhandhavagga Pali. In this text, it will be presented as concisely as possible)–

One day, when the Blessed One surveyed the world of beings at dawn, the Great Brahmin Pokkharasāti entered the net of His Omniscient Knowledge. When He further reflected on the Brahmin's past merits and supporting conditions (upanissaya), He saw the supporting conditions for the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga):

"When I travel to the district of Icchānaṅgala, the teacher Brahmin Pokkharasāti will send his disciple, the young Brahmin Ambaṭṭha, to investigate the major and minor marks of a Great Man. Ambaṭṭha will speak in competition with Me and utter the words of various low-born people. I will have to discipline that young man Ambaṭṭha and make the poison of his pride disappear. The young man Ambaṭṭha will then report the cause and effect to his teacher, the Great Brahmin Pokkharasāti.
512:
512
Upon hearing those words, his teacher, the Great Brahmin Pokkharasāti, will come to Me and investigate My major and minor marks. I will have to preach the Dhamma to that great teacher Brahmin. At the end of the teaching, that Brahmin will be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala)."

Having clearly foreseen these future events, the Buddha, surrounded by five hundred monks, traveled on a walking tour towards the Kosala country. In due course, He arrived at the Brahmin village of Icchānaṅgala within the Kosala country and stayed in the great forest named "Icchānaṅgala" near that village.

At that time, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti was governing the city of Ukkaṭṭha, which was populous and abundant in grass, firewood, water, rice, and grain, as an assignment from King Pasenadi of Kosala.

(The city was named Ukkaṭṭha because it was established and demarcated while torches were lit. Ukkā = torches + ṭhā = a city that is established).

About the Brahmin Pokkharasāti: During the time of Kassapa Buddha, this Brahmin was one who had mastered the three Vedas. After giving alms and listening to the Dhamma, he was reborn in the celestial realm.

When he passed away from the celestial realm and came to this human world, he felt loathing for staying in a mother's womb. Thus, he took a spontaneous birth (saṃsedaja) within a lotus thicket in a large lake near the Himalayas. Near that lake, a hermit lived in a leaf-hut. Standing on the shore of the lake, the hermit...
513:
513
...saw that great lotus bud as something extraordinary and thought, "This great lotus bud is superior and larger than other lotus buds. When it blooms, I will pluck that lotus."

That lotus bud did not bloom even after seven days. The hermit thought, "Why does this great lotus bud not bloom even after seven days? I will pluck that bud right now," and he went down into the lake to pluck it. As soon as the hermit cut the lotus from its stalk, it bloomed. Then, inside that lotus, he saw an extraordinary boy, pure white like silver, as if smeared with lotus pollen, resembling a silver statue sprinkled and smeared with gold dust.

The hermit thought, "This boy must be one of great merit. I will now clean and nurture him." He took him to the leaf-hut, cleaned and nurtured him, and from the age of seven, taught him the three Vedas. The boy mastered the three Vedas and became a very famous Brahmin teacher throughout the island of Jambudīpa. Later, this great Brahmin teacher demonstrated his skills to King Pasenadi of Kosala. Being impressed by his skills, King Pasenadi granted him the aforementioned great city of Ukkaṭṭha as a fief. Thus, because he was conceived and born in a lotus thicket, he was recognized by the people as the Brahmin Pokkharasāti.

The body of that Brahmin had the color of a white lotus and was as beautiful as a triumphal arch pillar erected at the gate of a celestial city. His head had a dark blue color like a sapphire. His beard appeared as if a small black line had been drawn on the orb of the moon. His eyes resembled blue lotuses, and his nose was well-rounded, clean, and pure like a silver tube. The palms of his hands, the soles of his feet, and his lips were like those finished with lac resin. The Brahmin's physical form was extremely beautiful.
514:
514
In a place where there is no king, this Brahmin was a suitable person to be made king; thus, he was very glorious. He was recognized as "Pokkharasāti" because he resembled a white lotus. (From the Commentary).

The Great Brahmin Pokkharasāti heard the news of the Buddha's virtues, just like the Brahmin Verañja mentioned below. That great teacher Brahmin Pokkharasāti had a resident disciple (antevāsika), a young Brahmin named "Ambaṭṭha," who was proficient in the three Vedas and various scriptures that Brahmins should master, and whom the teacher himself treated as an equal and highly esteemed.

Then, the teacher Pokkharasāti spoke to his resident disciple, the young man Ambaṭṭha, about the Buddha's reputation that he had heard, and commanded him, "Dear Ambaṭṭha, go. Go to where the ascetic Gotama is and investigate so that we may know: 'Has his fame spread according to the truth, or has it spread not according to the truth? Is he truly as famous as reported, or not?'"

Then the young man Ambaṭṭha asked, "O teacher, how shall I investigate the venerable Gotama to know: 'Has the fame of that venerable Gotama spread according to the truth, or has it spread not according to the truth? Is that venerable Gotama truly as famous as reported, or not?'" The teacher Pokkharasāti replied, "Dear Ambaṭṭha, in our Vedas, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man are directly mentioned. For a Great Man endowed with these marks, there are only two possible destinies:"
515:
"...there is no other way. If that great man remains in the household life, he will become a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) who rules over the four islands; if he renounces the world, he will certainly become a Buddha in the three worlds. Dear Ambaṭṭha, I am the one who teaches you the Vedas, and you are the one who has learned and heard the Vedas from me," he explained.

(The Brahmin Pokkharasāti was a man of reflection and thought: "In this world, many people like Pūraṇa Kassapa and others wander around using the name 'I am the Buddha, I am the Buddha.' Therefore, I should not approach him based on hearsay alone. Indeed, if one approaches certain individuals, it is difficult and burdensome to leave them, and it can also be disadvantageous. Thus, it would be better if I send my disciple, the youth Ambaṭṭha, to investigate and find out for certain whether he is truly a Buddha before I approach him myself." It was for this reason that he sent the youth Ambaṭṭha.)

Then the youth Ambaṭṭha replied, "Very well, teacher," and after rising from his seat and paying respects to his teacher, he mounted a carriage drawn by donkeys (or mules) used by his teacher and set out for the Icchānaṅgala forest together with many other youths. Upon reaching the Icchānaṅgala forest, he traveled by vehicle as far as possible, and when he reached the vicinity of the gate, he alighted from the vehicle and entered the monastery grounds on foot. (At that time, it was midday.)

At that time, many monks who were practicing their daytime meditation were walking to and fro in the open air. Then the youth Ambaṭṭha went to those monks and said to them:
516:
"Venerable sirs, where is the Venerable Gotama staying now? We have come to this place to see that Venerable Gotama."

Then, the following thought occurred to those monks:

"This youth Ambaṭṭha is born of a prominent family. He is also a disciple of the famous Brahmin Pokkharasāti. For the Blessed One, it will not be a burden to engage in conversation with such noble youths."

Having thought thus, they said to the youth Ambaṭṭha:

"Ambaṭṭha, approach that monastery (over there) with the closed door quietly, then enter the porch gently, cough, and knock on the door leaf. The Blessed One will open the door for you."

Then the youth Ambaṭṭha went as the monks had told him and knocked on the door. The Blessed One opened the door. The youth Ambaṭṭha entered the monastery. The other youths also entered the monastery, and after exchanging pleasant and friendly greetings with the Blessed One, they sat down in a suitable place.

(In this regard: It was not that the Buddha himself got up and opened the door. In fact, the Blessed One thought, "Let the door be opened," and extended his hand. Then, as if saying, "Venerable Blessed One, you who have given countless donations over many billions of world-cycles are not of the karma to have to open a door with your own hand," the door opened automatically.
517:
The door opened by itself; because it opened due to the Blessed One's will (to have the door opened), it is stated in the Pali as 'Vivari Bhagavā dvāraṃ.' In the Burmese translation as well, it is written as 'The Blessed One opened the door.')

## The Behaviors of the Youth Ambaṭṭha

The youth Ambaṭṭha, however, could not even feel devotion toward the splendor of the Blessed One's physical body. With the intention, "I will insult the Blessed One," he loosened the cloth tied around his chest and let it hang from his neck. Holding the edge of his lower garment with one hand, he stepped onto the walking path. While sometimes walking on the path himself and sometimes standing, he spoke to the Blessed One who was sitting, sometimes showing his arms, sometimes showing his chest, sometimes showing his back, sometimes making gestures with his hands, and sometimes making facial distortions (frowning).

"O Venerable Gotama, are your four elements in balance? Are you not fatigued in seeking alms-food? You appear to be without fatigue. Indeed, your major and minor limbs are full and very pleasant to behold. Wherever you go, all the people feel great affection for you, saying, 'He is a monk from the royal class' or 'He is the Blessed One,' and they offer you alms-food that is excellent and nutritious. Friends, look! (Venerable Gotama's) dwelling is like a magnificent hall. It is like a celestial
518:
palace. Look at this couch (on which he sleeps), look at this pillow (which he uses). For one who lives in such a fine place, how could there be any hardship or difficulty in practicing the path of a monk?"

In this manner, he continued to speak only mocking and ridiculing words, and words that were unbefitting of the practice of the virtuous (words which, for ordinary people, would be painful to remember for a lifetime).

At that time, the Blessed One thought: "This youth Ambaṭṭha is striving for what is impossible, like one who wants to reach out and grab the highest heaven (Bhavagga), like one who wants to wander into the Avīci hell by stretching out his legs, like one who wants to swim across the great ocean, or like one who wants to climb to the top of Mount Sineru. Now, I shall converse with this youth Ambaṭṭha." Having considered thus, he asked the youth Ambaṭṭha:

"Ambaṭṭha, do you speak to the aged Brahmin teachers and the teachers of teachers in this same (disrespectful) manner—speaking while walking and standing to me who am sitting—as you are now speaking these unbefitting words?"

When he asked this, the youth Ambaṭṭha replied:

"O Venerable Gotama, I do not speak in this way. O Venerable Gotama, a Brahmin disciple who wishes to speak with a Brahmin teacher who is walking must speak while walking. O Venerable Gotama, a Brahmin disciple who wishes to speak with a Brahmin teacher who is standing must speak while standing.
519:
O Venerable Gotama, a Brahmin disciple who wishes to speak with a Brahmin teacher who is sitting must speak while sitting. O Venerable Gotama, a Brahmin disciple who wishes to speak with a Brahmin teacher who is lying down must also speak while lying down."
