## The First Insult with the Word "Low-born"

(In this regard: Although it is customary for a Brahmin disciple to speak with a Brahmin teacher only in the three postures of walking, standing, and sitting, the youth Ambaṭṭha, because of his extreme pride and arrogance, included the posture of lying down. Therefore,) the Blessed One asked the youth Ambaṭṭha (according to his own words):

"Ambaṭṭha, it is acceptable among all Brahmin teachers for a walking disciple to speak with a walking teacher, a standing disciple with a standing teacher, and a sitting disciple with a sitting teacher. But you speak with a sitting teacher while you are walking and standing. (If so, it is very much like an ox.) Is your teacher an ox, or are you an ox?"

When asked thus, the youth Ambaṭṭha became very angry and said:

"O Venerable Gotama, with these shaveling menial monks, these low-born dark ones born from the heels of Brahma, my manner of speaking is just as I am speaking to the Venerable Gotama now."
520:
Thus, he first insulted them with the word "low-born."

(In this regard: Ambaṭṭha's belief was: "Brahmins were born from the mouth of Brahma; Kings were born from the chest of Brahma. Merchants (Vessas) were born from the navel of Brahma; poor laborers (Suddas) were born from the knees of Brahma; and monks were born from the heels of Brahma." Having this belief and placing monks at the lowest caste, Ambaṭṭha spoke without specifying anyone, yet he spoke with the intention, "I will speak only to the Buddha.")

Then the Blessed One thought: "From the moment he arrived, this youth Ambaṭṭha has spoken with me based only on pride. Like one who grabs a swift venomous snake by the neck, like one who embraces a great fire, or like one who grabs a rutting bull elephant by its trunk, he does not know his own measure. Now, I will make this youth Ambaṭṭha understand." Having considered thus, he said:

"Ambaṭṭha, your coming to this place was for a purpose. You should focus well only on that purpose for which you have come. (1)

Oh, the youth Ambaṭṭha is not yet skilled, yet he considers himself skilled. There is no reason other than his lack of skill for him to act and speak in this way. (2)"

(In this regard: In paragraph 1, it means: "Your teacher sent you for his own purpose; he did not send you
521:
to speak such overwhelming and insulting words to us. Therefore, focus on the purpose for which your teacher sent you." In this way, the Blessed One showed Ambaṭṭha the duty to be followed by those who visit others, and then spoke the words marked as (2) to humble Ambaṭṭha's pride.)

Then the youth Ambaṭṭha, because the Blessed One had called him "not yet skilled," became angry and displeased. Wishing to strike back at, insult, and accuse the Blessed One, and with the intention, "Friends, I will also offend the ascetic Gotama," he said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Gotama, the Sakyan race is fierce. They are rough and touchy. They are talkative. Being low-born, they do not respect, honor, esteem, worship, or pay homage to Brahmins. Venerable Gotama, it is not at all proper or fitting that your Sakyans, being of such a class, do not respect, honor, esteem, worship, or pay homage to Brahmins."

In this way, the youth Ambaṭṭha insulted the Sakyans for the first time with the word "low-born."

## The Second Insult with the Word "Low-born"

Then the Blessed One asked the youth Ambaṭṭha, "Ambaṭṭha, in what way have the Sakyans ever offended you?" The youth Ambaṭṭha replied:
522:
He said to the Blessed One, “Venerable Gotama, once I went to Kapilavatthu on some business for the teacher Pokkharasāti and arrived at the assembly hall of the Sakyans. At that time, many Sakyans (those who had been consecrated) and Sakyan princes (those not yet consecrated) were sitting on high seats in the assembly hall, poking each other with their fingers, laughing loudly, and playing together. Indeed, I thought they were laughing only at me; no one even invited me to a seat. Venerable Gotama, it is truly improper and unbefitting that these Sakyans, being of low birth, do not respect, honor, esteem, worship, or pay homage to Brahmins.” In this way, the youth Ambaṭṭha insulted the Sakyans for the second time with the words ‘low-born.’

(As for why the Sakyans behaved in such a mocking manner, it was because they knew Ambaṭṭha’s lineage. At that time, this youth Ambaṭṭha was walking as if intoxicated with pride, holding the hem of his garment which hung down to his toes with one hand, and with his shoulder hunched [if one holds the hem of the garment with one hand and clenches the other hand into a fist, looking down stiffly, the appearance of a hunched shoulder will become evident]. Then, saying, ‘Friends, look at the way Ambaṭṭha of the Kaṇhāyana lineage, who is our slave, is walking,’ they poked each other, laughed loudly, and played in that manner. Ambaṭṭha also knew his own lineage; therefore, he correctly thought and considered, ‘They are indeed mocking me.’)
523:
## The Third Insult with the Words ‘Low-born’
Then the Blessed One said to the youth Ambaṭṭha, “Ambaṭṭha, even a little quail-hen can chirp as she likes in her own nest. Ambaṭṭha, Kapilavatthu is the Sakyans' own city; you, Ambaṭṭha, should not bear a grudge over such a trifle.”

When the Blessed One spoke thus using the analogy of the quail-hen, the youth Ambaṭṭha thought, “This ascetic Gotama uses the analogy of a quail-hen for his own relatives, while making us out to be like hamsas, cranes, or peacocks; he has now become one free from pride.” Then, going a step further and mentioning the four castes, he said, “Venerable Gotama, there are these four castes: the Khattiya, the Brāhmaṇa, the Vessa, and the Sudda. Venerable Gotama, among these four castes, three—the Khattiya, the Vessa, and the Sudda—are indeed merely the servants of the Brāhmaṇa caste. Venerable Gotama, it is truly improper and unbefitting that these Sakyans, being of low birth, do not respect, honor, esteem, worship, or pay homage to Brahmins.”

In this way, the youth Ambaṭṭha insulted the Sakyans for the third time with the words ‘low-born.’

## Revealing that the Youth Ambaṭṭha is the Son of a Slave Girl
Then the thought occurred to the Blessed One, “This youth Ambaṭṭha severely oppresses the Sakyan clan with the words ‘low-born.’ It would be well if I
524:
were to ask about his lineage.” Having so thought, the Blessed One asked the youth Ambaṭṭha, “Ambaṭṭha, of what lineage are you?” The youth Ambaṭṭha shouted loudly three times, “Venerable Gotama, I am of the Kaṇha lineage.”

(In this matter, one might ask: Did Ambaṭṭha not know that the Kaṇha lineage was impure? [The answer is:] He knew of the impurity in a general sense, but he did not see the details of Kaṇha’s past life. Because he did not see it, he thought, ‘What can this Great Ascetic say? He will not be able to say anything at all,’ and being very stiff with pride, he spoke in this way.)

Then the Blessed One preached to the youth Ambaṭṭha the origin of the Sakyan lineage and the Kaṇha lineage in this way:

“Ambaṭṭha, if one were to trace back and examine your ancestral name and lineage on your father’s and mother’s side, the Sakyans would be the masters, and you are the son of a slave girl of the Sakyans.

Ambaṭṭha, the Sakyans regard King Okkāka as their ancestor. Ambaṭṭha, long ago, King Okkāka, wishing to bestow the kingship upon the son of his beloved younger queen, exiled his elder sons—Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍa, Hatthinika, and Sinisūra—from the country. (The five elder sisters of those princes—Piyā, Suppiyā, Ānandā, Vijitā, and Vijitaseṇā—also asked permission from their father and
525:
followed them). Those elder sons, having been exiled from the country, established a city and lived in a great teak forest near a lake on the slopes of the Himalayas. Those princes, fearing that their lineage would be mixed and corrupted, married their own sisters.

Ambaṭṭha, then King Okkāka asked his ministers and retinue, ‘Friends, where are the princes living now?’ The ministers and retinue replied, ‘Your Majesty, the princes have now established a city and are living in a great teak forest near a lake on the slopes of the Himalayas. Those princes, fearing that their lineage would be mixed and corrupted, have married their own sisters.’

Ambaṭṭha, then King Okkāka uttered this exclamation: ‘Friends, the princes are indeed capable (sakya)! Friends, the princes are indeed capable!’ Ambaṭṭha, it is because of that exclamation that the Sakyans are known as ‘Sakya.’ (Sakya means ‘those who are capable’). That King Okkāka was the first ancestor of the Sakyans.

## The Origin of the Kaṇha Lineage
Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka had a slave girl named Disā. That slave girl gave birth to a son named Kaṇha. As soon as Kaṇha was born, he spoke these words:

‘O mother, wash me! O mother, bathe me! Let me be free from this
526:
impurity! I shall be one who can carry out the welfare of my mothers.’

Ambaṭṭha, just as nowadays people recognize demons (pisāca) when they see them, in those days, people recognized demons as ‘Kaṇha.’ The people of that time said, ‘This child speaks as soon as he is born; a Kaṇha is born, a little demon (pisāca) is born.’ Ambaṭṭha, it is because of those words that the members of the Kaṇha lineage are known as Kaṇhāyana. That Kaṇha was the first ancestor of the Kaṇhāyana lineage.

Ambaṭṭha, if one were to trace back and examine your ancestral name and lineage on your father’s and mother’s side, the Sakyans would be the masters, and you are the son of a slave girl of the Sakyans.”

When he had spoken thus, the youths who had come with Ambaṭṭha surrounded the Blessed One and spoke loudly, saying, “Venerable Gotama, do not severely oppress Ambaṭṭha with the words ‘son of a slave girl.’ O Venerable Gotama, the youth Ambaṭṭha is well-born. He is of good family. He is very learned. He is a polished speaker. He is wise. The youth Ambaṭṭha is capable of debating and responding to Venerable Gotama in this matter (regarding being the son of a slave girl).”

(In this matter, the reason those youths spoke thus was only to escape blame when they returned to their teacher. In their minds, they thought, “Ambaṭṭha is the
527:
senior disciple of our teacher. If we do not intervene and say a word or two in such a debate, this Ambaṭṭha will speak to the teacher to cause a rift with us.” Thus, they spoke in this way only to be free from blame. In their hearts, however, they desired Ambaṭṭha to be oppressed; for indeed, because he was extremely proud, those youths also naturally hated Ambaṭṭha.)

Then the Blessed One thought, “If these young men, while sitting here, continue to make such a loud noise, this current conversation will never reach an end. I shall now silence these youths and speak only with Ambaṭṭha.” Having so considered, he said to those youths:

“Youths, if you think, ‘Ambaṭṭha is low-born, not of good family, of little learning, an unpolished speaker, and unwise, and is thus incapable of responding to the ascetic Gotama in this matter (regarding being the son of a slave girl),’ then let Ambaṭṭha be still, and you alone debate with me in this matter. But if you think, ‘Ambaṭṭha is well-born, of good family, very learned, a polished speaker, and wise, and is thus capable of responding to the ascetic Gotama in this matter,’ then you be still, and let the youth Ambaṭṭha alone respond to me.”
528:
Then the young men thought, “Once Ambaṭṭha has been told, ‘You are the son of a slave girl,’ he will not be able to lift his head again. This thing called lineage is difficult to know. If the ascetic Gotama were to say to anyone else, ‘You are a slave,’ who could meet the ascetic Gotama in a debate of Dhamma? (Indeed, no one could). Let Ambaṭṭha himself untie the great knot he has tied.” Having so thought, wishing to free themselves and throw the responsibility onto Ambaṭṭha, they spoke evasively to the Blessed One:

“O Venerable Gotama, the youth Ambaṭṭha is well-born, of good family, very learned, a polished speaker, and wise; he is capable of responding to Venerable Gotama in this matter (regarding being the son of a slave girl). We shall remain silent; let the youth Ambaṭṭha alone debate and respond to Venerable Gotama.”

Then the Blessed One asked the youth Ambaṭṭha this:

“Ambaṭṭha, this legitimate question has come to you. Even if you do not wish to, you must hear it. If you do not give a definite answer, or if you evade the question by talking of something else, or if you remain silent, or if you go away, your head will split into seven pieces right here.”
529:
“Ambaṭṭha, what do you think? How have you heard it said by the aged and elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers? From where did the Kaṇhāyana clan originate? Who was the founding ancestor of the Kaṇhāyanas?”

When this was asked, the youth Ambaṭṭha remained silent. (At this, the youth Ambaṭṭha thought: “The ascetic Gotama wants to make me personally admit and confess to being the son of a slave girl. If I personally admit and confess it, I will certainly become a slave. If this ascetic Gotama asks me two or three times and I do not give an answer, he will surely remain silent. Then I shall turn back and go away.” Thinking thus, he remained silent.) For a second time, the Blessed One said to the youth Ambaṭṭha:

“Ambaṭṭha, what do you think? How have you heard it said by the aged and elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers? From where did the Kaṇhāyana clan originate? Who was the founding ancestor of the Kaṇhāyanas?”

For a second time, the youth Ambaṭṭha (as he had planned) remained silent.

Then the Blessed One said to the youth Ambaṭṭha:

“Answer now, Ambaṭṭha. Now is not the time for you to remain silent. Ambaṭṭha, if anyone,”
530:
“when asked a legitimate question by the Tathāgata up to three times, does not answer, his head will split into seven pieces right then and there.”

At that moment, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, holding a huge iron sledgehammer, glowing, blazing, and flaming, stood in the sky above the youth Ambaṭṭha, thinking: “If this youth Ambaṭṭha, when asked a legitimate question by the Blessed One up to three times, does not answer, I shall split his head into seven pieces right here.” Only the Blessed One and the youth Ambaṭṭha saw Sakka in that form of a Yakkha.

(Here, it may be asked: Why did Sakka come? The answer is: He came to make him abandon his false view. Alternatively, in the previous section on the Request of Brahma (Brahmayācana), Sakka accompanied Sahampati Brahma and promised: “Venerable Sir, please teach the Dhamma. We shall make those who do not follow or who rebel against your authority comply. Let there be the Wheel of Dhamma from your side, and let there be the Wheel of Authority from our side.” Therefore, in accordance with that promise, he came with the intention: “Today, I shall terrify Ambaṭṭha and make him answer the question.”

Regarding the statement “Only the Blessed One and the youth Ambaṭṭha saw Sakka in the form of a Yakkha,” if others had also seen Sakka in that form, it would have been a cause for disrespect. They might have criticized: “This ascetic Gotama, knowing that the youth Ambaṭṭha does not subscribe to his doctrine, has summoned a Yakkha to show him. Therefore, Ambaṭṭha,”
531:
“speaks only because he is afraid and does not want to speak.” Thus they would have spoken words of blame. Therefore, Sakka manifested himself so that only the Blessed One and Ambaṭṭha could see him.)

As soon as he saw that Yakkha form, sweat poured from Ambaṭṭha’s entire body. His whole insides were churning and rumbling. The youth Ambaṭṭha, looking around to see if the other youths also saw the Yakkha as he did, did not see even a single person’s hair standing on end. Then he thought: “This danger is happening only to me. If I say ‘A great Yakkha,’ they might blame me, saying, ‘Do you alone have eyes? You alone see a Yakkha. At first, you did not see a Yakkha, but only after being thrown into the cage of the doctrine by the ascetic Gotama do you see a Yakkha.’” Thinking thus, he reflected: “Now, for me in this place, there is no other refuge but the ascetic Gotama.” Terrified, trembling, and with his hair standing on end, seeking the Blessed One as his shelter, his hiding place, and his refuge, he approached the Buddha, sat at a lower place, and said to the Blessed One:

“What did the Venerable Gotama say? May the Venerable Gotama please say it again.”

Then the Blessed One said:

“Ambaṭṭha, what do you think? How have you heard it said by the aged and elderly brahmins, the teachers of teachers? From where did the Kaṇhāyana clan originate?”
532:
“Who was the founding ancestor of the Kaṇhāyanas?”

When asked for the final time, the youth Ambaṭṭha said:

“Venerable Gotama, I have heard it just as the Venerable One has said. The Kaṇhāyanas originated from that Kaṇha (the son of a slave girl). That Kaṇha was indeed the founding ancestor of the Kaṇhāyanas.”

Thus he confessed and answered according to the truth.

## Concerning Ambaṭṭha’s Ancestry

When this was said, those youths shouted with a loud and piercing sound that echoed:

“Friends, it is said that the youth Ambaṭṭha is of low birth! He is not of good family! He is a slave-son of the Sakyans! Friends, it is said that the Sakyans are the masters of the youth Ambaṭṭha. We were mistaken in thinking that we should blame the ascetic Gotama, who speaks only the truth (Dhammavādī).”

Then the thought occurred to the Blessed One: “These youths are crushing the youth Ambaṭṭha severely with the word ‘slave-son.’ It would be well if I were to release Ambaṭṭha from such crushing.” Then the Blessed One said to those youths:

“Youths, do not crush the youth Ambaṭṭha so severely with the word ‘slave-son.’ That Kaṇha was a mighty seer (Rishi).”
533:
“That seer Kaṇha went to the Southern Country (Dakṣiṇāpatha), learned the noble mantras, and then approached King Okkāka to ask for his daughter named Maddarūpī.

King Okkāka, being angry and displeased, thought: ‘Friends, this seer Kaṇha, being a slave-son of mine, asks for my daughter Maddarūpī. What kind of person is this Kaṇha?’ and he fitted an arrow to his bow to shoot him. King Okkāka was unable to release that arrow, nor was he able to withdraw it.

Youths, then the ministers and the assembly approached the seer Kaṇha and said: ‘Venerable Seer, may there be safety for the King! Venerable Seer, may there be safety for the King!’ (Then the seer Kaṇha) spoke these threatening words: ‘There shall be safety for the King. However, if the King releases the arrow downwards, the earth throughout the King’s entire realm will be crushed and destroyed.’

(Here, the seer Kaṇha went to the Southern Country while still a layman and, by performing minor and major duties for a brahmin seer, obtained the arrow-halting mantra from him. He then dressed as a seer himself and came to King Okkāka. When he asked for the daughter, King Okkāka became angry and fitted an arrow to kill him, but Kaṇha halted the arrow with the mantra. The power of the mantra was only to halt the arrow. Saying ‘the earth will be crushed and destroyed’ was merely a threat and a falsehood. The subsequent statements are to be understood in the same way.)”
534:
When the ministers and the assembly again pleaded, saying: “Venerable Seer, may there be safety for the King, and may there be safety for the country and the realm!” the seer Kaṇha again spoke a threatening falsehood: “There shall be safety for the King, and there shall be safety for the country and the realm. However, if the King releases the arrow, it will not rain in the King’s entire realm for seven years.”

When the ministers and the assembly again pleaded, saying: “Venerable Seer, may there be safety for the King, and may there be safety for the country and the realm, and let it rain!” the seer Kaṇha said: “The King shall have safety, the country and the realm shall have safety, and it shall rain. However, let the King aim the arrow at his eldest son. The prince shall be safe, without even a single hair standing on end.” (The seer Kaṇha said this only after making the King promise to give him his daughter.)

Youths, then the ministers informed King Okkāka of this matter. Then King Okkāka aimed the arrow at his eldest son, and the prince was indeed safe, without even a hair standing on end. Then King Okkāka, being terrified and trembling with his hair standing on end because he was threatened by the weapon of the mantra, gave his daughter Maddarūpī to the seer Kaṇha (after having his head washed and releasing him from slavery).
535:
“Youths, do not crush the youth Ambaṭṭha so severely with the word ‘slave-son.’ That Kaṇha was a mighty seer.”

The Blessed One said this to provide relief to the youth Ambaṭṭha, showing that “Ambaṭṭha is, on one side (meaning from his own side), a relative of the Sakyans.” Therefore, the youth Ambaṭṭha, like one whose heat is cooled by water poured from a jar, became very relieved. He thought: “The ascetic Gotama, to comfort me, has made me a relative on my mother’s side. It is said that I am a Khattiya of royal lineage,” and he began to think highly of himself.

## Only the Khattiya is Supreme

Then the Blessed One thought: “This youth Ambaṭṭha is assuming ‘I am of royal lineage.’ He does not know that he is not a king. Now I shall make this youth Ambaṭṭha know that he is not a king.” To show the royal lineage, he expanded his teaching:

“Ambaṭṭha, what do you think? In this world, if a Khattiya youth were to marry a Brahmin girl, and a son were to be born from their union, would that son born of the Khattiya youth and the Brahmin girl receive the seat of honor and the first water among the Brahmins?”

When the youth Ambaṭṭha answered: “Venerable Gotama, he would,” the Blessed One continued again—
536:
“Would the Brahmins feed that son at the feast of Kupphī rice (rice offered in dedication to the deceased), at the festive meal, at the sacrificial meal, or at the meal for guests?”

He asked thus. When the young man Ambaṭṭha replied, “Venerable Gotama, they would feed him,” the Blessed One continued:

“Would the Brahmins teach the Vedas to that son, or would they not?”

When the young man Ambaṭṭha replied, “Venerable Gotama, they would teach him,” the Blessed One continued:

“Would he be prohibited from marrying Brahmin women, or would he not?”

When the young man Ambaṭṭha replied, “Venerable Gotama, he would not be prohibited,” the Blessed One asked decisively:

“Would the Khattiyas (the ruling class) perform the royal consecration (Abhiseka) for that son?”

Ambaṭṭha replied with sufficient reason, “Venerable Gotama, they would not. Why is that? Because, Venerable Gotama, that son is not of Khattiya descent on his mother’s side.” (In this section, just as a son born of a Khattiya father and a Brahmin mother does not receive the Khattiya consecration because of the lower caste on the mother’s side, similarly, a son born of a Brahmin father and a Khattiya princess is also ineligible because of the lower caste on the father’s side.)
537:
(To make it clearly known that such a son would not receive the Khattiya consecration, the Buddha questioned and the young man Ambaṭṭha answered as follows:)

(The Buddha:) “Ambaṭṭha, what do you think of this? Suppose a Brahmin youth were to marry a Khattiya maiden. If a son were born from their union, would that son born of a Brahmin youth and a Khattiya maiden receive the seat of honor and the first water among the Brahmins?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, he would.”

(The Buddha:) “Would the Brahmins feed that son at the feast of Kupphī rice, at the festive meal, at the sacrificial meal, or at the meal for guests?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, they would.”

(The Buddha:) “Would the Brahmins teach the Vedas to that son, or would they not?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, they would teach him.”

(The Buddha:) “Would he be prohibited from marrying Brahmin women, or would he not?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, he would not be prohibited.”

(The Buddha:) “Would the Khattiyas perform the royal consecration for that son?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, they would not. Why is that? Because, Venerable Gotama, that son is not of Khattiya descent on his father’s side.”
538:
(The Buddha’s Conclusion:) “Ambaṭṭha, thus, whether comparing women with women or men with men, the Khattiyas are superior and the Brahmins are inferior.”

In another way, the Buddha questioned and Ambaṭṭha answered to show that only the Khattiyas are superior and the Brahmins are inferior:

(The Buddha:) “Ambaṭṭha, what do you think of this? Suppose in this world, the Brahmins were to shave the head of a Brahmin for some offense, sprinkle ashes over his head, and banish him from the country or the town. Would that (banished) Brahmin receive the seat of honor and the first water among the Brahmins?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, he would not.”

(The Buddha:) “Would the Brahmins feed that (banished) Brahmin at the feast of Kupphī rice, at the festive meal, at the sacrificial meal, or at the meal for guests?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, they would not.”

(The Buddha:) “Would the Brahmins teach the Vedas to that (banished) Brahmin, or would they not?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, they would not.”

(The Buddha:) “Would that (banished) Brahmin be prohibited from marrying Brahmin women, or would he not?”
539:
(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, he would be prohibited.” (End of section.)

(The Buddha:) “Ambaṭṭha, what do you think of this? Suppose in this world, the Khattiyas were to shave the head of a Khattiya for some offense, sprinkle ashes over his head, and banish him from the country or the town. Would that person receive the seat of honor and the first water among the Brahmins?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, he would.”

(The Buddha:) “Would the Brahmins feed that person at the feast of Kupphī rice, at the festive meal, at the sacrificial meal, or at the meal for guests?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, they would.”

(The Buddha:) “Would the Brahmins teach the Vedas to that person, or would they not?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, they would teach him.”

(The Buddha:) “Would that person be prohibited from marrying Brahmin women, or would he not?”

(Ambaṭṭha:) “Venerable Gotama, he would not be prohibited.”

(The Buddha’s Summary:) “Ambaṭṭha, when the Khattiyas shave the head of a Khattiya for some offense, sprinkle ashes over his head, and banish him from the country or the town, even by this much, that person has fallen into extreme degradation. Ambaṭṭha, even when a Khattiya
540:
has fallen into such extreme degradation, the Khattiyas are still superior and the Brahmins are inferior.

Ambaṭṭha, the Brahma Sanankumāra also recited this verse:

‘The Khattiya is the best among those people
Who rely on lineage.
But one endowed with knowledge and conduct
Is the best among gods and men.’

Janetasmiṃ = among the multitude of people. Ye = those who. Gottapaṭisārino = are accustomed to relying on lineage. Tesu = among them. Khattiyo = the Khattiya. Seṭṭho = is praised as the most excellent. Devamānuse = among the assembly of gods and men. Vijjācaraṇasampanno = one endowed with knowledge (Vijjā) and conduct (Caraṇa). (Yo = whoever. Atthi = exists.) So = that person. Seṭṭho = is praised as the most excellent.

Ambaṭṭha, that verse was well-sung and well-recited by the Brahma Sanankumāra, not ill-sung or ill-recited; it is connected with the goal, not unconnected with the goal. I, too, agree with it. Ambaṭṭha, I also say the same as the Brahma Sanankumāra:

‘The Khattiya is the best among those people
Who rely on lineage.
But one endowed with knowledge and conduct
Is the best among gods and men.’

(The meaning is the same as before.)
Thus the Buddha spoke.
542:
Ambaṭṭha, those who are attached to talk based on birth (jātivāda), those who are attached to talk based on lineage (gottavāda), those who are attached to talk based on pride (mānavāda), and those who are attached to the taking and giving of daughters in marriage (āvāha-vivāha)—they are far from the attainment of the unsurpassed knowledge and conduct.

Ambaṭṭha, only by abandoning attachment to jātivāda, attachment to gottavāda, attachment to mānavāda, and attachment to āvāha-vivāha can one realize the attainment of the unsurpassed and most excellent knowledge and conduct.”

Thus the Buddha spoke. Then the young man Ambaṭṭha thought: “Until now, we thought we were established in knowledge and conduct. The ascetic Gotama has blown us away from that collection of knowledge and conduct like chaff in a violent storm. He encourages and praises only the unsurpassed collection of knowledge and conduct which we cannot reach. We should know the attainment of knowledge and conduct taught by this ascetic Gotama.” Thinking thus, he asked again: “O Venerable Gotama, what is that conduct (Caraṇa)? What is that knowledge (Vijjā)?”

Then, to the young man Ambaṭṭha, the Blessed One, as in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, starting from the appearance of a Buddha
543:
up to the Path of Arahantship, preached the unsurpassed and most excellent knowledge and conduct, section by section. (One should refer to the Burmese translation of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta.)

## Preaching the Four Causes of Decline

(I shall present this in brief.) Thereafter, the Blessed One told the young man Ambaṭṭha that there are four causes of decline (failure) in the attainment of knowledge and conduct (i.e., in the Dispensation). These four are:

(1) The state of a hermit or ascetic who, being unable to practice to the point of fulfilling knowledge and conduct, enters the forest and subsists only on fallen fruits; (2) the state of a hermit or ascetic who, being unable to practice even that much, enters the forest and subsists only on roots, tubers, and fruits; (3) the state of a hermit or ascetic who, being unable to practice even that much, builds a fire-hut near a town or village and serves the fire; (4) the state of a hermit or ascetic who, being unable to practice even that much, builds a four-sided pavilion at a crossroads and seeks a living by providing cool water and such to those coming from all four directions. These four types of persons who take the name of ascetics or Brahmins in this Isipabbajjā (hermitage) are merely servants to the monk who is endowed with knowledge and conduct in this Dispensation. Having explained this in detail, the Buddha questioned and made Ambaṭṭha explicitly confess that he and his teacher were still far from the practice of being endowed with knowledge and conduct, and (let alone being endowed with conduct) they were not even among those who possess the four states of hermits called the four causes of decline of knowledge and conduct (the Dispensation). After that—
544: “Ambaṭṭha, thus you and your teacher are deficient in the supreme perfection of knowledge and conduct (vijjā-caraṇa), and you are also deficient in the four causes of the ruin of that perfection of knowledge and conduct. Ambaṭṭha, your teacher, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, while unable to fulfill even the causes of ruin himself, spoke rudely, saying: ‘Who are these shavelings, wretched ascetics, menials, dark-skinned, born from the feet of Brahmā? How can there be any conversation between them and Brahmins learned in the three Vedas?’ Ambaṭṭha, look at this fault of your teacher, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti.” Thus, the Buddha rebuked him for the first time. (For details on this section, one should refer to pages 105, 106, and 107 of the Burmese translation of the Sīlakkhandhavagga Pāḷi.) Following this, the Blessed One continued to address the youth Ambaṭṭha: “Ambaṭṭha, your teacher, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, enjoys the wealth given by King Pasenadi of Kosala. Yet, King Pasenadi of Kosala does not grant him a face-to-face meeting; when consulting with him, he does so from behind a curtain. Ambaṭṭha, why does King Pasenadi of Kosala not grant a face-to-face meeting to one who receives a royally bestowed livelihood in accordance with the law? (Consider that reason). Ambaṭṭha, your teacher Pokkharasāti...”
545: “...look at this fault of your teacher, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti.” Thus, the Buddha rebuked him for the second time. (In this regard: The Brahmin Pokkharasāti was an expert in the ‘Sammukhā-āvaṭṭanī’ mantra, which can allure someone face-to-face. When the King wore very valuable ornaments, if the Brahmin stood near him, named the ornament, and recited the mantra, the King could not refuse and would give it to him. Later, on a festival day, when the King asked for the valuable ornament, saying, ‘Bring the precious ornament,’ the attendants would say, ‘It is no longer here, Your Majesty; you gave it to the Brahmin Pokkharasāti.’ When the King asked why he gave it, the ministers would say, ‘Your Majesty, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti knows the Sammukhā-āvaṭṭanī mantra; he deceived you with that mantra and took the valuable ornament.’ Other ministers, jealous of the close friendship between the King and the Brahmin, said, ‘Your Majesty, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti has a type of leprosy called kharu-thin. Your Majesty embraces and touches him upon seeing him; this leprosy can be transmitted through physical contact. Please do not do this.’ From that time on, King Pasenadi of Kosala no longer granted the Brahmin Pokkharasāti a face-to-face meeting. Even though he was not granted a face-to-face meeting, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti was a wise man learned in the nīti texts. Any matter consulted with him never failed. Therefore, the King would stay inside a curtain and consult with the Brahmin who remained outside the curtain.)
546: No one else besides the King and the Brahmin knew this matter. However, the Blessed One revealed this hidden matter, knowing that by doing so, Ambaṭṭha would conclude, ‘The ascetic Gotama is indeed the Omniscient One.’ (He did not say it merely to shame the Brahmin). Then the Blessed One continued to address the youth Ambaṭṭha: if a poor man or a slave sat in the place where King Pasenadi of Kosala consulted with a minister or a prince, and merely repeated the words they spoke, would that poor man or slave become a King or a minister? Having obtained Ambaṭṭha's admission that they would not, the Buddha used this as an analogy to state that Ambaṭṭha and his teacher, by merely reciting and teaching the Vedic texts composed and taught by ancient sages such as Aṭṭhaka and Vāmaka, do not thereby become sages or those practicing to become sages. Furthermore, he asked Ambaṭṭha whether those ancient sages, such as Aṭṭhaka and Vāmaka, lived in luxury like Ambaṭṭha and his teacher do today—wearing fine clothes, eating fine food, surrounded by women, riding fine chariots, and having guards at their fine dwellings—and whether they enjoyed sensual pleasures. Having obtained Ambaṭṭha's admission that they did not, the Buddha concluded to Ambaṭṭha:
547:
'Ambaṭṭha, thus you, along with your teacher, are neither a hermit nor one practicing to be a hermit. Ambaṭṭha, one who has doubts or uncertainty about whether I am a Buddha should clear that doubt by questioning me. I, the Buddha, shall clear that doubt by answering.'

(The Blessed One said this because He reflected: 'For the young man Ambaṭṭha, there is no possibility of attaining the Path and Fruit in this life; indeed, the day will only pass away. This young man Ambaṭṭha has come to investigate the Great Marks of the Buddha. But Ambaṭṭha has forgotten that matter. Now I shall give a hint to Ambaṭṭha so that he may remember.')

After saying this, since no one is able to investigate the marks of the Buddhas while they are sitting or lying down, but are able to investigate the marks of the Buddhas while they are standing or walking, and because it is the custom (dhammatā) of the Buddhas to rise from their seat and walk when they know someone has come to investigate their marks, the Blessed One came out of the monastery and walked towards the walkway (caṅkama). The young man Ambaṭṭha followed closely behind the Buddha.

## Showing the Two Marks

Then, while following the Blessed One who was walking on the walkway and investigating the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the Blessed One's body, the young man Ambaṭṭha clearly saw thirty of the marks, leaving aside two: (1) the male organ being enclosed in a sheath and...
548:
(2) the long, broad, and thin tongue. Not seeing these two marks, he remained in doubt and uncertainty, unable to decide or believe regarding those two marks.

Knowing that matter well, the Blessed One performed a feat of psychic power so that the young man Ambaṭṭha could see the male organ enclosed in a sheath. Then, the Blessed One extended His tongue and repeatedly touched both ear-holes (thereby showing the length of the tongue). He also repeatedly touched both nostrils (thereby showing the softness/flexibility of the tongue). He covered the entire surface of His forehead with His tongue (thereby showing the breadth of the tongue).

Then, the young man Ambaṭṭha reflected and decided: 'The ascetic Gotama is indeed fully and completely endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.' He then addressed the Blessed One: 'Well, Venerable Gotama, we shall go now; we are busy and have much to do.' Then the Blessed One said: 'Ambaṭṭha, you know the time for your departure (= your departure is according to your own will).' Then the young man Ambaṭṭha mounted his mule-drawn carriage and returned.

## The Teacher Pokkharasāti Waiting Outside the City

At that time, the great Brahmin teacher Pokkharasāti had come out of the city of Ukkaṭṭhā and was waiting for the young man Ambaṭṭha along with many other Brahmins.
549: Ambaṭṭha drove his vehicle as far as it could go into the garden, then dismounted and went on foot to the great teacher Pokkharasāti, paid homage, and sat down in a certain place. Then the teacher and pupil questioned and answered each other as follows: (Pokkharasāti) “Dear Ambaṭṭha, did you see that Master Gotama?” (Ambaṭṭha) “Sir, we have seen that Master Gotama.” (Pokkharasāti) “Dear Ambaṭṭha, has the reputation of that Master Gotama spread according to the truth, or not according to the truth? Is that Master Gotama as he is reputed to be, or not?” (Ambaṭṭha) “Sir, the reputation of that Master Gotama has spread according to the truth, not otherwise. That Master Gotama is indeed as he is reputed to be, not otherwise. That Master Gotama is indeed fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, not partially endowed.” (Pokkharasāti) “Dear Ambaṭṭha, did you have any conversation with the ascetic Gotama?” (Ambaṭṭha) “Sir, I had a conversation with the ascetic Gotama.” (Pokkharasāti) “Dear Ambaṭṭha, what kind of conversation did you have with the ascetic Gotama?”
550:
When the teacher asked thus, the young man Ambaṭṭha reported to the Brahmin teacher Pokkharasāti everything he had said to the Blessed One. Then the teacher Pokkharasāti said to Ambaṭṭha:
“Oh, our wise one! How wonderful! Oh, our learned one! How wonderful! Oh, our master of the three Vedas! How wonderful! Friends, with such a representative, a man is certain to fall into the four states of misery after the dissolution of the body, after death.
Hey, Ambaṭṭha! You insulted the Venerable Gotama again and again with such words; because of those words, the Venerable Gotama also exposed our faults again and again. Oh, our wise one! How wonderful! Oh, our learned one! How wonderful! Oh, our master of the three Vedas! How wonderful! Friends, with such a representative as this young man Ambaṭṭha, a man is certain to fall into the four states of misery after the dissolution of the body, after death.”
Having spoken these words of lamentation and blame, being angry and displeased, he kicked the young man Ambaṭṭha and knocked him to the ground. While still angry at Ambaṭṭha, he desired to approach the Blessed One to pay respects at that very moment. (As for Ambaṭṭha, the privilege he previously had of riding in the carriage with the teacher Pokkharasāti...
551:
...acting as the charioteer was revoked, and from that time on, he had to walk on foot in front of the carriage).
## The Brahmin Pokkharasāti Approaches the Buddha
When the Brahmin Pokkharasāti felt an intense desire to go and pay respects to the Blessed One, the Brahmins said to the teacher Pokkharasāti:
“Sir, it is too late today to go and see the recluse Gotama. Master Pokkharasāti can go to see the recluse Gotama tomorrow.”
Then the Brahmin Pokkharasāti had excellent food prepared in his house, and having had it loaded [into the carriage]* and torches lit and held, he departed from the city of Ukkaṭṭhā for the Icchānaṅgala wood. He traveled by carriage as far as the ground permitted, then alighted from the carriage...
* The translation “loaded into the carriage” is based on the Pali “yāne āropetvā” found in both the Sinhalese and Burmese Sixth Council editions. If the Pali were “yānam āropetvā,” it would be translated as “having mounted the carriage,” which would be very logical and appropriate.
To clarify further: Since both the Burmese and Sinhalese Pali editions consistently have “yāne āropetvā,” the Burmese translation teachers have translated it as “having loaded into the carriage.” Later (in the section where the Blessed One goes to the Brahmin's house for a meal), it was noted: “Since paragraph (292) states ‘having loaded the food into the carriage and departed from Ukkaṭṭhā,’ this house might not be inside the city of Ukkaṭṭhā; it might be in Icchānaṅgala village or...
552:
...some other place.”
He approached the Blessed One on foot, exchanged pleasant and memorable greetings with the Blessed One, and sat down at one side.
While sitting there, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti and the Blessed One conversed as follows:
(Pokkharasāti) “Venerable Gotama, did our pupil, the young man Ambaṭṭha, come here?”
(Buddha) “Brahmin, your pupil Ambaṭṭha did come here.”
(Pokkharasāti) “Venerable Gotama, did you have any conversation with the young man Ambaṭṭha?”
(Buddha) “Brahmin, I did have a conversation with the young man Ambaṭṭha.”
(Pokkharasāti) “Venerable Gotama, in what way did you have a conversation with the young man Ambaṭṭha?”
[Note continued]: If the Pali were “yānam āropetvā,” the direct meaning would be: “Having prepared food in his house, he mounted the carriage, and with torches lit, he departed from Ukkaṭṭhā, went to invite the Buddha, and offered the meal in his own house.” Only with such Pali would it be consistent with the passage in the Sāmaññaphala Sutta regarding King Ajātasattu's visit to the Buddha: “ārohanīyaṃ nāgaṃ abhiruhitvā ukkāsu dhāriyamānesu rājagahā niyyāsi”—having mounted the riding elephant, with torches being held, he departed from Rājagaha. Indeed, Icchānaṅgala is located within the district of Ukkaṭṭhā. It should be noted that “nivesana” is usually used for a permanent residence, while “parivesanā” is used for a temporary lodging in the story of Sunidha and Vassakāra.
553:
Then the Blessed One related to the Brahmin Pokkharasāti the entire conversation he had with the young man Ambaṭṭha. The Brahmin Pokkharasāti then apologized to the Blessed One, saying: “Venerable Gotama, the young man Ambaṭṭha is a fool. May the Venerable Gotama forgive the young man Ambaṭṭha.” Then the Blessed One spoke words of forgiveness:
“Brahmin, may the young man Ambaṭṭha be happy.”
## The Brahmin Pokkharasāti
## Examining the Great Marks
Then, when the Brahmin Pokkharasāti examined the thirty-two marks of a Great Man on the Blessed One's body, (just like the young man Ambaṭṭha) he clearly saw thirty marks, except for two: (1) the male organ being enclosed in a sheath, and (2) the long and broad tongue. Not seeing these two marks, he remained doubtful and uncertain, unable to decide or believe.
Knowing this, the Blessed One performed a psychic feat so that the Brahmin Pokkharasāti could see the male organ enclosed in a sheath. Then the Blessed One extended his tongue and stroked both ear-holes alternately (left and right). (By this, he made known the length of the tongue). He also stroked both nostrils alternately (left and right). (By this...
554:
...he made known the softness of the tongue). He covered the entire surface of his forehead with his tongue. (By this, he made known the breadth of the tongue).
Then the Brahmin Pokkharasāti thought and reflected, reaching the final conclusion: “The recluse Gotama is indeed fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.” He then addressed the Blessed One:
“May the Venerable Gotama, together with the community of monks, accept my meal today for the sake of merit.”
The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti said: “Venerable Gotama, it is time for the meal; the meal is ready.” According to the invitation of the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, the Blessed One, in the morning, went to the house of the Brahmin Pokkharasāti with the community of monks and sat on the prepared seat.
Then the teacher, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, and his pupils personally served the Blessed One and the community of monks with excellent food and delicacies. Then, knowing that the Blessed One had finished his meal and had removed his hand from the bowl, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti took a low seat and sat down at a respectful distance.
555:
To the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, who was sitting at a respectful distance, the Blessed One gave a graduated discourse, which is the noble path to the attainment of the Paths and Fruits: (1) Dānakathā = discourse on giving, (2) Sīlakathā = discourse on virtue, (3) Saggakathā = discourse on heaven, (4) Maggakathā = discourse on the noble practice leading to the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna. When the Blessed One knew that the Brahmin Pokkharasāti's mind was ready, pliant, free from hindrances, uplifted, and clear, he preached the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma-desanā (the Four Noble Truths) to him. Then the Brahmin Pokkharasāti was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry; he became a Sotāpanna.
## The Brahmin Pokkharasāti
## Special Declaration as a Lay Follower
Then the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, having become a Sotāpanna, said to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Venerable Gotama, it is as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what had been hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. In the same way, the Venerable Gotama has made the Dhamma clear in many ways.
556:
“Venerable Gotama, I go for refuge to the Venerable Gotama, to the Dhamma, and to the community of monks, together with my sons, daughters, wife, retinue, and ministers. May the Venerable Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forth as long as life lasts.
Just as the Venerable Gotama visits the houses of other lay followers in Ukkaṭṭhā, so may the Venerable Gotama visit my house, the house of Pokkharasāti. In my house, the young men and women will show respect, pay homage, and greet the Venerable Gotama. They will offer a seat or water, and (at the very least) they will gladden their hearts with faith and devotion. Such actions of those young men and women will be for their long-term welfare and happiness.”
Having thus taken the supramundane refuge, he extended the invitation to the Blessed One. (In this section of the Brahmin Pokkharasāti's taking of refuge, the points of (1) including sons, daughters, wife, retinue, and ministers in the refuge, and (2) inviting the Blessed One by explaining the reasons in the final paragraph, are more exceptional than the refuge-taking of others. Therefore,) the Blessed One, as a final conclusion:
557:
“Brahmin, you have spoken well.”
With these words of praise, he accepted the Brahmin Pokkharasāti's request with pleasure.
Here ends the account of the Brahmin Pokkharasāti.
## Here ends Chapter 35.
559:
Having said this, the Buddha preached this verse from the Dhammapada:

Te tādise pūjayato,
nibbute akutobhaye.
na sakkā puññaṃ saṅkhātuṃ,
imettamapi kenaci.

(To those who are such, who have attained the cooling peace of the extinction of defilements, who are fearless of any worldly object or existence; to such Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Ones, the merit of one who pays homage with faith cannot be precisely calculated by anyone—whether Brahma, deity, or human—as being only this much or that much.)

At the conclusion of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings became Noble Ones, such as Sotāpannas, and peacefully partook of the nectar of Nibbāna. (From the Commentary on the Sonadaṇḍa Sutta, Dīgha Nikāya, Vol. 1, page 254.)

Here ends the account of the Brahmin who measured the Buddha's height with a bamboo pole.
560:
## About King Pukkusāti
## (From the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa)

In the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), while King Bimbisāra was ruling the city of Rājagaha in the kingdom of Magadha, King Pukkusāti was ruling the city of Takkasilā on the outskirts of the Middle Country.

At that time, merchants from Takkasilā brought trade goods and arrived at Rājagaha. They took presents and went to pay respects to King Bimbisāra. The King, seeing the merchants who stood after paying homage and offering presents, asked, "Where do you live?" The merchants replied, "Great King, we live in the city of Takkasilā."

Then the King questioned the merchants about the peace, prosperity, and food supply of the district, as well as about the city of Takkasilā. He then asked, "What is the name of your sovereign king?" The merchants replied, "Great King, our sovereign king is named Pukkusāti." The King then asked, "Does your king practice the Ten Royal Virtues (Rājadhamma)?" The merchants replied, "Great King, our sovereign king (Pukkusāti) practices the Ten Royal Virtues. He supports the
561:
masses of people with these four bases of sympathy (saṅgaha-vatthu): Sassamedha, Purisamedha, Sammāpāsa, and Vācāpeyya. Established in the position of a parent to the people, he makes all the citizens as happy and joyful as a young child sleeping in its mother's bosom."

Furthermore, the King asked, "What is the age of your sovereign king?" When the merchants reported King Pukkusāti's age, it was found that the ages of the two kings were the same.

Then the King said to the merchants, "Friends, your king is a practitioner of Dhamma and is of the same age as I. Can you, friends, act so that your king becomes my great friend?" The merchants replied, "We can do so, Great King." The King then granted the merchants exemption from taxes and gave them a house for lodging.

1. Sassamedha = Skill in crops = Collecting one-tenth of the harvested produce as land tax.
2. Purisamedha = Skill regarding heroic officials = Giving rewards and providing salaries and rations to great heroic officials every six months.
3. Sammāpāsa = Acting to bind the hearts of the poor = Lending one or two thousand units of currency to the poor for three years without interest upon their signature.
4. Vācāpeyya = Speaking endearing words = Speaking affectionately according to age, such as "brother," "uncle," or "elder uncle." These four are called the four Rājasaṅgahavatthu.
562:
The King also said, "Friends, go now. After you have sold your goods and are about to return, see me before you depart."

The merchants did as the King commanded, and when they were about to return, they went to pay respects to the King. The King said to the merchants, "Friends, return in safety. On my behalf, repeatedly ask after the health of your sovereign king with my words, and introduce me by saying, 'King Bimbisāra desires friendship with Your Majesty.'"

The merchants agreed, saying, "Very well," and returned to the city of Takkasilā. Upon reaching the city, they stored their purchased goods properly. After eating their morning meal, they went to attend upon King Pukkusāti and paid him homage. King Pukkusāti asked, "Friends, where did you go? I have not seen you for all these days." The merchants reported the whole matter. King Pukkusāti said, "Very well, friends. Because of you, I have gained a royal friend in the Middle Country," and he was greatly delighted.

At another time, merchants from Rājagaha also went to Takkasilā for trade. King Pukkusāti, seeing those merchants who came to pay respects with presents, asked, "Friends, from where
563:
have you come?" Upon hearing the good news that they had come from Rājagaha, the King said, "You are those who have come from the golden city of my dear friend, King Bimbisāra." The merchants replied, "Yes, Great King."

Thereafter, King Pukkusāti asked after his friend's health and other matters. He then issued a royal decree throughout the kingdom: "From this day forward, let all foot-merchants and caravan-merchants coming from the kingdom of my friend King Bimbisāra be provided with houses for lodging and rations from the royal granary from the moment they enter my kingdom. Let them be exempt from taxes, and let there be no disturbance or oppression against them." King Bimbisāra likewise issued a similar decree in his own kingdom.

## How the Two Kings Exchanged Messages

Thereafter, King Bimbisāra sent a message to King Pukkusāti:

"My friend, precious gems such as rubies and pearls usually appear in the border regions. If various kinds of treasures worth seeing or hearing about should arise in my friend's kingdom, I would like to be informed and shared with."

King Pukkusāti also sent a reply to King Bimbisāra:
564:
"My friend, the Middle Country is a very noble region. If various kinds of treasures worth seeing or hearing about should arise in that Middle Country, I would like you, my royal friend, to inform and share them with me."

In this way, as days, months, and years passed, these two royal friends became firm allies without ever having seen each other.

## King Pukkusāti's Gift

While the two kings lived according to their agreement, a special gift first arose for King Pukkusāti. It happened in this way: King Pukkusāti received eight priceless woolen blankets (kambala) of five colors. The King thought, "These blankets are very excellent fabrics. I shall send these blankets as a royal gift to my friend." He ordered eight boxes made of sandalwood heartwood, the size of a lac-ball, to be turned. He placed one blanket in each of those sandalwood boxes, sealed them with lac to make them round, wrapped them in white cloth, and placed them in a chest. He then wrapped the chest in cloth, affixed the royal seal, and sent his ministers to King Bimbisāra with the instruction: "Present these to my friend King Bimbisāra." He also sent a message saying, "I wish for my friend to open and view this gift in the middle of the golden city, surrounded by his ministers and retinue."
565:
The ministers went and presented the gifts to King Bimbisāra. Upon hearing the message, King Bimbisāra ordered the drum to be beaten, proclaiming, "All ministers and troops must assemble as one." Surrounded by his ministers and troops in the center of the golden city, he sat upon a jeweled throne under a white parasol. He removed the royal seal, set aside the outer wrapping cloth, and opened the box. After untying the bundle inside the box and seeing the lacquered balls, he thought, "Oh, my friend King Pukkusāti must have thought, 'My friend King Bimbisāra is a lover of gambling,' and thus sent these lacquered dice as a gift." While thinking this, he took one lacquered ball and rolled it in his hand. Estimating its weight, he realized for certain, "There is a woolen garment inside."

Then, he struck the lacquered ball against the foot of the throne, and at that moment, the lacquer peeled off in layers. The King gently opened the scent-box with his fingernail and found a precious woolen garment inside. He then ordered the remaining seven boxes to be opened. Everyone clearly saw that all of them were priceless woolen garments. When those eight woolen garments were spread out and measured, they were found to be perfect in color and texture, each being sixteen cubits in length and eight cubits in width. Seeing the eight precious woolen garments, the multitude of people snapped their fingers in applause and tossed their turbans into the air in celebration. They said, "Our King's unseen friend...
566:
...King Pukkusāti, though they have never seen each other, has sent such priceless gifts. It is truly fitting and proper to maintain a friendship with such a king." Thus, they spoke and were filled with great joy and delight.

When King Bimbisāra had each woolen garment appraised, they were all found to be priceless. Of those eight woolen garments, he sent four to be offered to the Blessed One, and the remaining four he kept in his golden palace.

## King Bimbisāra's Return Gift

Thereafter, King Bimbisāra reflected, "One who sends a return gift later should send a gift that excels the one previously received. My friend King Pukkusāti has sent me priceless gifts; what kind of return gift should I send?"

In this regard, one might ask: "Was there no treasure in the city of Rājagaha superior to those eight woolen garments?" The answer is: It is not that there were none; there were. King Bimbisāra was a king of great merit. Therefore, it is not that there were no treasures superior to those eight woolen garments; indeed, there were. However, from the time the King became a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer), there was no worldly treasure or wealth that could delight his heart other than the Triple Gem: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.
567:
Thus, King Bimbisāra carefully selected a priceless treasure to send as a return gift, reasoning as follows:

"In this world, what are called delightful treasures are of two kinds: (1) Savinnāṇaka = animate treasures, and (2) Avinnāṇaka = inanimate treasures. Between these two, inanimate treasures such as gold and silver serve only as ornaments or requisites for animate treasures. Therefore, between animate and inanimate treasures, only animate treasure is praised as superior.

Animate (savinnāṇaka) treasures are also of two kinds: (1) Animal treasures, and (2) Human treasures. Animal treasures, such as precious elephants and horses, exist only for the use of humans. Therefore, between animal and human treasures, only human treasure is praised as superior.

Furthermore, human treasures are of two kinds: (1) Female treasure, and (2) Male treasure. Even if she were the jewel-consort of a Universal Monarch, a female treasure is merely a requisite for a man. Therefore, between female and male treasures, only male treasure is praised as superior.

Again, male treasures are of two kinds: (1) Āgāriya-ratana = the treasure of a householder who strives for domestic prosperity, and (2) Anāgāriya-ratana =
568:
the treasure of a monk or novice who does not strive for domestic prosperity. Even a Universal Monarch, the highest among householders, must pay homage with the fivefold prostration to a novice who has just been ordained this very day. Therefore, between the householder treasure and the homeless treasure, only the homeless (anāgāriya) treasure is praised as superior.

Furthermore, the homeless treasure is of two kinds: (1) Sekha-ratana = the treasure of worldlings and lower noble disciples who are still training in the three instructions (and have not yet finished), and (2) Asekha-ratana = the treasure of an Arhat. Even if there were a hundred thousand Sekha treasures, they could not equal a single Asekha Arhat in terms of great virtue and merit. Therefore, between the Sekha and Asekha treasures, only the Asekha treasure—the Arhat—is praised as superior.

That Asekha treasure is also of two kinds: (1) Buddha-ratana, and (2) Sāvaka-ratana (disciple treasure). Even if there were a hundred thousand disciple treasures, they could not equal a single Buddha in terms of great virtue and merit. Therefore, between the Buddha and disciple treasures, only the Buddha treasure is praised as superior.

Again, the Buddha treasure is of two kinds: (1) Paccekabuddha-ratana = the treasure of a Silent Buddha, and (2) Sabbaññu-buddha-ratana = the treasure of an Omniscient Sammāsambuddha.
569:
Even if there were a hundred thousand Silent Buddhas, they could not equal even a fraction of a single Omniscient Buddha in terms of great virtue and merit. Therefore, between the Paccekabuddha treasure and the Omniscient Buddha treasure, only the Omniscient Buddha treasure is praised as the most supreme.

Indeed, in the entire world of beings, including devas and brahmās, there is no treasure equal to the treasure of the Omniscient Buddha. Therefore, I shall send only this peerless treasure to my friend King Pukkusāti."

Having thus reflected, he asked the ministers from Taxila, "Friends, in your land of Taxila, do you ever see or encounter these three treasures: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha?" The ministers from Taxila replied, "Noble King, in our land of Taxila, we have not even heard the sound of the names 'Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha.' How then could we have the opportunity to see them?" The King said, "Very well, friends," and being exceedingly joyful and delighted that he had the opportunity to send a gift that did not exist in that land, he further reflected:

"Even if I were able to request and invite the Blessed One to go to Taxila, the residence of my friend King Pukkusāti, to bless the people, it is not the custom for Buddhas to let the dawn rise in frontier regions. Therefore, it is not possible for the Blessed One himself to go."
570:
Even if I were able to request and invite great Arahant disciples such as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahā Moggallāna to go, if I were to hear that 'Great Elders are residing in frontier regions,' I should send royal messengers to bring those Great Elders to my presence by any means and serve them with the four requisites. Therefore, it is also not possible for the Great Elders to go.

Instead, I shall send a royal message in such a way that it will be as if the Blessed One and the Great Elders have gone there themselves."

Having thus planned, he had a gold plate fashioned, four cubits long and one span wide, neither too thin nor too thick. On the day he was to write the letters upon that gold plate, he washed his head and bathed early in the morning, observed the eightfold Uposatha precepts, and after his morning meal, he completely abstained from wearing perfumes, flowers, or ornaments for that day. He took vermilion in a golden cup, closed the doors from the lower floor up, and ascended to the upper palace. To obtain more light, he opened the lion-supported eastern window. Sitting in the breezy chamber, wishing to write the letters on the gold plate, he wrote:

"The Blessed One, who is the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Well-gone One, the Knower of the worlds, the Incomparable Leader of persons to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and men, the Buddha, the Exalted One,
571:
has appeared in the world."

In this manner, he first wrote of the virtues of the Blessed One in part. Then he wrote: "In such and such a way He fulfilled the ten perfections; in such and such a way He passed away from the Tusita heaven and took conception in His mother's womb. At that time, such and such thirty-two great omens appeared, and the whole world became as if it were an open space. While He remained in His mother's womb, these specific wonderful and extraordinary events occurred. While living as a householder, these specific wonderful and extraordinary events occurred. In such and such a way He made the Great Renunciation, and in such and such a way He practiced the Great Striving. Having practiced the difficult austerities (dukkharacariyā) in such and such a way, He ascended to the terrace of the Great Bodhi tree, and sitting upon the Unconquerable Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka), He attained the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience. For the Blessed One who attained the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience, such and such wonderful and extraordinary psychic powers of world-revelation (lokavivaraṇa) occurred. In the entire world of beings, including devas and brahmās, there is no other treasure endowed with such virtues besides this Buddha-treasure." Having thus written about the Buddha, he added:

"Whatever wealth there is here or in the world beyond,
Or whatever precious jewel in the heavens,
None is equal to the Tathāgata.
In the Buddha is this precious jewel found.
By this truth, may there be well-being!"
572:
572
In this way, the qualities of the Buddha were partially described.

Then, wishing to praise the Jewel of the Dhamma, it was written: “The Dhamma well-expounded by the Blessed One is endowed with the qualities of being well-expounded (svākkhāta), visible here and now (sandiṭṭhika), timeless (akālika), inviting one to come and see (ehipassika), worthy of being applied (opanayika), and to be personally experienced by the wise (paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhi). The Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, consisting of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path, is endowed with such special qualities.” In this manner, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) were partially written, followed by:

Yaṃ buddhaseṭṭho paviṇṇayī suciṃ,
samādhimānantarikaññamāhu,
samādhinā tena samo na vijjati,
idampi dhamme ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ,
etena saccena suvatthi hotu.

In this way, the qualities of the Dhamma were partially described.

Then, wishing to praise the Jewel of the Saṅgha, it was written: “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is endowed with the foundational qualities of practicing well (suppaṭipanna), practicing uprightly (ujuppaṭipanna), practicing rightly (ñāyappaṭipanna), and practicing properly (sāmīcippaṭipanna). Being thus endowed with these four qualities as a cause, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, consisting of the four pairs or eight individuals, is also endowed with these five qualities as a result: being worthy of gifts (āhuneyya), worthy of hospitality (pāhuneyya), worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya), worthy of reverential salutation (añjalikaraṇīya), and being the unsurpassed field of merit for the world (anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ).
573:
573
“Noble sons of good birth and conduct, having heard the Dhamma of the Buddha, go forth from the household life into homelessness in this manner. Some noble sons renounce the white umbrella (royal sovereignty) to become monks. Some renounce the position of heir apparent, and others renounce the position of commander-in-chief and so forth to become monks. Having become monks, they fulfill the following practice (paṭipatti).” After this introduction, the small section on virtue (cūḷa-sīla), the middle section on virtue (majjhima-sīla), and the large section on virtue (mahā-sīla) from the Brahmajāla Sutta were partially written. Then, descriptions were given regarding restraint of the six sense faculties, the cultivation of mindfulness and clear comprehension, contentment with the four requisites, the nine types of dwellings suitable for meditation, the abandonment of the five hindrances, the commencement of kasiṇa preliminary work, the arising of the jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā), and the thirty-eight subjects of meditation—all these were partially written up to the path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga).

The meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) in its sixteen steps was written in detail, followed by: “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is indeed endowed with such qualities.”

Ye puggalā aṭṭha sataṃ pasatthā,
cattāri etāni yugāni honti.
te dakkhiṇeyyā sugatassa sāvakā,
etesu dinnāni mahapphalāni.
idampi saṅghe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ.
etena saccena suvatthi hotu.

In this way, the qualities of the Saṅgha were partially described, followed by: “The Blessed One’s Sāsana of the threefold training (sikkhā) is a Sāsana well-proclaimed, being good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
574:
574
It is a Sāsana that can definitely and certainly lead to liberation from the suffering of saṃsāra. If my friend King Pukkusāti is able, I wish for him to renounce the world and become a monk.” After writing these words of encouragement, the gold plate was rolled up and wrapped in a very soft woolen cloth. It was then placed in a casket of scented wood. That scented wood casket was placed in a gold casket, the gold casket in a silver casket, the silver casket in a ruby casket, the ruby casket in a coral casket, the coral casket in a red ruby casket, the red ruby casket in a masāragalla (variegated precious stone) casket, the masāragalla casket in a crystal casket, the crystal casket in an ivory casket, the ivory casket in a casket adorned with the ten kinds of jewels, and the ten-jewel casket in a bamboo casket. Then, that bamboo casket was placed in a scented wood box. Again, the scented wood box was placed in a gold box, and (following the previous sequence) into boxes of silver, ruby, coral, red ruby, masāragalla, crystal, ivory, ten-jewels, and bamboo, one inside the other.

Then, the bamboo box was placed in a scented wood chest. The scented wood chest was placed in a gold chest, and (following the previous sequence) into chests of silver, ruby, coral, red ruby, masāragalla, crystal, ivory, ten-jewels, and bamboo (lacquerware) chests, one inside the other. Finally, it was wrapped in a woolen cloth and sealed with the royal seal. The King then addressed his ministers:

“Decorate the road wherever my authority extends. The road must be eight usabhas wide. Within those eight usabhas,
575:
575
two usabhas on the left and two on the right—making four usabhas—shall be merely cleared. The middle four usabhas must be grandly prepared with royal decorations.”

Thus he issued the royal command. Then, he had the state elephant fully caparisoned, a throne placed upon it, and a white umbrella hoisted above it. He ordered the city streets to be sprinkled with water and swept clean, banners and streamers to be erected in rows, and both sides of the road to be decorated with live banana trees, full water pots, various kinds of incense, perfumes, and flowers. He also sent messengers with letters to the local governors and lords along the way, saying:

“In the territories under your rule, you must perform offerings and honors in this same manner.”

The King himself, magnificently adorned with all royal ornaments, surrounded by a grand army and the sound of various musical instruments, personally escorted the gift with great ceremony to the border of his kingdom. He then gave oral instructions to the envoy minister:

“Friend, when my friend King Pukkusāti receives this gift, I wish for him to receive it not in the midst of his harem, but after ascending to the upper terrace of his palace.”

Having given these instructions, the King
576:
576
reflecting that “The Blessed One has gone to the border regions,” paid homage with the fivefold prostration and returned to his kingdom.

The various local governors and lords also decorated the road in the same manner and passed the gift along from one to another.

## King Pukkusāti Receiving the Gift

King Pukkusāti also had the road decorated in the same manner from the border of his own kingdom, had the capital city beautifully adorned, and received the gift with great magnificence.

The gift arrived in the city of Takkasilā on a wonderful Uposatha day. The minister who brought the gift conveyed the oral message from King Bimbisāra to King Pukkusāti.

After hearing the message, King Pukkusāti made all necessary arrangements for those who had come with the gift. He then took the gift himself and ascended to the upper terrace of the palace. He stationed guards at the door, saying, “Let no one enter this palace.” He opened the lion-supported window of the pavilion, placed the gift on a high seat, and while he himself sat on a lower seat, he removed the royal seal and the outer woolen cloth. Starting from the lacquerware chest, he opened them one by one in order. When he saw the innermost scented wood casket, he thought:

“This preparation is
577:
It is very grand. This regalia cannot be the regalia of any other worldly treasure. Surely, some kind of treasure worthy of being heard of must have appeared in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa),' he reflected correctly.

After that, he opened the scent casket, removed the royal seal, held the very soft woolen cloth by its two ends, gently unwrapped it, and saw a roll of gold plate.

## King Pukkusāti's Great Joy and Happiness

King Pukkusāti unrolled the gold plate and was amazed, thinking: 'How delightful are these characters! How even are the tops of these characters! How even are the rows! They are as straight as if drawn with a square ruler!' He read it from the beginning without skipping a single word.

While reading the virtues of the Buddha, beginning with 'The Blessed One has appeared in this world,' great joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa) arose within the King. The hairs from his ninety-nine thousand (99,000) pores stood on end. He became unaware of whether he was standing or sitting. Then he continued to reflect: 'Oh, even after the passing of hundreds of thousands of millions of great aeons, I have gained the opportunity to hear news concerning the Buddha-treasure, which is so difficult to hear and obtain, by depending on my friend King Bimbisāra.' Thus, intense joy arose and increased manifold within the King.
578:
578
King Pukkusāti, unable to continue reading further, sat reflecting until the surge of joy subsided. Then he continued to read the qualities of the Dhamma, beginning with: “The Dhamma well-expounded by the Blessed One is also endowed with the quality of being well-expounded (svākkhāta).” While reading this, great joy and delight arose within the King just as before.

The King sat waiting and reflecting until the surge of joy subsided. Then he continued to read the qualities of the Saṅgha, beginning with: “The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is also endowed with the quality of practicing well (suppaṭipanna).” While reading this, great joy and delight arose within the King just as before.

## King Pukkusāti Attaining Jhāna and Renouncing

Then, he read the final section on the gold plate, which was the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati). By reflecting according to the instructions in the letter, he fully attained the jhānas of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara-jhāna). The King spent his time in the bliss of jhāna. No one else was allowed to see him; only one young attendant was permitted to enter and leave. In this manner, about half a month (15 days) passed.

The citizens gathered in the royal courtyard and said:

“Since the day the gift was received, the King has not held any royal audience to inspect the troops or to watch the dancers at all.”
579:
There was no judicial decision-making at all. The Great King wished to show the gifts sent by his friend King Bimbisāra to those who desired to see them. “Kings sometimes entice a neighboring king with gifts to make that country their own; what is our king doing?”—so they shouted and cried out. When the King heard the shouting, he thought, “Shall I promote the welfare of the country, or shall I uphold the teaching and instruction of the Blessed One?” Then, the King further reflected, “No official skilled in calculation can count the number of times I have existed as a king ruling a country; therefore, I shall only uphold the teaching and instruction of the Blessed One.” Having made this resolution, he took the sword kept near his bed, cut off his hair, opened the lion-supported window, and said, “Friends, take this hair of mine and assume the kingship.” He then threw the hair, together with the ruby-encrusted crest-gem, into the midst of the assembly.

The multitude of people caught the hair and the crest-gem, and they cried out and lamented, saying, “O Great King, are all the kings who receive gifts from your friend like Your Majesty?”
580:
King Pukkusāti’s hair and beard were only about two finger-breadths long, just like those of the Bodhisatta when he was about to renounce the world.

Then, King Pukkusāti sent a young servant to the market to buy two pieces of saffron-dyed cloth and an earthen alms-bowl. He declared, “My renunciation is dedicated to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, who is deserving of special offerings in the world.” Dedicating himself to the Blessed One, he put on one saffron-dyed cloth and draped the other over his shoulder. He hung the alms-bowl from his left shoulder, took up a staff, and paced back and forth two or three times on the palace terrace, thinking, “Is my appearance as a monk beautiful or not?” Feeling joyful and thinking, “My appearance as a monk is very beautiful,” he opened the main gate and descended from the palace.

Although the dancers and others standing at the three gates saw the noble Pukkusāti descending in the form of a monk, they did not recognize him as the King. They only thought, “A Paccekabuddha has come to preach the Dhamma to our King.” Only after they went up to the palace and carefully looked at the King’s usual standing and sitting places did they realize, “The King has gone!” and they all wept at once, like people on a sinking ship in the middle of the ocean.

As soon as the noble Pukkusāti, in the guise of a monk, descended to the ground, eighteen divisions of people, all the city dwellers, and the entire army surrounded him and wept loudly.
581:
They wept and lamented intensely. The ministers also said to the noble Pukkusāti:

“O Great King, the kings who live in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) are very deceitful. Please send messengers with letters to investigate and know for certain whether the Jewel of the Buddha has truly appeared in the world or not, and only then depart. For now, please return to the golden palace, Your Majesty.”

Then, the noble Pukkusāti, in the guise of a monk, said, “Friends, I believe the words of my friend King Bimbisāra without hesitation. Between my friend Bimbisāra and me, there has never been any double-talk. You all remain here,” and he departed. The ministers and the multitude of people followed him as they usually did.

The noble Pukkusāti drew a line on the ground with his staff and asked, “To whom does this country belong?” When the people replied, “O Great King, it is Your Majesty’s country,” he declared, “Whoever crosses this line shall be punished by royal authority.” In the Mahājanaka Jātaka, Queen Sīvalidevī did not dare to cross the line drawn on the ground by the Bodhisatta King Mahājanaka, so she rolled on the ground (to cross it by a stratagem) and followed the King. Following that Queen Sīvalidevī,
582:
the people followed along the path where the line was broken. However, in this case, the people did not dare to break the line drawn by King Pukkusāti. They remained there, bowing their heads to the line and rolling on the ground, weeping and lamenting.

## The Solitary Pukkusāti, the Son of Good Family

The noble Pukkusāti departed alone, without taking even a single servant, thinking, “This person would only provide me with water for washing my face and tooth-sticks wherever I go.” He traveled alone, reflecting, “My teacher, the Blessed One, also made the great renunciation and became a monk alone, without any companion.” He thought, “I would be ashamed before the Blessed One,” and “My teacher, the Blessed One, has not used a vehicle since he became a monk,” so he did not wear even a single-layered sandal.
