He did not even use a small leaf-umbrella. The multitude of people climbed onto trees, walls, and watchtowers, watching and saying, “Our King has gone away alone,” and they remained behind.

The noble Pukkusāti thought, “The journey ahead is very long. I cannot complete this journey alone,” and so he followed a group of bullock-cart traders. As he traveled on foot over ground that was rough and scorching hot, the soles of the very delicate noble Pukkusāti’s feet became blistered and cracked, causing him great pain. When the traders
583:
set up leaf-roofed huts to rest, the noble Pukkusāti would move away from the road and sit at the foot of a tree. In that place where he sat, there was not a single person to perform duties such as massaging his feet or hands. The noble Pukkusāti entered the fourth jhāna of Ānāpāna (mindfulness of breathing) to dispel the fatigue of the journey and spent his time enjoying the bliss of the jhāna.

The next day at dawn, after attending to his personal needs, he again followed the group of traders. When it was time for the morning meal, the traders took Pukkusāti’s alms-bowl, filled it with food and delicacies, and offered it to him. The food offered by those traders was sometimes undercooked, sometimes too soft, and besides being very coarse, it was impure with stones and grit. Sometimes it was very heavy, and sometimes very light. The noble son, without considering whether it was soft, hard, coarse, fine, heavy, or light, reflected only on the nature of the food as it entered his body and consumed it as if it were divine ambrosia.

In this manner, he traveled one hundred and ninety-two (192) yojanas to reach the city of Sāvatthī. Although the carts drove past the vicinity of the Jetavana Monastery upon reaching Sāvatthī, he did not ask, “Where does the Blessed One reside?” There were two reasons why he did not ask:
(1) Because of his great reverence for the Blessed One, and
(2) Because of the news in King Bimbisāra’s letter.
I shall elaborate on these two reasons—
584:
(1) Throughout the journey, the noble son did not entertain other thoughts but kept his mind focused only on the Blessed One. Being one who was inclined, leaned, and directed toward the Buddha, even when he reached the vicinity of the Jetavana Monastery, the thought “Does the Blessed One reside in this monastery?” did not even occur to him, so the intention to ask did not arise.
(2) In the letter sent by King Bimbisāra with the gifts, it was written, “Idha Tathāgato loke uppajjati = Here, the Tathāgata has arisen in the world,” which led him to believe that the Blessed One had appeared in the city of Rājagaha. Therefore, even though he passed close to the Jetavana Monastery, he did not ask about the Blessed One but continued his journey, traveling about forty-five (45) yojanas further to reach Rājagaha.

The noble Pukkusāti reached Rājagaha at sunset. Because of the news in King Bimbisāra’s letter, and because he thought the Blessed One would be residing in Rājagaha, and because there were many monasteries in Rājagaha, he asked the people he met, “In which monastery does the Blessed One reside?” When the people asked, “Venerable sir, from where have you come just now?” the noble Pukkusāti replied, “I have come from the north of this city of Rājagaha.” The people said, “Venerable sir, you have overshot your destination. The Blessed One is currently residing in Sāvatthī, which is about forty-five yojanas from Rājagaha on the very road you came by.”
585:
The noble Pukkusāti thought, “It is now late. I cannot go to the presence of the Buddha today. I will sleep in Rājagaha tonight and go to the Blessed One when dawn breaks tomorrow.” Then he asked those people, “Friends, where do the ascetics and monks who arrive in Rājagaha at sunset stay?” When the people pointed to a nearby potter’s shed and said, “Venerable sir, they stay in this potter’s shed,” the noble son asked the owner, the potter, for permission to stay the night in that shed and went in to sit there.

## The Arrival of the Blessed One

At dawn that day, the Blessed One surveyed the world of sentient beings and saw the noble Pukkusāti.

“This noble son, after reading the letter sent by his friend King Bimbisāra, has renounced the great kingdom of Takkasilā, which is over a hundred yojanas wide. Having become a monk for my sake, he has traveled one hundred and ninety-two (192) yojanas, overshot by forty-five (45) yojanas, and reached Rājagaha today.

If I do not go to him, he will stay for one night without attaining the three lower paths and fruits, and then he will meet a helpless death. I,”
586:
“If I go, he will reach, realize, and attain the three lower Ariya fruits. I have fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculable periods (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa) for the very purpose of showing compassion and uplifting sentient beings (veneyya-satta). I shall now show compassion to this clansman.”

Having reflected thus, the Buddha attended to his morning needs early in the day. Surrounded by a company of monks, he entered the city of Sāvatthī for alms. After returning from the alms round in the afternoon, he rested for a moment in the Gandhakuṭī chamber. Then, he reflected:

“This clansman, out of great respect and reverence for me, has performed a difficult task. He has abandoned the entire kingdom of Takkasilā, which is over a hundred yojanas in extent, and has set out alone without even bringing a single servant to provide him with water for washing.”

Reflecting thus, he did not take any of the great disciples such as the Venerable Sāriputta or the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Taking his own bowl and robes (patta-cīvara), he departed from Sāvatthī alone.

In departing thus, he did not fly through the air, nor did he shorten the distance of the earth’s path by psychic power. He thought: “This clansman has great respect and reverence for me. He did not travel by any vehicle such as an elephant, horse, chariot, or golden palanquin. He did not even wear simple sandals (which could be called a vehicle) nor did he carry a leaf-umbrella. I, too, should only go on foot.” Having made this decision, he traveled only on foot.
587:
“I should only go on foot,” he decided, and thus he traveled on foot.

The Blessed One, concealing his Buddha-glory—such as the major and minor marks (lakkhaṇa) and the six-colored rays (chabbaṇṇaraṃsi)—traveled in the guise of an ordinary monk, like the moon obscured by a bank of clouds. By evening (around 6:00 PM), he had covered forty-five yojanas. Just as the clansman Pukkusāti had entered the potter’s shed, the Buddha arrived near that same shed at sunset. The reason the Buddha traveled while concealing his glory was to allow the clansman Pukkusāti to rest from the fatigue of his journey freely and comfortably. Indeed, one whose fatigue from travel has not subsided is not a fit vessel for the teaching of the Dhamma.

Having arrived near the potter’s shed, the Blessed One did not enter forcefully by asserting, “I am the Omniscient Buddha.” Instead, standing at the entrance of the shed, he requested permission, saying: “O monk, if it is not a burden to you, we would like to stay in this shed for one night.” The clansman Pukkusāti, thinking the Blessed One was merely an ordinary monk, kindly gave permission, saying: “Friend, this potter’s shed is quiet and secluded. It is not cramped. May the venerable one stay as comfortably as you wish.”

(The clansman Pukkusāti, who had abandoned the kingship of Takkasilā—a realm over a hundred yojanas wide—to become a monk, how could he be stingy toward another fellow practitioner in a potter’s shed abandoned by others? He would not be stingy at all. However, some empty persons (mogha-purisa), after going forth in the Dispensation, are overcome and oppressed by stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsa-macchariya) and the like. They cling strongly to their own monastery or cell, thinking, “This is my hut, this is my precinct,” and strive to prevent other fellow practitioners from finding a place to stay. — Commentary Admonition).
588:
The Blessed One, who was exceedingly refined and delicate, had abandoned the Gandhakuṭī monastery which was like a celestial mansion. He spread a mat of grass in the potter’s shed—a place as repulsive as a rubbish heap, covered in ashes, broken pots, grass, straw, and the droppings of chickens and pigs. Spreading his rag-robe (paṃsukūla-cīvara) over it, he sat down without any change in his composure, just as if he were entering the Gandhakuṭī monastery, which was fragrant with celestial scents and like a divine palace.

Thus, these two—the Blessed One and the clansman Pukkusāti—both of noble Khattiya birth, both endowed with special merit from past aspirations, both having renounced royal luxury to become monks, both possessing golden complexions, and both having attained meditative absorptions (samāpatti), sat within the potter’s shed. Consequently, the small potter’s shed became exceedingly beautiful, like a crystal cave inhabited by two maned lion-kings.

Between the two, the Blessed One thought: “Although I am very refined and delicate, I have traveled a strenuous journey of forty-five yojanas by evening (6:00 PM).
589:
Without even letting the thought arise, “I will lie down on my right side and rest from the fatigue of the journey for a moment,” he remained sitting and entered the Fruition Attainment (phala-samāpatti) of the fourth jhāna.

The clansman Pukkusāti also did not let the thought arise, “I have traveled a journey of one hundred and ninety-two yojanas on foot. I will lie down for a moment to dispel the fatigue of the journey.” While sitting, he entered the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna).

(Here, one might ask: “Did the Buddha not come to preach the Dhamma to the clansman? Why then did he not preach the Dhamma but instead remain in Fruition Attainment?” The answer is: At that time, having just arrived, Pukkusāti’s fatigue from the journey had not yet subsided. If the Dhamma were preached then, he would not be able to receive the teaching properly due to his exhaustion. The Buddha refrained from preaching, considering that the clansman’s fatigue should first be calmed.

Other teachers (apare) say: “The city of Rājagaha is a populous capital, not quiet due to the ten kinds of sounds. These sounds only subside at midnight. The Buddha waited for that quiet time before preaching.” This reason given by those teachers is not the primary reason. Indeed, the Blessed One is capable of silencing even a sound that reaches up to the Brahma realm by his psychic power. (This means he could use his power to prevent the sound from reaching the clansman’s ears). In truth, he did not preach yet because he wished to wait for the clansman’s fatigue to subside).

The Blessed One had traveled from Sāvatthī to Rājagaha, a distance of 45 yojanas,
590:
on foot (without shortening the journey). He arrived at the potter’s shed at sunset (around 6:00 PM), requested permission, and entered. From that time (6:00 PM) until midnight (for about six hours), he remained in Fruition Attainment. Emerging from Fruition Attainment at midnight, he opened his eyes—which were adorned with the five kinds of clarity, like opening a lion-window of a golden mansion. He saw the clansman Pukkusāti sitting like a golden statue, without any movement of hands, feet, or head, as steady as a firmly planted doorpost, free from any restlessness, and absorbed in the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing. The thought arose in the Buddha’s mind: “This clansman maintains a posture (iriyāpatha) that inspires faith. It would be well if I were to begin a conversation with him.”

To clarify: Among the four postures (iriyāpatha), the three—walking, standing, and lying down—are not as graceful. Indeed, the limbs, hands, feet, and head of a walking monk move. The body of a standing monk is stiff. The posture of a lying monk is also not pleasing. In truth, only the sitting posture of a monk is truly beautiful—one who, in the afternoon, has swept his place of seclusion, spread his leather mat (cammakhaṇḍa), washed his hands and feet, and sat down cross-legged, forming the four-fold connection (at the two hip joints and two knee joints). This clansman Pukkusāti was also
591:
sitting cross-legged, absorbed in the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing. Thus, the Blessed One was greatly pleased by the sitting posture of the clansman Pukkusāti and thought: “This clansman maintains a posture that inspires faith.”

Regarding the thought, “It would be well if I were to begin a conversation,” one might ask: “Why did he need to ask? Did the Buddha not know that the man had gone forth intending to follow him?” The answer is: It is not that he did not know (he did know). However, if he did not ask, a connection for conversation would not be established. Without such a connection, the preaching of the Dhamma would not occur. Therefore, he asked in order to create an opening for the subsequent Dhamma teaching.

After having this thought, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Pukkusāti: “Monk, on whose account have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you delight in?” Then, the Venerable Pukkusāti answered in detail that he had gone forth on account of the Blessed One.

Again, the Blessed One asked: “Monk, where is that Blessed One, the Arahaṃ, the Sammāsambuddha, staying at this time?” The Venerable Pukkusāti replied: “Friend, in the northern districts, there is a city called Sāvatthī. In that city, the Blessed One, the Arahaṃ, the Sammāsambuddha, is currently staying.”
592:
When the Blessed One asked, “Monk, have you ever seen that Blessed One? If you saw him, would you recognize him?”, the Venerable Pukkusāti replied, “Friend, I have never seen that Blessed One, nor would I recognize him if I saw him.”

(In this regard: It is not surprising that everyone recognizes the Blessed One when he is adorned with the Buddha’s glory, thinking, “This is the Blessed One.” However, it is difficult for anyone to recognize the Blessed One when he travels in the guise of an ordinary monk, concealing his Buddha-glory while going for alms. Thus, Venerable Pukkusāti answered honestly according to his inability to recognize him, saying, “I would not recognize him.” He was simply stating the natural fact. For this reason, even though he was staying in the same potter’s shed as the Blessed One, he did not recognize him.)

Then, knowing that Venerable Pukkusāti’s fatigue from his journey had subsided, the Blessed One thought, “This clansman has gone forth as a monk dedicated to me. It would be well if I were to teach him the Dhamma.” He then addressed Venerable Pukkusāti, saying, “Monk, I will teach you the Dhamma. Listen to that Dhamma and pay close attention. I shall speak in detail.” (Up until this moment, Venerable Pukkusāti still did not know that this was the Blessed One.)

The clansman Pukkusāti was one who had gone forth after reading the royal letter sent by his friend, King Bimbisāra, renouncing his kingship with the great hope that “I shall hear the sweet Dhamma of the Blessed One.” After going forth and traveling such a long distance, he had not yet found anyone who would say even a single sentence such as, “Monk, I will teach you the Dhamma.”
593:
How could that clansman not listen respectfully to the words, “Monk, I will teach you the Dhamma”? (He would certainly listen.) Indeed, this Venerable Pukkusāti was one who thirsted for the water of Dhamma, like a person parched with thirst who desperately wants to drink water. Therefore, wishing to acknowledge with joy that he would listen respectfully, he replied, “Very well, friend.”

Then the Blessed One said to Venerable Pukkusāti:

“Monk, this person consists of six elements, six bases of contact, eighteen mental explorations, and four foundations. For a person who stands upon these four foundations, the currents of conceit—the notion of ‘I am’—do not flow. When the currents of conceit do not flow, that (khīṇāsava) monk is called a sage at peace. (1) One should not neglect wisdom (Vipassanā-paññā). (2) One should guard truth (vaci-sacca). (3) One should cultivate the relinquishment of defilements. (4) One should train only for the stilling of defilements. This is the summary (uddesa) of the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta.”

Having laid down this summary, he then explained and taught each group of words in the summary in detail (niddesa). (The detailed explanation should be noted as extracted from the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pāḷi in the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka.)
594:
## Venerable Pukkusāti Becoming an Anāgāmī Noble One

As the Blessed One thus explained and taught each group of words from the summary in detail, and when the detailed explanation of the summary statement “One should not neglect wisdom” was taught culminating in the knowledge of the Fruit of Arahatship, Venerable Pukkusāti, in accordance with his past merits and supporting conditions (upaniṣraya), reached the three lower Fruits and became an Anāgāmī (Non-returner).

For example, while a great king is eating various flavored foods from a royal golden bowl, if a young prince sitting on his lap, making a morsel of food according to the size of his own mouth, shows a sign of wanting to eat, the king would feed that morsel he had prepared for himself to the young prince. The young prince would eat only as much as the size of his mouth allows. The king himself would eat the remaining food or put it back into the royal golden bowl. Similarly, the Blessed One, the King of Dhamma, taught the Dhamma culminating in the Fruit of Arahatship according to the capacity of his own golden mouth of wisdom. (= He prepared and fed the morsel of Dhamma). The young prince, the clansman Pukkusāti, reached the three lower Fruits, which are like three-quarters of the morsel of Dhamma, according to the capacity of his past merits and supporting conditions, and became an Anāgāmī.

Specifically, in the earlier part before reaching the Fruit of Anāgāmī (before becoming a Noble One), while listening to the teaching of the Dhamma in terms of the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and bases of contact (phassāyatana), etc.,
595:
there was no doubt or hesitation at all in the mind of the clansman Pukkusāti regarding the nature of the Dhamma. However, regarding the Blessed One who was teaching in the guise of an ordinary monk, he had doubts, thinking, “The Buddhas often wander in an unmanifested form in some places. Could this noble person who is now teaching the Dhamma be the Blessed One himself?” Now, having reached the Fruit of Anāgāmī, he made a firm decision, free from doubt: “This noble one who is now teaching the Dhamma is indeed my teacher, the Blessed One.”

If that is so, one might ask, “Why did he not yet confess his fault and apologize for having mistakenly addressed him as ‘friend’ (before knowing he was the Buddha)?” The answer is: He did not yet confess because he had not yet found the opportunity to do so. To elaborate—the Blessed One continued to teach the Dhamma according to the sequence of the Dhamma summary he had laid down, without interrupting the flow of the Dhamma, like the flowing of a great celestial river. Therefore, because there was no opportunity to confess at that time, he remained without confessing yet.

## Venerable Pukkusāti Requesting Ordination

When the Blessed One finished the detailed teaching according to the sequence of the summary and reached the conclusion of the discourse, the sequence of the dialogue between Venerable Pukkusāti and the Blessed One was as follows:

(Venerable Pukkusāti:) “The Blessed One, the Teacher of gods and men, has indeed come to me out of great compassion! The Blessed One, who speaks the excellent Dhamma,
596:
has indeed come to me out of great compassion! The Blessed One, the Knower of all things, has indeed come to me out of great compassion!” (Having spoken thus with great joy, he rose from his seat, placed his robe over his left shoulder, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and said:) “Exalted One, a fault has overcome me, in that I was so foolish, so confused, and so unskilled as to have thought that I should address the Blessed One as ‘friend.’ (And as I thought, I mistakenly addressed you so.) Exalted One, may the Blessed One accept this confession of my fault as a fault, for the sake of future restraint.”

(The Buddha:) “Monk, indeed, a fault overcame you, in that you were so foolish, so confused, and so unskilled as to have thought that you should address me as ‘friend.’ (And as you thought, you mistakenly addressed me so.) Monk, since you see your fault as a fault and make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept your confession. Monk, it is growth in the discipline of the Noble One when one sees one’s fault as a fault and makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma and practices restraint in the future.”
597:
(Venerable Pukkusāti:) “Exalted One, may I receive ordination in the presence of the Blessed One.”

(The Buddha:) “Monk, are your (own) bowl and robes complete?”

(Venerable Pukkusāti:) “Exalted One, my (own) bowl and robes are not yet complete.”

(The Buddha:) “Monk, the Buddhas do not ordain those whose bowl and robes are not complete.”

Thereupon, Venerable Pukkusāti, greatly delighted and rejoicing in the words of the Blessed One (having expressed his appreciation), rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and departed to search for a bowl and robes.

(Here, it should be specially noted: One might ask, “Why did the clansman Pukkusāti not receive the miraculously created bowl and robes that ‘Ehi Bhikkhu’ monks receive?” The answer given by some is: “Because he had not donated the eight requisites in the past.” (The Commentator does not accept this answer.) Indeed, since the clansman Pukkusāti was one who had given gifts and was endowed with the aspiration (abhinīhāra), it should not be said that he had not donated the eight requisites. In truth, miraculously created bowl and robes only appear for those in their final existence (pacchimabhavika). This clansman Pukkusāti, however, was one who still had to undergo rebirth (in the Pure Abodes). Therefore, the miraculously created bowl and robes did not appear. (This is the answer.)

“If that is so, why did the Blessed One not search for the bowl and robes himself and ordain him?” one might ask. The answer is: He did not ordain him because there was no longer any time or opportunity to do so. Indeed, at that time,
598:
the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) of the clansman Pukkusāti was exhausted. It was as if a Great Brahmā from the Suddhāvāsa realm had come to stay in the potter’s shed for a brief moment. Therefore, the Blessed One did not search for the bowl and robes himself. (This is the answer.)

At the time the clansman Pukkusāti departed to search for a bowl and robes, it was just after dawn. To elaborate—the conclusion of the Blessed One’s Dhamma teaching, the rising of the dawn, and the emission of the six-colored rays occurred simultaneously.

As soon as the Dhamma teaching ended, the Blessed One emitted the six-colored rays, and the entire potter’s shed became brilliantly illuminated. The six-colored rays came forth in masses and clusters, spreading out and covering all directions as if they were being draped with golden cloth, or as if they were shining with a collection of various colored jewels and flowers. The Blessed One made a determination: “May the people of the city see the Buddha.” According to this determination, as soon as the people of the city saw the Blessed One, they said to one another, “The Blessed One has arrived! He is sitting in the potter’s shed!” and they reported this matter to King Bimbisāra.

## King Bimbisāra Arriving and Paying Homage

Upon hearing the report from the citizens, King Bimbisāra went out to the potter’s shed. After respectfully paying homage to the Blessed One, he said, “Exalted One...”
599:
“At what time did you arrive at this potter’s shed?” the King asked. The Blessed One replied, “Great King, I arrived at sunset yesterday.” The King then asked again, “For what purpose did you come, Bhante?” Thereupon, the Blessed One said:

“Great King, your close friend King Pukkusāti, after reading and hearing the royal message and gifts sent by you, renounced the world and went forth as a monk. Intending to seek me, he bypassed the city of Sāvatthī and traveled an extra distance of forty-five yojanas, eventually entering and staying in this potter’s shed.

I have come here on foot to favor that Pukkusāti. I have already preached the Dhamma to him. The clansman Pukkusāti has now attained the three lower noble fruits and has become an Anāgāmī (Non-returner).”

Surprised, the King asked, “Bhante, where is my dear friend King Pukkusāti now?” The Blessed One replied, “Great King, King Pukkusāti requested me to grant him full ordination, but as his bowl and robes were not yet complete, he has gone to seek them.” King Bimbisāra immediately and hurriedly followed in the direction where the clansman Pukkusāti had gone to search for his bowl and robes. The Blessed One, however, returned through the air.
600:
The Blessed One appeared at the Gandhakuṭī in the Jetavana Monastery.

## The Death of King Pukkusāti and His Rebirth in the Aviha Brahma Realm

While the clansman Pukkusāti was searching for a bowl and robes, he did not go to his close friend King Bimbisāra, nor did he go to the merchants who had come from Taxila. He thought to himself, “It is not proper for me to search for a bowl and robes by selectively choosing what is pleasing or displeasing in various places like a hen. Avoiding the great city, I shall search in water-landings, cemeteries, rubbish heaps, and alleys.” With the intention of seeking genuine rag-robes (paṃsukūla), he made an effort to find coarse rag-cloth in the rubbish heaps along the way.

While the clansman Pukkusāti was examining and searching for rag-cloth in a rubbish heap, a cow with a deranged mind (possessed by a female yakkha who was an enemy from a past life) rushed toward him and gored him to death with her horns. Because the clansman Pukkusāti was severely oppressed by hunger and thirst and was extremely weak in strength, his life ended even while he was upright, and as he fell to the ground, he appeared like a golden statue placed face down on the rubbish heap. After passing away, he was reborn in the Aviha Brahma realm. Immediately upon rebirth, he attained the fruit of Arahantship and became an Arahant Brahma.

There are seven individuals who attained the fruit of Arahantship immediately after taking rebirth in the Aviha Brahma realm: (1) Upaka, (2) Palagaṇḍa, (3) Pukkusāti, (4) Bhaddiya, (5) Khaṇḍadeva,
601:
(6) Bāhuraggi, and (7) Siṅgiya. This was taught in the tenth sutta of the Āditta Vagga and the fourth sutta of the Nānātitthiya Vagga in the Sagāthāvagga Saṃyutta Pāḷi.

King Bimbisāra thought, “My friend King Pukkusāti read the royal message and gifts I sent, renounced the kingship that was already in his hands, and traveled such a long and arduous journey. This clansman has performed a deed difficult for ordinary people to do. I shall honor my friend King Pukkusāti in the manner that monks are honored.” He then commanded his men, “Go and search until you find my friend King Pukkusāti,” sending them throughout the surroundings of the city. The messengers found King Pukkusāti, who had passed away and lay face down on a rubbish heap like a golden statue, and they returned to report the matter to King Bimbisāra.

When King Bimbisāra went to that place and saw the clansman Pukkusāti, he wept and lamented, saying, “Friends, we did not have the opportunity to pay our respects to our dear friend while he was alive. My friend King Pukkusāti has indeed become helpless!” He had the physical remains of the clansman Pukkusāti placed on a small couch and brought to a suitable place. Not knowing how to perform the honors for one who had become a monk, he summoned bath-attendants and others to wash the clansman. He then had him dressed in clean white cloth, adorned him in royal attire,
602:
placed him on a golden palanquin, and honored him with all kinds of musical instruments, perfumes, and flowers. He was carried outside the city, cremated with a great amount of scented wood, and after collecting the bone relics, the King had a stupa (cetiya) built.

Afterward, in Sāvatthī, many monks went to the presence of the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. They asked the Blessed One, “Bhante, the clansman Pukkusāti was exhorted by the Master with a brief instruction. That clansman Pukkusāti has now died. What is his destination? What is his future state?”

Then the Blessed One said, “Monks, the clansman Pukkusāti was a wise man. He practiced the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma (Vipassanā). He did not trouble me on account of the Dhamma. Monks, with the destruction of the five lower fetters (orambhāgiya saṃyojana) that lead to the lower sensual realms, the clansman Pukkusāti has been reborn in the Aviha Brahma realm, and he will attain Parinibbāna in that Suddhāvāsa realm. He is not subject to return from that Aviha realm (to the lower sensual world).”

This is the account of King Pukkusāti.
**********
604:
Having made this decision, the Buddha instructed, “Ananda, spread the small couch in the precinct outside the Gandhakuṭī.” He then lay down on that couch on his right side in the lion’s posture.

When Rāhu Asurinda approached the Blessed One and saw him lying down, he had to crane his neck and look up to behold the Buddha’s face, just as one looks up at the full moon in the middle of the sky. The Blessed One asked, “Rāhu Asurinda, what is the reason for your coming to behold me only after such a long time?” Rāhu Asurinda replied, “Bhante, I did not come because I mistakenly thought, ‘I will not be able to behold the Buddha without looking down.’”

Then the Blessed One said to Rāhu Asurinda, “Asurinda, I did not fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) with my face turned downward (meaning, by slackening effort). I gave gifts and practiced only with my head held high (meaning, without slackening effort).” On that very day, Rāhu Asurinda took refuge in the Triple Gem.

This is the account of Rāhu Asurinda.
**********
605:
## The Account of Devadatta
(Although the story of Devadatta, from the time of his ordination until he was swallowed by the earth, along with the many Jātakas preached concerning him, should be explained in detail, I shall summarize it as much as possible in this text.)

The account of Devadatta up to his ordination has been previously described (in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Volume 3, Page 145, Chapter 19, under the heading “The Ordination of the Six Sakyan Princes and Upāli the Barber”). If desired, it may be taken from there.

As described in the previous Chapter 19, from pages 145 to 160, after the six Sakyan princes and Upāli the barber went forth, among those seven monks:

(1) Venerable Bhaddiya became an Arahant with the Threefold Knowledge (te-vijja) within that very Rains Retreat.
(2) Venerable Anuruddha, after attaining the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu), reached the fruit of Arahantship after hearing the Mahāvitakka Sutta (as found in Aṅguttara Nikāya, Vol. 3, Page 62).
(3) Venerable Ānanda Thera was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) after hearing the discourse on the simile of the mirror-image preached by Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta (based on the Ānanda Sutta, Theravagga, Khandhavagga Saṃyutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Vol. 2, Page 86).
(4-5) Venerable Bhagu and Venerable Kimila later developed insight (vipassanā) and reached the fruit of Arahantship.
606:
(6) Venerable Devadatta, while still an ordinary monk (puthujjana), attained mundane jhāna and supernormal powers (abhiññā); he did not become an ariya (noble one).

Later, while the Blessed One was staying in the city of Kosambī, great gains, offerings, and honor accrued to the Blessed One along with a large community of disciples. Carrying robes, medicine, and other requisites, many people entered the monastery grounds and wandered about, looking for the places where the eighty great disciples resided, asking, "Where is the Blessed One? Where is the Venerable Sāriputta? Where is the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna? Where is the Venerable Mahākassapa? Where is the Venerable Bhaddiya? Where is the Venerable Anuruddha? Where is the Venerable Ānanda? Where is the Venerable Bhagu? Where is the Venerable Kimbila?"

However, there was not a single person who asked, "Where is the Venerable Devadatta sitting?" or "Where is he standing?"

## Devadatta's Plot to Gain Fame and Honor

Then, Venerable Devadatta thought: "I too went forth into the monkhood together with that Venerable Bhaddiya. They are those who went forth from the royal clan, and I too am one who went forth from the royal clan. These people who come carrying gains, offerings, and honor seek only those such as Venerable Bhaddiya. For me, there is not even a single person who mentions my name or asks about me. With whom should I associate, and whom should I inspire with faith, so that abundant gains, offerings, and honor may accrue to me?" Then he continued to think:
607:
"King Bimbisāra, upon his first meeting with the Blessed One, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) along with one hundred and ten thousand brahmin householders. It is impossible to win over King Bimbisāra. It is also impossible to win over King Pasenadi of Kosala. However, Prince Ajātasattu, the son of King Bimbisāra, is young and does not yet know the virtues or faults of anyone. I shall manage to win over Prince Ajātasattu."

Having thought thus, Venerable Devadatta went from Kosambī to Rājagaha. He manifested himself in the form of a young boy, wearing a snake on each of his two hands and two feet—making four—one snake around his neck, another snake on his head like a head-coil, and another snake on his left shoulder. Having entwined these six snakes by their tails like a waistband, he descended from the sky and sat on Prince Ajātasattu's lap.

Prince Ajātasattu was terrified and asked, "Who are you?" to which he replied, "I am Devadatta." The prince said, "Venerable sir, if you are indeed Devadatta, please appear in your natural form." Venerable Devadatta then vanished the form of the boy and stood before Prince Ajātasattu in his natural form, wearing his robes and carrying his bowl.

Then, Prince Ajātasattu, being greatly inspired by this miracle of psychic power, approached him regularly every morning and evening with five hundred chariots. Every day, he also established a regular offering of five hundred pots of rice,
609:
When Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied that he did know, the Blessed One said:

"Moggallāna, keep this matter to yourself. Moggallāna, keep this matter to yourself. Now, that hollow man (Devadatta) will reveal himself by his own actions."

Then the Blessed One taught that there are five types of teachers in the world: (1) a teacher who is not pure in virtue but claims, "I am pure in virtue"; (2) a teacher who is not pure in livelihood but claims, "I am pure in livelihood"; (3) a teacher who is not pure in teaching the Dhamma but claims, "I am pure in teaching the Dhamma"; (4) a teacher who is not pure in explanation but claims, "I am pure in explanation"; (5) a teacher who is not pure in knowledge and vision but claims, "I am pure in knowledge and vision."

Regarding these five types of teachers, although their respective disciples know the full truth, they do not inform the lay donors because they are supported by them with the four requisites and fear their teacher's displeasure. Instead, they remain indifferent, thinking, "He will become known by his own deeds one day." It is only such teachers whom disciples must protect, and such teachers who desire protection from their disciples.

However, the Blessed One taught that in His case, He is truly pure in virtue and thus claims, "I am pure in virtue." He is pure in livelihood... pure in teaching the Dhamma, pure in explanation,
611:
that dog would become even more fierce. In the same way, as long as Prince Ajātasattu approaches Devadatta with five hundred chariots every morning and evening, and as long as he sends five hundred pots of rice daily, one should expect only decline in Devadatta's wholesome qualities; growth is not to be expected.

Monks, Devadatta's gains, offerings, and fame have arisen for his own slaughter and destruction. Monks, just as (1) a banana tree bears fruit for its own slaughter and destruction; (2) a bamboo tree bears fruit for its own slaughter and destruction; (3) a reed bears fruit for its own slaughter and destruction; (4) a she-mule carries a fetus for her own slaughter and destruction; in the same way, Devadatta's gains, offerings, and fame have arisen for his own slaughter and destruction.

Phalaṃ ve kadaliṃ hanti,
phalaṃ veḷuṃ phalaṃ naḷaṃ.
Sakkāro kāpurisaṃ hanti,
gabbho assatariṃ yathā.

Monks, just as the fruit (phalaṃ) surely (ve) kills the banana tree (kadaliṃ); just as the fruit kills the bamboo (veḷuṃ); just as the fruit kills the reed (naḷaṃ); and just as the fetus (gabbho) kills the mother she-mule (assatariṃ);
612:
in the same way, honor and gains (sakkāro) kill the wicked man (kāpurisaṃ) of corrupt mind."

Thus He delivered the Dhamma teaching.

## Devadatta's First Grudge Against the Buddha

Then one day, while the Blessed One was sitting and teaching the Dhamma to a large assembly including the King, Devadatta rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over his left shoulder, and with palms joined in reverence toward the Blessed One, said:

"Exalted Buddha, the Blessed One is now old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and has reached the final stage of life. Blessed One, may the Blessed One now dwell in ease in this very life (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra) and remain unconcerned. Hand over the community of monks to me. I will look after and lead the community of monks."

When he said this, the Blessed One said to Devadatta, "It is not fit, Devadatta. Do not desire to look after and lead the community of monks."

A second time, Devadatta made the same request, and the Blessed One refused in the same way. When Devadatta made the same request for the third time, the Blessed One said to Devadatta:
613:
"Devadatta, I would not hand over the Saṅgha of monks even to Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Why then should I hand it over to you, a wretched person who consumes things like spittle?"

Then Devadatta thought, "The Blessed One rebuked me in the midst of the assembly, including the King, with the word 'kheḷāsaka' (spittle-eater, one who consumes impure requisites like spittle), while he praised only Sāriputta and Moggallāna." Angry and displeased, he paid respects to the Blessed One and departed.

This was Devadatta's first grudge against the Blessed One.

## Ordering the Act of Proclamation (Pakāsanīyakamma)
Then the Blessed One had the monks perform the Act of Proclamation (Pakāsanīyakamma) against Devadatta in Rājagaha (by a formal act consisting of a motion and a second). When the Saṅgha had performed the Act of Proclamation, the Buddha authorized Venerable Sāriputta, also by a formal act, to make Devadatta's character known in Rājagaha. Venerable Sāriputta, following the Buddha's command and having been authorized by the Saṅgha, made Devadatta's character known in Rājagaha.

When this was being proclaimed, people without faith or wisdom said, "These monks, who are Sakyan princes and sons of the Buddha, are jealous. They are jealous of Devadatta's gains and honors."

However, people with faith and wisdom said, "The Blessed One's making Devadatta's character known in Rājagaha will not be for a trivial reason."
614:
(In this context, the "Act of Proclamation" is a Vinaya matter. It means making it known that whatever the person (monk) against whom the act is performed does or says has nothing to do with the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, and is only the personal behavior or speech of that monk.

The manner of performing the Act of Proclamation against Devadatta was: "Formerly, Devadatta's behavior was of one kind; now it is of another kind. Whatever Devadatta does by body or speech, he should not be regarded as representing the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha; he should be regarded only as Devadatta himself." The Saṅgha performed the Act of Proclamation by reading the formal motion and second. Then, by the Buddha's command, the Saṅgha had to authorize Venerable Sāriputta (as the person who would clearly show and speak about Devadatta's character in Rājagaha) through a formal act. After being so authorized, Venerable Sāriputta, surrounded by monks, entered Rājagaha and proclaimed: "Formerly, Devadatta's behavior was of one kind; now it is of another kind. Whatever Devadatta does by body or speech, he should not be regarded as representing the Blessed One, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha; he should be regarded only as Devadatta himself." Thus he made Devadatta's character known in Rājagaha.) This is a brief note regarding the Act of Proclamation.

## Regarding Prince Ajātasattu
When the Act of Proclamation had been fully performed, Devadatta thought, "Now the ascetic Gotama has abandoned me. Right now, I shall cause harm to that ascetic Gotama..."
615: Thinking thus, he approached Prince Ajātasattu and said: "Prince, people in the past lived long lives, but people today have short lives. There is a possibility that you might die while still a prince. Therefore, you should kill your father and become King; I will kill the Buddha and become the Buddha." Then Prince Ajātasattu thought, "Venerable Devadatta is of great psychic power and majesty. He must know the reason for saying this." He fastened a dagger to his thigh and, in broad daylight, trembling with fear and anxiety, entered the palace hurriedly. The royal guards seized the prince and searched him, finding the dagger fastened to his thigh. They asked him: "Prince, what do you wish to do?" When the prince replied, "I wish to kill my father," the ministers asked, "Who incited you?" The prince honestly confessed, "Venerable Devadatta incited me." Then: (Group A) Some ministers held the view: "The Prince, Devadatta, and all the monks should be killed." (Group B) Some ministers held the view: "The monks should not be killed, for they have done no wrong. Only the Prince and Devadatta should be killed."
616: (Group C) Some ministers held the view: "Neither the Prince, Devadatta, nor the monks should be killed. We should report this to the King and do as he commands." Then the ministers seized the prince and went to King Bimbisāra, reporting the matter to him. The King asked, "Friends, what is the opinion of the ministers?" When they reported the three different views, the King said: "Friends, what fault could the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha have committed? Did not the Buddha already proclaim Devadatta's nature in Rājagaha, saying 'Formerly Devadatta's conduct was of one kind; now it is of another' (by performing the Pakāsanīya-kamma)?" Having said this, he removed the first group of ministers (Group A) entirely from their positions. He demoted the second group (Group B) to lower positions, and he promoted the third group (Group C) to higher positions. Then the King asked his son, "Prince, why do you wish to kill me?" When the prince replied, "Father, I desire the kingship," King Bimbisāra said, "Prince, if you desire the kingship, this royal splendor is yours, my dear son," and he handed over the throne and the kingdom entirely to Prince Ajātasattu.
617:
## Devadatta's Cruel Advice
Prince Ajātasattu, feeling satisfied, reported to Devadatta, "My heart's desire has been fulfilled." Then Devadatta spoke words of incitement to the prince: "You are like a man who beats a drum with a fox inside, thinking 'My task is successful.' If your father lives for two or three more days, he will reflect on the disrespect you have shown and will take back the kingship himself."

When the prince asked, "Venerable Sir, what then should I do?", Devadatta gave cruel advice, saying, "Kill your father outright." When the prince replied, "Venerable Sir, my father is of royal blood; is he not someone who should not be killed with a weapon?", Devadatta gave further rude and cruel advice: "Then kill your father by cutting off his food and starving him."

## Ajātasattu Causes His Father's Death
King Ajātasattu had his father, King Bimbisāra, imprisoned in an iron cage that was extremely hot and steaming. He issued an order: "No one except my mother is to be allowed to see him."

(1) At that time, Queen Videhī placed the King's meal in a golden bowl, tucked it into her garment, and entered the iron cage. The King ate that meal and was sustained. Ajātasattu asked, "By what means is my father..."
618: When he heard the reason, he issued a further order: "Do not allow my mother to enter with food hidden in her bosom." (2) From then on, Queen Videhī placed food in her hair-knot and entered the iron cage. The King ate that food and sustained himself. When Ajātasattu heard this news, he issued a further order: "Do not allow my mother to enter with food in her hair-knot." (3) Then Queen Videhī placed food inside her golden slippers, closed them, and entered wearing the slippers. The poor King sustained himself with the food she brought inside the golden slippers. The foolish King Ajātasattu asked again, "By what means does my father survive?" and upon hearing the reason, issued a further order: "Do not allow my mother to enter wearing slippers." (4) From then on, Queen Videhī bathed in scented water, smeared her body with the four sweet foods (catumadhura), covered herself with an outer robe, and entered the iron cage. The poor King sustained himself by licking the queen's body with his tongue. The foolish King Ajātasattu asked again and, upon hearing the reason, issued a final order: "From this time on, do not allow my mother to enter the cage at all." Queen Videhī, unable to enter, stood near the door of the iron cage and lamented, "O Lord Bimbisāra, you yourself did not allow that foolish son Ajātasattu to be killed when he was young. You have nurtured your own enemy. Now, this is the last time I shall see you. From this time on, I will no longer have the chance to see you, Great King. If I have committed any fault, please forgive me, Lord King Bimbisāra."
619:
"...did not allow you to be killed when you were young; he raised his own enemy himself. Seeing you now is the last time I shall see you. From this time on, I will no longer have the chance to see the Great King. If I have any faults, please forgive me, my Lord, King Bimbisāra..." she said, weeping and lamenting, and returned to her palace.

## The Passing of King Bimbisāra
From that time on, the King had no food. The King sustained himself by walking back and forth on the meditation path, entering the bliss of the Fruition of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphalasamāpatti) which he had attained. Because he was constantly entering that Fruition attainment, the King's physical body remained exceedingly beautiful.

The foolish King Ajātasattu asked, "Sirs, by what means is my father surviving?" and heard the attendants' report: "Your Majesty, the Great King survives by walking back and forth on the meditation path; the Great King's physical body is even more beautiful than before." Hearing this, he thought, "Now I shall stop that father's walking back and forth," and he commanded the barbers: "Go and slice the soles of my father's feet with a razor, rub them with oil and salt, and roast them over glowing embers of khadira wood."

When King Bimbisāra saw the barbers, he thought, "Surely someone has made my son see the truth..."
620:
620
“It must have been done. (Therefore) these barbers have come to shave and groom my hair and beard,” he thought and considered.

The barbers approached the King, paid homage, and stood there. When the King asked, “Why have you come?” they explained the reason. Then the King granted permission, saying, “Do as your King desires.” The barbers said, “O Great King, please sit,” and after paying homage to the King, they said, “O Great King, we shall act according to the command of King Ajātasattu; please do not be angry with us. This act is not at all suitable for righteous kings like Your Majesty.” Saying this, they firmly held his ankles with their left hands and, holding sharp razors in their right hands, they gashed the soles of the King’s feet, smeared them with oil and salt, and roasted them with smokeless, glowing Khadira embers.

(The teachers say: In a past life, the King had walked upon the courtyard of a cetiya wearing shoes. He had also stepped on a mat intended for sitting with unwashed feet. This present suffering of being gashed with knives, rubbed with oil and salt, and roasted with Khadira embers is the consequence of that unwholesome deed.)

King Bimbisāra experienced intense and painful feelings. King Bimbisāra thought, “Oh, how wonderful are the virtues of the Buddha! Oh, how wonderful are the virtues of the Dhamma! Oh, how wonderful are the virtues of the Saṅgha!”
621:
621
(Without any anger), reflecting only on the virtues of the Triple Gem, he withered and dried up like a flower discarded on the courtyard of a cetiya. He was then reborn in the Cātumahārājika deva realm as a great Yakkha general named “Janavasabha,” an attendant of King Vessavaṇa.

(In this regard: Because he had been a Sotāpanna Ariya while being the leader of 110,000 brahmin householders in his life as King Bimbisāra, the name of that Yakkha became known as “Janavasabha.” It means: Jana = of the 110,000 brahmin householders; Vasabha = the leader.

One might ask: “Why was such a great Sotāpanna Ariya reborn in the lower class of Cātumahārājika Yakkhas?” The answer to this question was given by the Yakkha Janavasabha himself.

The explanation is: He had circled in Saṃsāra, passing away from the Cātumahārājika realm to be a king in the human world for seven lives, and passing away from the human world to be in the Cātumahārājika realm for seven lives. Because he had lived and been in that Cātumahārājika realm for seven consecutive lives in the past, even though he was now a Sotāpanna Ariya who had performed many meritorious deeds for the Triple Gem and was capable of being reborn in higher deva realms due to the power of those merits, he had a strong attachment (bhava-nikanti) to the Cātumahārājika realm because he had been there for a long time over many lives. Due to this strong attachment to existence (bhava-nikanti) in the Cātumahārājika realm, he was reborn in that very Cātumahārājika realm now. This was confessed and answered by the Yakkha Janavasabha himself in the Janavasabha Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya, Mahāvagga:—

Seven here and seven there,
Fourteen rounds in Saṃsāra.
I remember my former dwellings,
Where I have lived before.—
(From Dīgha Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā, 2, 231).)
622:
622
## Regret After Foolishness
On the very day his father King Bimbisāra passed away, a son named Udayabhadda was born to the queen of the foolish King Ajātasattu. Two letters—one announcing the birth of the son and the other announcing the death of his father, King Bimbisāra—arrived at the palace at the same time from the respective palace officials and prison officials.

The courtiers in attendance consulted and agreed, “It would be appropriate to present the letter about the birth of the son first,” and they presented that letter into King Ajātasattu’s hand. At the very moment he read the letter, a powerful love for his son arose in Ajātasattu, trembling his entire body and penetrating to the marrow of his bones. At that moment, he remembered his father’s kindness, thinking, “When I was born, a similar powerful love for his son must have arisen in my father’s mind as well.”

King Ajātasattu issued an urgent command, saying, “Friends, go! Release my father!” Then the ministers said, “O King, how can he be released now?” and they presented the other letter (about the father’s death) into the King’s hand. When King Ajātasattu learned of his father’s death, he wept bitterly and went to his mother, Queen Videhī, asking, “O Mother, when I was born, did such love for a son exist in my father’s mind?” Queen Videhī replied, “Foolish son, what are you saying? When you were young, an abscess developed on your finger.
623:
623
At that time, the nurses could not soothe you to stop crying. Finally, they took you and handed you over to your father, who was sitting in the hall of justice. Your father took your finger with the abscess and put it in his mouth. Due to the warmth of his mouth, the abscess burst right inside your father’s mouth. At that time, because your father loved you so dearly, he did not spit out the pus mixed with foul blood (fearing he might wake you if he did), but swallowed it instead. Your father loved you this much.” When she explained this in detail, King Ajātasattu wept and lamented bitterly and performed his father’s funeral rites.

## Devadatta Sending Assassins
Thereafter, Ven. Devadatta went to Prince Ajātasattu and said, “Great King, send men to kill the Monk Gotama.” Prince Ajātasattu instructed the men, “Friends, do as Ven. Devadatta says,” and sent them to Devadatta.

Then Devadatta commanded the (first) man, “Disciple, go; the Monk Gotama is staying in such-and-such a place. After killing that Monk Gotama, return by this path.”

On the path by which that man would return, he stationed (a second group of) two men, saying, “Kill the
624:
624
man coming by this path and return by such-and-such a path.”

On the path by which those two men would return, he stationed (a third group of) four men, saying, “Kill the two men coming by this path and return by such-and-such a path.”

On the path by which those four men would return, he stationed (a fourth group of) eight men, saying, “Kill the four men coming by this path and return by such-and-such a path.”

On the path by which those eight men would return, he stationed (a fifth group of) sixteen men, saying, “Kill the eight men coming by this path and return by such-and-such a path.”

## The Assassins Established in Sotāpatti
Then the first man, taking his sword and shield and slinging his bow and quiver, went to the Blessed One. Upon reaching the vicinity of the Blessed One, he stood with a stiffened body, terrified, trembling, and shaken.

The Blessed One, seeing the man, called out, “Disciple, come; do not be afraid.” Then the first man (his fear subsiding) placed his sword and shield aside, laid down his bow and quiver, approached the Blessed One, prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, and confessed his fault, asking for forgiveness. The Blessed One expressed his forgiveness for the disciple’s fault and,
625:
625
by preaching the gradual discourse such as the talk on generosity (dāna-kathā) and the talk on morality (sīla-kathā) which lead to the attainment of the Path and Fruit, that first man became a Sotāpanna Ariya and took the supramundane refuge (in that very sitting).

Then the Blessed One said to that (first) man, “Disciple, do not go by this path; go by such-and-such a path,” and sent him away by another route.

Then the (second group of) two men thought, “How is it? That one man is very late in coming,” and as they went to meet him, they saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a tree as before. They approached the Blessed One, bowed down in homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Blessed One preached the gradual discourse to those (second group of) two men, showed them the Four Noble Truths, and established them in the Fruit of Sotāpatti. Those two men also became Sotāpanna Ariyas like the first man and took the supramundane refuge.

Then the Blessed One said to those (second group of) two men, “Disciples, do not go by this path; go by such-and-such a path,” and sent them away by another route.

Then the (third group of) four men (Peyyāla).
626:
626
Then the (fourth group of) eight men (Peyyāla).

Then the (fifth group of) sixteen men thought, “How is it? Those eight men are very late in coming,” and as they went to meet them, they saw the Blessed One as before. They approached the Blessed One, bowed down in homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Blessed One also preached the gradual discourse to those (fifth group of) sixteen men, showed them the Four Noble Truths, and established them in the Fruit of Sotāpatti. When those sixteen men had taken the supramundane refuge as before, the Blessed One said to those sixteen men, “Disciples, do not go by this path (the path Devadatta directed); go by such-and-such a path,” and sent them away by another route.

Then that (first) man approached Ven. Devadatta and said to him, “Venerable Sir, I cannot kill that Blessed One. That Blessed One is of great power and majesty.” When he said this, Devadatta said, “Disciple, enough; do not kill the Monk Gotama. I myself will kill the Monk Gotama.”

## Causing the Blessed One to Bleed
One day, after having favored the assassins with the attainment of the Fruit of Sotāpatti, the Blessed One was walking back and forth in meditation in the shade of Gijjhakūṭa Hill.
627:
At that time, Devadatta climbed Gijjhakūṭa Mountain and, plotting to kill the Buddha with a rock, rolled down a massive boulder. Then, two mountain peaks spontaneously arose and caught the falling boulder. A splinter from that rock flew off and struck the Blessed One's foot, causing blood to flow.

Then the Blessed One looked up and said to Devadatta, "Vain man, with a mind of malice and intent to kill, you have caused blood to flow from the Tathāgata; thus, you have accumulated much demerit."

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks, "Monks, because Devadatta, with a mind of malice and intent to kill, has caused blood to flow from the Tathāgata, he has committed this first ānantariya-kamma (an immediate-retribution weightier kamma)."

The monks then escorted the Blessed One to the Maddakucchi Monastery. From that Maddakucchi Monastery, the Blessed One said, "I wish to go to Jīvaka's Mango Grove Monastery. Carry me to that monastery." The monks escorted the Blessed One to Jīvaka's Mango Grove Monastery as he had instructed.

The great physician Jīvaka, hearing of this matter, went to the Blessed One and, to treat the wound, applied a very potent medicine and bandaged it. He then addressed the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, I have a patient in the city to whom I must give medicine.
628:
I will go to that patient and then return. I wish for this medicine to remain as it is (without removing the bandage) until I return." Having said this, the physician Jīvaka went to the patient in the city, performed what was necessary for him, and when he returned near the time the city gates were to be closed, he was unable to reach the gates in time.

At that moment, a thought arose in the mind of the physician Jīvaka: "I have applied a potent medicine to the Blessed One's foot and bandaged it as I would for an ordinary person; thus, I have committed a grave oversight. This is the time when that bandage should be removed. If that bandage is not removed, the Blessed One will experience intense burning throughout the night." He was thus filled with anxiety. At that very moment, the Blessed One called the Elder Ānanda and said, "Dear Ānanda, the physician Jīvaka returned late and was unable to reach the gates in time. He is now anxious, thinking that this is the time to remove the bandage. Dear Ānanda, remove that bandage." The Elder Ānanda removed the bandage as the Blessed One had instructed. The wound disappeared and was healed, just as bark falls from a tree.

As soon as the city gates were opened, the physician Jīvaka came quickly to the Blessed One within the dawn and asked, "Venerable Sir, how is it? Does Your Reverence still feel any burning in the body?" The Blessed One replied, "Jīvaka, for me, at the foot of the Great Bodhi Tree,
629:
all burning has been extinguished." Having thus connected the sequence of words and wishing to preach the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

Gataddhino visokassa, vippamuttassa sabbadhi.
Sabbaganthapahīnassa, pariḷāho na vijjati.

Jīvaka, the donor of the monastery: For the Arahant who has completed the journey of saṃsāra, who is free from all sorrow, who is completely released from all things such as the aggregates (khandhas), and who has abandoned all ties (gantha), no burning of the heart or distress exists even in the slightest.

(There are two types of burning: (1) kāyika-pariḷāha = physical burning/pain, and (2) cetasika-pariḷāha = mental burning/distress. In the continuity of an Arahant, because physical weariness occurs in connection with cold, heat, etc., physical burning/suffering is not entirely extinguished. The physician Jīvaka asked with reference to this physical burning. However, the Blessed One, being the King of Dhamma and uniquely skilled in the method of preaching, wished to direct the teaching toward the extinction of mental burning; therefore, he answered, "Jīvaka, for the Arahant endowed with the aforementioned qualities, there is no burning or suffering at all." This means Jīvaka asked about the presence of physical burning, and the Blessed One answered regarding the absence of mental burning.)

At the conclusion of the discourse, many beings attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth.
630:
## The Monks Specially Guarding the Blessed One

At that time, many monks who heard the report that "Devadatta is making an effort to kill the Blessed One" surrounded the monastery where the Blessed One was staying in multiple layers. They remained walking back and forth on the ambulatory paths (caṅkama), performing the recitation of the Dhamma texts with loud and resonant voices to provide protection, defense, and security for the Blessed One.

The Blessed One, hearing that sound (though he already knew), questioned the Elder Ānanda. When the Elder Ānanda reported the matter, the Blessed One had those monks summoned before him and said:

"Monks, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that one could deprive a Tathāgata of life by the violence of another. Monks, Tathāgatas pass into Parinibbāna without the violence of others."

Having said this (following the same method preached to the Elder Moggallāna on pages 609-610), he explained that there are five types of teachers in the world whom disciples need to guard, and only those five types of teachers desire the protection of their disciples. As for himself, because he possessed pure virtue, pure livelihood, pure teaching of Dhamma, pure speech, and pure knowledge and vision, he declared himself to have pure virtue, pure livelihood,
631:
(etc.), and declared himself to have pure knowledge and vision. Therefore, he stated that there was no need for disciples to guard him, nor did he desire their protection. He reiterated that it is impossible for anyone to kill a Tathāgata through their own efforts and that Tathāgatas attain Parinibbāna without the violence of others. He then said to those monks:

"Monks, go back to your respective dwellings. Monks, Tathāgatas are not persons whose lives are secure only through the protection of others."

## Sending the Elephant Nālāgiri

(The account of sending the elephant Nālāgiri appears in the Vinaya Cullavagga Saṅghabhedaka-khandhaka and in the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka Commentary of the Asīti Nipāta. Here, it shall be written based on the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka Commentary.)

The Blessed One, having been treated by the physician Jīvaka, returned to normal health and resided as before, surrounded by a company of monks, wandering with the great splendor of a Buddha. At that time, seeing the Blessed One, Devadatta thought, "When one sees the physical body of the recluse Gotama, which has reached the pinnacle of beauty, no human being is able to approach him to destroy or kill him. However, King Ajātasattu's elephant Nālāgiri is fierce and kills people; it does not know the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha. Only that fierce elephant Nālāgiri will be able to kill the recluse Gotama." Having thus plotted, he went to King Ajātasattu
632:
and told this matter to King Ajātasattu.

King Ajātasattu agreed and, having summoned the mahout, issued an order: "Friend, tomorrow you must make the fierce elephant Nālāgiri drunk and release him early in the morning on the path where the recluse Gotama will travel." Devadatta also asked the mahout, "On other days, how much liquor does the elephant Nālāgiri drink?" When the mahout replied, "He drinks eight pots, venerable sir," Devadatta further said, "If that is so, tomorrow you must give the elephant Nālāgiri sixteen pots of liquor to drink and release him face-to-face on the path where the recluse Gotama will travel." The mahout agreed, saying, "Very well."

King Ajātasattu had a proclamation made throughout the city by beat of drum: "Tomorrow, the elephant Nālāgiri will be made drunk and released into the city. Let all the citizens perform their various duties early and let no one travel on the city streets."

Devadatta also descended from the palace, went to the elephant stable, called the elephant keepers, and said, "Friends, we are royal teachers who can make those of low rank high and those of high rank low. If you desire a promotion in your rank and position, tomorrow morning, give the elephant Nālāgiri sixteen pots of very strong liquor. Then, at the time the recluse Gotama enters the city, provoke him by prodding him with goads and spears to make him angry, break him out of the stable, and release him on the path where the recluse Gotama travels."
633:
633
“Release the elephant face-to-face and kill the ascetic Gotama,” he said. The mahouts agreed, saying, “Very well.”

That news spread throughout the entire city. The Buddhist lay disciples, who cherished the Triple Gem, heard the news and approached the Blessed One, saying, “Venerable Sir, Devadatta, being of one mind and one purpose with the King, will release the fierce elephant Nāḷāgiri on the path where You will travel tomorrow. We do not wish You to enter the city for alms tomorrow; please stay here at the Veḷuvana Monastery. We shall offer alms to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha within the monastery itself.”

The Blessed One did not say, “I will not enter for alms tomorrow.” Instead, He reflected: “Tomorrow, I shall tame the fierce elephant Nāḷāgiri and, by performing the miracle of instruction (*anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya*), I shall subdue the heretics. Without wandering for alms in Rājagaha, I shall depart from the city surrounded by the assembly of monks and return to Veḷuvana Monastery. At that time, the lay devotees of Rājagaha will bring many alms-bowls and vessels of food to the monastery.”

* The Burmese word 'Pyatiha' (miracle) originates from the Pali word 'Pāṭihāriya'. It is called Pāṭihāriya because it occurs by subduing and removing opposing factors. There are three types of Pāṭihāriya: (1) Ādesanā-pāṭihāriya = the miracle of knowing and declaring the thoughts of others; (2) Iddhi-pāṭihāriya = the miracle of manifesting various psychic forms; (3) Anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya = the miracle of constant preaching and instruction by the Buddha and His disciples. Among these, the third, Anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya, is intended here. It is the practice of Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna to preach and instruct after manifesting psychic powers. It is the practice of Venerable Sāriputta to preach and instruct after declaring the thoughts of others. This is a special point to be noted.
634:
634
Knowing this, for this very reason, He accepted the invitation of those lay disciples. 

Those lay disciples, knowing well that the Blessed One had accepted, consulted with one another, saying, “We shall bring alms-bowls and vessels of food and offer alms at the monastery itself,” and then they departed.

The Blessed One, after preaching the Dhamma to the monks during the first watch of the night, and answering the questions asked by devas and brahmas during the middle watch, divided the last watch into three parts. In the first part, He lay down on His right side in the lion’s posture. In the second part, He entered the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (*arahatta-phala-samāpatti*). In the third part, He entered the attainment of great compassion (*mahā-karuṇā-samāpatti*). Rising from that attainment, He surveyed the beings who were ready to be liberated and saw clearly that eighty-four thousand beings would realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation upon the taming of the elephant Nāḷāgiri. When the dawn broke and it became light, He performed His morning ablutions and called Venerable Ānanda, saying, “Dear Ānanda, tell all the monks residing in the eighteen great monasteries around Rājagaha to enter the city of Rājagaha together with the Buddha today.”

Venerable Ānanda did as the Blessed One commanded. All the monks then assembled at the Veḷuvana Monastery.
635:
635
The Blessed One entered the city of Rājagaha surrounded by a great number of monks.

At that time, the mahouts acted according to the instructions given by King Ajātasattu and Devadatta. A very large crowd of people gathered. In that assembly, the people with faith said:

“Today, there will be a battle between the Great Elephant who is the Buddha and the great animal elephant Nāḷāgiri. We shall see the beautiful taming of the animal elephant Nāḷāgiri through the incomparable majesty of the Buddha-Elephant.”

Saying thus, they climbed onto the roofs of gabled houses, flat-roofed houses, and other buildings, and waited in readiness. However, the heretics who lacked faith said:

“This elephant Nāḷāgiri is fierce and a killer of men; he knows nothing of the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Today, this elephant Nāḷāgiri will destroy the golden-hued, radiant body of the ascetic Gotama and end his life. Today, we shall see the back of our enemy.”

Saying thus, they also waited in readiness on the gabled houses and so on.

When the elephant Nāḷāgiri saw the Blessed One approaching, he terrified the people, broke and destroyed houses, crushed carts to pieces, and with his trunk raised, he charged.
636:
636
With ears and tail erect, looming like a great mountain, he ran straight toward where the Blessed One was.

Seeing the elephant Nāḷāgiri running toward them, the monks said to the Blessed One, “Exalted Buddha, this fierce, man-killing elephant Nāḷāgiri is coming this way. This elephant knows nothing of the virtues of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. May the Exalted Buddha please turn away; may the Well-Spoken One please turn away.” Then the Blessed One said to the monks, “Monks, do not be afraid. I am capable of taming the elephant Nāḷāgiri.”

Then Venerable Sāriputta entreated the Blessed One, saying, “Exalted Buddha, whatever matter arises for a father is the responsibility of the eldest son. Let me be the one to tame this elephant Nāḷāgiri.” The Blessed One then forbade Venerable Sāriputta, saying, “Dear Sāriputta, the power of a Buddha is one thing; the power of a disciple is another. You, dear son, stay still.” In this same manner, most of the eighty great disciples made the same request. The Blessed One refused them all and forbade them.

## Venerable Ānanda’s Love Willing to Sacrifice His Life

Then, Venerable Ānanda, out of his great love for the Blessed One, could no longer remain patient. Thinking, “Let this elephant Nāḷāgiri first...
637:
637
...trample me to death,” he sacrificed his life for the Buddha, stepped forward, and stood in front of the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One said to Venerable Ānanda, “Ānanda, move aside. Do not stand in front of the Buddha.” Venerable Ānanda replied, “Exalted Buddha, this elephant Nāḷāgiri is extremely fierce; he kills men and is like the fire that destroys the world. Let him first trample me to death and only then come to You.” Although the Blessed One forbade him three times, he remained standing and did not move away. Finally, the Blessed One moved Venerable Ānanda by psychic power and placed him among the monks.

## The Situation of a Mother with Her Child

At that moment, a woman with a child saw the elephant Nāḷāgiri and, fearing death, ran away. In her flight, she dropped the young child she was carrying in her arms between the elephant Nāḷāgiri and the Blessed One and fled.

The elephant Nāḷāgiri, unable to catch the woman, turned back and moved toward the child. Then the child cried out loudly. The Blessed One radiated specific loving-kindness (*odissaka-mettā*) toward the elephant Nāḷāgiri and, with the very sweet voice of a Brahma, called out:

“O Nāḷāgiri, they did not give you sixteen pots of liquor to make you drunk so that you would...
638:
638
...seize others. Indeed, they did it so that you would seize and kill Me. Do not wander about troubling innocent travelers. Come straight to this place where I am.”

## The Power of the Buddha’s Majesty

As soon as the fierce elephant Nāḷāgiri heard the very sweet words of the Blessed One, he opened both eyes wide and, beholding the glory of the Buddha’s physical form, he was struck with awe and religious emotion (*saṃvega*). Due to the power of the Buddha’s majesty, his drunkenness vanished. Dropping his trunk and twitching his ears, he approached the Blessed One and prostrated at His feet.

Then the Blessed One said to the elephant Nāḷāgiri, “Nāḷāgiri, you are an animal elephant; I am the Elephant King who is the Buddha. From this time forth, do not be fierce, cruel, or a killer of men. Strive to achieve a mind associated with loving-kindness toward all beings.” Extending His right hand, He stroked the elephant’s forehead and said:

*Mā kuñjara nāgamāsado,*
*Dukkhaṃ hi kuñjara nāgamāsado.*
*Na hi nāgahatassa kuñjara,*
*Sugati hoti ito paraṃ yato.*

O animal elephant named Nāḷāgiri! Do not approach the Elephant King, who is I the Buddha who performs no evil, with the intention to kill. O animal elephant named Nāḷāgiri! Approaching the Buddha-Nāga with the intention to kill is indeed an evil that causes suffering. Truly, that word is true. O animal elephant named Nāḷāgiri! For one who has the intention to harm or kill the Buddha-Nāga, when he...
639:
639
...passes away from this present life to the next world, a happy destination (*sugati*) in the human or celestial realms is not possible in the slightest.

*Mā ca mado mā ca pamādo,*
*Na hi pamattā sugatiṃ vajanti te.*
*Tvaññeva tathā karissasi,*
*Yena tvaṃ sugatiṃ gamissasi.*

O animal elephant named Nāḷāgiri! Do not be intoxicated with pride and wickedness, thinking 'It is I'. Do not be negligent of the ten virtues. For the reason is: those people who are negligent and careless regarding the ten noble virtues do not reach a happy destination in the human or celestial realms. By whatever meritorious deed you shall reach a happy destination in the human or celestial realms, you yourself must perform that very merit.
640:
(=It means that only by performing meritorious deeds will you reach a happy destination).

Thus, the Buddha preached the Dhamma. The entire body of the elephant king Nālāgiri was suffused with a continuous thrill of joy (pīti). Had he not been an animal, he would have attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) right then and there.

Upon witnessing this miracle, the multitude of people shouted their acclaim, making the air ring with echoes. They clapped their hands and, in great delight, threw down various ornaments as rewards. These ornaments almost covered the entire body of the elephant. From that time onwards, the elephant Nālāgiri became known as "Dhanapāla" (Guardian of Wealth). Notably, at the assembly where the elephant Dhanapāla was tamed, eighty-four thousand beings drank the nectar of the Dhamma.

The Blessed One established the elephant king Dhanapāla in the Five Precepts. The elephant king tenderly took up dust from the Blessed One's feet with his trunk, sprinkled it upon his head, and retreated while kneeling. Standing at a place where he could still see the Blessed One for the last time, he paid respectful homage and entered his stable. From that time on, he became an exceptionally gentle and noble elephant, never harming anyone for the rest of his life.

As the Blessed One's wish was fulfilled, he made an aspiration: "May the heaps of ornaments and wealth return to the hands of their respective owners who threw them." Then, he reflected: "Today, I have performed a great miracle."
641:
Having performed this miracle, the Buddha reflected: "(Therefore), it is no longer appropriate to wander for alms within this city of Rājagaha." Having subdued the heretics, like a great king who has won a battle, he departed from Rājagaha surrounded by the community of monks and returned to the Veluvana Monastery. The townspeople brought many kinds of food, drinks, and snacks to the Veluvana Monastery and performed a great act of dana. At that time, the people sang this song of joy:

"Some tame with sticks, with hooks, and with whips;
But the Great Sage tamed the elephant without stick or weapon."

(Eke = some teachers tame elephants, horses, buffaloes, and oxen; Daṇḍena = with sticks or spiked rods; Aṅkusehi = with spears or hooks; Kasāhi ca = and with whips; Damayanti = they tame them through violent means such as beating and stabbing. Mahesinā = but the Buddha, the Lord of the Three Worlds; Adaṇḍena = without spiked rods or sticks; Asatthena = without any weapons of torture or killing; Nāgo = the elephant king Nālāgiri; Danto = was tamed by sprinkling the cool water of loving-kindness, causing all violence to vanish.)

They sang this verse with great joy.

## The Decline of Devadatta’s Gains
At that time, the multitude of people shouted and criticized loudly, saying: "It was Devadatta who caused King Bimbisāra to be killed; it was Devadatta who sent the assassins; it was he who rolled down the great rock. And now, it is he
642:
who has caused the elephant Nālāgiri to be released. King Ajātasattu wanders about making such a wicked person his companion and teacher."

King Ajātasattu, hearing the words of blame and criticism from the multitude, stopped the five hundred pots of rice that were regularly provided for Devadatta and no longer went to visit him. The townspeople also ceased to offer even a spoonful of alms-food to Devadatta when he came to their houses for alms.

## Requesting the Five Practices
As Devadatta’s gains and honors decreased day by day, he wished to sustain his life by performing a feat of wonder. He went to the Blessed One and said:

"Venerable Sir, I make this request:
(1) Let all monks be forest-dwellers for as long as they live; may any monk who stays in a village monastery be guilty of an offense.
(2) Let all monks be alms-food eaters only for as long as they live; may any monk who accepts an invitation to a meal from lay donors be guilty of an offense.
(3) Let all monks be rag-robe wearers only for as long as they live; may any monk who accepts and enjoys robes offered by lay donors be guilty of an offense.
643:
(4) Let all monks be tree-root dwellers only for as long as they live; may any monk who approaches a roofed monastery be guilty of an offense.
(5) Let all monks not eat fish or meat for as long as they live; may any monk who eats fish or meat be guilty of an offense."

He submitted these five points as a formal request.

Then the Blessed One said: "Enough, Devadatta. (1) Let him who wishes be a forest-dweller; let him who wishes stay in a village monastery.
