(2) Let him who wishes be an alms-food eater; let him who wishes accept an invitation to a meal from lay donors. (3) Let him who wishes be a rag-robe wearer; let him who wishes accept and wear robes offered by lay donors. (4) Devadatta, I have already allowed for eight months a dwelling at the foot of a tree. (5) I have already allowed the consumption of fish and meat that is pure in three aspects—that is, not seen, not heard, and not suspected [to have been killed specifically for the monk]."

(A special note here: Even when Devadatta made these five requests, the Blessed One knew, "This Devadatta requests this because he wishes to cause a schism in the Sangha." If He were to allow these five points, it would become an obstacle to the Path and Fruit for many noble sons. Therefore, He said, "Enough, Devadatta,"
644:
and refused him, saying, "(1) Let him who wishes be a forest-dweller," and so on.

In this matter, having understood the Blessed One's intention, a noble son should know what is suitable and appropriate for himself. The Blessed One's intention is as follows:

(a) A monk who, being very strong in both physical and intellectual power, would reach the Path and Fruit if he stays in the forest and develops his meditation.
(b) A monk who, having little physical strength, cannot stay in the forest but would reach the Path and Fruit only if he stays in a village monastery and develops his meditation.
(c) A monk who, being physically strong and endowed with patience, would reach the Path and Fruit whether he stays in the forest or in a village monastery.
(d) A monk who, though he practices meditation while staying in either the forest or a village monastery, will not attain the Path and Fruit in this life (a padaparama individual).
There are these four types of monks.

Among these four, the Blessed One wished for the monk described in (a) to stay only in the forest. This forest dwelling is suitable for that monk, and by his staying there, his disciples would also follow his example and be eager to stay in the forest.

The Blessed One wished for the monk described in (b) to stay in a village monastery.

The Blessed One wished for the monk described in (c) to stay only in the forest. This forest dwelling is suitable for that monk, and his disciples would also follow his example and be eager to stay in the forest.

The Blessed One also wished for the monk described in (d) (the padaparama) to stay only in the forest. For this monk, dwelling in the forest, observing the dhutaṅga practices, and practicing meditation
645:
can serve as a supporting condition (upanissaya) for attaining the Path and Fruit in future lives. Furthermore, his disciples would follow their teacher's example and be eager to stay in the forest.

Thus, referring to the monk described in (b), who has little physical strength and can only reach the Path and Fruit by staying in a village monastery, the Blessed One said, "(1) Let him who wishes stay in a village monastery." This monk, as it were, opens the door for other monks to stay in village monasteries.

If the Blessed One had accepted Devadatta's request, it would have been like cutting off the Noble Path for two types of monks: (1) the monk described in (b) who has little physical strength, and (2) the monk who stayed in the forest when young but, when old or when his elements are disturbed by phlegm, bile, or wind, can no longer stay in the forest and must stay in a village monastery to reach the Path and Fruit. For such monks, the Fruit of Arahantship would become unattainable. For these and other reasons, He did not accept Devadatta's request.)

## Devadatta’s Effort to Cause a Schism
Then Devadatta, with a joyful and uplifted mind thinking, "The Blessed One does not allow these five points," rose from his seat with his followers—Kokālika, Katamoraka Tissaka (the son of Queen Khaṇḍā), and Samuddadatta—paid homage to the Blessed One, and departed respectfully. (In this context, the monk Kokālika, the monk Katamoraka Tissaka, and the monk Samuddadatta were Devadatta's chief confidants.)
646:
Thereafter, Devadatta entered the city of Rājagaha with his followers and spread propaganda among the people, saying that although they had requested the five points—which lead to fewness of wishes and other benefits—by explaining the reasons, the Ascetic Gotama did not allow them, and that they themselves would undertake and practice those five points.

Among those people, those who lacked faith and wisdom praised Devadatta and his followers but criticized the Blessed One. However, those people endowed with faith and wisdom criticized and blamed Devadatta, saying, "Why does Devadatta strive to cause a schism in the Sangha and destroy the authority of the Blessed One?" The monks who heard the words of these people likewise criticized and blamed him, and then reported the matter to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, on account of the matter reported by those monks, had the Sangha assembled and, in the presence of the entire assembly, asked Devadatta: "Devadatta, is it true that you are striving to cause a schism in the Sangha and destroy its authority?" When Devadatta replied, "It is true, Blessed One,"

"Devadatta, it is not proper. Do not delight in a schism in the Sangha. Devadatta, causing a schism in the Sangha is a very grave matter. Devadatta, he who causes a schism in a harmonious Sangha produces demerit that lasts for an entire aeon (kappa) and is boiled in hell for an entire aeon.

Devadatta, he who brings about harmony in a divided Sangha produces great merit."
647:
“...to enjoy the celestial realms for an entire aeon. Devadatta, it is not proper; do not delight in the schism of the Saṅgha. Devadatta, causing a schism in the Saṅgha is a very grave matter.”

Thus, the Buddha gave him a profound admonition. Even though the Buddha had admonished him so deeply, Devadatta did not abandon his plan to cause a schism in the Saṅgha. After making the preliminary arrangements for the schism, he decided and resolved on the following day, “Today, I will certainly perform the Uposatha and Saṅghakamma separately.” That morning, he approached the Venerable Ānanda, who had entered the city of Rājagaha for alms, and said, “Friend Ānanda, from this day forth, I will perform the Uposatha and Saṅghakamma separately from the Buddha and separately from the Saṅgha (who follow the Buddha’s instructions).”

When the Venerable Ānanda reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha uttered this Udāna verse:

Sukaraṃ sādhunā sādhu,
sādhu pāpena dukkaraṃ.
Pāpaṃ pāpena sukaraṃ,
pāpamariyehi dukkaraṃ.

Good is easy for the good to do.
Good is difficult for the evil to do.
Evil is easy for the evil to do.
Evil is difficult for the Noble Ones to do.
648:
## Devadatta Causes a Schism in the Saṅgha

Then, on that Uposatha day, Devadatta rose from his seat in the assembly of the Saṅgha and announced, “Although we requested five points that would lead to fewness of wishes and other benefits, the ascetic Gotama did not permit them. We, however, shall undertake and practice these five points. Let those who favor these five points take a voting slip.” When he had the voting slips taken, five hundred monks from the Vajjī country residing in Vesālī, who were young in years and unskilled in the Vinaya, thinking, “This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the Teacher’s Dispensation,” took the voting slips. Then Devadatta, having caused a schism in the Saṅgha, took those five hundred monks and departed for Gayāsīsa.

## The Service of the Two Chief Disciples

Then the two great elders, Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna (the Chief Disciples), went to the Buddha. The Venerable Sāriputta informed him, “Exalted Buddha, Devadatta has caused a schism in the Saṅgha and has gone to Gayāsīsa taking five hundred monks with him.” The Buddha lamented, “Sāriputta, does not even compassion arise in your hearts for those young monks?” and urged them, “Sāriputta, go before those young monks are ruined and come to harm.” Saying, “Very well, Exalted Buddha,” the two great elders, Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, accepted the Buddha’s request, rose from their seats, and
649:
after paying respectful homage to the Buddha, they departed for Gayāsīsa.

## The Concern of a Young Monk

At that time, a certain monk stood weeping near the Buddha. The Buddha asked him, “Monk, why are you weeping?” The young monk replied, “Exalted Buddha, the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who are the Chief Disciples of the Exalted Lord, have also taken a liking to Devadatta’s teaching and have followed him to Devadatta’s place.” The Buddha explained to that monk, “Monk, there is no possibility at all that Sāriputta and Moggallāna would take a liking to Devadatta’s teaching. In fact, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have gone there to make those five hundred young monks who followed Devadatta understand (to gain the right view).”

At that time, Devadatta was sitting and preaching to a large following. Seeing the two Elders Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna coming from afar, Devadatta said to his following of young monks, “Monks, look! I have preached the Dhamma very well. Even Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the Chief Disciples of the ascetic Gotama, have taken a liking to my teaching and have come to join me.”

When Devadatta spoke thus, the monk Kokālika (one of the leaders in their group) said to Devadatta,
650:
“Friend Devadatta, do not be intimate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Sāriputta and Moggallāna are people of evil desires and are followers of those who lead them into evil desires.” Devadatta explained to the monk Kokālika, “Friend, you should not say such a thing. Because the coming of Sāriputta and Moggallāna is due to their liking my teaching, it is a good coming.”

When the two great Elders Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna arrived nearby, Devadatta said to Venerable Sāriputta, “Friend Sāriputta, come, sit here,” and invited him to sit on half of his seat. Saying, “Enough, friend,” Venerable Sāriputta took another seat and sat in a suitable place. Venerable Mahāmoggallāna also took another seat and sat in a suitable place. Then Devadatta, having preached the Dhamma to the monks for a great part of the night (throughout the three watches of the night), urged the Venerable Elder Sāriputta:

“Friend Sāriputta, the Saṅgha of monks is free from sloth and torpor. Friend Sāriputta, please preach the Dhamma to the monks. My back is very tired; I will stretch my back (I will lie down for a while).”

(His manner of speaking was an imitation of the Buddha; he was mimicking the Buddha.)

When Venerable Sāriputta replied, “Very well, friend,” Devadatta folded his double-layered robe (dukuṭa)
651:
into four, spread it out, and lay down on his right side. Being exhausted, and lacking mindfulness and clear comprehension, Devadatta fell asleep in an instant.

Then, Venerable Sāriputta, preceded by the miracle of mind-reading (ādesanā-pāṭihāriya), which is the accurate pointing out of the state of others' minds, admonished and restrained those five hundred young monks with the miracle of instruction (anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya), saying, “Abandon this and this quality; develop this and this quality.” The Elder Mahāmoggallāna, preceded by the miracle of psychic power (iddhi-pāṭihāriya), which is the manifestation of supernatural powers, admonished and restrained them with the miracle of instruction (anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya), saying, “Abandon this and this quality; develop this and this quality.” Consequently, those five hundred young monks attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) right there and became Noble Stream-enterers (sotāpanna ariyas).

(In this context, the three kinds of miracles are to be noted in brief: That which can dispel opposing unwholesome states is called pāṭihāriya in Pali, and prāṭihā in Burmese. These miracles are: (1) Ādesanā-pāṭihāriya = dispelling doubt in the Dispensation by accurately pointing out the state of another's mind, saying, “Your mind is in such and such a state”; (2) Iddhi-pāṭihāriya = dispelling doubt in the Dispensation by manifesting psychic forms; (3) Anusāsanī-pāṭihāriya = dispelling opposing defilements such as greed by teaching and admonishing what qualities to abandon and what qualities to develop, saying, “Abandon this and this group of qualities; develop this and this group of qualities.” Thus, there are three kinds of miracles.

Among them, admonishing with the miracle of instruction preceded by the miracle of psychic power was the practice of
652:
Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. (This means that if Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was to guide someone, he usually first made that person free from doubt in the Dispensation through the miracle of psychic power, and only then taught and admonished them on what to abandon and what to develop through the miracle of instruction.)

Admonishing with the miracle of instruction preceded by the miracle of mind-reading was the practice of Venerable Sāriputta. (This means that if Venerable Sāriputta was to guide someone, he usually first made that person free from doubt in the Dispensation through the miracle of mind-reading, accurately pointing out the state of that person's mind, and only then taught and admonished them on what to abandon and what to develop through the miracle of instruction.)

The Exalted Buddha himself, according to the inclination and temperament of the being, sometimes admonished with the miracle of instruction preceded by the miracle of mind-reading, and sometimes guided them with the miracle of instruction preceded by the miracle of psychic power. He used both methods. This is a brief note on the three miracles.)

After the five hundred young monks had become Noble Stream-enterers, Venerable Sāriputta called to them, “Friends, we shall go to the Buddha. Let any monk who delights in the Buddha’s Dhamma come with us.” Then, the two great Elders Sāriputta and Mahāmoggallāna took the five hundred young monks with them and, traveling through the air by means of meditative absorption (jhāna), went to the Veluvana Monastery.
653:
## Devadatta Vomits Blood

After the two great Chief Disciples had departed taking the five hundred young monks with them, the group leader Kokālika said, “Devadatta, get up! Sāriputta and Moggallāna have taken those young monks away. Did I not tell you, ‘Friend Devadatta, do not be intimate with Sāriputta and Moggallāna; Sāriputta and Moggallāna are people of evil desires and are followers of those who lead them into evil desires’?” and he struck Devadatta in the chest with his knee to wake him. At that moment, hot blood vomited out from Devadatta’s mouth right there.

## Preaching Many Jātaka Stories

The monks residing at the Veluvana Monastery saw Venerable Sāriputta arriving through the air, surrounded by the five hundred young monks, and reported to the Buddha, “Exalted Buddha, when Venerable Sāriputta departed, he went with only Venerable Mahāmoggallāna as his companion. Now, upon his return, he arrives surrounded by many followers, which is very beautiful.” The Buddha said, “Monks, Sāriputta is not beautiful only now; in the past, when he was an animal, my eldest son was also beautiful when he returned to my presence,” and he preached the Lakkhana-miga Jātaka (Ekaka Nipāta, 2-Sīlavagga) beginning with “Hoti sīlavataṃ attho.”

Again, the monks said, “Exalted Buddha, Devadatta, having the two Chief Disciples on his left and right, [imitated] the Buddha...”
654:
654

When the monks reported, "Lord, Devadatta is trying to imitate the Buddha, thinking he will preach the Dhamma with grace," the Buddha said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past as well, Devadatta endeavored to imitate me but was unable to do so." He then related the Vīraka Jātaka (No. 204, Natandhaḷha Vagga, Duka Nipāta), beginning with the verse "Api vīraka passesi."

On subsequent days, based on similar appropriate conversations, he preached other Jātakas such as the Kandagalaka Jātaka (No. 210, Natandhaḷha Vagga, Duka Nipāta), beginning with "Acari vatāyaṃ vitudaṃ vanāni."

Again, based on the topic that "Devadatta is ungrateful," he preached the Sakuṇa Jātaka (No. 308, Kāliṅga Vagga, Catukka Nipāta), beginning with "Akaramhasa te kiccaṃ."

Furthermore, regarding Devadatta's attempts to kill the Buddha, he preached the Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka (No. 21, Kuruṅga Vagga, Ekaka Nipāta), beginning with "Ñātametaṃ kuruṅgassa."

On another occasion, when many monks were discussing how "Devadatta has fallen away and lost both his gains and honors and his monkhood," the Buddha said, "Monks, not only now has Devadatta fallen and suffered loss; in the past too, he has fallen and suffered loss." He then preached the Ubhatobhaṭṭha Jātaka (No. 139, Asampadāna Vagga, Ekaka Nipāta), beginning with "Akkhi bhinnā paṭo naṭṭho."
655:
655

(Note: To briefly list the Jātakas preached concerning Devadatta as much as possible:

In the Ekaka Nipāta: Serivavāṇija, Lakkhaṇa, Kuruṅgamiga, Vānarinda, Tayodhamma, Sīlava, Saccaṅkira, Sigāla, Dummedha, Asampadāna, Ubhatobhaṭṭha, Virocana, and Sañjīva Jātakas.

In the Duka Nipāta: Vinīlaka, Dubbhiyamakkaṭa, Maṇicora, Vīraka, Kuruṅgamiga, Saṃsumāra, Kandagalaka, Dhammadhaja, Kāsāva, Cūḷanandiya, Kumbhīla, Upāhana, Mahāpingala, Sabbadāṭhi, and Guttila Jātakas.

In the Sattaka Nipāta: Kapi and Parantapa Jātakas.

These are the Jātakas. If one desires more detail, one should look into the 550 Jātaka stories.)
656:
656

## The Last Days of Devadatta

Thus, while the Buddha was residing in Rājagaha, he preached many past Jātaka stories concerning Devadatta. Later, he journeyed from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī and was staying at the Jetavana Monastery.

Devadatta, having been ill for nine months and wishing to see the Buddha in his final moments, pleaded with his disciples, "I wish to see my elder brother, the Buddha. Please take me so that I may behold him." When his disciples said, "When you were healthy and strong, you wandered about as a great enemy of the Buddha; we do not dare to take you to where he is," Devadatta replied, "Disciples, do not let me perish. In truth, it was only I who harbored malice toward the Buddha. The Buddha, however, does not have even a hair's breadth of malice toward me. Indeed, that elder brother of mine—

Vadhake Devadattamhi, core Aṅgulimālake.
Dhanapāle Rāhule ca, sabbattha samamānaso.

—is of equal mind toward all: toward (me) Devadatta, the brother-in-law who would kill him; toward the robber Aṅgulimāla who wore a garland of a thousand fingers; toward the fierce elephant Dhanapāla (also known as Nāḷāgiri) in his later moments; and toward his own dear son Rāhula."
657:
657

Toward all beings entirely, he possesses a mind that desires their welfare equally.

"Please take me so that I may behold my elder brother, the Buddha," he pleaded repeatedly. Then, his disciples carried Devadatta on a small litter and set out from Rājagaha toward Sāvatthī, where the Buddha was staying.

Upon hearing the news that Devadatta was coming, the monks informed the Buddha, "Exalted Buddha, it is said that Devadatta is coming to behold you." The Buddha told the monks, "Monks, Devadatta will never again have the opportunity to behold me with that very physical body in this life."

(From the time Devadatta requested the five points, he could no longer have the opportunity to behold the Buddha. This is the natural law.)

To the ordinary monks, it seemed that Devadatta was heading toward Sāvatthī to pay respects, and the Buddha remained there without moving elsewhere, yet he maintained, "Devadatta will by no means have the chance to behold me with this body." These two points created a state of suspense and uncertainty. Therefore, as Devadatta reached each stage of his journey, the monks repeatedly reported, "Exalted Buddha, Devadatta has now arrived at such-and-such a place; he has now arrived at such-and-such a place." Every time the monks reported this, the Buddha firmly stated, "Let him do as he wishes;
658:
658

Devadatta will by no means have the opportunity to behold me."

When the monks repeatedly reported, "Exalted Buddha, Devadatta has arrived about one yojana from Sāvatthī; he has arrived about half a yojana away; he has arrived about one gāvuta away; he has arrived near the pond close to the Jetavana Monastery," the Buddha gave his final word, "Even if he enters the Jetavana Monastery, Devadatta will never have the opportunity to behold me."

## Devadatta being Swallowed by the Earth

The disciples carrying Devadatta set the litter down on the bank of the pond near the Jetavana Monastery and went down into the pond to bathe. Devadatta rose from the litter and sat with both feet placed on the ground. His feet began to sink into the earth as if being pulled down. Devadatta sank into the earth gradually—up to his ankles, his knees, his waist, his chest, and his neck. Just as his jaw was about to sink into the earth, he recited this verse:

Imehi aṭṭhīhi tamaggapuggalaṃ,
Devātidevaṃ naradammasārathiṃ.
Samantacakkhuṃ satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ,
Vāṇehi buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ upemi.

"As my time of death approaches, I, Devadatta, with these bones and with this remaining life, go for refuge to that Buddha, the Supreme Person in the universe, the God of gods (Visuddhideva) who is superior to conventional gods (Sammuitideva) and gods by birth (Upapattideva), the Charioteer of men to be tamed who disciplines beings—humans, devas, and brahmas—by giving them the nectar of the Dhamma, the All-Seeing One endowed with the great Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), and the one endowed with the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa-lakkhaṇa) which are exceedingly beautiful to behold due to countless merits. With a mind that is sublime, associated with knowledge, and full of great wholesome joy, I approach and take refuge in him."
659:
659

It was because he foresaw this final act of taking refuge that the Buddha granted Devadatta ordination as a monk. If Devadatta had not become a monk, as a layman he would certainly have committed the extremely grave crime of wounding the Buddha (Lohituppādaka Anantariya-kamma), and he would definitely have been unable to perform this kind of wholesome deed which serves as a cause for liberation from the cycle of saṃsāra in the future.

Furthermore, it should be noted that although the Buddha knew that after ordaining, Devadatta would commit the two extremely grave crimes of wounding the Buddha and causing a schism in the Sangha (Saṅghabhedaka Anantariya-kamma), he also saw that Devadatta would be able to perform this wholesome deed that leads to liberation from saṃsāra. Therefore, the Buddha
660:
660

granted him ordination. Indeed, because of this wholesome deed, one hundred thousand eons from this present world-cycle, Devadatta will become a Paccekabuddha named Aṭṭhissara.

## Devadatta’s Suffering in the Avīci Hell

After reciting the aforementioned verse, Devadatta sank into the earth and was reborn in the Great Avīci Hell. As if it were said, "Because he offended the unshakable Buddha, let him be cooked in the unshakable hell," in the Great Avīci Hell, which is one hundred yojanas wide, Devadatta's body is one hundred yojanas tall. His head is submerged up to the ears in the upper iron cauldron. His two feet are submerged up to the ankles in the glowing red iron ground below. He stands facing the east while being cooked. One large iron stake, as thick as a palmyra trunk, comes out from the western wall of the hell-pot, pierces through the middle of Devadatta's back, comes out through his chest, and enters the eastern wall. Another large iron stake comes out from the southern wall, pierces through his right side, comes out through his left side, and enters the northern wall. Another large iron stake comes out from the upper iron roof (iron cauldron) of the hell-pot, pierces straight through the crown of his head, comes out through his lower orifice, and enters the iron ground at the bottom of the hell-pot. In this manner, Devadatta suffers the agony of being cooked without being able to move in the Great Avīci Hell.

(The Avīci Hell is so named because: (1) there is no interval between the beings, as it is crowded and packed; (2) there is no interval between the hell-fires, as they are continuous and pervasive; (3) there is no interval in the suffering of the beings, as it occurs at every moment.)
661:
...remained continuously and incessantly. Because there is no interval between these three—(1) the hell-being, (2) the flames of hellfire, and (3) the painful suffering—that hell is called the Great Avīci Hell.

## The Preaching of Jātaka Stories After Devadatta was Swallowed by the Earth

When Devadatta was thus swallowed by the earth, the monks started a conversation: "Even though he traveled with great difficulty to this place forty-five leagues away, Devadatta was swallowed by the earth without ever getting the chance to pay homage to the Blessed One."

The Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has been swallowed by the earth for offending me; he was swallowed by the earth in the past as well." He then related the Sīlavanāga Jātaka (Jātaka 72, Sīlavanāga Jātaka, Ekakanipāta, Varuṇavagga), telling how in the life when He was the Bodhisatta Elephant King (Sīlava), He carried a man who had lost his way in the forest on His back to safety. Yet, that man returned to the Bodhisatta Elephant King three times, cutting off the tips of the tusks the first time, the middle part the second time, and the base of the tusks the third time. To show how the earth swallowed that ungrateful hunter, the Bodhisatta's enemy, as soon as he passed out of the Elephant King's sight, the Buddha preached the Jātaka beginning with the verse "Akataññussa posassa."

Later, when the monks again raised a similar conversation, the Buddha preached the Khantivādī Jātaka (Jātaka 313, Catukkanipāta, Pucimandavagga) to show how Devadatta, as King Kalābu, was swallowed by the earth for offending the Bodhisatta when He was the ascetic Khantivādī. He also preached the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka (Jātaka 358, Pañcakanipāta, Maṇikuṇḍalavagga) to show how Devadatta, as King Mahāpatāpa, was swallowed by the earth for offending the Bodhisatta when He was the young prince Cūḷadhammapāla.
662:
...to show how Devadatta, as King Mahāpatāpa, was swallowed by the earth for offending the Bodhisatta when He was the young prince Cūḷadhammapāla.

After Devadatta was swallowed by the earth, the people were filled with joy. They raised banners and flags, planted banana trees, and set out full water pots, celebrating a great festival, saying, "It is a great gain for us!" When the monks reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that people rejoice at Devadatta's passing; they rejoiced in the past as well." He then preached the Mahāpiṅgala Jātaka (Jātaka 240, Dukanipāta, Upāhanavagga), beginning with the verse "Sabbo jano hiṃsito piṅgalena," to show how all the people rejoiced when the cruel and wicked King Piṅgala of Bārāṇasī, whom everyone hated, passed away.

The monks asked the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, where is Devadatta reborn now?" The Blessed One replied, "Monks, Devadatta has been reborn in the Great Avīci Hell." Then the monks remarked, "Venerable Sir, Devadatta lived in distress and suffering in this present life, and now that he has departed from this life, he has again been reborn in a place of distress and suffering."

Then the Blessed One said, "Indeed, monks. Whether they be monks or laypeople, all those who are negligent in wholesome deeds suffer in both this life and the next."

He then preached this verse of Dhamma:
663:
He then preached this verse of Dhamma:

Idha tappati pecca tappati,
pāpakārī ubhayattha tappati.
pāpaṃ me katanti tappati,
bhiyyo tappati duggatiṃ gato.

Monks, the evil-doer suffers in this life (Idha tappati) due to the anxiety caused by his kamma. He suffers in the next world (pecca tappati) due to the anxiety caused by the results (vipāka). He suffers in both worlds (ubhayattha tappati). He suffers in this present life thinking, "I have done evil" (Pāpaṃ me kataṃ). When he reaches a state of misery, a woeful destination (duggatiṃ gato), he suffers even more (bhiyyo tappati) due to the anxiety caused by the results.

At the conclusion of the Dhamma teaching, many beings attained the stage of a Sotāpanna and so forth. The Dhamma teaching was beneficial to the multitude.

The story of Devadatta ends here.

## Chapter 37
## The Story of King Ajātasattu

Regarding the story of King Ajātasattu, even before he was born, he was called Ajātasattu because he was the enemy of his father, King Bimbisāra. (Ajāta = before being born + Sattu = the prince who is the enemy of his father). The way he became his father's enemy before birth is as follows:

When Queen Vedehī, the chief consort of King Bimbisāra, conceived the prince, she developed a pregnancy craving (dohaḷa), thinking, "How good it would be if I could drink the blood from the King's right arm!" The Queen reflected, "My craving is for something very grave; it is not appropriate to tell anyone else." She did not dare to speak of her craving clearly, and as a result, she became thin, pale, and haggard.

Seeing her condition, King Bimbisāra asked the Queen, "My Queen, your physical appearance is not as it used to be. What is the reason?" When the Queen replied, "Great King, please do not ask," the King said, "My Queen, if you do not tell even me your desire, whom else will you tell?" He questioned her in various ways until she revealed her pregnancy craving.

Upon hearing of the Queen's craving through his persistent questioning, the King, overcome by affection, exclaimed, "O foolish Queen, why did you think this matter was so grave?" He then summoned a physician, had his arm lanced with a small golden knife, collected the blood in a golden bowl, mixed it with water, and gave it to the Queen to drink.
665:
When the court astrologers who read omens heard this news, they predicted, "The child now conceived in the Queen's womb will surely be the King's enemy; this prince will kill the King." Upon hearing this, the Queen became greatly distressed, thinking, "The son born from my womb will kill the King." Wanting to abort the fetus, she went to the garden and had her abdomen massaged and pressed, but the fetus did not drop. The Queen went to the garden many times and did the same. (That garden later became known as Maddakucchi, the garden where the womb was pressed).

King Bimbisāra investigated why the Queen went to the garden so frequently. When he learned the reason, he forbade her, saying, "My Queen, it is not yet known whether the child in your womb is a son or a daughter. If it is said, 'They did such a thing to the child born to them,' it will be a great dishonor and a bad reputation for us throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Do not do this, my Queen." He then placed guards over her. The Queen then thought, "I will kill him only when he is born."

When the child was born, the royal attendants took the infant to a safe place (so that the Queen could not kill him). Later, when the prince had grown up, they presented him to the Queen.
666:
As soon as the Queen saw the prince, she felt a strong love for her son. (The desire to kill him vanished completely). Therefore, she could not kill the prince. His father, King Bimbisāra, eventually appointed the growing Prince Ajātasattu to the position of Crown Prince (Uparāja).

(The events from this point until he associated with the bad friend Devadatta, killed his father the King, and took the throne have already been described in the "Story of Devadatta" above; they should be noted from there).

From the day King Ajātasattu had his father, King Bimbisāra, killed as previously described, the moment he closed his eyes to sleep, he would see signs of his destiny (gati-nimitta) like a dream, as if he were being pierced by hundreds of spears. He would tremble and cry out, unable to sleep. (Considering this incident of King Ajātasattu, one should take note that for those who have committed great evil, signs of a woeful destination can appear early on, not just at the moment of death). When the King trembled and cried out, and the guards asked, "What is this? What happened?", King Ajātasattu would only reply, "Nothing happened at all." Because he would tremble and cry out whenever he tried to sleep due to the hellish visions, King Ajātasattu found no pleasure in sleeping. Consequently, he used to hold royal assemblies for long hours every night to keep himself awake. (This is an extract from the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary, Vol. 1, p. 128).
667:
I shall further present the explanation from the Commentary on the Sañjīva Jātaka (Jātaka 150, Ekakanipāta, Kakaṇṭakavagga) here:

King Ajātasattu, having faith in the immoral Devadatta who was like a thorn to the Buddhas, supported that wicked man. Intending to honor Devadatta, he spent a great deal of wealth to build a large monastery for him at Gayāsīsa. By following Devadatta's advice and killing his father the King, who was a Sotāpanna Ariya, he destroyed his own merit which was a supporting condition (upanissaya) for attaining the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga) in that very life, and thus met with great ruin.

When King Ajātasattu heard the news that "Devadatta has been swallowed by the earth," he became terrified, thinking, "Will the earth swallow me too?" He could no longer enjoy his royal luxury. He found no comfort or peace in sleep. He lived in a state of constant trembling and agitation, like a young elephant being prodded with a sharp iron goad. In his mind, it always seemed as if the earth were about to crack open, as if flames from the Avīci Hell were bursting forth repeatedly, as if the earth were about to swallow him, and as if the wardens of hell were making him lie on his back on a glowing hot iron floor and piercing him with iron spears. Thus, for King Ajātasattu, he was trembling like a beaten cock, unable to find a moment's rest or stability; he could not remain still.

For this very reason, although King Ajātasattu wished to see the Blessed One, pay homage to Him, and ask Him questions...
668:
Because his crime was so grave, he did not dare to approach the Blessed One.

Later, in the city of Rājagaha, on the full moon night of the month of Kattikā, when the Kattikā festival was being celebrated, the entire city was adorned like a celestial city. While the festivities were underway with torches and lamps shining brightly, King Ajātasattu sat upon his golden throne in the royal assembly hall, surrounded by his ministers. Seeing the physician-minister Jīvaka sitting nearby in attendance, the thought occurred to him: “I shall go to the Blessed One, taking Jīvaka as my guide. However, it would not be appropriate to speak directly, saying, ‘Friend Jīvaka, I do not dare to go before the Buddha myself. Come, escort me to the presence of the Blessed One.’ Instead, I shall praise the beauty and perfection of the night by way of a pretext and then ask, ‘Which ascetic or brahmin should we visit today, whose presence might bring faith and clarity to our minds?’ Upon hearing this, the ministers will each speak of the virtues of their own teachers. Jīvaka, too, will speak of the virtues of his teacher, the Blessed One. Only then shall I take Jīvaka and go to pay respects to the Blessed One.”

Having formed this plan, King Ajātasattu said:

(a) “Friends, how delightful is this night, free from the five obscurations: frost, mist, clouds, Rāhu, and smoke!”
(b) “Friends, how beautiful is this night, free from the five obscurations: frost, mist, clouds, Rāhu, and smoke!”
669:
(c) “Friends, how lovely is this night, free from the five obscurations: frost, mist, clouds, Rāhu, and smoke!”
(d) “Friends, how clear and serene is this night, free from the five obscurations: frost, mist, clouds, Rāhu, and smoke!”
(e) “Friends, how auspicious and memorable is this night, free from the five obscurations: frost, mist, clouds, Rāhu, and smoke!”

After praising the full moon night of Kattikā with these five sentences, he continued:

“Which ascetic or brahmin should we visit today, whose presence might bring faith and clarity to our minds?”

In saying this, he gave a hint to Jīvaka. Indeed, as mentioned before, King Ajātasattu had committed two great wrongs: (a) he had killed his father, King Bimbisāra, who was a devoted lay disciple and a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer) serving the Buddha; and (b) he had supported Devadatta, who had caused great harm to the Blessed One. Because of these grave offenses, he did not dare to go to the Buddha on his own. He thought, “Jīvaka is a devoted lay supporter and the primary donor of the monastery to the Blessed One. I shall go to see the Buddha by relying on his protection.” Thus, he gave the hint to Jīvaka.

Jīvaka, for his part, was not unaware that King Ajātasattu was hinting at him; he knew it well.
670:
However, in that assembly, there were many disciples of the six heretical teachers (Titthiyas). Jīvaka thought: “These people have approached unwise teachers, and thus they themselves are unwise and do not understand the etiquette of an assembly. If I begin to speak of the virtues of the Blessed One, they will repeatedly stand up and interrupt to speak of the virtues of their own teachers. If they do so, the praise of the Buddha’s virtues will never reach its conclusion. The King, however, will find nothing of essence to follow even if he visits the six heretical teachers whom these ministers worship. He will not be pleased with the ministers' words and will eventually ask me directly. Only then shall I speak of the virtues of the Blessed One without distraction and escort the King to the presence of the Buddha.” Having reflected deeply, although he knew the King was hinting at him, he remained silent (tuṇhībhāva) to cut off any potential distraction.

The ministers who were disciples of the six heretical teachers also thought: “Today the King praises the full moon night of Kattikā with five sentences. Surely he wishes to approach some ascetic or brahmin to ask questions and listen to the Dhamma. This King will surely bestow great offerings and honors upon the teacher he listens to and finds faith in. It would be a great blessing for the minister whose teacher becomes the King’s preceptor.” Having thus planned,
671:
“I shall speak of my teacher’s virtues and take the King to him,” each minister intended. One minister spoke of the virtues of his teacher, Pūraṇa Kassapa. Another minister spoke of the virtues of his teacher, Makkhali Gosāla; another of Ajita Kesakambala; another of Pakudha Kaccāyana; another of the great teacher Sañjaya; and another minister spoke of the virtues of his teacher, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta. (The manner in which these six ministers praised their respective heretical teachers should be noted from the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, the second discourse of the Sīlakkhandhavagga in the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka).

King Ajātasattu had seen these heretical teachers before. Even then, merely seeing their appearance was far from inspiring faith; it had caused him displeasure. Now, upon hearing the ministers' words, he felt like a man who, wishing to eat a golden-hued, sweet, ripe mango, is instead given a very sour wood-apple (kapittha) placed in his hand. Although he longed to hear the sweet Dhamma that reaches the Three Marks of Existence (Tilakkhaṇa) and is associated with virtues such as the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and higher knowledge (abhiññā), hearing the praise of these heretical teachers (on top of his prior displeasure with their appearance) made him extremely dissatisfied, and he remained silent.
672:
Although King Ajātasattu was dissatisfied upon hearing the ministers' words, he reflected: “If I were to scold these ministers and have them dragged by their necks out of the royal hall, others would be terrified, thinking, ‘The King treats everyone who speaks this way,’ and no one would dare to utter another word.” Therefore, despite his displeasure, he did not speak any words of blame and remained silent.

## The Bold Words of Jīvaka

Upon hearing the ministers' words, King Ajātasattu thought: “Only the ministers I do not wish to hear have spoken. Jīvaka, whom I wish to hear, remains silent like a king of Garudas who has swallowed the brain of a Naga. This is of no benefit to me.” He further reflected: “Jīvaka is a devoted lay disciple of the peaceful Blessed One; therefore, he is peaceful himself. He remains silent like a monk who is perfected in conduct. This Jīvaka will not speak unless I ask him. If one is trodden upon by an elephant, one must grasp the foot of that very elephant.” Having thus decided to consult Jīvaka, he said:

“Friend Jīvaka, why do you remain silent? These ministers seem to have no end of praise for the teachers they worship. Do you not have a teacher to worship as these ministers do?
673:
“Is it because my father did not grant you rank and wealth that you are a poor man without a teacher to worship? Or is it because you are lacking in faith that you have no teacher?”

Thus, he questioned him directly.

Then Jīvaka thought: “This King has now prompted me to speak of the virtues of my venerable teacher. Now is not the time for me to remain silent. It is not appropriate for me to speak of the Blessed One’s virtues while remaining seated, as these ministers did when they praised their heretical teachers while merely bowing to the King.” Having thus reflected, he rose from his seat, faced the direction of the “Jīvaka Mango Grove Monastery” where the Blessed One was residing, paid homage with the five-point prostration, and with hands raised in prayer above his head, he said:

“Great King, do not think of me as one who reveres just any ordinary person who merely bears the name of a monk. Indeed, when my teacher, the Blessed One, descended into his mother’s womb, when he was born, when he renounced the world, when he attained Enlightenment, and when he turned the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten thousand world systems shook. In this manner, he performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire.
674:
“In this manner, he made his descent from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to the world of men. I shall speak of the virtues of the Blessed One to Your Majesty to the best of my ability. Please listen with a steady and concentrated mind, O King.

“Your Majesty, the Blessed One, the Worthy One (Arahaṃ), the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), my teacher, is currently residing in the Mango Grove Monastery donated by us, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty (1,250) monks.

“That teacher of mine, the Blessed One, is the Worthy One (Arahaṃ) because he is worthy of the special offerings of men, devas, and brahmas, being endowed with the virtues of morality (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana). (Et cetera). He is the Blessed One (Bhagavā) because he is endowed with the six supreme glories. The excellent reputation and fame of my teacher, the Blessed One, has spread even to the highest heavens.

“I wish for Your Majesty to approach my teacher, the Blessed One. If you approach the Blessed One, your mind will surely become clear and serene.”

Thus, he spoke these bold and brilliant words.

## Preparing the Elephant Vehicles for the Pilgrimage

While listening to the words praising the virtues of the Blessed One, King Ajātasattu's entire body was continuously suffused with the five kinds of rapture (pīti). Consequently, at that very moment, the King desired to go and pay homage to the Buddha. He thought, "At this time, for me who wishes to visit the Buddha, no one other than Jīvaka the Physician will be able to quickly harness the vehicles." He then commanded, "Friend Jīvaka, go and have the elephant vehicles prepared."

(In this regard: Although there were various types of vehicles such as horse-carriages and chariots, the elephant vehicle is considered the most noble vehicle according to worldly convention. The King thought, "One should go to the presence of the most noble Buddha only with the most noble vehicle." Furthermore, horse-carriages and chariots make noise; the sound of those horse-carriages and chariots can be heard from afar. As for the elephant vehicle, even when moving with heavy steps, no sound is heard. Thinking, "One should go to the presence of the peaceful and calm Buddha only with peaceful and calm vehicles," King Ajātasattu ordered the elephant vehicles to be harnessed.)

Then, Jīvaka the Physician replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and had the royal state elephant prepared along with five hundred female elephants, fully adorned with harnesses and trappings. Regarding the manner of preparation:

Although Jīvaka the Physician was not directly commanded by King Ajātasattu to "prepare five hundred female elephants," being a wise man, he had the five hundred female elephants fully adorned with harnesses and trappings. In doing so, Jīvaka reflected in his mind: "The King says he will go to visit the Buddha at this evening hour.
676:
Kings are known to have many enemies. If any danger should occur along the way, the people might reproach me, saying, 'Jīvaka the Physician, without investigation or reflection, simply followed the King's words and led him out of the golden palace at an untimely hour of the night.' Not only that, people might also reproach the Buddha, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama, thinking that many people follow his words, preaches the Dhamma without regard for the proper time (without setting rules).' Therefore, I shall act and plan so that no reproach falls upon me, no reproach falls upon the Blessed One, and the King is well-provided with protection."

Then he further reflected, "Men do not feel fear when they are supported by women. Therefore, I shall let the King travel comfortably, surrounded by the assembly of royal women." Having reflected thus, he had the five hundred female elephants fully adorned with harnesses and trappings. He then had five hundred women of the palace dress in male attire and instructed them, "Mothers, you must each carry a sword and a spear in your hands and follow, surrounding the King."

Furthermore, Jīvaka the Physician reflected, "For this King Ajātasattu, because he is one who has committed the great ānantariya-kamma of patricide (pitu-ghātaka), there is no special merit as a decisive support (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit in this life and in this body. It is the natural custom of the Buddhas to preach the Dhamma only when they see the special merit of the decisive support for the Path and Fruit (in someone). Now, I shall cause a great multitude of people to assemble. If they are thus assembled, the Blessed One will preach the Dhamma because of the past merit—
678:
He proceeded to the Mango Grove monastery of Jīvaka the Physician, where the Blessed One was residing.

(In this regard: Concerning the phrase "with great royal pomp," King Ajātasattu was the ruler of the two great kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha, which spanned three hundred yojanas. For King Ajātasattu, who was endowed with such a mass of sovereign glory, although there was no prior arrangement or plan made early on saying, "On such a day, the King will go to pay homage to the Blessed One," at that very moment, five hundred royal women (according to Jīvaka's arrangement) came out ready, dressed in male attire with turbans, carrying swords slung over their shoulders and holding spears with handles made of precious ruby gems.

Furthermore, sixteen thousand court dancers followed, surrounding the King. At the edge of those dancers, the elderly women who were the attendants and servants of those dancers followed on foot.

At the edge of those elderly women were the eunuchs who guarded the golden palace. Behind those eunuchs, sixty thousand ministers, looking splendid and beautiful in various types of attire, followed on foot.

Behind those ministers, ninety thousand provincial princes, adorned with various ornaments and carrying various weapons like young vijjādhara youths, followed on foot.

Behind those princes, ten thousand Brahmins, wearing waistcloths worth a hundred and upper robes worth five hundred draped over their left shoulders, having bathed, anointed themselves with perfumes, and adorned themselves with golden flowers and such, followed on foot with their right hands raised, shouting the auspicious cry of victory: "Jayatu Mahārājā—May the Great King be victorious over all dangers!"
679:
Behind those Brahmins followed the five types of musical instruments; behind those five types of musical instruments, the archers; behind those archers, the elephant corps; then the cavalry as far as the eye could see; then the continuous line of the chariot corps; then the infantry with arms touching; and then the eighteen guilds, dressed in various ornaments according to their rank, followed on foot.

In this way, Jīvaka the Physician organized the royal retinue so that an arrow shot from the edge of the crowd could not reach the King. He himself followed close to the King with great alertness, intending, "If any danger arises, I shall be the first to ensure the King's safety."

As for the torches, they were so many that they could not be numbered in hundreds or thousands. With this royal pomp, King Ajātasattu went to the Buddha's monastery.)

## King Ajātasattu's Fear

When he had left the city and reached the vicinity of the Mango Grove monastery, King Ajātasattu was overcome by intense fear, trembling, and horripilation. To make it clearer:

King Ajātasattu became intensely terrified, becoming suspicious of Jīvaka the Physician because of the silence. Indeed, while they were still in the golden palace, Jīvaka the Physician had informed him, "Great King, the Blessed One desires silence. You will have to approach the Blessed One in silence." Therefore, King Ajātasattu had forbidden the playing of musical instruments. The relevant officials merely carried the instruments as they followed. They were not allowed to speak loudly, and everyone had to move—
680:
using only finger snaps as signals. In the great Mango Grove monastery, not even the sound of a single monk sneezing could be heard. Kings are generally those who find delight and pleasure only when there is sound.

King Ajātasattu became bored and weary because of the aforementioned silence, and suspicion towards Jīvaka the Physician arose in him as follows: "This Jīvaka says, 'In the great Mango Grove monastery which I have donated, there are twelve hundred and fifty (1,250) monks.' Even though he says so, not even the sound of a sneeze is heard within this great Mango Grove monastery. I do not think what he says is true. This Jīvaka, having deceived me and led me out of the city, likely intends to capture me with the army in front, and then set up the white parasol himself to rule as king. It is true—this Jīvaka possesses the strength of five bull elephants. He is also hovering close to me. There is not a single royal attendant carrying a weapon near me. Alas, what a great misfortune for me!" Thus, suspicion towards Jīvaka the Physician arose, and he became greatly terrified.

After King Ajātasattu became thus terrified, he could no longer even maintain his royal composure to pretend he was not afraid. He clearly revealed his state of fear to Jīvaka the Physician, saying:

"Friend Jīvaka, is it true that you are not deceiving me? Friend Jīvaka, is it true that you are not betraying me? Friend Jīvaka, is it true that you are not handing me over to my enemies? How can there be twelve hundred and fifty monks..."
681:
“Why is there no sound of sneezing, coughing, or talking from such a large assembly of bhikkhus?” he asked Jīvaka.

Then Jīvaka said to King Ajātasattu:

“Do not be afraid, Great King; do not be afraid, Great King. I am not deceiving you, Your Majesty; I am not misleading you, Your Majesty; I am not handing you over to enemies, Your Majesty. Proceed forward, Great King; proceed forward, Great King. There are lamps burning brightly within the pavilion.”

(In this context: Jīvaka thought, “This King does not know that I am one who does not take the life of others. If I do not speak to reassure him, he might perish right here.” Having thought thus, wishing to speak firm and comforting words, he said, “Do not be afraid, Great King,” repeating it twice. Then he comforted him with the three phrases starting with “I am not deceiving you, Your Majesty.”

Afterwards, to strengthen his confidence, he said the phrase “Proceed forward, Great King” twice. Then he said, “Great King, a gang of wicked thieves does not remain with lamps lit. Because this is not a gang of wicked thieves, the lamps are burning brightly within the pavilion. Great King, by the sign of those lit lamps, enter with confidence, knowing it is the dwelling of virtuous people.” This was the meaning intended when he said, “There are lamps burning brightly within the pavilion.” How profound is the intended meaning!

Wise men speak briefly,
Yet their words are full of meaning.
Deep and subtle is their speech,
Such is the nature of the wise.)
682:
## King Ajātasattu
## Inquiring about the Benefits of the Ascetic Life

Then King Ajātasattu went by elephant as far as the ground permitted, and upon reaching the entrance of the monastery, he dismounted. As soon as his feet touched the ground, the power and majesty of the Blessed One struck and permeated his entire body. At that moment, beads of sweat poured from his whole body so profusely that he almost had to change his royal robes. Remembering his own crime (of killing his father), he became intensely afraid. Therefore, King Ajātasattu did not go directly to the Blessed One but held Jīvaka by the hand. Like one wandering around looking at the monastery buildings, he said, “Friend Jīvaka, you have had this building well constructed; you have had this building well constructed,” praising the monastery as he walked. When he reached the door of the circular assembly hall (the Dhamma hall), King Ajātasattu asked Jīvaka with royal dignity, “Friend Jīvaka, where is the Blessed One?” Indeed, it is the custom of royalty to ask even when they already know, as if they do not.

Upon hearing those words, Jīvaka thought, “This King, while standing on the earth, asks ‘Where is the earth?’ like one looking up at the sky and asking ‘Where are the moon and sun?’ or like one standing at the foot of Mount Sineru and asking ‘Where is Mount Sineru?’ Even so, while standing in the presence of the Blessed One, he asks ‘Where is the Blessed One?’ Now...
683:
...I shall show the Blessed One to the King.” Having thought thus, he raised his joined palms in reverence towards the Blessed One and replied, “Great King, that person sitting against the central pillar, facing East, in front of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, is the Blessed One.”

Then King Ajātasattu approached the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, and stood at one side. Seeing the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, who were endowed with a calm demeanor like a very clear lake, and who remained perfectly still without any coughing or sneezing, the King gazed steadily at the Blessed One and the silent Saṅgha without losing his composure for even a moment despite his large royal retinue. He then uttered this inspired exclamation (udāna):

“May my son, Prince Udayabhadda, be endowed with such peace as the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is now endowed with!”

(In this context: King Ajātasattu did not utter this exclamation with the intention of wishing, “It would be good if my son, Prince Udayabhadda, were to become a monk like these bhikkhus and be peaceful.” Rather, when the King saw the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, his heart became very clear and he remembered his son, Prince Udayabhadda. Indeed, it is the natural way of the world to remember one’s beloved relatives and friends when one obtains a rare object or sees something wonderful. Thus, when King Ajātasattu saw the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he remembered his beloved son and uttered this exclamation. It was not because he wished for his son to become a monk.)
684:
Alternatively, King Ajātasattu uttered this exclamation because he was anxious about his son and desired his son’s peace. To elaborate: In King Ajātasattu’s mind, he thought, “One day my son, Prince Udayabhadda, will ask, ‘My father is still young; where is my grandfather?’ At that time, if my son hears in some way that ‘Your father has killed your grandfather,’ he might think, ‘I too shall kill my father and become king one day.’” Because he was anxious about his son in this way, he desired his son’s peace and thus uttered this exclamation.

Furthermore, although King Ajātasattu uttered this exclamation out of anxiety for his son, his son, Prince Udayabhadda, would indeed kill him. To clarify: In that royal lineage, for five consecutive generations, the son killed the father. (1) Prince Ajātasattu killed his father, King Bimbisāra, and became king. (2) Prince Udaya killed his father, King Ajātasattu, and became king. (3) Prince Mahāmuṇḍika, the son of King Udaya, killed his father, King Udaya, and became king. (4) Prince Anuruddha, the son of King Mahāmuṇḍika, killed his father, King Mahāmuṇḍika, and became king. (5) Prince Nāgadāsa, the son of King Anuruddha, killed his father, King Anuruddha, and became king. As for King Nāgadāsa, the citizens and the public consulted together, saying, “These kings are those who sever the royal lineage; what benefit is there from these kings?” and they killed and removed him.)

Even before King Ajātasattu uttered his exclamation, the Blessed One reflected, “This King has come into my presence and stands in silence; what is he thinking?” When he considered...
685:
...the King’s state of mind, He knew: “This King does not dare to speak with the Buddha, and while repeatedly looking at the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, he is remembering his son. If I, the Buddha, do not initiate the conversation, he will not dare to say anything. I shall converse with him.” Having reflected thus, immediately after King Ajātasattu uttered his exclamation, the Blessed One initiated the conversation, saying:

“Great King, your thoughts have turned to that which you love.”

At that moment, King Ajātasattu thought: “Oh, how wonderful are the qualities of the Blessed One! There is no one like me who has committed such offenses against the Blessed One. Indeed, I have killed the Great King (my father), who was the most excellent attendant and a noble lay follower (ariya dāyaka) of the Blessed One. Not only that, following the wrong advice of Devadatta, I sent assassins. Not only that, I also released the elephant Nālāgiri. It was because of me that Devadatta rolled down a rock from Gijjhakūṭa Hill (to kill the Blessed One). The mouth of the Blessed One, who initiates conversation with me who has committed such great crimes, is truly beyond satiety. Oh, the Blessed One stands firm in the *five characteristics of Tādi.”

* The five characteristics of Tādi are: (1) Being able to maintain an equal mind without love or hatred towards desirable and undesirable worldly conditions. (2) Having abandoned the defilements. (3) Having crossed the flood of saṃsāra. (4) Having been freed from passion, etc. (5) Being one who can be pointed out as “one with virtue,” “one with faith,” etc., by those specific qualities of virtue and faith.
686:
“...He stands firm. We shall no longer seek any other refuge outside of such a Blessed One.” Such was his thought.

Having thought thus, King Ajātasattu was filled with joy and, wishing to respond to the Blessed One, he said:

“Venerable Sir, I love my son (Prince Udayabhadda) very much. Venerable Sir, may my son, Prince Udayabhadda, be endowed with such peace as the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is now endowed with!”

He spoke exactly as he had uttered in his exclamation.

Then King Ajātasattu thought, “If I pay homage to the Blessed One and then go here and there to pay homage to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, I will have to turn my back on the Blessed One. If that happens...”

(Alternative definition of the five characteristics of Tādi): (1) Being able to dwell with the perception of the agreeable in disagreeable beings and formations, if one so desires. (2) Being able to dwell with the perception of the disagreeable in agreeable beings and formations, if one so desires. (3) Being able to dwell with the perception of the agreeable in both agreeable and disagreeable beings and formations, if one so desires. (4) Being able to dwell with the perception of the disagreeable in both agreeable and disagreeable beings and formations, if one so desires. (5) Being able to dwell with equanimity, observing with a neutral mind, in both agreeable and disagreeable beings and formations, if one so desires. These five aspects, accomplished through the five kinds of Ariyan power (ariya-iddhi), are called the five characteristics of Tādi. (Extracted from the New Sub-commentary to the Sīlakkhandhavagga, Vol. 2, pages 27, 28, 29.)
687:
687
“It would be disrespectful to the Buddha. Indeed, one who pays respects to the King and then goes to pay respects to the Crown Prince where he is, is being disrespectful to the King,” he thought and reflected. Therefore, after paying respectful homage to the Buddha, he remained in his place and saluted the Saṅgha with joined palms, then sat down in a place free from the six faults.

After sitting down, King Ajātasattu addressed the Buddha:
“Magnificent Buddha, if the Exalted One would permit me to ask a question, I would like to ask the Exalted One a little about a certain matter.”
When he requested permission in this way, the Buddha invited King Ajātasattu with the invitation of the Omniscient Ones, saying, “Great King, ask whatever you wish.”

## Two Types of Invitation
(When someone asks a question, the invitation of the person being asked is of two types: (1) Sabbaññu-pavāraṇā = the invitation of the Omniscient Buddhas, and (2) Sāvaka-pavāraṇā = the invitation of the disciples.

Among these, when someone asks a question, the Omniscient Buddhas give a bold and unconditional invitation, saying, ‘Ask whatever you desire; I shall answer everything you ask to the very end,’ without leaving anything out. This kind of Sabbaññu-pavāraṇā is offered only by the Buddhas and the Bodhisattas whose perfection-knowledge (pāramī-ñāṇa) is fully matured.)
688: Disciples, when someone asks a question, do not invite them by saying "Ask whatever you wish," but rather with a reservation, saying "Sutvā vedissāma = Having heard your words, I shall answer if I know." These are the two kinds of invitations. (From Dĩghaᅩᅩhakathā, Vol. 1, page 141, etc.). When the Blessed One had thus boldly invited him with the Sabbaupavāraᅇā, King Ajātasattu became very pleased and encouraged, and wishing to ask the question, he said: "Venerable Sir, there are many crafts, such as: elephant riders, horsemen, charioteers, archers, standard-bearers, military strategists, those who can charge into the enemy's army and cut off their heads, princes famous for their excellence in war, those who can charge and fight with great speed, warriors like great elephants, the very brave, mail-clad warriors, loyal servants, cooks, barbers, bath-attendants, chefs, garland-makers, laundrymen, weavers, reed-mat makers, potters, accountants, finger-calculators, and besides these, many other similar crafts. These people live their lives in this very life depending on the fruits of the crafts they have mastered. With those crafts they have mastered, they make themselves happy, as well as their parents, children, wives, friends, and companions..."
689: "...they make them strong and prosperous, and for the sake of the world beyond, they establish meritorious deeds that lead to heaven among recluses and brahmins—that is, they give alms. Is it possible, Venerable Sir, to point out a fruit of the ascetic life that is visible in this very life, similar to the fruits of these crafts?" At that time, the Blessed One did not yet answer the question, thinking: "Many ministers who are disciples of heretical teachers (titthiyas) from outside the Dispensation have come here. If I were to preach by dividing the teaching into two parts—the dark side (kaᅇhapakkha), which is the heretical doctrine, and the bright side (sukkapakkha), which is the Buddha's doctrine—these ministers might disparage me, saying, 'Our King has come here with great effort to listen to the Dhamma, but from the moment he arrived, the recluse Gotama has been speaking only about the contradictions and disputes among the doctrines of recluses.' They would not listen to the Dhamma respectfully. If the King himself speaks about the doctrines of the heretics, they will not be able to disparage him; they will only follow the King's wish. (Issarānuvattako hi loko) = Indeed, it is the nature of the masses to follow the King. Now, I shall make it the King's responsibility to speak about the heretical doctrines." Having thought thus, He asked King Ajātasattu, "Great King, do you remember ever asking this question to other recluses and brahmins?" At that, King Ajātasattu replied, "I remember asking this question to other recluses and brahmins."
690: When he replied, "I remember," the Blessed One encouraged him, saying, "Great King, how did those recluses and brahmins answer? If it is not a burden to you, please tell me." King Ajātasattu replied, "Venerable Sir, in the presence of the Blessed One or someone like the Blessed One, it is no burden for me." (The intention in King Ajātasattu's reply is: It is difficult to speak in the presence of those who pretend to be wise; such pretenders only look for faults in every phrase and every letter. True wise persons, upon hearing words spoken in answer, praise them if they are faultless, and if they are faulty, they correct the Pali, phrases, meanings, and letters that are contradictory or erroneous. There is no one in the world who is a true wise person like the Blessed One. Therefore, he replied as mentioned before.) When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One encouraged him, saying, "In that case, Great King, speak." Thus encouraged, King Ajātasattu recounted how he had approached the six heretical teachers—Pũraᅇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambala, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Nigaᅇᅩha Nāᅩaputta, and Sajaya Belaᅩᅩhaputta—and asked about the visible fruits of the ascetic life. He explained how each of these six teachers answered only according to their own views, so that the question and answer were mismatched, like being asked about a mango tree and answering about a breadfruit tree, or being asked about a breadfruit tree and answering about a mango tree.
691: Although he was not pleased with those answers, he thought, "How could a king like me think of disparaging the recluses and brahmins—the virtuous ones—living within my kingdom?" Reflecting thus, he neither accepted nor rejected the various erroneous doctrines of those six heretical teachers. Though dissatisfied, he did not voice his dissatisfaction, and without taking their words to heart, he stood up and left. Having recounted this, he asked the Blessed One again, as before, about the visible fruits of the ascetic life. Then the Blessed One gave a detailed explanation to King Ajātasattu on the visible fruits of the ascetic life, starting with (1) the example of a slave who becomes a monk and receives the King's honor, (2) the example of a tax-paying farmer who becomes a monk and receives the King's honor, and (3) to show even higher and more noble fruits, starting from the appearance of a Buddha, a person of either low or high birth hears the Dhamma, gains faith, and enters the monkhood. He then practices (a) Cũᄱasĩla, (b) Majjhimasĩla, and (c) Mahāsĩla. Moving further, he practices restraint of the senses, possesses mindfulness and clear comprehension, is easily contented, abandons the five hindrances, and attains the first jhana, (4) the second jhana, (5) the third jhana, (6) the fourth jhana, and (7-14) moving further, he attains the eight types of higher knowledge: Insight Knowledge (Vipassanā-āᅇa), the Mind-made Body (Manomayiddhi), Supernormal Powers (Iddhividha), the Divine Ear (Dibbasota), Knowledge of Others' Minds (Cetopariya-āᅇa), Recollection of Past Lives (Pubbenivāsānussati), Knowledge of the Passing Away and Rebirth of Beings (Cutũpapāta-āᅇa), and the Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints (Āsavakkhaya-āᅇa), which is the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship.

(The detailed explanation should be extracted and noted from the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, the second sutta of the Sīlakkhandhavagga in the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka).

(When the Great Elders who performed the Recension (Saṅgāyana) recited the texts, a section of about 12 pages of recitation is called one bhāṇavāra.
