## King Ajātasattu
## Taking Refuge and Asking for Forgiveness
In this way, when the Buddha preached in detail the Sāmaññaphala—the visible fruits of recluseship—culminating in the Fruit of Arahantship, King Ajātasattu expressed his appreciation (Sādhu) at every section of the Sāmaññaphala. He listened respectfully to the beginning, the middle, and the end, and reflected: “For a long time in the past, I asked these questions to many recluses and brahmins, but like one pounding husks, I did not obtain any essence. Oh, how wonderful are the qualities of the Buddha! The Buddha has answered these questions by creating a great light of wisdom, like one setting up and lighting a thousand lamps. For a long time, delusion (moha) has deceived me, preventing me from seeing and knowing the power of the Buddha’s attributes.” Thus, with his body touched by the five types of joy (pīti) arising from the recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati), and wishing to make clear his devotion to the Triple Gem, he said:

“Magnificent Buddha, it is excellent! Magnificent Buddha, it is excellent!”
693:
“Magnificent, Lord! Magnificent, Lord! It is as if, Lord, one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what had been hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the dark so that those with eyes might see forms. In the same way, the Blessed One has explained the Dhamma in many ways. I, Ajātasattu, go to the Blessed One for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka) who has taken refuge from this day forth as long as life shall last.

Lord, a transgression (accaya) overcame me, in that I was so foolish, so confused, and so unskilled that, for the sake of lordship, I killed my father, that righteous king who ruled righteously. May the Blessed One accept this confession of my transgression as such, for the sake of future restraint.”

Thus, he took the refuges and confessed his transgression. Then, the Blessed One spoke to King Ajātasattu:

“Indeed, Great King, a transgression overcame you, in that you were so foolish, so confused, and so unskilled that you killed your father, that righteous
694:
king who ruled righteously. Great King, because you see your transgression as a transgression and make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you. For, Great King, it is growth in the discipline (vinaya) of the Noble One when one sees one's transgression as a transgression, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, and practices restraint in the future.”

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, King Ajātasattu said to the Blessed One:

“Well then, Lord, we must go now. We have many duties and much to be done.”

“Now is the time, Great King, for you to do as you think fit.” Then King Ajātasattu, having rejoiced and appreciated the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed.

## Points to Note Regarding the Refuges (Saraṇagamana)

Here, a brief explanation regarding the refuges will be presented. In the matter of the refuges, these seven points should be understood:

(a) Saraṇa (Refuge),
(b) Saraṇagamana (The act of taking refuge),
(c) Saraṇagata (The one who has taken refuge),
(d) Varieties of refuge,
(e) Benefits of the refuge,
(f) Defilement of the refuge,
(g) Destruction of the refuge.
695:
## (a) Saraṇa

Among these seven, the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—is called 'Saraṇa' (Refuge) because it dispels (sarati hiṃsatīti saraṇaṃ) the various fears, anxieties, physical and mental sufferings, and the miseries of the states of deprivation (apāya) and unhappy destinations (duggati) for all those who take refuge in them. Alternatively, the Buddha is the refuge because he dispels the various dangers of beings by establishing them in what is beneficial (happiness) and preventing them from what is not beneficial (suffering). The Dhamma is the refuge because it dispels the various dangers of beings by enabling them to cross the wilderness of saṃsāra and by providing relief. The Saṅgha is the refuge because it dispels the various dangers of beings by causing even small meritorious deeds to yield great and abundant fruits. Therefore, according to the aforementioned etymology, the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha—is called Saraṇa. (Saraṇa refers to the three true objects that can dispel the various dangers and sufferings of beings.)

## (b) Saraṇagamana

Saraṇagamana (Taking Refuge) refers to the collection of mental states (citta-cetasika) of the Great Wholesome (Mahā-kusala) consciousness, the Great Functional (Mahā-kiriya) consciousness (for Arahants), or the Path (Magga) consciousness (for Ariyas at the stage of the Path). These arise in a manner of bowing and inclining towards the Triple Gem, removing the unwholesome states that cause defilement through faith and reverence in those three gems. (Saraṇanti gacchati anenāti saraṇagamanam. Anena = by this collection of mental states; Saraṇanti = as the three true objects that dispel various dangers and sufferings; Gacchati = one knows
696:
and approaches. Iti tasmā = therefore; Taṃ = that collection of mental states; Saraṇagamanam = is called Saraṇagamana. Saraṇagamana is the collection of mental states that serves as the means of knowing and approaching the three true objects that dispel various dangers and sufferings. This is how the grammatical definition should be constructed.)

## (c) Saraṇagata

A person endowed with the aforementioned collection of mental states is called 'Saraṇagata' (one who has taken refuge). (Saraṇagata means one who knows the three true objects that dispel various dangers and sufferings; or, it refers to a person endowed with the collection of mental states that so knows.) Thus, one should first understand these three: (a) Saraṇa, (b) Saraṇagamana, and (c) Saraṇagata.

## (d) Varieties of Refuge

The aforementioned Saraṇagamana is of two kinds: (1) Supramundane Refuge (Lokuttara-saraṇagamana) and (2) Mundane Refuge (Lokiya-saraṇagamana).

(1) Of these two, the Supramundane Refuge occurs in the mental continuum of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who have realized the Four Noble Truths. At the moment of the respective Paths (Magga-khana), it takes Nibbāna as its object and, by the accomplishment of its function (kicca-siddhi), it is fully completed regarding the Triple Gem in a single thought-moment, by totally eradicating the unwholesome defilements (upakkilesa) that cause the refuge to be defiled. (The meaning is: Supramundane Refuge refers to the mental states of the Path. Although these Path-consciousness states arise taking Nibbāna as their object, they arise while totally uprooting the unwholesome defilements that defile the refuge. By doing so, even though these mental states do not take the Triple Gem as their object—taking only Nibbāna—the function of knowing the true nature of the Triple Gem is already accomplished. This accomplishment of the function is what is called 'knowing the true nature of the Triple Gem through kicca-siddhi.' This is what is meant by 'the Supramundane Refuge is completed at the moment of the Path.' For example, when it is said 'one knows the Four Noble Truths at the moment of the Path,'
697:
at the moment the Path-consciousness arises, it knows by taking Nibbāna as its object, which is the Truth of Cessation (Nirodha-sacca). As for the remaining three Truths, when the Path-consciousness arises, it totally uproots the darkness of delusion (moha) that covers and hides the Four Noble Truths. Because the delusion that prevents one from knowing the Truth of Suffering as suffering, the Truth of Origin as origin, the Truth of Cessation as cessation, and the Truth of the Path as the path is eradicated, the Noble One has completed the function of knowing the remaining three Truths, even though he does not take them as objects (taking only Nibbāna). This completion of the function is called 'knowing the remaining three Truths through kicca-siddhi.' This is very profound; reflect and consider it repeatedly to understand.)

(2) Mundane Refuge (Lokiya-saraṇagamana) occurs in the mental continuum of worldlings (puthujjanas) by taking the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha as objects, while setting aside the unwholesome defilements that defile the refuge. In terms of ultimate reality (paramattha), this refuge is the acquisition of faith (saddhā) in the three true objects—the Buddha and so on—and the wisdom (paññā-cetasika) or Right View (Sammā-diṭṭhi) which has faith as its root. Among the ten bases of meritorious action (puñña-kiriya-vatthu), it is called 'Diṭṭhijukamma' (straightening of views).

In this context, faith alone is called refuge. Both faith and wisdom together are also called refuge. Indeed, Mundane Refuge is of two kinds: 1. Refuge associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta) and 2. Refuge dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta). Of these two, the refuge taken by children and others through the encouragement of parents and others is the refuge dissociated from knowledge. In this refuge, the mental factor of faith (saddhā-cetasika) is taken as the essence. The refuge taken by knowing the virtues and grace of the Triple Gem is the refuge associated with knowledge. In this refuge, both faith (saddhā-cetasika) and wisdom (paññā-cetasika) are
698:
taken as the essence. The reason for stating faith and wisdom as the refuge here is because they are predominant (padhāna). In reality, the collection of mental states led by faith and wisdom is what is called 'refuge.'

That Mundane Refuge is further divided into four types:

(1) Attasanniyyātana-saraṇagamana = Refuge by way of dedicating oneself to the Triple Gem.
(2) Tapparāyaṇa-saraṇagamana = Refuge by way of reliance and inclining towards the Triple Gem.
(3) Sissabhāvūpagamana-saraṇagamana = Refuge by way of accepting the status of a disciple.
(4) Paṇipāta-saraṇagamana = Refuge by way of supreme veneration to the Triple Gem.

(1) Among these four, the refuge that occurs by dedicating oneself to the Triple Gem thus: 'Ajjādiṃ katvā ahaṃ attānaṃ buddhassa niyyātemi, dhammassa niyyātemi, saṅghassa niyyātemi = From this day forth, I dedicate myself to the Buddha, I dedicate myself to the Dhamma, I dedicate myself to the Saṅgha,' is called Attasanniyyātana-saraṇagamana.

(2) The refuge that occurs by way of reliance on the Triple Gem thus: 'Ajjādiṃ katvā ahaṃ buddhaparāyaṇo dhammaparāyaṇo saṅghaparāyaṇoti maṃ dhāretha = From this day forth, please recognize me as one who relies upon and is inclined towards only the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha,' is called Tapparāyaṇa-saraṇagamana.

(3) The refuge that occurs by way of accepting discipleship thus: 'Ajjādiṃ katvā ahaṃ buddhassa antevāsiko, dhammassa antevāsiko, saṅghassa antevāsikooti maṃ dhāretha = From this day forth, please recognize me as a disciple of the Buddha, a disciple of the Dhamma, a disciple of the Saṅgha,'
699:
“Please regard me as your close disciple.” Taking refuge in this manner, by accepting the status of a disciple of the Triple Gem, is called Sissabhāvūpagamana Saraṇagamana (Taking Refuge by Approaching as a Disciple). (In this context, in the Mahājanaka Jātaka, the Bodhisatta King Mahājanaka pointed to two inanimate mango trees—one with fruit and one without—as his teachers, saying, “Phalo ambo aphalo ca, te satthāro ubho mama.” Just as the Dhamma points the way to benefit, the Dhamma is spoken of as the teacher and oneself as the disciple).

(4) “Ajjādiṃ katvā ahaṃ abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalikammasāmīcikammaṃ buddhādīnaṃyeva tiṇṇannṃ vatthūnaṃ karomīti maṃ dhāretha = Please regard me as one who, from this day forward, performs the acts of prostration, rising to welcome, saluting with joined palms, and showing proper respect only to the three objects: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.” Taking refuge in this manner, by showing extreme respect to the Triple Gem starting with the Buddha, is called Paṇipāta Saraṇagamana (Taking Refuge by Veneration). (It is Paṇipāta, not Pāṇipāta).

A person who performs any one of these four described manners is said to have taken refuge.

Alternatively: (1) “Bhagavato attānaṃ pariccajāmi” etc. = “I sacrifice myself to the Blessed One. I sacrifice myself to the Dhamma. I sacrifice myself to the Saṅgha.” Or, “I sacrifice my life to the Triple Gem.” Or, “My body is already sacrificed to the Triple Gem.” Or, “My life is already sacrificed to the Triple Gem.” Or, “I approach and know the Blessed One as my refuge until the end of my life; I approach and know the Dhamma... the Saṅgha as my refuge.” Or, “The Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha are my refuge, my support, and my shelter.” Uttering such words and surrendering oneself to the Triple Gem is Attasanniyyātana Saraṇagamana (Taking Refuge by Self-dedication).
700:
(2) The young Brahmin Pippali, who would later be known as the Venerable Mahākassapa, took the form of a monk on his own and departed from his native Brahmin village of Mahātittha. While traveling toward where the Buddha was, the Buddha came out to meet him from a distance of three gāvutas and sat alone at the foot of a banyan tree named Bahuputtaka, located between the city of Rājagaha and the town of Nāḷandā. Upon seeing the Buddha, Pippali made a firm decision without any doubt: “This noble person is the Satthā (Teacher) of gods and humans; He is the Sugata (Well-gone) because He has truly reached Nibbāna through the right practice; He is the Sammāsambuddha (Fully Enlightened One) because He has realized all Truths and knowable phenomena by Himself without error.”

He then uttered the following to take refuge:
“Satthārañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ = If I were to look for a noble person called Satthā, the Teacher of gods and humans, I would look only to the Blessed One. Sugatañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ = If I were to look for a noble person called Sugata, I would look only to the Blessed One. Sammāsambuddhañca vatāhaṃ passeyyaṃ, bhagavantameva passeyyaṃ = If I were to look for a noble person called Sammāsambuddha, I would look only to the Blessed One. (This means: “I do not look upon or see anyone other than the Buddha as the Teacher, the Sugata, or the Fully Enlightened One with my eye of wisdom; I see and know only the Buddha as the Teacher, the Sugata, and the Fully Enlightened One with my eye of wisdom.”)”

In this way, he took refuge by verbalizing his commitment. This is Sissabhāvūpagamana Saraṇagamana, taking refuge by accepting the status of a disciple of the Triple Gem, similar to the way Venerable Mahākassapa accepted the status of a disciple.

(3) As mentioned in the previously cited Āḷavaka Sutta and Hemavata Sutta:
“So ahaṃ vicarissāmi, gāmā gāmaṃ purā puraṃ.
Namassamāno sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammataṃ.” (And)
“Te mayaṃ vicarissāma, gāmā gāmaṃ nagā nagaṃ.
Namassamānā sambuddhaṃ, dhammassa ca sudhammataṃ.”
701:
In this way, like the refuge of the ogre Āḷavaka, the deva king Hemavata, and the deva king Sātāgira, there is Tapparāyaṇa Saraṇagamana, which is the refuge characterized by leaning and inclining toward the Triple Gem. (The meanings of the verses have been written below).

(4) As stated in the Brahmāyu Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, when the Buddha finished answering the eight questions asked by the Brahmin Brahmāyu, the great Brahmin Brahmāyu was so inspired by the Buddha that he rose from his seat, bowed his head to the Buddha's feet, and even kissed the Buddha's feet with his mouth. He massaged them vigorously with both hands and announced his name, saying, “O Venerable Gotama, I am the Brahmin Brahmāyu; O Venerable Gotama, I am the Brahmin Brahmāyu.”

Like this great Brahmin Brahmāyu, Paṇipāta Saraṇagamana occurs through the act of extreme physical veneration of the Triple Gem.

In summary, one should not consider the four types of refuge, such as Attasanniyyātana, as having only one single mode of action. Since there are various actions and various ways of speaking that constitute respectful devotion to the Triple Gem, the Great Commentator explained this latter method so that one can appropriately recognize: “This kind of action or speech is Attasanniyyātana Saraṇagamana; this kind is Tapparāyaṇa Saraṇagamana; this kind is Sissabhāvūpagamana Saraṇagamana; and this kind is Paṇipāta Saraṇagamana.”

## Four Types of Paṇipāta Veneration
That veneration or act of respect called Paṇipāta is further divided into four types: 1. Veneration due to kinship, 2. Veneration due to fear, 3. Veneration due to being a teacher, and 4. Veneration of the Triple Gem as the true object worthy of supreme offerings.
702:
Among these four types, only the veneration of the Triple Gem as the true object worthy of supreme offerings (number 4) constitutes Paṇipāta Saraṇagamana. Veneration or respect shown through the other three types does not constitute taking refuge.

Indeed, taking refuge is only achieved when one respects, cherishes, and venerates the Triple Gem as the true, praiseworthy, and noble Jewel. The refuge is broken only if one abandons the true Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha and instead respects, cherishes, and venerates false claimants to those titles as if they were the true Triple Gem.

Therefore: 1. If a certain Sakyan or Koliyan prince prostrates thinking, “The Buddha is our great relative,” that person is not said to have taken refuge.

2. If a certain person prostrates out of fear, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama is a person honored by kings and possesses great power and majesty; if I do not show him respect, he might cause me harm,” that person is also not said to have taken refuge.

3. If a certain person prostrates thinking, “He was my teacher,” remembering that he had learned some art or science from the Bodhisatta before he became the Buddha, or if a certain person, after the Bodhisatta became the Buddha, hears:

“Catudhā vibhaje bhoge, paṇḍito gharamāvasaṃ.
Ekena bhogaṃ bhuñjeyya, dvīhi kammaṃ payojaye.
Catutthañca nidhāpeyya, āpadāsu bhavissati.”

“A wise man living at home should divide his acquired wealth into four parts. He should enjoy one part of the wealth for his own consumption. He should employ two parts for his business or work. He should set aside the fourth part, intending it for use when misfortune arises.” (For example, if one earns a profit of 100 kyats from trade, that 100 kyats should be divided into four parts: one part of 25 kyats should be used for household expenses; two parts, totaling 50 kyats, should be reinvested in the business; and the fourth part of 25 kyats should be saved for use in case of emergencies).
703:
If one prostrates with the intention and thought, “He is my teacher,” because he taught such advice for worldly prosperity and provided guidance for worldly success, both of these types of people are not said to have taken refuge.

4. However, if a person prostrates thinking, “This Blessed One is the true and genuine Jewel, worthy of receiving supreme offerings planted for the benefit of future lives in the world,” only that person is said to have taken refuge.

Furthermore, for a lay devotee (upāsaka or upāsikā) who has understood the Buddha as the Aggadakkhiṇeyya (the person worthy of supreme offerings) and has taken refuge, the refuge is not broken even if they prostrate to a relative who is an ascetic of an outside sect (titthiya), thinking, “This person is my relative.” If this is the case for an ascetic relative, what need is there to mention a relative who is an ordinary layperson? The refuge is certainly not broken (1). Similarly, for a lay devotee who has taken refuge, the refuge is not broken even if they prostrate to a ruler of the country out of fear that the ruler might cause harm if respect is not shown. Indeed, since a king is one honored by the whole country, he might cause harm if not respected; therefore, one must show respect. Even if one prostrates to a king out of fear, the refuge is not broken (2). Similarly, for a lay devotee (who is established in refuge), the refuge is not broken even if they prostrate to a person of an outside sect who was once their teacher, thinking, “This person was once my teacher,” because they learned some art or science from them (3). In this way, as described, the different types of refuge should be understood.
704:
## (e) The Benefits of Refuge
Between the two types of refuge mentioned—mundane refuge (lokiya) and supramundane refuge (lokuttara)—the four noble fruits (ariya-phala) are the primary benefits of supramundane refuge (the arising of the Path consciousness). The exhaustion and cessation of the suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa-dukkha) is called the secondary benefit or the advantage (ānisaṃsa). Alternatively, never perceiving conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), which are impermanent, suffering, and non-self, as permanent, pleasant, or self is called the secondary benefit of supramundane refuge. Attaining success in existence (bhava-sampatti), such as reaching a happy destination, and attaining success in wealth (bhoga-sampatti), such as being endowed with riches, are the benefits of mundane refuge. This is the benefit of taking refuge.

## (f) The Defilement of Refuge
Between these two—mundane refuge and supramundane refuge—mundane refuge is defiled by ignorance of the qualities of the Triple Gem, by doubt, and by wrong or distorted perceptions. It becomes lacklustre, narrow, and insignificant. As for supramundane refuge, there is no such thing as defilement; it remains pure and clean at all times.

## (g) The Destruction of Refuge
Between the two types of refuge, supramundane refuge never suffers destruction. Indeed, a noble person (ariya) who is established in supramundane refuge will never point to anyone other than the Triple Gem as their teacher, even in a future life in the hereafter. Only mundane refuge is subject to destruction.

The destruction of mundane refuge is of two types: 1. Blameworthy destruction, and 2. Blameless destruction. Of these two, 1. [Blameworthy destruction occurs] when one [turns] to teachers of other sects besides the Triple Gem...
705:
705
Among the four modes previously mentioned, such as “the mode of dedicating oneself,” if one seeks refuge through any of these modes, the refuge is broken and, because it occurs together with unwholesome faults such as craving (taṇhā) and wrong view (diṭṭhi), it yields the result of evil suffering. 2. When the body of this life breaks and one passes away, the mundane refuge (lokiya-saraṇagam) that was taken is broken; however, since it is merely the breaking of the refuge and not any unwholesome act, there is no fault. (The refuge observed by the virtuous Buddhist people today is mundane refuge. Since this mundane refuge is taken without a time limit, unlike the undertaking of precepts, the refuge ends and breaks only when life ends. Such breaking of refuge through death is a blameless breaking, as it does not involve unwholesome states like craving and wrong view. This is the explanation regarding the breaking of refuge. From the Commentary on the Sīlakkhandhavagga, pages 205 to 209).

## Points to Note Regarding a Lay Follower (Upāsaka)
Here, I shall briefly mention points to be noted regarding a lay follower. In this matter of a lay follower, one should understand these six points:
(a) Who is called a lay follower,
(b) Why one is called a lay follower,
(c) The virtue (sīla) of a lay follower,
(d) The livelihood of a lay follower,
(e) The decline of a lay follower,
(f) The perfection of a lay follower.

## (a) Who is Called a Lay Follower
Among these six, as to “What kind of person is called a lay follower?”: regardless of whether their status is low or high, anyone who is established in the Three Refuges is called a lay follower. (Take the relevant evidence from Saṃyutta Nikāya, Vol. 3, page 344).
706:
706
## (b) Why One is Called a Lay Follower
As to “Why is one called a lay follower (upāsaka)?”: one is called an upāsaka because one attends to the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. (Upāsatīti upāsako. Upāsati = he attends to the Triple Gem. Iti tasmā = therefore. Upāsako = he is called an upāsaka. Upāsako = a donor who attends to the Triple Gem. This is the etymological definition).

## (c) The Virtue of a Lay Follower
As to “What is the virtue of a lay follower?”: the Five Precepts are called the virtue of a lay follower. (Take the evidence from Saṃyutta Nikāya, Vol. 3, page 345).

## The Livelihood of a Lay Follower
As to “What is the livelihood of a lay follower?”: avoiding these five types of wrong trade: 1. Trading in weapons, 2. Trading in human beings, 3. Trading in meat, 4. Trading in intoxicants, 5. Trading in poison; and making a living in accordance with the Dhamma through cattle farming, trade, or agriculture is called the livelihood of a lay follower. (Take the evidence from Aṅguttara Nikāya, Vol. 2, page 183).

## (e) The Decline of a Lay Follower
As to “What is the decline of a lay follower?”: the failure of the previously mentioned Five Precepts and righteous livelihood is called the decline of a lay follower. (It means that if the Five Precepts are broken, or if one makes a living by trading in any of the five types of wrong trade, the status of a lay follower is ruined). Furthermore, there are five qualities that make one a coarse, defiled, and loathsome lay follower: 1. Lack of faith, 2. Lack of moral conduct (sīla), 3. Being endowed with and following only worldly omens (maugala) based on what is seen, heard, or sensed as devised by foolish people, 4. Not believing in wholesome and unwholesome kamma but believing only in omens as the essence, 5. Seeking and looking for a worthy recipient of alms in the doctrines of heretics (titthiyas) outside the Dispensation of the Omniscient Buddha,
707:
707
and if performing meritorious deeds, giving priority to the doctrines of heretics first and only then performing them in the Buddha’s Dispensation—these five qualities are called the decline of a lay follower. (It means that if these five qualities arise, the status of a lay follower is ruined). (Take the evidence from Aṅguttara Nikāya, Vol. 2, page 181).

## (f) The Perfection of a Lay Follower
As to “What is the perfection of a lay follower?”: being endowed with the previously mentioned Five Precepts and righteous livelihood is called the perfection of a lay follower. (It means that if the Five Precepts and righteous livelihood are not ruined, the status of a lay follower is perfect). Furthermore, there are five qualities that make one a lay follower who is like a jewel, like a red lotus (paduma), or like a white lotus (puṇḍarīka): 1. Having faith, 2. Not failing in moral conduct, 3. Not following worldly omens, 4. Not believing in worldly omens but believing only in wholesome and unwholesome kamma, 5. Not seeking or looking for a worthy recipient of alms in the doctrines of heretics outside the Dispensation, and if performing meritorious deeds, giving priority to this Dispensation first and only then performing them in the doctrines of heretics—these five qualities are called the perfection of a lay follower. (It means that if these five qualities are present, the status of a lay follower is perfect). (Take the evidence from Aṅguttara Nikāya, Vol. 2, page 11).

## King Ajātasattu’s Loss and Gain
Thereafter, not long after King Ajātasattu had departed, the Buddha addressed the monks: “Monks, King Ajātasattu has dug up and destroyed his own foundation. Monks, if this King Ajātasattu had not killed his father, King Bimbisāra, who was a righteous king who ruled according to the Dhamma, the vision of the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga) would have arisen in King Ajātasattu’s continuum right in this very place. (This king would have become a Stream-winner, an Ariya, right in this very place).”
708: 708. In this regard: 'If this King Ajātasattu had not killed his father, he would have reached the Path of Stream-entry while sitting right here upon hearing this Sāmaññaphala Sutta. Now, however, because of his association with the evil friend Devadatta, there has arisen an obstacle to the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry. Nevertheless, because this King Ajātasattu approached me and took refuge in the Triple Gem, and because the three branches of my Sāsana in which he took refuge are so noble and great—just as a man who has committed murder and is due to receive the death penalty might be released from death by offering a gift of a handful of flowers (or by paying a fine of a handful of wealth) because he has found a good protector—similarly, although he deserved to be reborn in the Avīci hell due to the weight of the heinous crime (ānantariya-kamma) of killing his father, because he found a good refuge in the Buddha's Sāsana, he will instead be reborn (after death) only in the Lohakumbhī hell. After sinking for thirty thousand years until reaching the bottom, and then rising for another thirty thousand years until reaching the upper rim (after a total of sixty thousand years), he will be released from that Lohakumbhī hell.' Thus the Blessed One continued to speak. (In this regard, I shall further present special points to note from the Commentary regarding King Ajātasattu's gain: A question may be asked, 'Did King Ajātasattu obtain any benefit or advantage from hearing this Sāmaññaphala Sutta?' The answer is: He obtained a great benefit. The manner of his gain is as follows: From the time he killed his father, signs of an unhappy destination (duggati-nimitta) appeared to him, and he could not sleep day or night.
709:
709
From the time he approached the Buddha and heard this Sāmaññaphala Sutta discourse, which is very sweet and essence-filled, he obtained the opportunity to sleep peacefully day and night. He also performed great acts of veneration and offerings to the Triple Gem. Among worldlings (puthujjanas) like this King Ajātasattu, there is no other person endowed with such faith (pothujjanika-saddhā). (He obtained benefits in the present life, such as the opportunity to sleep peacefully, the merit of making offerings to the Triple Gem, and an incomparable worldling’s faith). For the future world as well, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Vijitāvī, attain Parinibbāna, and end the cycle of suffering. This is the benefit for the hereafter.

## Points to Note Regarding King Ajātasattu’s Enlightenment
In this matter, there is a question to be asked: “If King Ajātasattu did not have the obstacle of the immediate kamma (ānantariya-kamma) of patricide, and if the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry would have truly arisen right there, how could he become a Paccekabuddha and attain Parinibbāna in the future? If he is truly to become a Paccekabuddha and attain Parinibbāna in the future, how could the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry have arisen right there? For Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa, one’s prayer is fulfilled only when endowed with these 5 factors: 1. Human state (manusatta), 2. Perfection of gender (liṅgasampatti), 3. Seeing those free from taints (vigatāsavadassana), 4. Extraordinary service (adhikāra), 5. Strong desire (chandatā). For Sāvaka-bodhi-ñāṇa, the prayer can be fulfilled if endowed with 2 factors: 1. Extraordinary service, 2. Strong desire. Regarding the duration of fulfilling perfections (pāramī), for Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa, one must fulfill perfections for two asankhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons (kappas); for Sāvaka-bodhi-ñāṇa, one fulfills perfections for one asankhyeyya and a hundred thousand aeons to be a Chief Disciple, and for a hundred thousand aeons to be a Great Disciple. Regarding the manner of realizing the Four Noble Truths, Paccekabuddhas realize the Four Noble Truths by their own intuitive wisdom without a teacher, while disciples (sāvakas) realize the Four Noble Truths only by depending on a teacher. Therefore, are not Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa and Sāvaka-bodhi-ñāṇa different in their fundamental causes?” (This is very deep; consider it with great mindfulness).
710: 710. The answer is: There is no contradiction or impossibility as the questioner asks. The reason is that for this King Ajātasattu, after passing away from this life and suffering in the Lohakumbhī hell for sixty thousand years, he will then fulfill the requirements for Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa. Indeed, even those who are to be liberated through Sāvakabodhi-ñāṇa, if the causes for that Sāvakabodhi-ñāṇa do not converge, they will be liberated through Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa at another time in the future. The reason is that such a prayer for liberation through Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa is possible. (This is the answer of the first group of teachers. According to these first teachers, if conditions had been right, King Ajātasattu was one who would have been liberated through Sāvakabodhi-ñāṇa in this very life (one who would have attained the Path of Stream-entry). However, because he associated with the evil friend Devadatta, the causes for liberation through Sāvakabodhi-ñāṇa failed to converge and were destroyed, so he did not attain the Path of Stream-entry in this life. Nevertheless, it is meant that the king will later fulfill the meritorious foundations for Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa and will be liberated through that Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa). According to the other teachers (apare-ācariya): This King Ajātasattu is one who had already made past prayers and performed merits specifically for Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa. Indeed, even though they have made past prayers for Paccekabodhi, if they have not yet received the definite prophecy (niyata-byākaraṇa) for that Paccekabodhi, and because they have not yet reached the maturity for that Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa, they might reach Sāvakabodhi-ñāṇa in the presence of a living Buddha. Therefore, the Blessed One preached: 'Monks, if this King Ajātasattu had not killed his father, the vision of the Path of Stream-entry would have arisen in his continuity of aggregates right here while hearing the Sāmaññaphala Sutta.' To continue: Among the three types of aspirants—Bodhisatta (aspirant for Full Enlightenment), Paccekabodhisatta (aspirant for Paccekabuddhahood), and Sāvakabodhisatta (aspirant for Disciple's Enlightenment)—only the Great Bodhisattas are free from the five heinous crimes (pañcānantariya-kamma)...
711:
They are exempt. The remaining two types of aspirants (bodhisattas) are not exempt from the heinous crimes (anantarika-kamma). This statement is true: although the Venerable Devadatta was one destined for the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa), having received a definite prophecy (niyata-byādita), he committed the extremely heavy anantarika-kammas of causing a schism in the Saṅgha (saṅghabhedaka) and wounding the Buddha (lohituppādaka) due to a long-standing grudge (āghāta) against the Buddha. Based on this, it should be understood that aspirants for Paccekabuddhahood and aspirants for the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi) are not yet exempt from anantarika-kamma. Therefore, because of the obstacle of kamma (kammantarāya) consisting of patricide, King Ajātasattu no longer has the convergence of conditions to attain the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa) in this very life. However, by the certainty of Paccekabodhi (paccekabodhi-niyāma), he will in the future become a Paccekabuddha named Vijitāvī and attain Parinibbāna. This is the view of other teachers (apare). Between these two views, one should investigate and consider which is appropriate. (From the New Sīlakkhandhavagga-ṭīkā, Volume II, Commentary on Sāmaññaphala Sutta, page 198).

The account of King Ajātasattu ends.
